This course uses the UAE as a case study for examining the defining challenge of the 21st century: how rapid urbanization can proceed in places already shaped by environmental constraints. Throughout Abu Dhabi and the wider Emirates, students examine the high-stakes balance between development, ecological limits, infrastructure demands, and climate risk. Targeted seminars are interwoven with guided fieldwork, including natural and urbanized site visits across coastal, terrestrial, and marine settings; inspections of major infrastructure projects; introductory environmental impact assessment (EIA) site surveys; and engagements with local experts and diverse stakeholders. These experiences enable a balanced appraisal of the constraints and opportunities that shape urbanization under challenging environmental conditions. By integrating ecology, urban metabolism, design, and policy, the course develops transferable insights into the future of cities in a warming world.

title: CCOL-UH 2113J Information Design: Berlin as Data
text:
CCOL-UH 2113J Information Design: Berlin as Data (3 credits)
Typically offered January term
What can we learn about a city, and what stories can we tell from the data it makes public? Berlin is one of Europe's most data-rich cities—its history, migration, infrastructure, and urban transformation are extensively documented. Using the living city as subject and inspiration, this course immerses students in transforming data into clear, compelling visual narratives. Class sessions cover visualization principles, geospatial mapping, and narrative structure using AI tools and industry-standard software. Daily warm-up exercises draw on Berlin, EU and global open datasets—building visual fluency and judgment. Students move between datasets and lived urban form, learning how data becomes legible—and how it can reveal, obscure, simplify, or distort reality. The final project is an original data-driven narrative about Berlin's neighborhoods, histories, economic or social trends. Ultimately, the course trains students to treat data as raw material and craft sound, targeted data-driven narratives.
This is an away course in Berlin.

title: CCOL-UH 2114J Bringing Imagination to Life: Immersive Worlds & Experiential Entertainment
text:
CCOL-UH 2114J Bringing Imagination to Life: Immersive Worlds & Experiential Entertainment (3 credits)
Typically offered January term
In an era of digital saturation, why are we flocking to physical theme parks, mega-concerts, and "pop-up" worlds at record rates, and how does the global entertainment industry continue to up the game and evolve experiential entertainment into a cultural force? Using the Disney model of immersive storytelling, placemaking, and operational excellence as a framework, we will audit the machinery of enchantment to understand how theme parks transform media into high-stakes destinations that create shared meaning and economic value. Through case studies and fieldwork in Abu Dhabi, one of the world’s fastest-growing entertainment hubs, we will investigate the logistical, ethical, and psychological architecture of entertainment destination spaces and interview experts from experience designers and engineers to hospitality staff and data collectors of consumer sentiment. Students will analyze how these environments are financed and marketed, who they benefit or exclude, and how they drive tourism and diversify global economies. Ultimately, the course invites students to rethink “fun” itself: as a business strategy, a cultural language, and a powerful engine of human connection.

title: CCOL-UH 2115J AI: Emergence or Emergency?
text:
CCOL-UH 2115J AI: Emergence or Emergency? (3 credits)
Typically offered January term
Questions about whether AI represents a fundamental shift in the human trajectory, a transient phenomenon, or an existential threat animate public debate as automated tools remake daily life. What often goes missing is the broader history of science in which AI is embedded as well as new perspectives on science and technology that emerge when we foreground the intellectual labor of the Gulf. How is the UAE remaking AI, and how is AI remaking the UAE? In this course, blending academic inquiry, practical coding, and fieldwork, students investigate Abu Dhabi's active role in global AI innovation. They compare AI's modes of reasoning with cultural practices of human inquiry across the Hellenistic era, Islamic Golden Age, and Scientific Revolution. Students learn machine learning, neural networks, deep learning, unsupervised and reinforcement learning, and large language models, exploring practical applications in UAE healthcare, public administration, science, and education. Direct encounters with regulatory authorities promoting responsible AI complement discussions on societal impact, culminating in a fieldwork-based debate on the UAE’s role in developing and governing AI.

title: CCOL-UH 2116J Harnessing the Power of Video Games for Cultural and Social Impact
text:
CCOL-UH 2116J Harnessing the Power of Video Games for Cultural and Social Impact (3 credits)
Typically offered January term
Can video games improve lives and change the world? The $200 billion video game industry is larger than the film and music business with 3 billion gamers generating billions of ‘lean-forward’ hours of engagement every week. The medium has unique potential to foster cultural and social impact because video games are interactive and participatory. Games enable players to step into diverse roles, confront challenges, make choices, get feedback, and fail safely. They give players agency – the ability to make a difference in the game and ‘real’ world. Students will play and analyze games that have cultural and social impact goals, meet with local gaming studios and organizations, and research and develop a proposed Emirati culture game highlighting Emirati National Identity Values. Specific case studies such as the BAFTA-winning Never Alone will be reviewed; topics covered will range from aligning core game mechanics with cultural objectives to understanding the business and market dynamics for funding, developing, and releasing social impact games. Students will present their pitch for an Emirati culture game before a board of cultural and industry experts.

title: CCOL-UH 2117J Listening to the Mangroves
text:
CCOL-UH 2117J Listening to the Mangroves (3 credits)
Typically offered January term
What does the environment say through sound? Are we equipped to listen? This course acoustically investigates the health of one of the most valuable and threatened coastal ecosystems on Earth, Abu Dhabi’s mangroves. Hearing is immersive, three-dimensional, and continuous, and this makes listening a powerful tool to understand environments, relationships, places, and histories that vision alone cannot provide. Through fieldwork consisting of recording sessions in the mangroves of Abu Dhabi, complemented by a hands-on lab with the Sounding the Mangroves project research team, students will build a comprehensive sound map of the mangroves’ health. As part of this work, students will get a primer on the fundamental concepts of acoustic ecology, soundscape analysis, and ecoacoustics; learn to operate professional sound equipment; and interview research teams from Environment Agency Abu Dhabi (EAD) in the areas of Jubail and Al Mirfa. Becoming acoustemologists, or scholars of sound, students will gain a greater understanding of sound as a fundamental component of human and natural wellbeing, and of listening as a mode of ecological knowledge.

title: CCOL-UH 2118J Belle Epoque Paris: An Urban Quilt of Literature, Music, Art, and Architecture
text:
CCOL-UH 2118J Belle Epoque Paris: An Urban Quilt of Literature, Music, Art, and Architecture (3 credits)
Typically offered January term
An Urban Quilt of Literature, Music, Art, and Architecture: "Life imitates art far more than art imitates life," wrote Oscar Wilde in his 1899 essay "The Decay of Lying: an Observation." What effect does art have in society? Can it open new ways of seeing, make us question our beliefs, reveal uncomfortable truths? Can it change the world? Or does it merely reflect prevailing power structures? And how should we make sense of the patriarchal and colonial perspectives common among artists from the past, even those most critical of their time? Students will explore Paris as an intertextual urban space, where the creative genius of 19th- and 20th-century artists reverberates throughout the city. We study fiction, poetry, painting, music, theater, opera, and film, focusing on literary works by Zola, Balzac, Colette, and Proust, and artworks by the impressionists, fauvists, pointillists, and cubists. Through interviews, research, and project-based visits to theaters, cafes, monuments, and museums, we will build a collective mindmap to make sense of the contradictions and intersections of Paris's urban space. Beyond learning about the past of a single city, we will seek to become critical navigators of the present and future.
This is an away course in Paris.

title: CCOL-UH 2119J Cosmopolis
text:
CCOL-UH 2119J Cosmopolis (3 credits)
Typically offered January term
Cosmopolis examines contemporary cosmopolitanism—its promises, limits, and critics—through Abu Dhabi as a living city within the UAE: a place that has staked its global ambitions on plurality while navigating the tensions that often arise around issues such as security, governance, migration, heritage, and culture. How is Abu Dhabi redefining cosmopolitanism? How does society function in a city built for the world? How do design, narratives, public space, law and policy shape who feels at home—and who does not? Students connect moral and political theory to on-the-ground experience through site visits to public and civic spaces, practicing rapid ethnographic methods to map where pluralism thrives and where it strains. Ethnographic fieldwork and two short writing reflections on themes of heritage, culture, religion, social initiatives, and education build analytical skills throughout the course; a final team project proposes a practical intervention to foster civic life. By the end, students can evaluate cosmopolitan ideas and design proposals grounded in field evidence and thus track how debates over cosmopolitanism shape the UAE’s and even the world’s joint futures.

title: CCOL-UH 2120J The Business of Attention
text:
CCOL-UH 2120J The Business of Attention (3 credits)
Typically offered January term
What will command human attention in the future, and who will control it? In an era of infinite content, algorithmic feeds, AI-generated media, and constant digital distraction, attention has become one of our most valuable, contested resources. This course examines how entertainment, media, technology, sports, advertising, and social platforms compete to capture, shape, and monetize human attention. Drawing from business, psychology, and cultural studies, we explore how audiences discover and assign meaning to content in a fragmented marketplace. Through fieldwork in Abu Dhabi, students will study how algorithms shape culture and taste, and how societies balance global media influences with local traditions, and why some stories, brands, and creators break through while others struggle to be seen. Examining examples from global sports leagues, social media creators, and gaming to emerging cultural institutions across the Gulf, we ask: in a world of infinite choice, what continues to earn human attention and trust? If we are what we pay attention to, attention may be the defining currency of modern life, shaping how we understand ourselves and the future.

title: CCOL-UH 2121J Sports Psychology: Fields, Fandoms, Communities
text:
CCOL-UH 2121J Sports Psychology: Fields, Fandoms, Communities (3 credits)
Typically offered January term
How does sport shape who we are, where we belong, and the ways we build community? Abu Dhabi has emerged as a model of sports-led development, investing in infrastructure, events, and partnerships that advance economic diversification and social transformation. As the emirate transitions from hosting events that attract fans to creating experiences that connect people, sport takes on new meaning in daily life. This course explores how sports cultures take root, grow, and bring people together in ways that result in changed lives. Grounded in the local sports scene while giving attention to global contexts, the course examines the physical, psychological, and social dimensions of human engagement with sport. Through fieldwork across sports facilities and training grounds, students analyze how participation and fandom shape identity, belonging, and wellbeing. Learning interlaces current events, historical examples, industry case studies, behavioral theories, and management principles across business, government, and non-profit sectors that can be applied to understanding the role of the individual in building a functioning society.

title: CCOL-UH 2122J Pandemics and Plagues
text:
CCOL-UH 2122J Pandemics and Plagues (3 credits)
Typically offered January term
Throughout recorded history, pandemics and plagues have occupied an outsized significance in human culture. How are pandemics shaped by the intersections of pathogens, people, and place? What do plagues reveal about the fault lines and fractures in society? Can lessons from past pandemics – especially our recent experience with COVID-19 – help us better prepare for the next outbreak? Using global literature and film, we explore how people have narrated, interpreted, and imagined infectious diseases through time and across continents. Case studies include the Black Death, tuberculosis, cholera, the Spanish flu, HIV/AIDS, and COVID-19. Fieldwork with medical centers, public health resources, and disease-monitoring data initiatives in Abu Dhabi brings our study of pandemics into the present day by providing first-hand insights into the scope, monitoring, and prevention of infectious diseases.

title: CCOL-UH 2123J Futurism and Art
text:
CCOL-UH 2123J Futurism and Art (3 credits)
Typically offered January term
What happens when a state makes futurism a core priority? And how can artists, curators, and developers engage with this agenda, by speculating alternatives for a future worth living and building? This course examines how intellectuals and state officials have approached the idea of the future in the past and in the present. What were the political stakes of modernization theories and oppositional movements, such as Italian Futurism, Bolshevism, Afrofuturism, and Arab Futurism? And what can these histories tell us about Gulf/UAE futurism as both an aesthetic and a political project? Using the UAE's cultural and economic sectors as examples, we explore how the future of the UAE and its region is being imagined and constructed at arts institutions, such as the Guggenheim Abu Dhabi, Sharjah Art Foundation, and Diriyah Art Futures in Riyadh, and through the connections of the art world to real estate developers, oil companies, and AI. By researching these institutions’ language and aesthetics and co-designing and curating a group exhibition as the final project, students learn how art can transform the imagination into a space of active resistance and defiance against despair.

title: CCOL-UH 2124J English
text:
CCOL-UH 2124J English (3 credits)
Typically offered January term
Who does English belong to, and in a globalized society, does the concept of "native speaker" still hold meaning? This course examines the shifting boundaries of language ownership and identity in a globalized world. We will analyze the unseen power of English as both a tool for commerce and digital exchange and as a site of struggle over who defines the language. By exploring English as a Lingua Franca (ELF), we contrast traditional notions of linguistic "correctness" with how English is actually used by more than a billion speakers worldwide. We will investigate how educational policies, assessments, and classroom practices often uphold rigid standards that marginalize certain varieties of English as well as local and home languages, in addition to the role of AI in shaping global English and whether it empowers multilingual speakers or marginalizes those outside the "standard." Students will reflect on how their identities and opportunities are shaped by the perceived "nativeness" of their speech. Fieldwork in Abu Dhabi’s high-stakes, multilingual ELF context allows students to analyze how diverse communities reclaim and reshape English to suit their own needs.

title: CCOL-UH 2125J Sound, Voice, and Place in the Age of AI
text:
CCOL-UH 2125J Sound, Voice, and Place in the Age of AI (3 credits)
Typically offered January term
What does it mean for a place to have a "sound," and how do geography, migration, and community shape a local musical identity block by block? How have technologies of capture and reproduction, from the 78 rpm disc to generative AI, changed who gets to make music, and who gets credit for it? As AI becomes capable of generating convincing music and voices, what remains irreducibly human about music? Every city has a sound, but few offer students the chance to make music inside it. This intensive, studio-based course uses Tulsa, home to Western swing, singer-songwriter Americana, gospel, jazz, and hip-hop, as both subject and workshop. Students spend most of their time composing, recording, and performing original work alongside two lead instructors: a multi-platinum producer and mixer, and a Tulsa-based songwriter, multi-instrumentalist, and vocalist for Hanson and Tinted Window. Classroom study on the neuroscience of music alongside encounters with Tulsa's musicians, venues, and traditions, including its Americana heritage and legacy of Black musicians, culminate in an original body of recorded work each student will write, perform, and produce.

title: CCOL-UH 2126J Architecture and Landscape Design for an Uncertain Future
text:
CCOL-UH 2126J Architecture and Landscape Design for an Uncertain Future (3 credits)
Typically offered January term
How do we design for an uncertain future? How can design respond to the climate crisis in ways that mitigate impacts of the built environment? What are potential tradeoffs and unintended consequences of designing during the energy transition? Using Abu Dhabi as a practical lens, this course explores architectural and landscape sustainability, a method using design to respond to climate’s environmental impacts and strengthen community wellbeing. Students investigate the philosophical roots of environmentalism, navigate regional climate challenges, and cultivate design thinking skills through resilient technologies and AI performance modeling. Fieldwork visits to Masdar City, Guggenheim Abu Dhabi, and Abu Dhabi Sustainability Week 2027 allow students to examine different visions of sustainability in practice and explore the values and interests they serve. Through daily design exercises, students integrate fieldwork and multiple perspectives on sustainable and resiliency principles with design. As a final project, students create an applied campus project for NYUAD, presenting their sustainable solutions to a faculty jury.

title: CCOL-UH 2127J Bitter and Sweet: The Business of Chocolate
text:
CCOL-UH 2127J Bitter and Sweet: The Business of Chocolate (3 credits)
Typically offered January term
The cocoa industry today serves as a microcosm of the global economy and faces considerable ecological, economic, social and cultural challenges that need addressing on a global scale. Students will study the world of chocolate over its entire value chain, exploring its history and culture, cultivation and economic development, business and economics, marketing and branding, politics and trade, science and nutrition, sustainability and labor issues as well as the future of the industry amidst climate and development challenges. Why is one of the world's most beloved foods - chocolate - built on a foundation of systemic inequities, and how can industry multinationals address this imbalance? Students will engage in interviews with local stakeholders and directly experience chocolate through workshops and tastings to explore the unique challenges and opportunities that this important industry faces in Ghana. Insights derived from this course will be relevant not only to the chocolate industry, but also to others that grapple with similar issues on a global scale.
This is an away course in Accra.

title: CCOL-UH 2128J Politics of Culture: Ethnographic Fieldwork in the UAE
text:
CCOL-UH 2128J Politics of Culture: Ethnographic Fieldwork in the UAE (3 credits)
Typically offered January term
What is the role of culture in political life? Why do modern states organize all aspects of daily life from holidays and public rituals to citizens’ language, dress, leisure, and social comportment? How does culture legitimize political power? This colloquium examines the relationship between politics and culture through ethnographic fieldwork. Students will read primary texts on ethnographic methods and on cultural theories of power, while utilizing Abu Dhabi’s vibrant cultural institutions, public spaces, and community settings to practice fieldwork techniques. In these sites, students will conduct participant observation and interviews, take field notes, and produce reflective writing. Class seminars will tie together the readings, discussions, and hands-on fieldwork experience. Drawing on their ethnographic research, students will develop an original analysis of how cultural symbols reinforce the state’s political vision in the UAE and beyond.

title: CCOL-UH 2129J Contemporary Art Jewelry
text:
CCOL-UH 2129J Contemporary Art Jewelry (3 credits)
Typically offered January term
Why is jewelry such a powerful means of expression in today's globalized world? Why have humans across virtually every culture developed the practice of adorning themselves with jewelry? Through cultural and artistic lenses, students examine jewelry in its broadest significance, with particular emphasis on contemporary art jewelry as a form of communication. The course begins with an anthropological inquiry into human self-adornment, investigating decoration practices across cultures as vehicles for identity and expression, before shifting to the UAE context and the rich history of pearl diving. Working with an internationally recognized contemporary jeweler, students will explore the relationship between jewelry, light, and reflection as vehicles for meaning, experimenting with materials to develop concepts into a wearable piece. Fieldwork across the Abu Dhabi Gold Souk and Sheikh Zayed National Museum will allow students to explore the cultural narratives jewelry embodies in the UAE and beyond. Finally, students present their work in an exhibition at the Arts Center Cube, showcasing jewelry’s rich intersection with art, culture, economics, and personal expression.

title: CCOL-UH 2130J Making the Desert Home: The Archaeology of Al Ain Oasis
text:
CCOL-UH 2130J Making the Desert Home: The Archaeology of Al Ain Oasis (3 credits)
Typically offered January term
The Archaeology of Al Ain Oasis: How do societies make an arid environment habitable, and what does archaeology tell us about the ancient origins of the UAE's thriving economy? This course investigates how communities in Al Ain have created, maintained, and reimagined oasis life over five millennia. Focusing on the UNESCO World Heritage Site of Al Ain and its ancient system of falaj underground aqueducts, students will consider whether oases are best understood as engineered environments, ecological systems, economic enterprises, cultural landscapes, or a blend of each. Students will undertake an archaeological survey as part of the Al Ain Oasis Mapping Project, examining how water technology, agricultural practices, trade opportunities, labour availability, and political organisation shaped the landscape. The course will combine morning fieldwork in the oasis with afternoon seminars and site visits, exploring theoretical perspectives in archaeology and case studies in cultural heritage management. Creating an archaeological map of the oasis as a final product, students will contribute directly to documenting Emirati heritage while developing evidence-based perspectives on how desert environments become - and remain - home.
This is a fully off-campus fieldwork intensive course. Students will stay in Al-Ain for two weeks with a day off in Abu Dhabi on the weekend. They will work outside in the heat/dust so practical clothing, sturdy shoes, sunhats, sunglasses, water bottles, etc., are essential. Students should dress in respectful clothing while in Al-Ain. Abayas are unsuited to archaeological fieldwork, and students have opted to wear a lab coat. This course counts as an Abu Dhabi based course.

title: CCOL-UH 2131J What It Costs Us to Win: Lessons on Success from Athletics
text:
CCOL-UH 2131J What It Costs Us to Win: Lessons on Success from Athletics (3 credits)
Typically offered January term
Lessons on success from athletics: What does it mean to win, to succeed? Who defines winning, what are the costs, and why does it matter? Can you achieve a "win" and still "lose"? In athletics, answers are clear: points, trophies, records, and awards. However, these questions also show up in life: in school, parenting, career, and relationships, we desire to "win" and be seen as "winners" at whatever we do. In this course, we use athletics to explore the parallels and pitfalls of success on the field of play and in life, with particular attention to success trajectories in the UAE and how the emerging sports scene is redefining what it means to win. We discuss how cultural values and political ideologies shape how we define and approach success and the costs and benefits for individuals and societies. Students will learn from the most "successful" coaches, athletes, and scholars of human development. We prioritize learning from athletic dynasties that show how success rooted in care, collaboration, commitment, and contentment - counterintuitive to success driven by individualism, dominance, and competition - offers a blueprint not only for building winning individuals but also for a more just and humane society.

title: CCOL-UH 2132J The Science of Smell
text:
CCOL-UH 2132J The Science of Smell (3 credits)
Typically offered January term
Of all our senses, why is smell the most neglected yet the most emotionally explosive? Is scent a mere luxury, or is it the primary architect of our memories, social boundaries, and cultural identities? This interactive, discussion-based course explores the chemistry behind our sense of smell and its emotional, cultural, and psychological impact. The course makes immediate the invisible molecules of scent around us by examining the molecular basis of smell, olfactory biology, perfume composition, and scent’s role in memory, culture, identity, and politics. Students will map the topography of everyday scents and trade routes across the UAE, decode perfume structures, and even create their own fragrances. No prior science background required—just a curious nose and an open mind.

title: CCOL-UH 2133J Europe Between Washington and Moscow: Can Western Values Survive?
text:
CCOL-UH 2133J Europe Between Washington and Moscow: Can Western Values Survive? (3 credits)
Typically offered January term
Europe is not just a continent; it is a thousand-year-old culture, a political project, a set of moral ideals. Modern Europe was founded on a belief in individual liberty and social equality, the rule of law, reason and secularism. That ethos is now endangered by, among other things, an increasingly belligerent Russia and an illiberal America. This colloquium will ask how, and whether, Europe can preserve its identity and values amid these grave challenges. Through visits to cathedrals, palaces, museums, libraries, concert halls, and memorials treating Prague as one of our main texts, and through readings and discussion, students will examine how Europe has been shaped by art and philosophy, by empire and religion, by nationalism, communism and democracy. We will then move on to the contemporary struggle over the survival of this project, focusing on the war in Ukraine, the rise of right-wing populism, immigration, and deteriorating relations with Washington, which has compelled Europeans to recognize that they can no longer count on protection from across the ocean. Students will engage firsthand with journalists, security analysts, and policy scholars shaping contemporary Europe.

title: CCOL-UH 2134J The New Silk Roads: China, the UAE, and the Making of Globalization
text:
CCOL-UH 2134J The New Silk Roads: China, the UAE, and the Making of Globalization (3 credits)
Typically offered January term
How do China and the United Arab Emirates shape each other, and how do ordinary people experience their political, economic, cultural, and social connections to make globalization? This course examines the historical and contemporary realities of China–UAE ties and the making of new silk roads. Moving beyond Western narratives, we approach China and the Gulf as participants in a dynamic South–South exchange shaped by trade, migration, religion, language, education, and state-led development. Students will study the long history of interaction between China and the Arab and Islamic worlds and the Gulf's evolving position in global networks as the foundation for analyzing recent developments, including China’s economic expansion, the Belt and Road Initiative, and Chinese migration to the UAE. Fieldwork across diasporic markets, Chinese-language schools, and mosques reveals how globalization is not solely driven by states or corporations, but produced by migrants, merchants, teachers, religious leaders, consumers, and families. Completing a final digital ethnography, students will analyze globalization as a lived and contested reality shaped through everyday intercultural encounters.

title: CCOL-UH 2135J Connection by Design: Can AI Strengthen Human Connection?
text:
CCOL-UH 2135J Connection by Design: Can AI Strengthen Human Connection? (3 credits)
Typically offered January term
We are facing a global crisis of connection, reflected in the rising levels of depression, loneliness, partisan divides, suicide, and violence. While technology is often blamed, there is a growing consensus that the problem is not technology but the way it is designed with a wide variety of design features that inevitably promote disconnection and isolation. How can digital technology and AI be designed to deepen human-to-human connection? Drawing on the science of human connection, this course examines the skills that enable human to human connection and bridge divides, and has students work in pairs to develop research grounded proposals for Connection-by-Design technology that strengthens human relationships rather than disconnecting them. The UAE will serve as the first country to offer such opportunities within a rapidly changing, technologically ambitious, and culturally diverse society. Students will learn and practice the skills necessary for human connection through interviews with local community members and apply this fieldwork to their UAE-specific product designs.

title: CCOL-UH 2136J Body in Balance: Discovering Sleep, Nutrition, and Exercise
text:
CCOL-UH 2136J Body in Balance: Discovering Sleep, Nutrition, and Exercise (3 credits)
Typically offered January term
What does it mean to have a healthy body, and can we rehack our biology in a rapidly changing world? Who among us has not struggled to balance fatigue, eating well and exercise against competing pressures of work and personal life? This course explores the interconnected science of sleep, nutrition, and exercise, and the tension between fast-paced lives and healthy lifestyles. With the UAE a key player in global food and energy systems, we explore biological and ethical costs of our modern, high-stress life, considering how to break free from these cycles and live healthier lives. Our inquiry into who gets to live a healthy life tracks the UAE's transition from a lifestyle centered on physical labor, traditional whole-food diets, and natural sleep patterns to one characterized by sedentary work, ultra-processed foods, and artificial light, taking us into fieldwork in health clinics, food markets, historic communities, national museums, and UNESCO Heritage sites. Students conduct two caffeine timing experiments, maintain a sleep diary, exercise log, and food journal, carry out an Abu Dhabi food environment audit, and produce a cross-national comparative analysis of health behaviors.

title: CCOL-UH 2137J Rebels, Punks, and Bohemians
text:
CCOL-UH 2137J Rebels, Punks, and Bohemians (3 credits)
Typically offered January term
This course about counterculture explores how the young and not-so-young reject mainstream society to embrace something wilder and more authentic, whether in art, music, literature, politics, or love. Can misfits and rebels bring about social change? What happens to society when today’s punks become tomorrow’s politicians, when anti-art winds up in a museum? Our setting for these questions is Madrid. We’ll tackle the subject genealogically, tracing countercultural movements back in time from the present day to the early 20th century. Starting with Spain’s “15-M” Occupy demonstrations in the 2010s, we’ll plunge into the punk explosion of the 1970s and 80s known as the Movida. We’ll then examine local echoes of the global 1960s, and finally look at the artistic ferment of the “Silver Age” of the 1910s and 20s. The goal is to understand the aesthetics of rebellion in its original context. In streets, plazas, museums, and bars, we’ll study Madrid’s countercultural spirit up close. As a final project, students will invent their own movement, complete with its own zine and style of clothing.
This is an Away course in Madrid.

title: CCOL-UH 2138J When Home is a Photograph: Vernacular Archives of the Arab World and Black Life
text:
CCOL-UH 2138J When Home is a Photograph: Vernacular Archives of the Arab World and Black Life (3 credits)
Typically offered January term
What insights about photography come to light when vernacular photographs from the Arab world and African American life are put in dialogue? How do archives of photographs create home and frameworks of belonging or omission? This course explores the rich photographic cultures represented in two archives: the Akkasah Photography Archive at NYU Abu Dhabi and the Peter J. Cohen Collection of Black life in NYC. Both archives feature vernacular photographs – those that capture everyday life through studio portraits, travel albums, identification photographs, and snapshots. A key component of the course is the hands-on engagement with these photographic objects, allowing students to explore their cultural significance as photographs and their status as objects to be physically held while centering questions of home. Students will culminate their studies by curating a photo exhibition as a final project. Engaging the vibrant photographic arts scene of the UAE, the course includes local speakers and field visits are planned to the Alserkal Avenue arts district, Gallery 421, the NYUAD Arts Center photography darkroom and the Akkasah Photography Archive.

title: CCOL-UH 2139J Photography and Witnessing
text:
CCOL-UH 2139J Photography and Witnessing (3 credits)
Typically offered January term
What does it take to be a witness rather than look at events passively, without feeling compelled to respond? What are the ethical, political, cultural, legal and personal stakes in witnessing? Can photographic images turn us into witnesses and motivate us to respond to what we see, or do we have to witness an event personally to be moved to act? This seminar uses contemporary Berlin as a case study for how images are used (in memorials, museums and public life) to confront viewers with pictures so that they take responsibility for a shared but often contested future. Through the creation of image-based projects in small, rotating teams, students learn how images can either document or distort the past, compel us to action or numb us, and either be tools or obstacles for individuals or groups to be socially and politically recognized. Readings include key texts from the history and theory of photography, some texts on the political and social use of images, as well as important critical responses to iconic images.

title: CCOL-UH 2140J Wealth and Inequality in the Global City
text:
CCOL-UH 2140J Wealth and Inequality in the Global City (3 credits)
Typically offered January term
Wealth and Inequality in the Global City: The rapid increase in wealth and income inequality in many countries is concentrated in the world’s leading cities. What is driving the concentration of wealth, and what are its consequences? Using New York City as our laboratory, we will explore some of the ways in which wealth and power are created and maintained, as well as examining some of the social consequences of high levels of inequality for families and individuals who are being left behind. Readings and class discussions will explore the social and political economy of inequality in the work of contemporary social sciences. We will deepen our understanding of key issues through field trips, films, and conversations with key leaders in the world of finance and business, government, as well as NGOs working to alleviate some of the most serious consequences of poverty and inequality in New York.
This is an Away course in New York.

title: CCOL-UH 2141J Mediterranean Foodways
text:
CCOL-UH 2141J Mediterranean Foodways (3 credits)
Typically offered January term
A bottle of olive oil, a basket of warm bread, platters of fresh produce, grilled fish: these are stock images of the Mediterranean diet. But whose Mediterranean, whose diet, and whose interests does this image serve? How does Mediterranean food relate to memory? How do Mediterranean foodways relate to forms of social difference, including ethnicity, gender, class, and nationality? How do Mediterranean foodways engage with the processes of globalization? What have been the effects of migration across the Mediterranean on its foodways? How do Mediterranean foodways respond to the pressures of climate change and industrial agriculture? In this class students will explore the intersections of food and culture through critical analysis of the Mediterranean diet and the Slow Food movement, and through field excursions to local food markets, an olive oil producer, and an experimental university food lab. Through case studies from around the Mediterranean as well as cooking and tasting, students will interrogate the multiple and contradictory ways traditions are created and recreated in a globalized world.
This is an Away course in Florence.

title: CCOL-UH 2303J Histories of - and in - Greece: Golden Age to Independence and Resistance
text:
CCOL-UH 2303J Histories of - and in - Greece: Golden Age to Independence and Resistance (3 credits)
Typically offered January term
What did the Greeks contribute to human history? Is it their philosophy, cultural heritage, or mythology? The Greeks pioneered the concepts of democracy, citizenship, ethics, philosophical inquiry, mythology, drama & literature, and the ‘philosopher king’. This course examines the lasting contributions of Ancient Greece to history, philosophy, politics, and cultural heritage. Students will study key texts such as Plato’s Republic and concepts including the Socratic method, the Allegory of the Cave, and the Theory of Forms, exploring their impact on ethics, politics, metaphysics, and science. Field visits to sites such as the Parthenon, theaters, and museums will ground discussion of Greece’s political, cultural, and religious institutions, as well as its interactions with neighboring civilizations. The course also addresses how societies remember the past, asking why certain narratives are promoted while others are marginalized. The course studies how Greece’s legacies continue to shape democracy, governance, and identity today.
This course includes travel to Greece. This course will be offered in January-Term. For the January-Term offering the course will be open for enrollment to NYU Abu Dhabi AEP students only.

title: CCOL-UH 2304J Global Discoveries: From Athena to Athens, Myth - Past and Present
text:
CCOL-UH 2304J Global Discoveries: From Athena to Athens, Myth - Past and Present (3 credits)
Typically offered January term
Greece has been associated with several quintessential images promoted to entice tourists: olive groves, the Parthenon, and white-washed buildings on sun-drenched islands. Beneath this branding lies a rich and contentious past inscribed in the country’s architecture, monuments, art, dance, music, poetry, and cuisine. This course introduces students to Greek history and examines myths as templates for understanding the human experience that echoes across cultural boundaries. Students will examine how myths connect human narratives, social contracts, and expressions of human existence to understand: “Is there a pattern of being and a way of thinking tied to the past, present, and future?” The exploration of Athenian landmarks, history, literature, and culture will challenge students to establish criteria for determining whether these sites and their attached histories have a broader, universal significance. The course explores different approaches to memorialization: the desire to showcase “golden ages,” why and how societies remember the past, how they decide which/whose pasts are worth remembering, and what motivations drive the promotion of specific pasts.
This course includes travel to Greece. This course will be offered in January-Term. For the January-Term offering the course will be open for enrollment to NYU Abu Dhabi AEP students only.

title: CCOL-UH 2307J Histories of - and in - Greece: Ancient Greece
text:
CCOL-UH 2307J Histories of - and in - Greece: Ancient Greece (3 credits)
Typically offered January term
The Greek brand is associated with quintessential images promoted to entice tourists: olive groves, the Parthenon, and white-washed buildings on sun-drenched islands. Beneath this pleasantly reductive picture lies a rich, contentious past inscribed in the country’s architecture, monuments, art, dance, music, poetry and cuisine. What did the Greeks contribute to human history? How do Greek concepts and practices of democracy, citizenship, ethics, philosophy, mythology, drama, and literature shape society today? Through tours, lectures, and experiential learning at the Parthenon, theaters, and museums, students will study Ancient Greece’s lasting contributions to history and culture and the often-suppressed Byzantine, Ottoman, Jewish, Romá, communist, migrant and refugee pasts. Students will examine how debates about commemoration, secularism, cultural preservation, textbooks, and national identity reflect ongoing contests over Greek history. The course addresses how societies remember the past and how they decide whose pasts are worth remembering.

title: Core: Data and Discovery (CDAD-UH)
text:
CDAD-UH 1001 Data (4 Credits)
Typically offered Spring
Data are everywhere. We have massive datasets keeping track of humanity's everyday minutiae from babies born to calories consumed, friends made to crimes committed. How can we use these data to make useful predictions and gain insights into ourselves and humanity in general? This course introduces the basics of learning from data and covers topics such as wrangling, exploration, analysis, prediction, and storytelling through data visualization.

Grading: Ugrd Abu Dhabi Graded
Repeatable for additional credit: No

CDAD-UH 1002 Space (4 Credits)
Typically offered Fall
What's out there? For centuries, curious astronomers peered up into the night sky and saw stars, planets, and the occasional comet. Nowadays, astronomers have a suite of tools at their disposal to observe objects in space and help to answer the fundamental questions about the intricate workings of the Universe. From arrays of radio dishes spanning continents to gamma-ray detectors on satellites orbiting the Earth, astronomy is now truly Multi-Wavelength. This course is a journey of discovery, where students peer at objects such as quasars, stellar nurseries, galaxy clusters, supernovae, black holes, extrasolar planets, neutron stars, molecular clouds and gamma-ray bursts through various telescopes. Research and presentation will form a core part of the course, and experimental and quantitative methods will be brought to bear on our understanding of other worlds. How these results can be communicated to the scientific community and the public will be discussed, along with the relevance to society, including spin-off technologies. Data & Discovery Core courses develop the ability to use experimental and quantitative methods to understand the world - and in this course - other worlds!

Grading: Ugrd Abu Dhabi Graded
Repeatable for additional credit: No

- AD Curriculum Attributes: Core: Data Discovery

CDAD-UH 1004 Microbes (4 Credits)
Typically offered occasionally
Microbes are the most abundant organisms on Earth. They practically exist in every environment on our planet and play major roles in defining our atmospheric composition, sustaining the food webs that feed us and significantly influencing our health. Yet, microbes are diverse; they vary in size from 0.2 micrometers (1/300th diameter of a human hair) to a few millimeters. Some microbes are loners while others live in communities that talk to each other and coordinate behavior. The class will introduce students to microbes by examining their importance, ecology and diversity. The class will take students on a journey of how early microbiologists classified microbes, isolated and cultured them and how today DNA sequencing has revolutionized the way scientists classify microbes. Throughout the course, students will isolate samples to image and culture microbes and isolate their DNA from around the NYU Abu Dhabi campus and the emirate of Abu Dhabi. DNA samples will be sequenced using portable DNA sequencing technology (MinION technology), which generates data rapidly.

Grading: Ugrd Abu Dhabi Graded
Repeatable for additional credit: No

- AD Curriculum Attributes: Core: Data Discovery
- AD Curriculum Attributes: Experimental Inquiry

CDAD-UH 1005 Forensic Science: Guilty or Not Guilty? (4 Credits)
Typically offered occasionally
"Every contact leaves a trace." This phrase, coined by the pioneer of forensic science Edmond Locard, is the starting point of all forensic investigations. Scientific measurements are used to discover traces left at the crime scene and connect them to a person, object, or place. But what is it about science that allows us to make these connections? And how are facts determined by scientific measurements different from those recorded during an interrogation? Does the word "fact" carry the same meaning in the legal system as it does to you or to an experienced scientist? In this course, students explore these questions while analyzing samples left at a crime scene using biological, chemical, and physical laboratory techniques used in forensics. Exploring the underlying scientific principles and analyzing adjudicated cases, they discuss the capabilities and limitations of forensics, how it relates to the criminal justice system, and its impact on society.

Grading: Ugrd Abu Dhabi Graded
Repeatable for additional credit: No

CDAD-UH 1007 The Mind (4 Credits)
Typically offered Fall and Spring
This course explores definitions and theories of the mind and how it may work. Students will learn how philosophers, psychologists, computer scientists, and neuroscientists have studied the mind and will consider several demanding but stimulating questions about thought, memory, and behavior. Readings and discussions will review the historical and scientific developments that led to contemporary understandings of the mind and the challenges and answers that these views pose to our common-sense understanding of, for instance, the unconscious mind, the irrational mind, and the subjective nature of memories.

Grading: Ugrd Abu Dhabi Graded
Repeatable for additional credit: No

- AD Curriculum Attributes: Core: Data Discovery
- AD Curriculum Attributes: Experimental Inquiry

CDAD-UH 1008 Seven Wonders of the Invisible World (4 Credits)
Typically offered Fall and Spring
"In the year of 1657 I discovered very small living creatures in rain water." This quote is attributed to Anton van Leeuwenhoek, a Dutch merchant whose skillful use of glass lenses allowed him to peer into a world of microorganisms that would otherwise be invisible to the naked eye. His careful observations gave way to advances in microscopy that have allowed scientists to observe detailed structures of plants, viruses invading cells, intricate crystal lattices, and the seemingly chaotic motion of small particles. In this course, microscopy is explored, first by examining the fundamental optical systems used to magnify objects, and eventually by using sophisticated microscopes to make observations. We explore seven wonders of the invisible world - natural animate and inanimate phenomena that include micro-animals, plant and animal cells, bacteria and viruses, fungi, proteins, and naturally occurring crystals.

Grading: Ugrd Abu Dhabi Graded
Repeatable for additional credit: No

- AD Curriculum Attributes: Core: Data Discovery
- AD Curriculum Attributes: Experimental Inquiry

CDAD-UH 1010 Diversity (4 Credits)
Typically offered Fall
Diversity is everywhere. We see it in the 8+ billion human beings and the 4-7,000 languages they speak. It is present at every scale from the cell types making up complex organisms to the different species present in an ecosystem. It is even present in the opinions people have on diversity itself. Talking about the worldwide loss of biodiversity and languages or about present and past human diversity thus requires clarifying and discussing important concepts. Understanding patterns of genetic diversity within species to unravel their evolutionary history requires a critical analysis of patterns and processes. This has consequences for our understanding of human evolution but also for our understanding of endangered species. During this course we will need a common language to clarify and discuss important concepts (what is diversity, how can it be quantified, how is it represented across scales, but also what is science, is it just a narrative among others, diverse narratives, can the idea of model and consistency be useful to identify scientific from other types of discourses?)

Grading: Ugrd Abu Dhabi Graded
Repeatable for additional credit: No

- AD Curriculum Attributes: Core: Data Discovery
- AD Curriculum Attributes: Experimental Inquiry

CDAD-UH 1016 Where the City Meets the Sea: Studies in Coastal Urban Environments (4 Credits)
Typically offered Fall and Spring
Over half of the human population lives within 100 km of a coast and coastlines contain more than two-thirds of the world's largest cities. As a result, the world's natural coastal environments have been substantially modified to suit human needs. This course uses the built and natural environments of coastal cities as laboratories to examine the environmental and ecological implications of urban development in coastal areas. Using data from multiple coastal cities, student teams use field-based studies and Geographic Information System (GIS) data to examine patterns and processes operating in coastal cities. This course uses the local terrestrial, marine, and built environments as a laboratory to address these issues, and team projects requiring field work form a core component of the learning experience. As part of the NYU Global Network University this course is being offered simultaneously in several NYU sites globally and students are collaborating extensively with students from their sister campuses through the duration of this course.

CDAD-UH 1017 Symmetry (4 Credits)
Typically offered Spring
Symmetries are ubiquitous in nature and permeate the arts. Beginning with both intuitive definitions and more formal mathematical descriptions, the course will explore the symmetries in the subatomic constituents of matter and their interactions, larger-scale chemical and biological compounds, and the macroscopic natural world. Students will explore ways in which the human psyche is primed to find symmetry beautiful and examine the symmetries that underlie artistic creations, from geometrical patterns in artwork, to rhythm and chord progression in musical composition, and meter and rhyme in poetry. After a thorough study of symmetry, the course will end with a discussion of asymmetries and broken symmetries in nature and aesthetics.

Grading: Ugrd Abu Dhabi Graded
Repeatable for additional credit: No

CDAD-UH 1019 Heat and the Universe (4 Credits)
Typically offered Spring
The study of temperature and of heat, as formulated in the laws of thermodynamics, will be used as a unifying guide to examine a variety of phenomena in our natural world. In the physical world, course topics will encompass the cooling of the Universe in its early minutes as well as the dramatic expansion in the first seconds after the Big Bang and the role that temperature fluctuations have played in the Earth's history. In the animal world, the course covers the surprising discovery of heat-loving bacteria and the techniques mammals, including humans, have adopted for temperature regulation. Readings will include materials from various scientific realms such as cosmology, biology, and geology.

Grading: Ugrd Abu Dhabi Graded
Repeatable for additional credit: No

- AD Curriculum Attributes: Core: Data Discovery

CDAD-UH 1024 Reading Like a Computer (4 Credits)
Typically offered Fall
How do computers "read" text, and how can computer-assisted analysis of texts give us new access to information about ourselves and the cultural legacies we have inherited? This course explores quantitative methods for discovering and analyzing diverse texts of the human record. It also offers a glimpse into possible futures of reading. Students will both discuss, and put into practice, forms of computer-assisted textual analysis that have revolutionized research in humanities and social science fields in recent years. They will also take a critical look at the "ubiquitous analytics" and the "ubiquitous virtuality" of everyday life. By engaging with the idea of data in the humanities, the course encourages students to reconsider our common-place assumptions about how reading works. Course materials, discussions, and classroom exercises will push students to examine how basic ideas about a text such as author, subject, setting, character or even style might look different when a non-human is involved in the interpretation. The course assumes no prior computer or coding skills, but a willingness to explore new technologies is essential for success.

Grading: Ugrd Abu Dhabi Graded
Repeatable for additional credit: No

CDAD-UH 1032 Stability (4 Credits)
Typically offered Spring
What makes a system stable or unstable? How does a lack of stability translate into chaos or turbulence? Every new device, experiment, or idea, requires a check for system stability. Important in science, engineering, politics, economics, and daily life, understanding stability enables predictability and control. In the late nineteenth century, philosophers, physicists, and mechanical engineers laid the foundations of hydrodynamic stability, the field which analyzes the stability and onset of instability of fluid flows. How have these breakthroughs helped us to determine whether a given flow is stable or unstable, or to describe how possible instabilities can cause turbulence? And how might insights drawn from such fields offer insight into other areas of our lives, from monetary or political systems to bridges to interpersonal relationships?

Grading: Ugrd Abu Dhabi Graded
Repeatable for additional credit: No

- AD Curriculum Attributes: Core: Data Discovery

CDAD-UH 1033 Data and Human Space (4 Credits)
Typically offered Fall
Societies have traditionally used maps to represent, even construct, the spaces in which we live as well as the territories over which we assert control. But what has become of the map in the (post-)digital age? Has our relationship to human space changed in our data-rich world? Are we unknowingly map-makers by virtue of walking around with our devices? This course explores the specific role that technology can play in our understanding of both historical and contemporary map making. Through regional and global examples of urban culture mapping, the course’s focus on data discovery extends beyond working with official data to creating our own data within familiar environments. In addition to seminar discussion of readings and audiovisual materials, the course will host guest speakers. It also has a lab component with two main assignments. First, we focus on the larger Arabian Gulf region through the eyes of historical cartographers and colonial geographers. Second, we will turn to the city of Abu Dhabi itself to see how (and why) we might map some of its spaces of human culture using simple technology. The course assumes no prior computer skills.

Grading: Ugrd Abu Dhabi Graded
Repeatable for additional credit: No

CDAD-UH 1034 Numbers, Models, and Chaos (4 Credits)
Typically offered Spring
The hallmark of a successful scientific theory is its ability to predict the outcome of experiments. Yet the last century's most shocking scientific development is the mathematical theory of chaos, with the subsequent realization that predictability has intrinsic limits. Such limits may have no practical importance (as in many engineering problems). Sometimes they shape an entire branch of science (as in meteorology). This course provides a challenging, but accessible, way to understand predictability's limits, while still appreciating the bedazzling richness of phenomena that only theories which face these limits can possibly describe. The course brings together, in a cohesive whole, ideas about numbers and infinities; the inner working of computing machines; nuances and concessions occurring in model-building; the meaning of randomness and of determinism. Students will participate in the construction of mathematical models (mostly inspired by population biology) under the form of iterated maps, and interact with simple computer simulations of those models to illustrate key concepts of nonlinear dynamics: stability, limit cycles, attractors, and predictability.

Grading: Ugrd Abu Dhabi Graded
Repeatable for additional credit: No

CDAD-UH 1037 Cyberwarfare (4 Credits)
Typically offered Spring
Einstein once said, "I know not with what weapons World War III will be fought, but World War IV will be fought with sticks and stones." The answer to part one of his statement is here: World War III will likely be a cyber war. Election hacking, power grid cyberattacks, troll farms, fake news, ransomware, and other terms have entered our daily vocabularies and are here to stay. This course aims to introduce students to the cyberwarfare landscape: the actors, capabilities, techniques, impacts, legal and geopolitical issues, and defense systems it necessitates. How has the threat of cyber war transformed our definitions of privacy and security, on individual, national, and international planes? We will dive in with specific case studies, such as power grid cyberattacks, and we will perform cyber tabletop exercises. The first half of the course establishes the technical foundations needed for understanding cyberspace; the second half approaches the problem from different angles, attempting to understand the repercussions of technological, legislative, and political changes.

CDAD-UH 1039 Search (4 Credits)
Typically offered Spring
How do we find what we're looking for? How do we know when we've found it? If we can't tell the future, how do we make choices that impact the rest of our lives, such as finding a life partner, a fulfilling career, or even a good Core course? This course examines the nature and implications of such search processes. Questions addressed include why marital selection (when and whom to marry) has changed so much over time. Why do more women than men now go to college in some parts of the world? What does the data suggest explains these major societal changes? Students will be tasked with obtaining country-level evidence on how changing legislation in different countries is observed to affect societal outcomes. Students will not only learn the nature of causal inference in data, but will better understand how and why society is changing. Additional topics include the search for knowledge (scientific method and causality), navigation (the search for home [and time dilation with GPS]), returns to matching (insect swarms and Tinder) and even shopping at the carpet souk.

CDAD-UH 1040 Artificial Intelligence and Human Decisions (4 Credits)
Typically offered Spring
This course explores how humans and intelligent systems make decisions, with a focus on the opportunities and risks of AI-driven decision technologies in shaping judgment and action. Students begin by examining the foundations of decision-making and the role of AI across domains such as data collection, data quality, and visualization. Core approaches in statistical learning and machine learning are introduced, including methods for pattern discovery, prediction, and model evaluation, reinforced through weekly laboratory coding practicals in a data science computing environment. Building on these methods, the course considers how AI systems interact with human decision-makers, covering topics such as collaborative intelligence, auditing for bias, and ethical frameworks for responsible deployment. Advanced sessions highlight emerging adaptive systems that learn, optimize, and respond in uncertain environments. By the end of the course, students will be able to apply core AI methods, while critically assessing their ethical and societal implications.

Grading: Ugrd Abu Dhabi Graded

CDAD-UH 1041 Decisions and the Brain (4 Credits)
Typically offered Spring
Where do errors come from? How can we make better decisions? Should intuition be trusted? Can we nudge others to make better decisions, and should we? This course examines neural bases for human decisions and cognitive biases. Drawing from economics, psychology, and neuroscience, it takes an interdisciplinary perspective on topics including decision-making under risk (how humans deal with probabilities), intertemporal decisions (saving for the future), and social decisions (interpersonal allocations and fairness). Students will explore different notions of rational behavior, how data on human behavior and brain activity is collected, and how we can use these data to improve decisions. Hands-on experience will include lab visits (both behavioral and brain imaging) and data collection through online platforms as students gain familiarity with different models of decision-making (including expected utility theory vs. prospect theory for decisions under risk, exponential vs. hyperbolic discounting for intertemporal decisions, and selfish vs. social preferences for interpersonal decisions) and examine how these models reflect available neural evidence.

CDAD-UH 1043 Data and Society (4 Credits)
Typically offered Fall
Why is data science so influential and popular in business, government and academic research? What are the benefits we gain with expending resources to collect and analyze data, and what is lost when we make decisions about how to classify events? In this class, students will gain a foundational understanding of statistics, data science, and computational data analysis using data sets drawn from real-life problems, primarily with the R statistical software package. They will also be exposed to the philosophical underpinnings of quantitative analysis via scientific inquiry, along with criticism of methods and the way that data-driven analysis can be used to obscure as much as inform. Students will also undertake a group project that will involve independent data analysis on a topic of relevance to world affairs.

CDAD-UH 1044 Human-Centered Data Science (4 Credits)
Typically offered Fall and Spring
Data science is changing our lives. While the importance of data science is widely acknowledged, there are also great concerns around it. How are data generated? How can they be used to make predictions and inform insights? What can be the potential dangers of applying data science techniques? What are the social and human implications of their uses? This multidisciplinary course explores these questions through hands-on experience on key technical components in data science and critical reviews of human and social implications in various real-world examples, ranging from social science to arts and humanities to engineering. In the course, students will 1) learn basic concepts and skills in data science (e.g., crawling and visualization); 2) apply these skills in a creative project; 3) discuss social and human implications of data science, including data privacy; algorithmic bias, transparency, fairness, and accountability; research ethics; data curation and reproducibility; and societal impacts. This course encourages students to reconsider our common-place assumptions about how data science works and be critical about the responsible use of data.

What is the real shape of your food? How do you define cooking on a molecular sense? Are all calories the same? Is industrial food really as diverse as it seems? The ever-rising wave of general interest in food has helped to knock down the barriers of science and cooking, where science found its way into house-kitchen and cooking into laboratories and industrial plants in the past three decades. This course attempts to integrate some of the broad questions, as the ones given above, by taking food as a molecular architecture and its preparation as a hypothesis-driven scientific event. The answers to these questions would touch upon matters of health, nutrition, environment and ethics of eating. The laboratory sessions would complement the in-class topics by providing hands-on activities on elucidating the science of cooking, preparation of chemical cuisines and quantitative/qualitative analysis of food components in commercial food and drinks.

What determines how a disease spreads in human populations? Biomedical scientists have greatly expanded our knowledge of the diseases caused by viruses, parasites, fungi or bacteria. Yet every year, epidemics of infectious diseases still cause large amounts of suffering, bereavement and economic loss throughout the world. Climate change, deforestation, and the globalization of economic activity might even accelerate the emergence of new infections and usher in an "era of pandemics." In this course, students will draw on literature from the biomedical and social sciences, as well as historical accounts of outbreaks, to understand the dynamics of contagion. They will learn the tools used by epidemiologists and public health specialists to prevent the emergence, limit the spread, or even eliminate infectious diseases. They will investigate the ethical, behavioral, and political obstacles that might limit the adoption of protective behaviors during epidemics. Students will engage in debates and research related to the current COVID-19 pandemic, as well as in case studies of diseases including smallpox, influenza, malaria, HIV/AIDS, and Ebola.

What is self? What is identity? Do our perceptions of self and identity change over our lifetimes? This course discusses fundamental questions about biological concepts of self and identity, which are changing in the current era of genomics, as we are starting to appreciate ourselves better in the context of our environments. An emerging concept in biology is the link between self and the microbiome. Historically viewed as harmful pathogens, non-pathogenic microbes are vital for our existence and they are omnipresent in human bodies and the environment. These microbes change over our lifetimes mirroring our development from infancy to adulthood. Does this microbial development influence our perception of self?

Can randomness be classified or characterized? Giving examples from natural and social sciences, mathematics, engineering as well as computer science, the course launches an interdisciplinary survey into the world of Stochastic processes and considers ways in which randomness is shaping our daily lives.

CDAD-UH 1072 Nothing (4 Credits)
Typically offered Fall
How can a course be about nothing? How can anything be about nothing? We all use the word "nothing" (probably several times a day) without hesitation, but if we stopped to think about its meaning, we would realize that "nothing" is a complex, multi-faceted, ever-changing concept. To talk about "nothing," we need to first set rules and boundaries. This course explores the evolution of the concept of nothing in mathematics, philosophy and, especially, physics over the centuries. We will discuss the history of the concept of zero, ideas of nothing and everything in ancient philosophy, the concept of limit, which is at the heart of modern mathematics, and the theories of relativity and quantum physics, which represent the foundations of our modern understanding of the universe. We will ask age-old questions that have occupied natural philosophers for millennia: Why is there something rather than nothing? Where does everything come from? Can something come from nothing? What is nothing anyway? Along the way, we will see how developing scientific theories requires taking basic concepts---like the concept of "nothingness"---and making them precise enough to support scientific inquiry. We will discover that such a process can lead to a radical revision of basic concepts we might have thought were unambiguous.

In this course, we study the science of complexity through examples from the physical sciences, the social sciences, and the arts.
