title: PhD in Astrophysics and Space Systems
breadcrumbs: PhD in Astrophysics and Space Systems
text:
Join an information session










The PhD in Astrophysics and Space Systems is the first program of its kind in the UAE and the wider region. This program, founded and developed by NYUAD, aligns with the UAE’s strategic vision to position itself as a global leader in space science and innovation, nurturing a new generation of pioneers in this dynamic and rapidly evolving field.

Bridging the disciplines of Physics and Engineering, the program offers an interdisciplinary framework to explore fundamental questions in astrophysics while addressing the practical complexities of space systems design and implementation. Doctoral candidates will engage in rigorous academic coursework and carry out a multi-year research project under the guidance of world-class faculty. This comprehensive training equips graduates with the expertise and independence to lead and execute complex projects across a wide range of professional disciplines.










Program Structure

People

Funding

Apply












Key Program Details

- Four semesters of graduate coursework followed by dissertation

- Potential for collaborative work and research at the NYU campus in New York

- Cutting-edge research opportunities in NYU Abu Dhabi’s labs

- Tuition, fees, and health insurance provided throughout the program

- Generous research assistantship and stipend provided by NYU Abu Dhabi throughout the program.

- Campus accommodation at no cost in Abu Dhabi
- Career development assistance

- New York University Abu Dhabi degree upon graduation









Learn more about the program































































Online Information Sessions

Click on the Register button to view upcoming info sessions.

Learn more about the program, our campus, and the unique experience a graduate program in the UAE offers.










Register for Information Sessions





















The establishment of a PhD program in Astrophysics and Space Systems at NYU Abu Dhabi underscores our unwavering commitment to advancing academic excellence and innovation in fields critical to the UAE and the future of humanity. By harnessing our world-class research facilities, interdisciplinary expertise, and collaborations with leading space agencies, we are preparing our students to lead in the burgeoning UAE space sector. This program elevates NYUAD’s standing as a hub for groundbreaking research and education and aligns with our mission to cultivate talent that will drive the UAE’s ambitious vision for space exploration and technological leadership.







Meet Our Faculty










Andrea Valerio Macciò

Professor of Physics; Global Network Professor of Physics







Francesco Arneodo

Professor of Physics; Global Network Professor of Physics







Mohamad Eid

Associate Professor and Global Network Associate Professor of Electrical and Computer Engineering





















- View all Faculty














This PhD program represents a significant milestone for space research and education at NYU Abu Dhabi. Humanity’s fascination with the stars predates recorded history, and our recent advancements in exploring the cosmos have revolutionized global communication and environmental monitoring. These transformative technologies stem directly from breakthroughs in understanding phenomena ranging from subatomic particles to the largest galaxy clusters. Through this program, we aim to cultivate the next generation of scientists and researchers, equipping them to lead the future of scientific space exploration.


The National Space Strategy 2030 aims to enhance the space sector’s contribution to the national economy and promote the UAE's regional and international presence in the space sector. The strategy sets the general framework for UAE's space industry and activities for the years leading up to 2030, including government activities related to space, commercial activities, scientific activities carried out by the public and private sectors and academic institutions and research and development centres.







Research News

Exciting research is happening at NYU Abu Dhabi.



Mind Over Dark Matter

Professor Andrea Macciò has been searching his entire life for something that science knows is there but has never seen.

Astronomers Closely Study a Scorching Hot Exoplanet That Possibly Swallowed a Smaller Neighbor

Mohamad Ali-Dib, along with an international team led by the Université de Montréal, announced a detailed study of the extremely hot giant exoplanet WASP-76 b in the journal Nature .

Traces of Water in a Super-hot Gas Giant’s Atmosphere

Jasmina Blecic, together with a team of international experts, identified water vapor in the atmosphere of WASP-18 b.

Unsolved Mystery

Scientists like Francesco Arneodo and Lotfi Benabderrahmane have spent decades searching for something they can’t see.

Why Are Space Scientists so Interested in Black Holes?

“By looking at black holes, we can learn something about the evolution of galaxies," say physicists Ingyin Zaw and David Russell.

NYU Abu Dhabi's Universe of Virtual Galaxies

The simulated birth and evolution of a virtual galaxy — billions of years of space activity was envisioned by Andrea Macciò, Associate Professor and Program Head of Physics.








Female Emirati Aerospace Engineer who Found Her Place in Space

Marwa Saeed Al Mamari is pursuing a PhD at NYU Abu Dhabi while helping the next generation of Emiratis see a future in space.







NYU Abu Dhabi Students’ Music Now Orbiting Earth on the International Space Station

Musical compositions by NYU Abu Dhabi students are now on board the International Space Station







NYU Abu Dhabi Researchers Call for Strengthening Sustainability Regulations in Laws Governing Space Exploration

NYUAD Researchers Highlight the Need for Sustainabiliuty Legislation in Space Exploration

title: Apply
breadcrumbs: PhD in Astrophysics and Space Systems
text:
Apply











Candidates must have completed at least a bachelor's degree before commencing the PhD program. Candidates need to provide information about any graduate-level courses and degrees have completed. While degrees do not have to be in a particular discipline, a successful application will need to demonstrate the mastery needed to engage effectively with doctoral-level work in this program.

The goal for the selection committee is to choose highly promising students for this program, and admissions decisions are made without knowledge of an applicant's financial need.









Apply Now

Deadline January 4, 2027

Questions before you apply?

Join an information session

Physics at NYU Abu Dhabi








-





In addition to the information below, the online application provides instructions to guide you. All sections of the application and the required supporting documents must be submitted online by the deadline. Incomplete applications will not be reviewed. Do not submit any hard copy materials to NYU Abu Dhabi as part of the application process.

If you have any difficulties with the online application, please email the Graduate Admissions office from the email address associated with your application: nyuad.graduateadmissions@nyu.edu .

After submitting the application, you will not be able to change or add information. You will receive a link to the Application Status Portal where you can track the status of your application.








Required Information

Prepare the following required information when you are ready to start an application:

- Copies of transcripts from all post-secondary institutions you have attended. If you are admitted to the program, you will need to provide official documents.
- Official English language proficiency test scores or receive a test waiver
- You are from a designated list of English-speaking countries.
- You have completed at least four years in a university program taught entirely in English.
- Self-reported test scores for proof of English proficiency. Minimum scores: Academic IELTS = 6.0 / TOEFL iBT = 79 / EmSAT English = 1400. Official results will be needed if you are admitted.

- Current curriculum vitae
- Research interest letter: Explain why you want to pursue the PhD in Astrophysics and Space Systems at NYU Abu Dhabi. Describe your research interests and past research experience.
- Three recommendation letters: You will provide the name, title, and email of three recommenders. They will receive a request from NYUAD to upload a letter of recommendation for your application.
Any information or materials submitted to NYU Abu Dhabi after the final application deadline are not guaranteed to be reviewed or considered by the Selection Committee.

You will receive an email when there are updates to your application status that can be viewed on the Application Status Portal . Your final official decision will be posted to your status page, and an admission decision from any other source of communication will be not considered official or binding.

NYU Abu Dhabi reserves the right to validate the accuracy of your application information with appropriate sources, including the right to contact relevant individuals and organizations.



-






- Verification : After submitting your application, the admissions office checks that all supporting documents have been uploaded correctly and are readable. After this verification, the applications are made available to the Selection Committee for the initial review.

- Initial review : The Selection Committee begins reviewing submitted applications after the application deadline. The committee looks at information from all parts of the application to form a complete picture of the applicant’s potential fit with the program.

- Shortlist : The Selection Committee places applicants who are the best fit for the program on a “shortlist.” These applicants are invited to an interview with the selection committee.

- Interview : During the interview, the applicant has the opportunity to provide more details about their motivations, education, and experience. This gives the Selection Committee a more complete understanding of the applicant before making the admissions decision.

- Admissions decision : Applicants who are offered admission will be notified by email to check the Application Status Portal where the admission letter can be viewed and downloaded. The applicant needs to confirm acceptance of the offer.

- Offer acceptance : The applicant confirms acceptance of the admission offer via the Application Status Portal and begins the onboarding process.

Note: You must receive a UAE security clearance, and obtain an appropriate UAE visa if required by your residency status. NYU Abu Dhabi will facilitate these processes for admitted students. If for any reason you cannot obtain the security clearance or visa, your admissions offer may be rescinded.











Contact Us

If you have any difficulties with the online application, then send an email to the Graduate Admissions office. Send this email from the same address used in your application.

Apply











Candidates must have completed at least a bachelor's degree before commencing the PhD program. Candidates need to provide information about any graduate-level courses and degrees have completed. While degrees do not have to be in a particular discipline, a successful application will need to demonstrate the mastery needed to engage effectively with doctoral-level work in this program.

The goal for the selection committee is to choose highly promising students for this program, and admissions decisions are made without knowledge of an applicant's financial need.

sections.title: Apply Now · Required Information
sections.text:
Prepare the following required information when you are ready to start an application:

- Copies of transcripts from all post-secondary institutions you have attended. If you are admitted to the program, you will need to provide official documents.
- Official English language proficiency test scores or receive a test waiver
- You are from a designated list of English-speaking countries.
- You have completed at least four years in a university program taught entirely in English.
- Self-reported test scores for proof of English proficiency. Minimum scores: Academic IELTS = 6.0 / TOEFL iBT = 79 / EmSAT English = 1400. Official results will be needed if you are admitted.

- Current curriculum vitae
- Research interest letter: Explain why you want to pursue the PhD in Astrophysics and Space Systems at NYU Abu Dhabi. Describe your research interests and past research experience.
- Three recommendation letters: You will provide the name, title, and email of three recommenders. They will receive a request from NYUAD to upload a letter of recommendation for your application.
Any information or materials submitted to NYU Abu Dhabi after the final application deadline are not guaranteed to be reviewed or considered by the Selection Committee.

You will receive an email when there are updates to your application status that can be viewed on the Application Status Portal . Your final official decision will be posted to your status page, and an admission decision from any other source of communication will be not considered official or binding.

NYU Abu Dhabi reserves the right to validate the accuracy of your application information with appropriate sources, including the right to contact relevant individuals and organizations.



-






- Verification : After submitting your application, the admissions office checks that all supporting documents have been uploaded correctly and are readable. After this verification, the applications are made available to the Selection Committee for the initial review.

- Initial review : The Selection Committee begins reviewing submitted applications after the application deadline. The committee looks at information from all parts of the application to form a complete picture of the applicant’s potential fit with the program.

- Shortlist : The Selection Committee places applicants who are the best fit for the program on a “shortlist.” These applicants are invited to an interview with the selection committee.

- Interview : During the interview, the applicant has the opportunity to provide more details about their motivations, education, and experience. This gives the Selection Committee a more complete understanding of the applicant before making the admissions decision.

- Admissions decision : Applicants who are offered admission will be notified by email to check the Application Status Portal where the admission letter can be viewed and downloaded. The applicant needs to confirm acceptance of the offer.

- Offer acceptance : The applicant confirms acceptance of the admission offer via the Application Status Portal and begins the onboarding process.

Note: You must receive a UAE security clearance, and obtain an appropriate UAE visa if required by your residency status. NYU Abu Dhabi will facilitate these processes for admitted students. If for any reason you cannot obtain the security clearance or visa, your admissions offer may be rescinded.

title: Program Structure
breadcrumbs: PhD in Astrophysics and Space Systems
text:
Program Structure











There are two interconnected tracks for this program: Astrophysics and Space Systems. Elective classes will be track-specific.

Each track consists of 70 credits:

- 40 credits from formal coursework, with 16 credits from Master-level classes, and 24 from PhD-level classes,
- 30 credits are awarded for the PhD dissertation, which is to be defended at the end of the 5th year.







Coursework

Classwork is divided into two different categories, Master-level classes and PhD-level classes.

- The Master-level classes offer students a common, large panoramic view of the concepts and techniques at the foundation of astrophysics and space science. These classes, for a total of 16 credits, are organized into three core classes for all students and two lab classes to be chosen.
- The PhD-level classes are instead meant to give an in-depth view of specific subjects and current research topics in one of the two tracks selected by the student. They are organized in four elective classes to be chosen according to the selected track, and two research rotations.








Tracks

- Astrophysics
- Space Systems 










Learn How To Apply

Applications for Fall 2027 will open in October












Students will finish their coursework within their second year, after which they will have to pass a comprehensive exam. At the end of their fifth semester, we expect the students to present their thesis proposal to the faculty members. A thesis has to be presented and defended by the end of the fifth year.



Courses

|
| Intro/core Classes (Master Level) | Radiative processes, Astrophysics, Detectors, and Telescopes
| Laboratory Classes (Master Level) - two courses | Radio Astronomy Lab, X-ray Astronomy Lab, Optical Spectrometry Lab, AstroParticle Lab, Optics and Photon Detection Lab
| Electives
| | Astrophysics Track | AstroChemistry, AstroParticle Physics, Compact Objects, Foundations of Spacetime, General Relativity, High Energy Astrophysics, Numerical Methods in Astrophysics, Observational Cosmology, Planetary Physics, Quantum Gravity and Black Holes, Quantum Gravity and Cosmology, Theory of Galaxy Formation
| Space Systems Track | Human-Computer Interaction for Space Exploration, Radiative Transfer, Rocket and High-speed Propulsion, Robotics, Space Instrumentation, Spacecraft Dynamics, Space Economy and Sustainability, Sensors and Actuators for Space Applications, Tele-operations
| Common Electives | Radiative and Mechanical Transport, Fluid Mechanics

title: Research
breadcrumbs: PhD in Astrophysics and Space Systems
text:
Research






Astrophysics and Space Systems at NYU Abu Dhabi













The Universe spans all scales, from the subatomic particles believed to comprise Dark Matter, which dominates the mass in the Universe, to large-scale structures that span the observable universe. Astrophysics research at NYUAD spans all of these scales, as described below:








- Cosmology, origin, and nature of Dark Matter and Dark Energy
- Theory and simulations of galaxy formation
- Galaxy dynamics
- Active Galactic Nuclei
- Accretion onto stellar mass and super-massive black holes
- Formation and physics of compact objects (black holes and neutron stars)
- Sun and stars physics, astroseismology, modeling, and observations
- Composition and evolution of our universe








Questions before you apply?

Physics at NYU Abu Dhabi

PhD Student Research













Space Systems Research at NYUAD

NYUAD research in the domain of Space Systems spans the fields of Telescope Instrumentation for Space Exploration, Space Communications with Satellites and Space Stations, Space and Spacecraft Robotics, Mechatronics, Photon Detection, Sensors and Actuators, Rocket Combustion and Propelling Systems. Faculty members with expertise in these domains are primarily Electrical Engineering and Mechanical Engineering scholars who will be contributing to this program through their teaching and research.



Center for Astrophysics and Space Science

Composed of a unique combination of theorists, observers, and instrument builders dedicated to understanding the nature of the cosmos. Our research spans a vast range of temporal and spatial astronomical scales, from our own Sun and its planets to the whole Universe.


Applied Interactive Multimedia Lab

The Applied Interactive Multimedia (AIM) research group works with diverse facets of interactive multimedia and immersive multimodal systems. Our interests include the conception, engineering, and utilization of novel haptic interfaces as a new media in Human-Computer Interaction (HCI).







Research Highlights

Exciting research is happening at NYU Abu Dhabi.










Astronomers Closely Study a Scorching Hot Exoplanet That Possibly Swallowed a Smaller Neighbor

Mohamad Ali-Dib, along with an international team led by the Université de Montréal, announced a detailed study of the extremely hot giant exoplanet WASP-76 b in the journal Nature .








Traces of Water in a Super-hot Gas Giant’s Atmosphere

Jasmina Blecic, together with a team of international experts, identified water vapor in the atmosphere of WASP-18 b — an ultra-hot gas giant 10 times more massive than Jupiter — and made a temperature map of the planet.








Unsolved Mystery

Scientists like Francesco Arneodo and Lotfi Benabderrahmane

have spent decades searching for something they can’t see.
















Why are Space Scientists so Interested in Black Holes?

“By looking at black holes, we can learn something about the evolution of galaxies," say physicists Ingyin Zaw and David Russell.










NYU Abu Dhabi's Universe of Virtual Galaxies

The simulated birth and evolution of a virtual galaxy — billions of years of space activity was envisioned by Andrea Macciò, Associate Professor and Program Head of Physics.








Mind Over Dark Matter

Professor Andrea Macciò has been searching his entire life for something that science knows is there but has never seen.

title: PhD Student Research
breadcrumbs: PhD in Astrophysics and Space Systems
text:
PhD Student Research






Academic Year 2025-2026




















Dalya Akl

Project : High-energy Transients, Powerful and Luminous Phenomena Arising from Compact Objects







High-energy transients, powerful and luminous phenomena arising from compact objects, serve as exceptional probes of the universe’s most extreme physical processes. My research focuses on the physics of outflows in these systems, investigating how ejecta are launched, shaped, and observed across the electromagnetic spectrum.

As part of major international collaborations, including the GRANDMA (Global Rapid Advanced Network for Multi-messenger Addicts) Network and the Zwicky Transient Facility (ZTF), I contribute extensively to rapid follow-up of transient events and gravitational-wave alerts. By integrating coordinated observations from ground- and space-based facilities with physical modeling of jet emission and transient evolution, I study sources ranging from gamma-ray bursts to X-ray binaries and other compact-object explosions. During my PhD, I aim to unify these directions, relativistic jet physics, time-domain and multi-wavelength studies, and multi-messenger response, to investigate energy transport, shock interactions, and the observable signatures of compact objects.

My work extends to the search for and characterization of electromagnetic gravitational-wave counterparts, particularly kilonovae. Driven by the search for GW170817-like events, I seek to understand how these transients constrain neutron-star merger physics, r-process nucleosynthesis, and multi-messenger emission mechanisms. Together, these efforts move toward a coherent understanding of the engines powering high-energy transients and the universe’s brightest flashes and most fleeting signals.



























Sara Alameeri

I am investigating how much we can learn about the atmospheric dynamics of Hot Jupiters given our current observational capabilities.







I obtained my Bachelor of Science (honours) majoring in astrophysics from Monash University, where my undergraduate research covered the dynamics of celestial three-body systems. I explored the gravitational effect of companions on protoplanetary disk structures computationally and analytically. Such studies of the interactions between planet and disk particles ultimately answer the question of how our very own solar system was formed.

Having researched the earlier stage of planetary evolution, I moved on to studying the dynamics of exoplanetary atmospheres, specifically Hot Jupiters with Ian Dobbs-Dixon. Hot Jupiters, as the name alludes to, are planets of the size of Jupiter that orbit very closely to their host stars. A year on hot Jupiter is equivalent to a few Earth days. These extreme orbital conditions (in comparison to our own Jupiter) lead to drastic changes in these planet’s atmospheres. In my first research rotation, I am investigating how much we can learn about the atmospheric dynamics of Hot Jupiters given our current observational capabilities. Additionally, I am working on identifying the current theoretical and computational limitations and the improvements needed to be done in order for us to optimize our observations and push our understanding further of these extreme worlds.

I am passionate about the intersection between science and art, how creative thinking can inform our science processes, and how science can inspire artistic expression. I value interdisciplinary conversations that bring together natural and social sciences, cultural studies, history, and philosophy, so I am always happy to listen and discuss different perspectives.



























Amna Alhosani

Project : Optimization of Hybrid Rocket Fuel Grain Geometry through Numerical Simulation







Hybrid rockets combine the simplicity and safety of solid propulsion with the controllability of liquid systems, offering a promising route toward more flexible and sustainable launch technologies. Yet, their internal design remains a key factor limiting performance and predictability. Understanding how fuel grain geometry influences combustion behavior, regression rate, and overall efficiency is central to advancing hybrid propulsion systems.

During my PhD, I aim to address this challenge by optimizing the internal geometry of hybrid rocket fuel grains through high-fidelity numerical simulations. My work focuses on developing a predictive framework that connects grain design, internal flow behavior, and regression rate to overall motor performance, ultimately contributing to the design of more efficient and reliable hybrid propulsion systems.

Alongside my doctoral studies, I work as a Researcher at the Technology Innovation Institute’s Propulsion and Space Research Center, where I contribute to the design, manufacturing, and testing of hybrid rocket technologies as part of the Rocket Propulsion Team. I hold a bachelor’s degree in Aerospace Engineering from Khalifa University (2021) and a master’s degree in Aerospace Vehicle Design from Cranfield University (2022). My broader interests include aerospace propulsion, aircraft design, and applied research in rocket and flight systems.



























Aisha AlYazeedi

Project : Measuring the spatially-resolved properties of large-scale outflows and their host galaxies.







Large-scale outflows from galaxies are typically associated with star formation or AGN activity from the central supermassive black hole; however, it’s still unclear how these outflows are generated and how the properties of the outflow are connected to their origins or their hosts. My research focuses on measuring the spatially-resolved properties of the outflow and its host galaxy across multiple wavebands, such as the morphology, kinematics, and energetics, allowing us to better understand the structure of the radio emission and suggest a possible connection between the type of outflow and mode of accretion onto the black hole. During my PhD, I aim to broaden my research to include stellar-mass black holes and binary systems, integrating these studies with my current focus on AGN to investigate whether the underlying physics of accretion and outflows are similar across different scales.

I obtained my Bachelor of Science in physics from Sorbonne University Abu Dhabi and spent several years working on research projects related to AGN. I am deeply passionate about space science, and I value the diversification of research areas within this field. I am keen on not only advancing knowledge through academic research but also contributing to the development of applied projects in the space sector.



























Federico Baraggioni

My research focuses on one of the most significant unsolved problems in modern astrophysics: the nature of dark matter.







Although first suggested by Fritz Zwicky in 1933, dark matter only became the object of extensive studies in the 1970s thanks to the work of Vera Rubin and Kent Ford. They demonstrated that galaxies rotate much faster than expected based on their visible matter alone. According to the current standard cosmological model, dark matter accounts for approximately 85% of the total mass of the universe.

Today, there are numerous candidates for dark matter, with masses spanning many orders of magnitude. My work aims to distinguish between these competing theories. To achieve this, I analyze large-scale cosmological simulations to see how different dark matter frameworks would shape the universe.

Specifically, I investigate the effect of these models on the Inter-Galactic Medium (IGM), the diffuse gas found between galaxies. I study the physical properties of the IGM by processing the outputs of these simulations, particularly the distribution of neutral hydrogen and the emission of fluorescent Lyman-alpha.

A key part of my research involves introducing a novel morphological analysis using Minkowski functionals. This approach allows me to quantify the differences between simulations using different dark matter candidates. My goal is to design a new method to constrain the properties of dark matter and provide new insights into our understanding of the cosmos.



























Swetha Lakshmi

Project : Stable and unstable ram mode operation in ramjet engines, critical to understanding and controlling combustion stability in high-speed propulsion systems.







In my current research, I focus on stable and unstable ram mode operation in ramjet engines, critical to understanding and controlling combustion stability in high-speed propulsion systems. Unstable ram mode operation, such as the unstart phenomenon, causes sudden disruptions in airflow and pressure that significantly impact engine performance and reliability, making their study essential for advancing supersonic flight technologies.

During my PhD, I plan to extend this work to rotating detonation technology, which promises higher efficiency and thrust by harnessing continuous detonation combustion. The aim is to deepen insights into the complex flow and combustion dynamics in these engines through a combination of experimental investigations, computational modeling, and theoretical analysis, contributing to innovative combustion mechanisms for next-generation propulsion systems.

By integrating coordinated observations from ground- and space-based facilities with physical modeling of jet emission and transient evolution, I study sources ranging from gamma-ray bursts to X-ray binaries and other compact-object explosions. During my PhD, I aim to unify these directions, relativistic jet physics, time-domain and multi-wavelength studies, and multi-messenger response, to investigate energy transport, shock interactions, and the observable signatures of compact objects.

My work extends to the search for and characterization of electromagnetic gravitational-wave counterparts, particularly kilonovae. Driven by the search for GW170817-like events, I seek to understand how these transients constrain neutron-star merger physics, r-process nucleosynthesis, and multi-messenger emission mechanisms. Together, these efforts move toward a coherent understanding of the engines powering high-energy transients and the universe’s brightest flashes and most fleeting signals.

sections.title: Academic Year 2025-2026 · Sara Alameeri
sections.text:
I am investigating how much we can learn about the atmospheric dynamics of Hot Jupiters given our current observational capabilities.







I obtained my Bachelor of Science (honours) majoring in astrophysics from Monash University, where my undergraduate research covered the dynamics of celestial three-body systems. I explored the gravitational effect of companions on protoplanetary disk structures computationally and analytically. Such studies of the interactions between planet and disk particles ultimately answer the question of how our very own solar system was formed.

Having researched the earlier stage of planetary evolution, I moved on to studying the dynamics of exoplanetary atmospheres, specifically Hot Jupiters with Ian Dobbs-Dixon. Hot Jupiters, as the name alludes to, are planets of the size of Jupiter that orbit very closely to their host stars. A year on hot Jupiter is equivalent to a few Earth days. These extreme orbital conditions (in comparison to our own Jupiter) lead to drastic changes in these planet’s atmospheres. In my first research rotation, I am investigating how much we can learn about the atmospheric dynamics of Hot Jupiters given our current observational capabilities. Additionally, I am working on identifying the current theoretical and computational limitations and the improvements needed to be done in order for us to optimize our observations and push our understanding further of these extreme worlds.

I am passionate about the intersection between science and art, how creative thinking can inform our science processes, and how science can inspire artistic expression. I value interdisciplinary conversations that bring together natural and social sciences, cultural studies, history, and philosophy, so I am always happy to listen and discuss different perspectives.

sections.title: Academic Year 2025-2026 · Amna Alhosani
sections.text:
Project : Optimization of Hybrid Rocket Fuel Grain Geometry through Numerical Simulation







Hybrid rockets combine the simplicity and safety of solid propulsion with the controllability of liquid systems, offering a promising route toward more flexible and sustainable launch technologies. Yet, their internal design remains a key factor limiting performance and predictability. Understanding how fuel grain geometry influences combustion behavior, regression rate, and overall efficiency is central to advancing hybrid propulsion systems.

During my PhD, I aim to address this challenge by optimizing the internal geometry of hybrid rocket fuel grains through high-fidelity numerical simulations. My work focuses on developing a predictive framework that connects grain design, internal flow behavior, and regression rate to overall motor performance, ultimately contributing to the design of more efficient and reliable hybrid propulsion systems.

Alongside my doctoral studies, I work as a Researcher at the Technology Innovation Institute’s Propulsion and Space Research Center, where I contribute to the design, manufacturing, and testing of hybrid rocket technologies as part of the Rocket Propulsion Team. I hold a bachelor’s degree in Aerospace Engineering from Khalifa University (2021) and a master’s degree in Aerospace Vehicle Design from Cranfield University (2022). My broader interests include aerospace propulsion, aircraft design, and applied research in rocket and flight systems.

sections.title: Academic Year 2025-2026 · Aisha AlYazeedi
sections.text:
Project : Measuring the spatially-resolved properties of large-scale outflows and their host galaxies.







Large-scale outflows from galaxies are typically associated with star formation or AGN activity from the central supermassive black hole; however, it’s still unclear how these outflows are generated and how the properties of the outflow are connected to their origins or their hosts. My research focuses on measuring the spatially-resolved properties of the outflow and its host galaxy across multiple wavebands, such as the morphology, kinematics, and energetics, allowing us to better understand the structure of the radio emission and suggest a possible connection between the type of outflow and mode of accretion onto the black hole. During my PhD, I aim to broaden my research to include stellar-mass black holes and binary systems, integrating these studies with my current focus on AGN to investigate whether the underlying physics of accretion and outflows are similar across different scales.

I obtained my Bachelor of Science in physics from Sorbonne University Abu Dhabi and spent several years working on research projects related to AGN. I am deeply passionate about space science, and I value the diversification of research areas within this field. I am keen on not only advancing knowledge through academic research but also contributing to the development of applied projects in the space sector.

sections.title: Academic Year 2025-2026 · Federico Baraggioni
sections.text:
My research focuses on one of the most significant unsolved problems in modern astrophysics: the nature of dark matter.







Although first suggested by Fritz Zwicky in 1933, dark matter only became the object of extensive studies in the 1970s thanks to the work of Vera Rubin and Kent Ford. They demonstrated that galaxies rotate much faster than expected based on their visible matter alone. According to the current standard cosmological model, dark matter accounts for approximately 85% of the total mass of the universe.

Today, there are numerous candidates for dark matter, with masses spanning many orders of magnitude. My work aims to distinguish between these competing theories. To achieve this, I analyze large-scale cosmological simulations to see how different dark matter frameworks would shape the universe.

Specifically, I investigate the effect of these models on the Inter-Galactic Medium (IGM), the diffuse gas found between galaxies. I study the physical properties of the IGM by processing the outputs of these simulations, particularly the distribution of neutral hydrogen and the emission of fluorescent Lyman-alpha.

A key part of my research involves introducing a novel morphological analysis using Minkowski functionals. This approach allows me to quantify the differences between simulations using different dark matter candidates. My goal is to design a new method to constrain the properties of dark matter and provide new insights into our understanding of the cosmos.

sections.title: Academic Year 2025-2026 · Swetha Lakshmi
sections.text:
Project : Stable and unstable ram mode operation in ramjet engines, critical to understanding and controlling combustion stability in high-speed propulsion systems.







In my current research, I focus on stable and unstable ram mode operation in ramjet engines, critical to understanding and controlling combustion stability in high-speed propulsion systems. Unstable ram mode operation, such as the unstart phenomenon, causes sudden disruptions in airflow and pressure that significantly impact engine performance and reliability, making their study essential for advancing supersonic flight technologies.

During my PhD, I plan to extend this work to rotating detonation technology, which promises higher efficiency and thrust by harnessing continuous detonation combustion. The aim is to deepen insights into the complex flow and combustion dynamics in these engines through a combination of experimental investigations, computational modeling, and theoretical analysis, contributing to innovative combustion mechanisms for next-generation propulsion systems.

text:
Global PhD Student Fellowship in Biology





The NYU Abu Dhabi Global PhD Student Fellowship in Biology is offered in collaboration with the Graduate School of Arts and Science at NYU New York. The program offers training in a broad range of biological research fields, including developmental genetics, genomics and systems biology, molecular and cellular biology, evolutionary biology, and infectious disease.

The program generally involves one to two years of classwork at NYU New York, followed by three to four years of research at NYU Abu Dhabi. If selected, the doctorate is fully funded under the NYU Abu Dhabi Global PhD Student Fellowship.














Key Features of the Fellowship

- New York University degree upon graduation
- Access to the extraordinary resources of the NYU Graduate School of Arts and Science
- Graduate coursework in New York
- Cutting-edge research opportunities in NYU Abu Dhabi’s labs
- Tuition, fees, and health insurance provided throughout the program
- Generous research assistantship and stipend provided by NYU Abu Dhabi throughout the program
- Assistance for degree-related travel between Abu Dhabi and New York
- Campus accommodation at no cost in Abu Dhabi
- A contribution toward accommodation costs in New York
- Career development assistance at both campuses

title: Undergraduate Academic Policies
text:
Undergraduate Academic Policies

The Academic Policies of NYU Abu Dhabi are summarized below. Unless otherwise noted, students should direct all questions or concerns regarding these policies to their Faculty Mentor, who will liaise with the appropriate members of the university administration as needed.

-





Guidance on Student Absences:

NYUAD’s absence guidelines are grounded in honesty, trust, and academic integrity. Academic integrity includes being truthful in all verbal and written communication between students and faculty.

In line with policy at NYU New York, effective since fall 2023, NYUAD students are not required to submit a doctor’s or NYUAD Health Center note for missing class on a short-term basis.

Guidelines:

- Short-term Absences : For medical efficacy and equity reasons, faculty should take students’ reports of unanticipated, brief illness or other circumstances (e.g., family emergencies or personal issues) at face value and excuse short-term absences without requiring a doctor’s note. This reduces the burden on students whose illnesses do not require clinical intervention, and relieves burden on the Health Center. The NYUAD Health Center will not issue doctor’s notes for such situations, and faculty should not ask students to divulge their private health-related information. At the faculty member’s discretion, absences that are not adequately explained to the satisfaction of the professor can be considered “unexcused” and handled in accordance with the attendance policy as stated on the course syllabus.
- Defining and Accommodating Short-term Absences : Up to one calendar week of absences (modified as appropriate for 7-week and J-Term courses) from class should be excused. Faculty should direct a student experiencing a short-term illness towards alternative forms of class participation or engagement such as reviewing notes or slides posted on NYU Brightspace, getting notes from other students, viewing class recordings (if available), or attending office hours. Faculty should keep in mind that in the case of illness, some recovery period may be necessary before the student is able to engage fully with these kinds of course resources. Unless related to chronic conditions, short-term absences based on illness typically do not involve formal accommodations via the Moses Center for Student Accessibility.
- Students’ Responsibility : In all cases, students should notify faculty in advance, when possible , when they will not be able to attend class. Each semester, the Office of Undergraduate Education, Student Affairs, and the Dean of Students remind students that they must notify their instructors in the event of any absences from class.
- Longer-term Absences : When a student misses more than one week of class, or has repeated short-term absences totaling more than one week, faculty may require appropriate documentation (e.g., a medical note, record of a family emergency, military service, etc). The Dean of Students Office ( nyuad.dos@nyu.edu ) can advise on what documentation may be requested appropriately. At the same time, faculty should raise an “Academic Concern” flag in NYU Connect or report the issue to the Academic Resource Center (ARC).

With the Academic Concern flag, faculty have the opportunity to provide comments that will support meaningful student outreach. These comments are not shared with the student, but rather only with those individuals in the student’s network who can support them. The goal of this action is to ensure that there is a coordinated effort to enable the student’s academic progress in all of their courses. Should faculty become aware of a mental health issue, please follow the Distressed Student Protocol. Faculty can also raise a flag in NYU Connect, but this will be received by the student’s adviser first. If there is a known time sensitivity, please alert NYUAD’s mental health professionals directly.
All other current attendance policies remain the same and the administration supports the standards established by individual faculty as presented in their course syllabi in accordance with guidance from the Undergraduate Curriculum Committee (UCC).

Faculty should continue to monitor attendance in classes and continue to employ classroom policies and practices that accommodate students who are managing health issues — whether involving physical or mental health — or who have other legitimate reasons for missing class.



-





At NYU Abu Dhabi, a commitment to excellence, fairness, honesty, and respect within and outside the classroom is essential to maintaining the integrity of our community. By accepting membership in this community, students, faculty, and staff take responsibility for demonstrating these values in their own conduct and for recognizing and supporting these values in others. In turn, these values create a campus climate that encourages the free exchange of ideas, promotes scholarly excellence through active and creative thought, and allows community members to achieve and be recognized for achieving their highest potential.

As part of the NYU global network, NYUAD students are also subject to NYU’s all-school policy on Academic Integrity for Students at NYU . Alleged integrity violations are resolved using NYUAD’s Academic Integrity Procedure. View the Academic Integrity Policy and Procedure .

Statement of Principles

Upon matriculation, students bring a wide variety of experiences, hopes, and goals to NYU Abu Dhabi. These backgrounds create and continually shape our communal goals and ideals. The NYUAD Community’s Commitment to Integrity is an important element of life together at NYU Abu Dhabi. Simply stated, it means that each member of the community is responsible for maintaining the student’s own integrity and the integrity of the NYU Abu Dhabi community. While broad in its applications, it provides a guideline for decision making which holds each community member to principles of good conduct toward oneself and others. While this principle allows for a significant degree of individual freedom, a general framework of values is necessary. In choosing to join the NYUAD academic community, community members agree to integrate the following standards into their own definition of personal honesty as outlined in the following explanation of the NYUAD Community’s Commitment to Integrity:

Responsibility : Though each member’s individual conception of responsibility is unique, NYU Abu Dhabi trusts that everyone will demonstrate ownership of their actions and will recognize the ways in which their actions affect their peers, NYU Abu Dhabi, and the greater community. Each member of the NYUAD community maintains the ability to express themselves with integrity, which is crucial to the development of a community that is personally challenging, both intellectually and socially. Membership in the community also includes an obligation to help others maintain the highest level of integrity through encouraging compliance and, if necessary, making the community aware of possible violations.

Students have a responsibility to be aware of what constitutes an academic integrity violation and are encouraged to review the NYU-wide statements about academic integrity references above. For their part, faculty have a responsibility to help educate students about what constitutes an infraction and to report possible infractions to the Office of Undergraduate Academic Policies (OUAP).

When possible, faculty members have a responsibility to design assignments in ways which encourage academic integrity. As part of this responsibility faculty are permitted, but not required, to utilize similarity detection software and such other methods of detecting possible violations as may become available.

Honesty : A sense of honesty is fostered by the individual’s ability to express oneself in a candid and forthright manner.

Respect : Respecting oneself and others requires that every individual maintain the integrity of their own values, while acting in a way that is careful and considerate of others. In our community, mutual respect can be obtained only by valuing free inquiry, respect for difference, and intellectual honesty.

NYUAD’s integrity procedure assumes adherence to the rules and regulations of the University that are designed to promote intellectual and social pursuits and to ensure personal safety. In addition, the University is committed to an inclusive and diverse community. A NYUAD student demonstrates their respect for individual freedom by conducting themselves with maturity and honor, and by showing due concern for the welfare of other members of the community.

Dishonorable academic conduct, such as plagiarism and cheating, discredits the individual student. Such behavior is detrimental to the well-being of the NYUAD community. Abiding by community standards indicates a mature acceptance of community responsibility.








Levels of Academic Integrity Violations with Examples

Because NYU Abu Dhabi is a diverse institution and because some types of integrity violations are more serious than others, it is useful to provide some examples of possible violations.. The list below is not exhaustive; other conduct not mentioned below may violate standards of integrity. It is also possible that additional contextual factors may be present that could affect how a particular listed violation is evaluated and addressed.

The following list provides examples of some of the most common types of violations:

- Plagiarism – Copying and pasting from or paraphrasing minor or substantial portions of someone else’s words, ideas, or work and presenting them as your own without proper credit or citation
- Collusion – unauthorized collaboration with others to purposely cheat or influence the outcome of an assignment
- Cheating – the unauthorized use of information, materials, devices, or other sources during an exam, quiz, or test
- Fraud – Intentionally deceiving or misrepresenting academic work, such as, creating false data or the alteration of data to mislead on an assignment deliberately; Submitting an assignment, essay, code, or research written wholly or partly by Generative AI tools and/or AI-assisted technologies; Editing Generative AI tools and/or AI-assisted technologies output and presenting it as one’s original work; And using Generative AI tools and/or AI-assisted technologies to generate fake sources, data, or citations and presenting them as real.
- Seeking or receiving unauthorized guidance or support for an assignment, exam, quiz, or test
- Using material written for one class in another, without prior approval from the instructor
- Signing the attendance sheet for an absent student
- Knowingly facilitating dishonesty by another student on an exam or assignment.
- Intentionally misleading NYUAD faculty or staff in an attempt to circumvent a policy or prior decision
While all integrity violations are serious, most can be reviewed through an informal process that is described below. However, some are so egregious that they can be considered only through a more formal set of procedures. While most typical violations result in sanctions wholly within the class such as a lower mark on an assignment or in the course as a whole, particularly egregious violations are likely to lead to more severe sanctions including the revocation of study away privileges, academic probation, suspension, or dismissal from NYU Abu Dhabi. Among the most severe violations are the following:

- Repeat violations by a student who has been found responsible for a previous academic integrity violation.
- Having a substitute take an examination or complete an assignment for you
- The buying, selling, or distribution of an exam, paper, or coursework
- Intentionally destroying or obstructing another student’s work
- Tampering with or fabricating evidence related to integrity violation cases
- Giving or obtaining exam questions in advance
- Falsifying or altering records or documentation (e.g., grades, transcripts, medical notes, etc.)
- Using someone else's netID or password
- Failure to secure IRB approval when required where significant harm to individuals or the University is present
- Knowingly violating laboratory protocols in a manner that endangers people or property







Procedure When an Infraction Is Suspected

Definition

This policy incorporates by reference the definitions of plagiarism and cheating contained in the University-wide Academic Integrity for Students at NYU policy .

Faculty Member/Instructor : As used in this policy, the term “Faculty Member” or “Instructor” refers to the person initiating the academic integrity review, even though the initiator may not always have that status. Typically, a faculty member initiates a case of an alleged academic integrity violation. However, the University recognizes that there may be cases where a university administrator initiates an integrity violation review; in such cases, the faculty member of record will be consulted and involved, as appropriate, in accordance with the administrator initiating the charge.

Academic Day/Week : An academic day is any day during the spring or fall semesters in which NYUAD classes are held. An academic week is any five consecutive academic days. While all parties are encouraged to proceed as quickly as careful deliberation allows, exam periods, holidays, and January or summer terms are not included as academic days.

Office of Undergraduate Academic Policies : The Office of Undergraduate Academic Policies (OUAP) is responsible for implementing the Academic Integrity Policy and the Procedures that support that policy. If the OUAP should have a real or perceived conflict of interest or be unavailable, they may appoint a designee to carry out their responsibilities as described below. As used in this document, the term OUAP means the Office of Undergraduate Academic Policies or their designee.








Integrity Review Process

A faculty member who suspects a student of an academic integrity violation will report the apparent incident to the OUAP shortly (typically within one academic week with the expectation of delays during breaks) after identifying or being informed of the suspicious act, specifying the particular circumstances and supporting evidence of misconduct. The identification of an alleged violation may occur at any time, including after the course ends and a grade is reported. However, in the ordinary course, cases of alleged violations related to a single class will be brought not later than the end of the first month of the regular semester following the completion of the course. The University, in its discretion, may proceed with suspected major violations of this policy when discovered subsequent to this timeframe. While cases should be initiated within one week of identifying the alleged infraction, there is no ultimate statute of limitation for bringing cases that relate to multiple courses or to infractions unrelated to a course.

The OUAP will determine if there is sufficient evidence to proceed further and the apparent severity of the alleged violation — specifically taking into account whether or not the student has been previously found responsible for an integrity violation. If the alleged infraction is determined to be minor or a first offense, the faculty member may seek to resolve the matter directly with the student through the following informal process.

Both the student and the faculty member have the right to proceed directly to the formal process described below. However, unless the case is determined to be egregious, review will ordinarily begin with the informal process. Cases involving repeat offenders, egregious alleged violations, or multiple potential violations must utilize the formal procedures described later in this document.

Students may not drop or withdraw from a class while an integrity proceeding is taking place; and a drop or withdrawal will not erase or eliminate records of the incident, finding or sanction. The sanction for an integrity violation may include requiring a student to withdraw from a course or may preclude a student from withdrawing from a course or converting it to pass/fail grading. Unless specified in the sanction, normal rules pertaining to course withdrawal and pass/fail are assumed to apply. If a student is sanctioned to withdraw from a course for an academic integrity violation, they will not be eligible for a tuition refund for that course, regardless of when the withdrawal occurs during the semester.

If an academic integrity matter has not been resolved by the final grade submission deadline, the instructor should contact the OUAP before submitting a final grade. The office will coordinate with the Registrar to determine the appropriate temporary grade and next steps.








Informal Process

When it is the first offense, the OUAP will inform the faculty member of the typical range of sanctions based on the records of sanctions utilized in similar prior cases, although such precedent is not binding.

Within one academic week of consulting with the OUAP, the faculty member then seeks to resolve the matter independently with the student, advise the student on the conventions and expectations of academic integrity, as pertinent, and reach a mutually acceptable agreement (1) on the facts, (2) whether these facts constitute a violation, and (3) on a sanction. If the matter is resolved between the faculty member and the student, the faculty member will submit a report on the incident to the OUAP within one academic week that includes a brief summary signed by both the student and the faculty of fact, an admission of responsibility on the part of the student, and the agreed upon sanction, if any. While the expectation is that the OUAP will affirm the agreement reached between the student and the faculty member, the OUAP may insist that the case be continued through the formal process when the sanction is deemed inappropriate or the case involves significant questions of precedent that merit further review.

Second offenses will also be managed using the informal process.

The sanction for second offenses will be automatic course failure, unless the course instructor recommends to the OUAP an alternative sanction depending on the level of the offense and such a recommendation is deemed appropriate.

While the OUAP will maintain a record of the determination in all cases, a student who was found not to have been responsible for a violation will not be considered a repeat offender nor otherwise adversely impacted in any future integrity proceedings.

The student has no more than one week after a sanction is applied through the informal process to dispute it and request to move forward with the formal process. If neither party appeals within one academic week of the decision, the sanction will be implemented and the finding will stand.








Formal Process

If the faculty member and student cannot reach an agreement on the facts and sanction, or if either the faculty member or OUAP believes that the violation is of sufficient gravity to warrant a more official treatment, the faculty member will provide a formal, written complaint to the OUAP within one academic week of the discovery of the alleged infraction or if applicable, the end of the informal process, unless circumstances warrant extending this timeframe, requesting to resolve the matter through the formal process of an academic hearing.

In all cases, a third charge following a finding of responsibility or multiple concurrent charges will automatically trigger a formal review. The OUAP will promptly inform the student of the allegation, providing the student with a copy of the formal written complaint.

Although individual faculty members have broad latitude in assigning sanctions for violations in their classes, the expectation is that faculty will assign sanctions consistent with historical precedent as outlined by the OUAP. Sanctions may be appealed and the determination of the Academic Integrity Hearing Committee may alter the sanction initially proposed by the faculty member. With this in mind, faculty members are encouraged not to list specific sanctions in their course syllabi and must be aware that sanctions are ultimately subject to review and revision by the Academic Integrity Hearing Committee (AIHC) as described below.

Make-up of the Academic Integrity Hearing Committee (AIHC)

Formal cases of alleged academic integrity violations are considered by the Academic Integrity Hearing Committee (AIHC), a panel consisting of three faculty members and two students. The panel for each individual hearing is randomly selected by the OUAP from two Committee Pools: one for Faculty and one for Students. Each year the Division Deans will appoint up to four representatives from each division for inclusion in the AIHC Faculty Pool. Similarly, each year Student Government, as well as any individual member of the NYUAD community may nominate students to serve as student representatives to the AIHC Student Pool. The OUAP will review all nominations and appoint eight or more of these nominated students to serve as AIHC Pool members. Appointment to the Pools typically takes place in the fall semester for service for the following year. However, replacement appointments, including the appointment of academic administrators, may be made at any time to fill vacancies in the Pool.

The OUAP may select the tentative members for each ad hoc panel from the two respective pools and may consider availability, disciplinary expertise, or any other factor that she or he deems appropriate in making the selection. Panelists who believe that they may have a real or apparent conflict of interests must ask to be recused. The accused may also request that particular panel members be recused for specific cause. The OUAP will determine the final make-up of the panel.








Committee Process

The Associate Vice Provost of Undergraduate Education (AVP), or their designee, will serve as the non-voting Chair of the Hearing — assuring that the procedures are followed, that all participants have an opportunity to be heard, and that a proper written record of the decisions of the Committee is maintained.

The student may be advised by a non-faculty member of the NYUAD community who may be present at the hearing. However, the adviser may not address the proceedings. Witnesses may be called as required, but may only be present during their own testimony. Other than those persons required to conduct the review, the hearing is closed.

The hearing consists of two parts:

The initial phase is the determination of responsibility.

The AVP will share the official written complaint with the AIHC at the hearing.

The Faculty Complainant will summarize the accusation and present whatever evidence they believe bears on the question of responsibility.

The Student Respondent will have an opportunity to speak and provide evidence in their defense.

The chair may allow any relevant evidence to be included. Formal legal rules of evidence do not apply.

Committee members, including the chair, may ask questions at any time.

Although it may become apparent during the hearing that a student had been found responsible for a previous integrity violation, prior findings of responsibility may not be considered as evidence in the current case.

Upon conclusion of all presentations, the complainant and student are excused.

The members of the AIHC deliberate as needed. The decision as to responsibility is based on a preponderance of evidence as determined by a majority of the voting members of the AIHC.

If the student is not found responsible, the case is closed and the instructor may not sanction the student in any way.

If the decision of the AIHC is that the student is responsible for a violation, the process proceeds to the second step of recommending a sanction.

The AVP will inform the AIHC at this time if there are any previous integrity findings against the student and will provide the AIHC with historic precedents for similar cases.

AIHC members may ask questions as needed.

The AIHC is charged with recommending a sanction within the class and must consider both historical precedent as well as exacerbating and mitigating circumstances. While the AIHC is expected to consider both faculty and student statements about an appropriate sanction, including syllabus statements, the AIHC is not constrained by any syllabus statement nor by the sanction initially proposed during the informal procedure, if any. The faculty member is expected to implement the sanction proposed by the AIHC . However, they retain the right to modify any class-based sanction for cause and with the written approval of the AVP. The AIHC may also make a recommendation for a sanction outside of the class structure including but not limited to revocation of study away privileges, academic probation, suspension, or dismissal from NYU Abu Dhabi.

Upon conclusion of all presentations, the AVP will announce the sanction (if applicable), and the complainant and student respondent will then be excused.

The decision of the AIHC will be sent to the student and the complainant in writing within one academic week.

Consistent with law, the AVP will implement any outside-of-class sanction determined by the AIHC. If the recommended sanction is dismissal, the AVP will refer the AIHC’s recommendation to the Vice Chancellor. As per UAE law, any decision to dismiss a student remains the sole prerogative of the Vice Chancellor – although it is expected that in most cases they will support the recommendation of the Committee. If the Vice Chancellor determines that dismissal is not the appropriate sanction, they may impose the lesser sanction of suspension for a period to be determined by the Vice Chancellor or may refer the case back to the AIHC for further discussion of alternative sanctions. In such a case, the AIHC has discretion to impose any sanction less severe than dismissal.








Appeal

If a student is found responsible and sanctioned for an academic integrity violation, the student can appeal to the NYUAD Vice Provost of Undergraduate Education (VPUE) but only on one of the grounds described below. A faculty member may also initiate an appeal based on one of those grounds.

If neither party appeals within one academic week of the date of the AIHC decision, the sanction will be implemented and the finding will stand.

Grounds for Appeal

Material procedural irregularity : A procedural irregularity is a failure of a decision-making body/ decision maker to follow the process or rules in place for making decisions. However, an appeal based on a procedural irregularity requires not only that an irregularity occurred but also that the irregularity is sufficiently significant so as to have likely prejudiced the outcome.

New Evidence : An appeal may be made if evidence has come to light following the decision of the AIHC which: a) was not available at the time of the initial hearing and b) might reasonably be expected to have materially affected the outcome. New evidence may, for example, include a witness whose identity and information was unknown at the time of the original hearing and whose testimony might have materially affected the hearing committee's decision at that time.

Appeal Process

A student or faculty complainant who wishes to appeal the decision of the AIHC shall follow the following procedure:

- The appellant notifies the OUAP in writing that they are appealing the outcome of the hearing, briefly summarizing the event, the supporting evidence, and their reasons for challenging the finding and/or sanction. The appeal must be submitted to the OUAP within one academic week of receiving the finding and sanction.
- The OUAP forwards the appeal to the Vice Provost (VPUE) and may, at their discretion, provide comment on the merits of the appeal or on any other matter pertinent to the case.
- The VPUE will review the case and determine whether or not the appeal has merit.
- If the VPUE determines that the appeal is without merit, the original finding and sanction are final.
- If the VPUE determines that the case for appeal is sufficient to suggest that the finding or sanction may have been prejudiced due to procedural error or new evidence, they will refer the case back to the OUAP for another hearing.
- In cases where a new hearing is required, the OUAP will form another AIHC via a new lottery and the case will be reheard as described previously.
- Although unlikely, an appeal of the findings or sanctions of a case heard a second time is possible and, if appropriate, would be subject to the same process as previously described.
- In cases where the initial sanction includes removal from an individual class, suspension, or dismissal, the Provost may allow the student to attend classes while the appeal is pending; in such cases it is understood that while all course work can be completed, no course credits can be given if the original decision is upheld.
- An unresolved academic integrity case will automatically place a hold on degree conferral and the release of the final transcript. The hold will be lifted once the formal hearing process has concluded and a final decision has been issued.







Multi-school Cases

Academic integrity violations at NYU Abu Dhabi occasionally involve students from other NYU schools. Similarly, NYUAD students may commit violations at other schools within NYU or while attending classes outside of the NYU network. Whenever feasible, the NYUAD OUAP will inform the host school of any prior violations of academic integrity prior to a sanction being imposed.

In cases involving more than one NYU school, the administrators responsible for overseeing integrity violations at the involved schools will work together to determine the procedures to be followed in adjudicating the particular case. Generally, the policies of the host school are followed.

If an NYUAD student is charged with an academic integrity violation outside of the NYU network, the student may be subject to sanctions concerning their attendance at the host institution according to that institution’s procedures and may also be subject to additional sanctions at NYUAD at the discretion of the OUAP - except that only the Vice Chancellor of NYU Abu Dhabi is empowered to dismiss an NYUAD student from NYU Abu Dhabi.

NYU Abu Dhabi will maintain records of any situations in which a student is found responsible for an academic integrity violation and will ordinarily consider any such violations as prior violations when adjudicating future alleged violations. If a student is approved for an internal transfer to another NYU school, the record of the violation will remain part of the student’s university record and may be shared with the receiving school for internal record-keeping and consideration in any future academic integrity matters.








Maintenance of Records

The OUAP is responsible for maintaining written records of all cases, formal or informal, in which a student has been found responsible for an integrity violation.

The file will typically contain the name of the complainant, the name of the student, the date of the infraction, indicative evidence of the violation, the ultimate sanction, and in cases where a formal hearing was held, the formal written complaint and the membership of the AIHC that reviewed the case.

The primary use of this file is to enable the OUAP to determine whether or not an alleged violator of the integrity policy has been found responsible for a prior violation; otherwise, the file is maintained as confidential.

The Dean of Students or other appropriate individuals may be granted access to some or all of the information in the file when considering non-academic disciplinary matters.

Students who have been found responsible for an academic integrity violation may have their academic integrity record reviewed when applying for internal or external awards, prizes, scholarships, or participation in academic competitions and on academic boards. Depending on the nature and severity of the violation and the sanction imposed, a student may be ineligible for certain opportunities.

A prior academic integrity violation will not necessarily result in automatic disqualification. Minor violations, including unintentional violations or misunderstandings, will ordinarily not adversely affect eligibility. Decisions will be made on a case-by-case basis in accordance with the applicable criteria for the award, prize, scholarship, or competition.

Submitting a reference form to a member of the NYU community that requests information about the student’s prior integrity or disciplinary history constitutes written permission to access the information and for that reference to include pertinent details from the case file.

Students who are suspended or dismissed as a result of an academic integrity violation will have a notation posted on their transcript once the case has been finalized. The notation will appear for the semester in which the violation occurred and will indicate that the student was suspended or dismissed. The transcript notation will not state that the suspension or dismissal resulted from an academic integrity violation.








Revocation of Degrees

If an academic integrity violation is discovered after a degree has been conferred, and the violation is determined to be sufficiently serious that it would have affected the student’s eligibility to graduate had it been known at the time, NYU Abu Dhabi reserves the right to revoke the degree.

Any such case will be reviewed through an appropriate university process, with the former student given notice of the allegation and an opportunity to respond before a final determination is made.

Where a degree is revoked, the university may update its records accordingly and notify any relevant internal or external offices, as appropriate.
