title: Digital Preservation Statement
text:
Digital Preservation Statement





Digital preservation at NYU Abu Dhabi Library is informed by both the vision and mission of NYU Abu Dhabi at large and the mission and values of NYU Libraries as a global organization. Digital preservation is also informed by the information professions at large. The following statement acknowledges the importance of articulating and defining shared understandings of work happening across Library departments and outlines priorities and areas involved in leading a digital preservation program on the NYU Abu Dhabi campus. This statement is also a way for NYU Abu Dhabi Library to emphasize that digital preservation is important and a central priority and service we provide to the University and our global network.








Our Charge

The NYU Abu Dhabi Library is committed to taking a lead role in preserving knowledge, scholarship, heritage and history – primarily through its local Archives and Special Collections program, which exists to provide access to rare and unique primary source materials that support the teaching and research needs of students and faculty, and promote scholarship and interest in the history of the UAE, the Gulf, the Arabian Peninsula, the wider region, and the University’s history. Our charge is situated in the context of being an institution that is both part of the NYU global network and in and of Abu Dhabi, and for the World.

Digital preservation is challenging due to the risk and urgency around potential technological obsolescence, leading to the risk of inaccessibility or loss of records and archives. As technologies and digital preservation processes evolve in the field, so too will we assess our local approaches and evolve and change our platforms and processes as necessary. Additionally, digital preservation extends the reach of our physical collections to scholars inside and outside the NYUAD community.








Our Commitment

Digital preservation is a program, not a project, at NYU Abu Dhabi. The NYUAD Library is committed to providing resources that include staff, technology, time, infrastructure, expertise, and budget. The continued allocation of university resources toward the digital preservation program will allow us to continue preserving collections in perpetuity.

The NYUAD Library intends to preserve its digital collections with the same level of commitment as its physical collections. Since this work is not limited to physical or analog formats, the Library’s mission includes preserving materials in both native born-digital formats as well as digitized surrogates of analog materials.








Our Responsibility

Digital preservation is not a promise of "forever," as stated in NYU Libraries' own digital preservation policy statement. Our aim is to utilize present-day technologies and processes to extend the life of materials for as long as possible. Digital preservation is also more than simply storing digital objects and resources. It requires employment of processes and standards, and it is the responsibility of the digital preservation team to stay current in these processes and standards, while at the same time, it may be necessary to consult and collaborate with external partners.







The NYUAD Library digital preservation team includes a variety of specialists and experts:

- Library Administration and Strategy: Executive Director, Associate Director
- Archives and Special Collections (ASC): Head of ASC, NYUAD Archivist
- Digitization Program and Digital Preservation Leadership: Digital Content Specialist
- NYUAD Library Staff: Responsible for compliance with this statement
- External Partners: NYUAD/NYU IT are partners, especially in the sustainability of technical infrastructure
The digital preservation policy will be reviewed regularly against University and Library missions and goals to ensure that it continues to support the core work of the institution.








Our Scope

Collections identified for digital preservation at NYU Abu Dhabi include both born-digital and digitized copies of analog materials. Identified materials should fall within the overarching collection scope of Archives and Special Collections. These materials include primary and secondary sources acquired to support the teaching and research needs of the campus, to build an archival collection of institutional history (University Archives), and to provide access to our specialized collections for our remote international scholars. The goal is not to digitize every source or object in our holdings.

Within the scope of our mission and collections, we prioritize digital preservation according to a set of transparent criteria and priorities:

- Heavily used collections : Collections for which there are well-defined anticipated uses for the materials in digital format and evidence of past use of the materials in their original formats. This may mean digital reformatting and preservation of only some parts of analog collections.
- Value for research : Priority is given to materials with significant intrinsic value because they represent the unique holdings and subject strengths of ASC and NYUAD Library. Other high-priority collections support the long-term scholarly interests of the NYUAD community and documentation of the history of NYUAD itself.
- Items difficult to access in their current format or at risk of deterioration : Digitization of rare and/or fragile items can protect them from repeated handling. However, fragile items will be evaluated prior to digitization and will not be put at risk to digitize. Other items that are difficult to access include obscure formats and audio and visual formats that may not be accessible without digitization.
- Disaster Preparedness : Materials may be prioritized for digitization and digital preservation to preserve the informational content of unique primary sources in the event of natural disasters or other forms of destruction.
- Copyright Acknowledgement : Most archival and special collections content requires consideration of copyright. Collections prioritized for digitization and digital preservation are either in the public domain or have a lower risk of copyright infringement.
Out of Scope for this policy are:

- Research data and research records that have not been accessioned by ASC and are more appropriate for another type of institutional repository.
- University records that have not been accessioned by ASC.
- Commercial or open-access digital content that the Library does not manage and where the Library has only access rights.
- Materials that are digitized on demand to meet reference requests may not fit into digital preservation priorities.
Digital preservation curators will regularly assess priorities.








Our Values

In the work of digital preservation, we value collaboration, transparency, an iterative approach, and accessibility. We commit to these values while also recognizing that materials will be as open as possible and only restricted when necessary. The Library is committed to providing access to digital materials while respecting and upholding the intellectual property rights of authors and obtaining prior consent when the creator’s identity is known. We aim to understand our global audience and consider, in the daily work of digital preservation, our broad user community and the preservation and access needs of the collections within the context of being both part of the United Arab Emirates and part of the NYU global network.

Our values are also informed by the larger digital preservation professional community and the importance of shared knowledge.








Our Stewardship

Being good stewards of preserved digital collections involves the following:

- Investing in a technical infrastructure that is sustainable and supports digital preservation work.
- A commitment to having dedicated digital preservation staff with the required expertise to support digital preservation work and to their continued professional development.
- Engagement in systematic planning and strategy that includes regularly assessing digital materials to understand and mitigate risk (such as loss of accessibility and technical obsolescence).
- A commitment to ensuring the authenticity of preserved materials.
- A commitment to building a literacy and knowledge base for digital preservation and our processes.
- A commitment to providing access to digital materials while respecting and upholding the intellectual property rights of authors.







Operating Principles

NYU Abu Dhabi endeavors to ensure that digital objects, either born-digital or digitized content, will remain robust in both bitstream and logical preservation. By combining internal storage solutions, workflows, and external cloud-based systems that conform to ISO 14721 (the Open Archival Information System reference model) and align with ISO 16363 standards (Certification of Trustworthy Digital Repositories). Digital objects will be preserved and migrated as formats become obsolete, ensuring long-term accessibility and mitigating digital obsolescence.

- File fixity values will be calculated at the earliest opportunity to ensure file transfers can be validated throughout these processes and workflows.
- Where possible, the utilisation of robust backup strategies, such as the 3-2-1 rule, will be implemented, whilst being mindful of the implications to the environmental impact of large data storage and digital sustainability.
Technical, preservation, and descriptive metadata will be gathered and aligned with the files utilizing the appropriate metadata schemas that both meet the collections’ requirements and ensure compliance with established standards and best practices.

The Library commits to maintaining safe and secure hardware and software dedicated to Digital Preservation work. We provide isolated, non-networked machines for specific tasks to mitigate risks to campus network infrastructure and ensure access is only granted to digital preservation staff.



Stakeholders

- Ron Berry, Executive Director, Educational Technology and Library Services
- Beth Russell, Associate Director for Research Services and Strategy; Academic Librarian
- Brad Bauer, Head of Archives and Special Collections; Academic Librarian
- Lauren Kata, Associate Academic Librarian for Archives and Special Collections and NYUAD Archivist
- Rebecca Pittam, Manager of Digital Preservation

title: Faculty Digital Archive
text:
Faculty Digital Archive











The Faculty Digital Archive (FDA) is a highly visible repository of NYU scholarship, allowing digital works — text, audio, video, data, and more — to be shared and securely stored. Collections may be made freely available worldwide, accessible to NYU only, or restricted to a specific group.









Read More

Get more information on the FDA.













About the Service

- Full-time faculty may deposit their research — unpublished and, in many cases, published — in the FDA.
- Departments, centers, or institutes may also use the FDA to distribute working papers, technical reports, or other research material.
- The FDA allows scholars to provide open access versions of their publications, presentations and other research, and faculty are encouraged to use Creative Commons licenses where possible in order to maximize the impact and reach of their work.
- By default, content in the FDA is world-readable, unless collection owners choose to restrict access.

title: Project Collaborations
text:
Project Collaborations






Winter Institute in Digital Humanities

The Digital Scholarship and Preservation program is co-founder and co-host of the Winter Institute in Digital Humanities , an event aimed at researchers and educators interested in the intersection of technology and the humanities. Now in its third iteration, the Winter Institute has drawn instructors and scholars worldwide to engage in an intensive digital humanities learning environment. The Winter Institute features hands-on courses, lunchtime presentations, a poster session, cultural and academic visits, and networking opportunities.

Topics addressed in the courses vary from year to year. Recent offerings have focused on computational analysis of cultural heritage, artificial intelligence and the classroom, spatial analysis of societies, Arabic text analysis, and the data of culture. The courses share a common vision of how the digital has changed and continues to change, the way that we learn, teach, do research, and disseminate knowledge. Certain courses also address new responsibilities and horizons for the arts and humanities in an age of automation.

To stay in touch about these and other similar events, consider joining our NYUAD Digital Humanities listserv by sending a request to nyuad.dh@nyu.edu .

Music and Sound Cultures Research Group

As partners in the Music and Sound Cultures research group , we created a digital compendium of regional heritage music for computational analysis using a collections-as-data approach. We also capture and preserve sound culture materials about the Arab Mashriq, accessible via our preservation repository. This collection continues to grow, expanding our collection of audio materials with the Andrew Eisenberg collection of East African commercial sound recordings .

The Capstone Archives

The Capstone Archives is an accumulating collection of NYUAD Capstone senior research projects, beginning with the Class of 2014, which the Archives and Special Collections department partners with the Digital Scholarship and Preservation program to make accessible as an online digital collection. A living, growing digital archive that represents a diverse sampling of the research, innovation, and creative endeavors of NYUAD undergraduate students, the online collection includes open Capstone project essays and reports. For questions about submitting your Capstone project or other related questions, contact nyuad.archive@nyu.edu for assistance. Graduate students should contact the Graduate Program Office for questions and information about Electronic Theses and Dissertations.

Arabic Collections Online

The Digital Scholarship and Preservation program is the home of the Arabic Collections Online project at NYUAD, a publicly available digital library of public domain Arabic language content. ACO provides digital access to nearly 18,000 volumes across 10,473 subjects drawn from rich Arabic collections of distinguished research libraries, including NYU Libraries, Princeton, Cornell, Columbia , American University in Cairo , American University of Beirut, United Arab Emirates National Archives, and Qatar National Library .

title: Streaming Services
text:
Streaming Services





In general, popular streaming services like Netflix, Hulu, Disney+, and Amazon Prime do not grant rights for institutional or educational use. The Library cannot provide access to these services for classroom use.

Physical Formats

The Library provides access to a collection of physical formats (DVD, Blu Ray) of films that support the curriculum. Faculty and instructors may schedule a loan to ensure the physical format is available for their course.

Supported Streaming Services

The Library provides access to academic streaming services such as Kanopy Streaming , Alexander Street Press, and Swank Digital Campus. These resources are supported in classrooms by the NYUAD IT Team ( nyuad.it@nyu.edu ).

Request Specific Films

If a specific film is required as course material and is not already part of the physical or electronic collections, please contact nyuad-acquisitions-group@nyu.edu as soon as possible. Depending on availability, film acquisition requests will take a minimum of two weeks or longer to fulfill.

One-time Documentary Screenings

Providers, such as Netflix , offer one-time educational screenings of documentaries. These single-use screenings must be arranged by the faculty’s department or another entity on campus because the Library’s policy is to direct funds towards the development of the permanent collection.

title: Name Authority Records (NAR) and NACO Services
breadcrumbs: Name Authority Records (NAR) and NACO Services
text:
Name Authority Records (NAR) and NACO Services






What is a Name Authority Record (NAR)?

A Name Authority Record (NAR) is a standardized library record that uniquely identifies an individual, organization, or entity associated with scholarly work. It ensures that all publications by the same author are correctly attributed — even when names appear in different forms (e.g., with initials, name changes, or transliteration variations).

For example, a NAR connects so that they are recognized as one person in library systems:

- J. A. Smith
- John A. Smith
- Smith, John Andrew







What is NACO?

The Name Authority Cooperative Program (NACO) is part of the Library of Congress’s Program for Cooperative Cataloging (PCC). Through NACO, trained librarians at participating institutions can:

- Create new Name Authority Records.
- Update or correct existing records.
- Contribute directly to international authority databases.
As a participant in this program, NYU Libraries can actively ensure accurate representation of its faculty and researchers in global catalogs.








Why NARs Matter for Faculty

Accurate Name Authority Records are essential for scholarly visibility and attribution.

They help ensure that:

- All of your publications are correctly grouped together , even across different databases.
- Your work is discoverable by students, researchers, and collaborators.
- Your academic profile is consistent , regardless of name variations.
- Your citations and impact are accurately tracked .
Without a properly maintained NAR, publications can be split across multiple identities — making your scholarly record incomplete or harder to find.








When Should an NAR Be Updated Through NACO?

A NAR may need to be created or updated in situations such as:

- You publish under multiple name variations (e.g., initials, full name, transliteration differences).
- You have experienced a name change .
- Your work is being confused with another author of a similar name .
- Your publications are not consistently grouped together in library catalogs.
- Additional identifying information (e.g., affiliation, field) needs to be added for clarity.
In these cases, NACO-trained librarians can revise the record to ensure accuracy and proper disambiguation.



Get Help with Your Name Authority Record

If you believe your Name Authority Record needs to be created or updated, the Library is here to help.

Please contact us at nyuad-acquisitions-group@nyu.edu , and we will:


- Review your current authority record (if one exists).
- Assess any discrepancies or ambiguities.
- Submit updates through NACO as needed.

title: NYUAD Library AI Resources
text:
NYUAD Library AI Resources


















NYUAD Library Statement on Artificial Intelligence and AI Literacy

As information professionals, we approach Generative AI as a new information tool and support a critical look at the use of AI, as we do with all information sources. We promote the use of AI that advocates and encourages human metacognition and critical thinking. Current and future learners must learn how to recognize high-quality information and understand their personal responsibility in using AI tools and AI-generated information ethically and responsibly. Information Literacy will become increasingly important as our world changes alongside AI. 1

The NYUAD Library teaches workshops covering the ethical and responsible use of Generative AI. The teaching complies with the NYU Statement on Academic Integrity . Our workshops are grounded in information literacy principles centered around the ACRL Framework for Information Literacy for Higher Education , encouraging students to understand the implications and pitfalls of using such tools by exploring:

- Critical thinking, skepticism, and questioning​
- Critical pedagogy, focusing on social justice and what inequalities it may exacerbate or create​
- Critique of the outputs and potential harms 2
We follow local guidelines concerning AI Ethics, UAE Ethics: Principles and Guidelines , and we align with the UAE National Strategy for Artificial Intelligence 2031 . We also abide by the Research Libraries Guiding Principles for Artificial Intelligence , created by the Association of Research Libraries. We encourage students, staff, and faculty to review NYU's AI and Sustainability and NYU's AI LLM FAQ page to learn more about the environmental impact of using AI tools.

All of our e-resources are licensed, and these resources may have guidelines about using their content with Generative AI tools (ex., uploading a journal article into an AI tool for synthesis). Please follow the guidelines listed on the homepage of these e-resources.

When choosing AI tools, we recommend reviewing NYU’s consideration of 3rd party tools , which emphasizes Personally Identifiable Information (PII) and Intellectual Property (IP), the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act (FERPA) and Privacy, and accessibility.

This statement was written without the use of AI.

Updated October 6, 2025

1 Adapted from The American University's Artificial Intelligence and Libraries guide.

2 Adapted from Babson College Horn Library AI Literacy guide.










Adopted from the paper " Building an AI Literacy Framework: Perspectives from Instruction Librarians and Current Information Literacy Tools ." (PDF)



NYUAD Library AI Literacy Framework

-






Competencies

- Establish a base knowledge for artificial intelligence; learn the difference between narrow and general AI.

Learning Objectives

- Recall the definitions of artificial intelligence, machine learning, and generative AI.
- Recognize the difference between narrow and general AI and how much human intervention each requires.

(Narrow AI, a type of technology, which includes generative AI, that can follow predefined tasks, and general AI, a theoretical AI technology that is self-aware and does not rely on humans to complete tasks.)


-






Competencies

- Understand the different types of AI; understand how technologies branch into subcategories

Learning Objectives

- Express how artificial intelligence includes many subcategories and how they relate to each other.
- Summarize which subtypes of AI are used in certain tools.


-






Competencies

- Undertake elective experiences; develop your own AI.

Learning Objectives

- Experiment with different available AI tools.
- Implement effective strategies for creating prompts for generative AI tools.


-






Competencies

- Analyze and critique on a micro-level.

Learning Objectives

- Appraise the quality of the output created by an AI tool and question if it is appropriate for the user’s purposes.
- Distinguish content created by humans and artificial intelligence.


-






Competencies

- Discuss issues on a macro-level; evaluate societal impact; engage in ethical considerations of AI.

Learning Objectives

- Comment on the impact that AI can have on the environment.
- Critique the bias that can be present in artificial intelligence and algorithms.


-






Competencies

- Engage in AI discourse; stay involved in the conversation.

Learning Objectives

- Plan ways to stay active in conversations about artificial intelligence.
- Collaborate with other learners to keep up to date on AI developments.






All workshops should emphasize the University of Newcastle's four topics (Intersection of IL and AI) which are:

- Criticality
- Questioning
- Making Judgements
- Seeking Evidence









The Library offers several research guides related to the effective and ethical use of AI tools:

- Citing and Acknowledging AI-Generated Text
- Evaluating Generative AI Tools for Academic Research
- Images and AI
- Generative AI and Large Language Models (LLMs)
- Machines and Society
- Media and Misinformation
In addition, AI @ NYU Abu Dhabi is a central hub for faculty and staff to learn about AI-related resources, initiatives, and updates across the University.











- What We've Learned: Confronting AI's Challenges in Libraries (November 16-17th, 2026)
- NYUAD Library AI Literacy Program (September 14th-October 9th)
- NYUAD Library Workshops on AI Tools
- NYU Shanghai Library Workshops (login required)
- NYU New York Libraries Workshops









Contact Us

Academic Librarian for Engineering, AI Initiatives, and Reference Services Coordinator

Email: am6087@nyu.edu





Follow Us

title: Library Instruction and Research Expertise
text:
Library Instruction and Research Expertise






Research Librarians

Research librarians at NYUAD combine subject expertise with teaching, supporting students in developing information literacy skills and collaborating with faculty across disciplines.

Information Literacy and Library Instruction

Information literacy is the ability to recognize when information is needed and to locate, evaluate, and use it effectively. Beyond supporting academic success, information literacy fosters independent, lifelong critical thinkers prepared to navigate information in all areas of their lives.

At NYUAD, research librarians draw on the ACRL Framework for Information Literacy in Higher Education to guide their teaching. This framework emphasizes effective information discovery while also examining the systems that shape knowledge and the ethical responsibilities of information use.

Librarians bring these concepts into the classroom through course-integrated instruction sessions. Scheduled on request and tailored to assignments, these sessions connect information literacy directly to student learning. Working in close collaboration with faculty, librarians design sessions that introduce the resources and research skills students require for their courses and assignments.

Sessions may include, but are not limited to:

- Developing search strategies using catalogs, databases, and discovery tools

- Comparing scholarly, popular, and other types of information to understand how knowledge is created in different forms

- Evaluating credibility across sources, including online information, and understanding the peer review process

- Working with primary and secondary sources across disciplines

- Tracing scholarship through citations and influential works to engage with scholarly conversations

- Examining the ethical and economic dimensions of information use, including citation, attribution, and avoiding plagiarism

- Understanding copyright, open access, and publishing models, and how they affect access to scholarship

- Approaching research as an iterative process of questioning, evidence-gathering, and reflection

- Exploring AI and algorithmic literacy to understand how technologies shape access to information and knowledge creation

To schedule a session, contact your Research Librarian or email nyuad.library@nyu.edu








First-Year Writing Seminar (FYWS) and the Library













The First-Year Writing Seminar (FYWS) is a cornerstone of the NYUAD experience, introducing undergraduate students to the reading, writing, and critical-thinking skills essential to a liberal arts education.

Research librarians are embedded in every seminar, ensuring that students build a strong foundation in information literacy alongside their writing and communication skills.

All students enroll in FYWS during one of their first two semesters, ensuring that the Library becomes an early and integral part of their academic journey. Through this partnership, students develop research methods that support them across disciplines.

As part of this commitment, the Librarian for Instruction, First-Year Experience, and Student Success coordinates FYWS instruction, collaborates with faculty, and develops programs that support research, foster belonging, and strengthen the first-year learning experience.









Rebecca Hastie

Support Beyond the Classroom

The Library extends support through:

- One-on-one research consultations

- Guidance for Capstone and other advanced research projects

- Customized instruction incorporating Archives and Special Collections

- Discipline-specific resources and research guides

- Assistance for using library collections, resources, and services








Workshops and Events

The Library regularly hosts open workshops and events on research, digital tools, and academic skills. These sessions are available to all students, faculty, and staff.

title: Student Research Help
text:
Student Research Help






Connect with NYUAD librarians with research expertise in your field of study

Whether you’re starting your first-year writing project or tackling your Capstone, research librarians are here to support you at every stage of your NYUAD journey.

Get to know the librarian in your subject area as they’ll support you to find, evaluate, and use information effectively across your fields of study.














One-on-One Research Support

Research librarians can help you to:

- Approach research as a process of exploring ideas, identifying questions, and discovering information through strategic searching

- Discover and evaluate different kinds of sources, including scholarly, popular, professional, primary, and secondary

- Understand how ideas grow as researchers build on each other’s work, analyze the arguments in your sources, and learn how to contribute your own voice to the discussion

- Use information ethically by citing sources, giving credit, and avoiding plagiarism

- Recognize how generative AI and algorithms shape the information you find online









Find a Research Librarian in Your Subject Area













Archives and Special Collections

Archives and Special Collections are open to all NYUAD students. The collection provides access to rare and unique primary source materials that explore the social, cultural, and historical contexts of the UAE, the Gulf, and the surrounding region.

Working with primary source materials such as rare books, posters, letters, diaries, and maps helps you connect directly with the people and events of the past. These sources strengthen research skills by encouraging you to question, interpret, and analyze evidence and the knowledge collected across different time periods in history. Archivists in the department are resources for students who have questions about archival management, public history, heritage and oral history methods.

Archives and Special Collections is also home to the undergraduate Capstone Archives , which is managed as part of the NYUAD University Archives .

Find details about the collections, how to plan your visit, and what to expect on the Archives and Special Collections webpage .








Support for Capstone Projects

NYUAD research librarians provide subject-specific support at every stage of your Capstone project, from advanced research strategies to using specialized resources and tools.

Research librarians can help you:

- Develop subject-specific research skills and refining your literature review

- Use citation management software including Zotero , RefWorks , and EndNote

- Identify and access data sets, industry standards, and other specialized materials

- Request sources not held by the libraries at NYU Abu Dhabi or NYU New York

- Access rolling lockers for seniors to store Capstone research materials

Explore the Capstone Archives to see completed NYUAD Capstone projects, and reach out to the Data Services Team at Bobst Library in New York for help at any stage of the research data lifecycle.

title: Borrow and Request
text:
Borrow and Request





The NYU Abu Dhabi Library provides resources and technologies needed for research and teaching, and an extensive range of physical and electronic resources. The Library is fully connected to NYU Libraries' e-resources in New York, providing seamless access for our global community.








Our Collection

Our growing collection includes:














- over 91,000 books
- over 7,400 DVDs
- over 416,000 e-journals












- over 1,400 databases
- nearly 5 million ebooks



















The print collection is designed to support the undergraduate curriculum taught at NYUAD and is primarily in English. However, works in major research languages, including languages taught at NYUAD, are also represented.

Borrowing

To borrow materials from the NYUAD Library, users may search our catalog , locate the item on the shelves, and bring it to the library circulation desk near the entrance of the library. The borrower must show their NYU ID card in order to borrow. See our loan periods in the chart below.

If the NYUAD Library does not have an item, see instructions for requesting from other libraries .

Other libraries interested in borrowing material from NYUAD Library via interlibrary loan should contact us .










Interlibrary Loan



























Suggest an Item for the Collection

Can't find what you're looking for? Students and faculty may nominate books, journals, e-resources, audio, and video recordings to be acquired by the library.










Connection to NYU Libraries

The NYUAD Library is closely connected to NYU Libraries. Visit their website for more information and resources.








Library E-Resources

Learn how to connect to the Library's E-Resources.

Library Policies

See the Library's policies on borrowing, conduct, food, and study rooms.

title: Course Reserves
text:
Course Reserves






Faculty and Instructors

Course reserves ensure that essential readings and resources are readily accessible to students throughout the semester. Faculty and instructors may request that materials be placed on course reserve for any course that's currently being taught. Course reserve requests can be submitted at any time. While not required, including a course syllabus can help library staff process requests more efficiently and ensure accurate placement of materials.

Library items can be pulled from the stacks by circulation staff. Any personal books for reserve should be brought to the library’s circulation desk by the faculty and instructors.

Physical items (library books/textbooks/personal books, DVDs, etc.) may be placed on reserve, depending on availability.

Please allow up to two days for processing, and kindly plan ahead to ensure the materials are ready when your students need to use them.

How to place items on Course Reserve

To place an item on course reserve, contact the Access Services Department by emailing: lib-nyuad-circ@nyu.edu and include the following information in your email:

- Faculty/Instructor Name
- Faculty/Instructor Email
- Course Name
- Course Number
- Semester
- Material Type (e.g., book, DVD, personal copy)
- Loan Schedule: choose one
- Two-hour loan
- Three-hour loan
- Five-hour loan

A confirmation email will be sent to you once the request has been completely processed.

For any further clarifications, please email: lib-nyuad-circ@nyu.edu OR visit the Library Information Desk.








Students

Course Reserves Access

Students can visit the Library Information Desk to request course reserves by providing staff with the name of the course, the instructor's name, or the title of the book. Items will have a loan period of two, three, or five hours.

Email : nyuad.library@nyu.edu

Phone : +971-2-628-5544

Ask questions nearly 24/7 using the live chat service at the bottom of the website or visit our chat page .

Find specific staff members on the Library Team page .

title: Request from Other Libraries
text:
Request from Other Libraries






















Faculty, researchers, and staff may request books or items from the collections in NYU New York, or other university libraries.

-





Faculty and staff can request whole items be held at the NYUAD Library Information Desk.

Available items requested for hold at the library are typically available within 1-2 business days.

- Log in to the Library Catalog for personalized request and delivery options.
- Search for the item you need in the Catalog. Click the title of your desired item.
- This screen will inform you of your access options, including full-text online, if available.
- Click Request or More Info .
- On the next screen, select NYU Abu Dhabi Library . Click Submit .


-





You can request whole items be shipped to Abu Dhabi from New York, or request article/chapter scans from items owned by Bobst or Courant libraries. Whole items typically arrive within seven days of the request; article/chapter scans of available items typically arrive within 24 hours.

- Log in to the Library Catalog for personalized request and delivery options.
- Search for the item you need in the Library Catalog. Click the title of your desired item.
- This screen will inform you of your access options, including full-text online, if available.
- Click GET IT FROM OTHER NYU LIBRARIES (FASTER) for a chapter or article scan, or to have the entire item sent to Abu Dhabi.
- On the next screen, select NYU Abu Dhabi Library as the Pickup/Delivery location and complete the relevant fields if you are requesting an article or chapter scan. Click Submit .
Requests are available for circulating items from Bobst, Bobst Offsite, and Courant General Collections.

Items not available for shipment to Abu Dhabi:

- Items on reserve
- Reference items
- Non-circulating items
- Consortium items (New School, Cooper Union, New-York Historical Society, Brooklyn Historical Society Othmer Library, Villa La Pietra Library)
You may instead prefer to recommend a purchase by our library or request the item from a non-NYU library through the Interlibrary Loan (ILL) .



-






- Please fill out this Inter-Library Loan Form .
- You will receive an email confirmation of your booking within two New York business days. If you do not receive this confirmation, contact the NYUAD Access Services Department at lib-nyuad-circ@nyu.edu .
- Abu Dhabi faculty will be granted a seven-day loan period.


-






- Please fill out this Inter-Library Loan Form .
- You will receive an email confirmation of your booking within two New York business days. If you do not receive this confirmation, contact the NYUAD Access Services Department at lib-nyuad-circ@nyu.edu .
- Abu Dhabi faculty will be granted a seven-day loan period.


-






- Interlibrary Loan (ILL) is a service by which the library requests materials from other libraries on your behalf.
- There is no charge for this service, although due to the high cost of delivery, judicious use is encouraged.
- Log in to the Interlibrary Loan Request System and select the appropriate form.
- Requests may be placed for the following:

-A maximum of five (5) articles from any one journal title (as per copyright restrictions)

-Books (be sure check the appropriate box for Abu Dhabi pickup)

-Book chapters (limited to one chapter or about 10 percent of the page count per copyright)

-Dissertations and theses

-Microforms (note that the NYUAD Library does not have a microform reader)

-Photocopies of journal/newspaper articles
- Non-print materials, such as videos, sound recordings, and computer files, can be requested but are often difficult to obtain.
- Items owned by NYU that are checked out.
- Items in NYU's full-text e-journal collection are not available via ILL.
- Requests take anywhere from one to four weeks, depending upon location and availability. Most interlibrary loan requests for journal articles or book chapters take four days or less from the time you submit a request until you have the item in hand. Requests for whole items (e.g., books, dissertations, etc.) typically take ten days.
- See complete NYU ILL policies and information .


-






- Books from the NYUAD Library will be due back at the end of the semester and are eligible for renewal.
- DVDs from the NYUAD Library are due back in one week, and are eligible for renewal one time . If additional renewals are needed for research or teaching, please contact the library .
- Past issues of periodicals are due back in one week. Renewals are not possible. Current issues must stay in the library.
- CDs are due back in one week. Renewals are not possible.
- Items borrowed from the NYU Division of Libraries are loaned to users based on the owning location's local policies. All items are subject to recall. For complete loan policies of NYU Bobst Library, please visit our Library Policies section .
- Renewals of NYU library materials can be made by accessing your " My Library Account " in the catalog.
- Materials on loan from non-NYU libraries are generally loaned for four weeks.

text:
Suggest an Item for the Collection











NYUAD students and faculty are invited to nominate books, journals, e-resources, audio, and videos to be acquired in accordance with the Library's collection development strategy . You may contact your divisional research librarian or nyuad-acquisitions-group@nyu.edu with your suggestions.

Most non-rush items typically arrive on campus within 60 days, so planning ahead is strongly advised.

If you have an urgent research or teaching need, please note that rush-ordered print or physical items require a minimum of two weeks to arrive shelf-ready. However, delivery times ultimately depend on vendor shipping schedules and cannot be guaranteed.

In general, electronic resources will need to match the library's subscription model and access configuration. Acquiring e-resources can be a lengthy process depending on several factors.

While the library appreciates all suggestions, we purchase items based upon their academic quality, relevance to NYUAD programs, and budgetary prudence.

title: Collection Development Strategy
text:
Collection Development Strategy





Last updated: February 26, 2026








Objectives













The purpose of this Collection Development Strategy is to ensure that the Library’s resources directly support the University’s academic programs and research needs.

The policies, standards, and resources of the NYU Abu Dhabi Library are aligned with the guidelines of the Association of College & Research Libraries (ACRL), the largest division of the American Library Association (ALA), as well as the global standards established by the Online Computer Library Center (OCLC) and the International Federation of Library Associations and Institutions (IFLA).









Library Policies








-





The Library welcomes purchase requests from students, faculty, and staff in support of the University’s mission. While all suggestions are considered, materials are selected based on academic quality, relevance to NYUAD programs, and budgetary considerations.

Rush-ordered print books and other physical materials typically require a minimum of two weeks to arrive shelf-ready. Delivery times depend on vendor shipping schedules and, therefore, cannot be guaranteed. Non-rush orders may take up to sixty days to arrive shelf-ready.

New subscription databases may be acquired in partnership with NYU colleagues in New York. Subscriptions typically involve a trial period, during which user feedback is collected, followed by a contractual agreement. This process generally requires several months.

To suggest a purchase, please contact your divisional Research Librarian or email nyuad-acquisitions-group@nyu.edu



-





The Library encourages faculty to submit their syllabi to syllabi-to-library-group@nyu.edu for review. Recommended readings will be purchased for the main collection.



-





To conserve space and ensure the efficient use of resources, the Library does not acquire duplicate print materials for the collection, except in special circumstances. Whenever possible, the Library gives preference to e-books with unlimited user access.



-





The Library acquires non-commercial films in streaming or physical formats, provided they meet the licensing requirements of the Avery Fisher Center for Music and Media .



-





The Library does not acquire textbooks, as their publishing and usage models differ fundamentally from those of research library collections.

All required course textbooks must be reported to the NYUAD Bookstore at nyuad.bookstore@nyu.edu .

Required course readings (not textbooks) may be provided through e-books with unlimited user licenses. However, not all e-books in the Library’s collection are licensed for unlimited simultaneous users, and timely access for all students cannot be guaranteed. Please contact the Library at nyuad.library@nyu.edu with any questions regarding specific e-book licenses.



-





The Library does not collect test preparation or similar materials, as they quickly become obsolete and lose instructional value. Students seeking test preparation or career assistance are encouraged to contact the Career Development Center .



-





The Library accepts donations under the following conditions:

- The materials are not duplicated in the main collection.
- The materials are consistent with the Library’s Collection Development Strategy.
- The materials are in good physical condition and do not contain extensive highlighting or underlining.
Please send a list of titles to nyuad-acquisitions-group@nyu.edu for review. All titles will be evaluated in accordance with the Library’s Collection Development Strategy.

The Library does not accept unsolicited donations delivered via dropbox or mail.



-





Exceptions to this policy may be granted on a case-by-case basis when necessary to support the University’s mission.

title: About the Library
text:
About the Library





Service to faculty, students, and scholars is the primary mission of the NYU Abu Dhabi Library. We provide the resources necessary for research and teaching, and offer assistance in their use. Members of the NYU community have access to our extensive range of physical and electronic resources, including:














- over 91,000 physical books
- over 7.400 DVDs
- over 416,000 e-journals
- over 1,400 databases
- nearly 5 million ebooks



















The NYUAD Library is fully connected to the electronic resources of NYU Libraries in New York, providing seamless access for our global community. These e-resources are accessible within the library and remotely. Eligible borrowers may request print resources from NYU Bobst Library or other libraries worldwide via Interlibrary Loan . NYUAD students and faculty are invited to nominate books, journals, e-resources, audio, and videos to be acquired in accordance with the Library's collection development strategy .

Comfortable reading areas and small and large group study rooms create a productive atmosphere for research. The dedicated Reading Room on the Mezzanine level provides plenty of space for students to focus on their research in a relaxed environment. Research assistance is available via phone, email, chat, and in-person at our Research Help Desk. By appointment, librarians are available to meet individually with students and faculty to help them with their research needs.

title: Library Policies
text:
Library Policies

Policies and Guidelines

-






- The individual that checks out any item is responsible for it and any accessories while they are checked out and until they are appropriately returned. A due date will be given at the time of checkout based on the type of item being checked out and/or for the checkout purpose.
- The item and all accessories must be returned by the due date to the NYUAD Library.
- The item must be returned in the same condition in which it was received at the time of checkout. Normal wear and tear is acceptable.
- Borrowers remain solely responsible for the item(s) and any accessories throughout the checkout period. If items are lost or damaged, the borrower will be asked to pay for the item(s).
- Borrowers returning items past their due date, failing to return an item in the same condition as when it was checked out, or failing to return an item altogether will be subject to disciplinary procedure. This includes, but is not limited to, suspension of the individual's borrowing privileges from the NYUAD Library. The library has loan rules that govern when and for how long users are blocked for returning materials overdue.
- Depending on the item and its loan period, items that are excessively overdue will be considered lost and the borrower will be billed for replacement. If items are declared lost and subsequently returned, lost charges will be waived but late charges, if any, remain.
- Borrowers owing more than AED 20 (USD 5.45) will be blocked from borrowing from the NYUAD Library.
- Borrowers owing more than AED 100 (USD 27.34) will be blocked from Albert and from borrowing from the NYUAD Library.
- The maximum late charge is AED 180 (USD 49.01) per item.
- If you have a question about your fine, please contact lib-nyuad-circ@nyu.edu .

- If you need to pay a fine, please contact nyuad-library-admin@nyu.edu .


-






- NYU Libraries support the educational goals of New York University Abu Dhabi (NYUAD) by providing access to all forms of information to support research, study, teaching, and the general pursuit of knowledge. In order to be successful in this mission, the Library and its community of users observe a relationship of reciprocal rights and responsibilities. While most users conduct themselves in a responsible manner, in the interest of protecting the rights of all Library users, it is necessary to define what constitutes infringements on the rights of others.
- The NYU Libraries Conduct Code affirms a commitment to protecting an environment conducive to intellectual pursuits. Such an environment is characterized by respect for the rights of others, respect for the Library's resources, and respect for appropriate conduct in a public forum. The Code ensures that users of NYUAD Library find themselves in an environment that will enable them to achieve their educational objectives.
- The Code also acknowledges that the Library fulfils an important educational function in the University. Educational settings, unlike other public forums, require special considerations in defining violations, investigating allegations of violations, and imposing disciplinary action. This document affirms our commitment to addressing and resolving charges of misconduct in a speedy manner, while upholding the rights of due process.
Read the complete Library Code of Conduct (PDF).



-






- The consumption of food and drinks, within reason, is permitted in the Library unless otherwise indicated. Snack food, sandwiches, and drinks in closed containers are permitted in all areas of the Library, except for Archives and Special Collections.
- Please be considerate of others and avoid consuming food items that create messes, smells, and/or noise.
- Kindly recycle and dispose of the trash as appropriate.
- Take responsibility for cleaning spills, food crumbs, etc., OR report spills to any Library staff member.
- Food ordered for delivery to the Library should be picked up outside of the Library.
- No food or drink is permitted near the Library’s scanning stations, microfilm machine, printers, or in Archives and Special Collections.
- Unattended food and/or drink openly displayed in public areas may be confiscated and discarded.
- Users violating this policy may be asked to remove the food and/or drink from the area.


-





Students can choose from a variety of room types:

Small study rooms

- Rooms # 430-441, up to two persons
- No reservations needed, available on a first-come, first-served basis.
- Individuals occupying small study rooms cannot be asked to vacate for groups of two students.

Large study rooms

- Rooms # 414- 428 up to four persons
- Rooms # 401-406 up to six persons
- Rooms # 409 and 410 up to 10 persons
- No reservations needed, available on a first-come, first-served basis.
- Individuals occupying any large study room can be asked to vacate for groups of two or more students.
Please note that selected study rooms are reserved by the Writing Center and Academic Resource Center for academic purposes, details of which are clearly identified on the room booking system. Students are welcome to use these rooms when not reserved by the Writing Center or Academic Resource Center.

The Library reserves the right to remove student personal belongings that are left unattended in individual or group study rooms for more than 20 minutes. All belongings will be transferred to Campus Safety Officers for safekeeping.

Camping in the rooms is not permitted. For purposes of this policy, "camping" includes:

- Sleeping in the room with or without one’s belongings

- Excessive use of the room that interferes with its usage for other students, faculty, or staff

- Storing personal belongings or other similar behavior that amounts to reserving the room

- Whether a given use constitutes “camping” will be determined based on the facts and circumstances of specific situations.
Doors to the rooms should be kept closed when in use. Sound travels, even with the door closed. Please keep the volume at a reasonable level.

Students requiring quiet study space should proceed to the Reading Room. No reservations needed, available on a first-come, first-served basis.

Drinks in covered containers and small snacks are permitted in group study rooms. (Please refer to the Library’s Food Policy.)



Collection Development Strategy

title: Library Student Advisory Committee
text:
Library Student Advisory Committee





The NYUAD Library Student Advisory Committee provides a venue for the Library and student body to work together on a shared vision for our programs, collections, services, and spaces. The committee is composed of two rotating Librarians and a small group of students from across divisions that are elected by their peers.

Recent initiatives include:

- Implementing search capabilities for our equipment holdings in our Library catalog
- Engaging with students on usability studies of both Library spaces and digital interfaces
- Helping with advertising new Library classes and programs
- Introducing a fine structure for late equipment returns based on feedback from the student body
- Modifying loan policies and periods based on student feedback

title: Library Study Spaces
text:
Library Study Spaces






Library Main Floor

In addition to housing the Library’s print collection, the main level of the Library provides several different areas to meet academic needs.














Computers

Numerous Mac and PC machines with a wide array of hardware and software are available for use. Computers are available on a first-come-first-serve basis. Numerous printer/scanner/copier machines are also located throughout both floors of the Library.





















Meeting Rooms

The Library has several small and large group meeting rooms that are available for reservation through the EMS Space Reservation System . Please note that the booking of all Library spaces is limited to NYUAD staff and faculty. More information on booking spaces across campus can be found in the student portal and faculty/staff intranet .

Leisure Reading

Take a break from your academic reading! Our Leisure Reading collection of popular fiction and nonfiction titles are available for checkout for a two-week period. We also welcome suggestions for the Leisure Reading collection in our suggestion box located on the shelves.

Seating Areas

Multiple soft-seating areas where students relax and take a break from academics.


























































Library Mezzanine Floor

Reading Room

Looking for a quiet space to study? The dedicated Reading Room upstairs on the Mezzanine level provides plenty of space for students to focus on their research in a relaxed and quiet environment. The Library’s print periodicals collection is also found here.

Group Study Rooms

The Library has several Group Study Rooms available on a first-come, first-serve basis for student use only. These range in size from two- to ten-person rooms, some with AV systems to support group presentations.














Rolling Lockers for Senior Students

Rolling lockers, located on the Mezzanine Level, are available for senior students to check out. Senior study rolling lockers provide you a personal space so ongoing work may be left in the Library.

To apply for a rolling locker, please email lib-nyuad-circ@nyu.edu . You will be notified within a week as to which rolling locker you have been assigned.









Rolling lockers are available for senior students.








-






- Rolling lockers are assigned on a first come, first served basis. If more seniors request rolling lockers than there is availability, we will develop a waiting list and notify students as space becomes available.
- Rolling locker reservations will be assigned on a per-semester basis.
- Any Library materials left in the Rolling Locker will need to be checked out and will be checked regularly by authorized Library staff to ensure adherence to policy.
- NYUAD Library assumes no responsibility for loss or theft of personal items left in the rolling locker.
- Personal decorations on the rolling locker are not allowed, as rolling lockers are part of the Library furniture and décor.

title: Services for People of Determination
text:
Services for People of Determination





The NYUAD Library and the Student Persistence and Wellbeing departments partner together with the Moses Center in New York to provide a range of services for people of determination.

- Information on Student Persistence and Accessibility at NYUAD

- Information from the Moses Center for Student Accessibility

- Information on Assistive Technology

Within the Library, we can provide:

- priority use computer terminals equipped with readers and supporting applications

- conversion of course materials to accessible formats

- guidance for choosing citation software with accessibility features

- assistance with research and using library resources with accessibility features

- accessible spaces for studying, including elevators for Mezzanine level access.

- Alternative formats of research materials available through the Accessibility Team in New York

- A Guide to support academic accommodations and accessibility at NYU Libraries.

Sensory Room (coming soon)

Located on the fourth floor of the Library, the Sensory Room provides students with an academic environment that helps them center their sensory needs to be more academically successful. This includes sensory-seeking and sensory-avoidance features such as adjustable individual lighting, sound-dampening panels, adjustable privacy panels, and sensory manipulatives like noise-canceling headphones and fidget devices.

Access to the Sensory Space is granted to those with academic accommodations that would benefit from using the space. Please contact the Student Persistence and Accessibility (SPA) team to request accommodations at nyuad.spa@nyu.edu.



Contact Us

Student Persistence and Accessibility (SPA), NYUAD Liaison for Moses Center for Accessibility and Inclusive Culture

nyuad.spa@nyu.edu

Services for People of Determination





The NYUAD Library and the Student Persistence and Wellbeing departments partner together with the Moses Center in New York to provide a range of services for people of determination.

- Information on Student Persistence and Accessibility at NYUAD

- Information from the Moses Center for Student Accessibility

- Information on Assistive Technology

Within the Library, we can provide:

- priority use computer terminals equipped with readers and supporting applications

- conversion of course materials to accessible formats

- guidance for choosing citation software with accessibility features

- assistance with research and using library resources with accessibility features

- accessible spaces for studying, including elevators for Mezzanine level access.

- Alternative formats of research materials available through the Accessibility Team in New York

- A Guide to support academic accommodations and accessibility at NYU Libraries.

sections.title: Sensory Room (coming soon)
sections.text:
Located on the fourth floor of the Library, the Sensory Room provides students with an academic environment that helps them center their sensory needs to be more academically successful. This includes sensory-seeking and sensory-avoidance features such as adjustable individual lighting, sound-dampening panels, adjustable privacy panels, and sensory manipulatives like noise-canceling headphones and fidget devices.

Access to the Sensory Space is granted to those with academic accommodations that would benefit from using the space. Please contact the Student Persistence and Accessibility (SPA) team to request accommodations at nyuad.spa@nyu.edu.

title: Visitors
text:
Visitors





The NYU Abu Dhabi Library is primarily intended for use by current faculty, students, and staff. However, we do welcome all NYU alumni and offer special access to high school students in Abu Dhabi, and allow other guests via our Community Access Program below.



















As part of NYU Abu Dhabi’s mission to support the research and scholarship needs of the broader community, the NYUAD Library welcomes individuals with research needs to access its collections via the Community Access Program.

Members of the community are granted in-person access to the library to conduct research, study, and read using our collections, through an online application process.










Apply







View our Archives and Special Collections
















High School Programs







The NYUAD Library welcomes visits from high schools in Abu Dhabi. A scheduled visit to the NYUAD Library gives students the unique opportunity to utilize the library's rich collection of print and electronic resources.

The library encourages student groups working on advanced-level research projects, such as the IB Extended Essay, to attend a personalized library workshop followed by hands on research time.

NYUAD librarians collaborate with teachers and school administrators to create active and engaging library workshops. Library instruction efforts focus on teaching the basics of academic research such as, locating sources, identifying scholarly sources, and citation management.








Preparing Your Students

A visit to the NYUAD Library is most successful when students are doing research for a real assignment. Working towards a common research goal helps students stay motivated and make the most of their library experience. NYUAD librarians are happy to tailor the session to best meet the individual needs of your students and their assignment.








Planning Your Visit

In order to best meet your needs and maximize your experience, we encourage all high school groups to follow the steps below when planning their trip:

- Please email the NYUAD Library three weeks in advance of your scheduled visit. All requests can be sent via email to nyuad.library@nyu.edu .
- Share class learning objectives and assignment descriptions with NYUAD librarians in order to design engaging and thought-provoking library workshops that meet your students needs. All workshops should last no more than 2.5 hours.
- Ensure every ten students are accompanied by one school official such as a teacher, librarian, or administrator. No more than 40 students can attend one scheduled session.










Alumni

All alumni are given access to the NYUAD Library and the NYU Alumni eLibrary . Show your Alumni ID and register at the Information Desk for access to our library services. Alumni do not have borrowing privileges. Read more on the NYUAD Alumni page .














Contact the Library

NYUAD librarians have specific subject expertise to help you with your research. Find your research librarian .

Hours : Check today's opening hours before visiting.

Email : nyuad.library@nyu.edu

Phone : +971-2-628-5544

Ask questions nearly 24/7 using the live chat service at the bottom of the website or visit our chat page .

Find specific staff members on the Library Team page .

title: Community Access Program
text:
Community Access Program






Community Access to the NYUAD Library

As part of NYU Abu Dhabi’s mission to support the research and scholarship needs of the broader community, the NYUAD Library welcomes individuals with research needs to access its collections via the Community Access Program (CAP).

Members of the community are granted in-person access to the library to conduct research, study, and read using our collections, through an online application process, below. Community Access is granted on an annual basis.

To ensure the NYUAD Library contains the material most suitable to patrons’ work, applicants should include their area of research and, where possible, the specific resources they need. The available resources can be found by searching the library catalog .

Due to university policy regarding minors on campus, we can only accommodate visitors aged 18 and above through our Community Access Program. If you are seeking to use the NYUAD Library for research related to your IB Extended Essay or other secondary school projects, please contact your IB coordinator or school librarian to see if a class visit is planned. The NYUAD Library often hosts high school visits for students working on their extended essays. Alternatively, a guardian may complete the CAP application form below and accompany you during your visit.



Questions?

Questions about the Community Access Program should be directed to

nyuad.library.communityaccessprogram @nyu.edu .




Access to Archives and Special Collections

Community members who need to conduct research using primary source materials are also encouraged to visit the university’s Archives and Special Collections , which is the University's repository for rare books and archival materials, specialized subject collections, manuscripts, photographs, and map collections.


How to Access Archives and Special Collections

Submit questions and requests directly to Archives and Special Collections at nyuad-asc-group@nyu.edu . The Collection is open for in-person services by appointment only, and appointments should be made at least 48 business hours in advance.







Community Access Program Application Form








Please complete the registration form below.

Upload a Copy of Your Government-issued ID (e.g., Emirates ID, passport)

Please note that photos should be in a single file and should follow this file name structure "Last name_First name" (e.g., Smith_Jill.pdf) .





Agreement




Terms and Conditions *


Members of the community are granted in-person access to the library to conduct personal scholarly research of our collections. Use of our collections for corporate research, i.e, research on behalf of a business, organization, or employer, is not permitted.

Community Access to the library is granted on an annual basis. NYUAD Library will make every reasonable effort to inform Community Access Program (CAP) members of any updates, changes, or restrictions affecting availability

These terms and conditions are not exhaustive and are subject to additional applicable library policies and guidelines:



- I agree to act as a respectful and courteous member of the academic community while engaged in library research and in all interactions with faculty, staff, and students of NYUAD. 

- I understand that access to all library resources and assets is governed by license agreements, copyright laws, and policies established by the library. 

- I acknowledge that priority and immediate access to library resources are reserved for NYUAD students, faculty, and authorized affiliates, and I agree to give priority to them if my use limits their access. 

- A valid Community Access Program (CAP) access pass must be presented at each visit to the Library’s Public Safety desk, and members are required to sign the visitor logbook each time they visit. 

- The access pass must be presented to the Information Desk staff when requesting Wifi or Library network access for the week. 

- Borrowing privileges and offsite electronic access are not included in the Community Access Program. 

- Access to the library may be limited to certain hours or days of the week as established by the Library’s Senior Director. Users are expected to bring and use their own personal devices, and no equipment other than a laptop is permitted inside the Library. For those unable to do so, we have clearly marked Quick Access Kiosks (Mac and Dell) available for short-term use of up to 30 minutes. 

- Approved CAP members must remain within the designated main collection area (ground floor) during their visit. Access to the upstairs Group Study Rooms and the Quiet Study Room is not permitted, as these spaces are reserved exclusively for NYUAD community members. 

- CAP members are also prohibited from entering staff offices, departmental areas, and all reservable spaces within the Library. These areas are restricted to authorized NYUAD community members only. 

- Printing privileges are not available; however, the Information Desk staff can assist with printing a limited number of pages as a courtesy. 

- Food and Drink Policy: Snacks and drinks in covered containers are permitted. Meals or hot food are not permitted. 

- Family members, friends, or personal guests of CAP members are not permitted into the Library. Non-members must apply separately to the Community Access Program (CAP) and receive approval before entry.

text:
NYUAD Students: Working for the Library





The NYUAD Library employs currently enrolled and registered NYUAD students on an hourly basis — through the Student Assistantship program — in positions that are both challenging and responsible. We offer a supportive working environment; opportunities to interact with members of NYUAD community, public, and Library staff; varied duties and valuable work experience allowing students to learn more about the Library while gaining a hands-on experience with the operations of academic libraries.

Our student assistants report that, through their work in the Library, they learn about new resources and services, acquire new skills and proficiency with new technologies that can be transferred to their academic endeavors and future roles.

Benefits of working in the Library:

- No experience required
- Flexible hours scheduled around your classes
- Gain experience to begin building your resume
- Learn successful researching tips













Student Assistant Positions

Our needs for these positions change and there may not always be an opportunity to apply for one of these. We encourage you to get in touch with us at nyuad.library@nyu.edu with your queries about Library employment.

Recent Student Assistant positions include:

- Reference and Research Assistants
- Center for Digital Scholarship Assistants
- Access Service Assistants
- Archives and Special Collection Assistants








More Information

Get details on the Student Assistantship Program (NetID and password required).













Current Open Positions

No Student Assistant positions available at this time. Please check back for openings.

TONIGHT | The Composer's Profession: Creation, Performance, Copyright & Artificial Intelligence

Wednesday, October 14, 2026 | 8 PM | C3-006
A talk by Richard Dubugnon
How can musical plagiarism be assessed when the comparison of works reaches its limits? In this talk, composer and court-appointed expert Richard Dubugnon explores how expert analysis can usefully be extended to examine the creative process itself. This approach, which has become particularly relevant in the age of digital tools and artificial intelligence, provides the court with additional insight into the plausibility of claimed authorship. Through audio examples and a case drawn from his expert practice, Dubugnon considers the methods and limits of musical comparison and the value of examining sources and creative processes.

The third edition of the Dakar Translation Symposium (DTS) will take place at NYU Abu Dhabi under the theme Africa and Her Hospitality . Security Alert: Beware of Phishing That Uses Fear and Urgency

Alarming emails about harassment complaints, legal matters, or disciplinary actions can create pressure to respond immediately. Scammers exploit this reaction to encourage clicks on malicious links, the opening of unsafe attachments, or the disclosure of sensitive information.
Pause, verify, and report:

- Recognize the pressure. Treat unexpected messages that use fear, urgency, or threats to demand action with caution.
- Look beyond the sender’s address. Even an internal or .edu address can be compromised. “Undisclosed recipients” or an unusual recipient list can be warning signs, but do not prove a message is fraudulent.
- Verify before clicking. Avoid links and attachments in suspicious messages, especially those claiming to contain confidential complaints or incident details.
- Confirm through a trusted channel. Contact the relevant office using contact details from the official directory and not those provided in the suspicious email.
- Report suspicious emails. Use the Report Phishing option. If a suspicious link has already been clicked or sensitive information disclosed, contact IT promptly. For assistance, contact NYU Abu Dhabi IT:
Call: +971 2 628 8888
Email: nyuad.it@nyu.edu

MRI Study Here on Campus!

NYUAD’s Center for Brain and Health invites you to participate in a MRI study here on campus. The institute’s mission is to gain a better understanding of conditions prevalent in the region.
What will you do?
The study will take approximately 2.5 hours. We will collect demographic data, behavioral and visual data, brain scans in the MRI scanner, a saliva sample for whole-genome sequencing, and an OCT scan. You will be compensated up to 150 AED in vouchers.
Are you eligible?
You can participate if you are above 18 years of age, do not have a history of neurological conditions, are not pregnant at the time of the study, and do not have non-removable metal. You can only participate once.
If you are interested please email one of the researchers below:

The Principal Investigator of this study is Dr. Bas Rokers.

TONIGHT | The Composer's Profession: Creation, Performance, Copyright & Artificial Intelligence

Wednesday, October 14, 2026 | 8 PM | C3-006
A talk by Richard Dubugnon
How can musical plagiarism be assessed when the comparison of works reaches its limits? In this talk, composer and court-appointed expert Richard Dubugnon explores how expert analysis can usefully be extended to examine the creative process itself. This approach, which has become particularly relevant in the age of digital tools and artificial intelligence, provides the court with additional insight into the plausibility of claimed authorship. Through audio examples and a case drawn from his expert practice, Dubugnon considers the methods and limits of musical comparison and the value of examining sources and creative processes.

The third edition of the Dakar Translation Symposium (DTS) will take place at NYU Abu Dhabi under the theme Africa and Her Hospitality . Taking majlis (gathering place) and karam (hospitality and generosity) as points of departure, the symposium will explore questions of language, belonging, migration, care, and the possibilities and limits of welcome. The three-day program includes scholarly panels, literary conversations, student roundtables, film screenings, music, and practice-based gatherings. This event is open to all members of our NYU Abu Dhabi community. RSVPs required for planning purposes. For more updates, please visit the DTS website and follow DTS on Instagram .

-
Security Alert: Beware of Phishing That Uses Fear and Urgency

Alarming emails about harassment complaints, legal matters, or disciplinary actions can create pressure to respond immediately. Scammers exploit this reaction to encourage clicks on malicious links, the opening of unsafe attachments, or the disclosure of sensitive information.
Pause, verify, and report:

- Recognize the pressure. Treat unexpected messages that use fear, urgency, or threats to demand action with caution.
- Look beyond the sender’s address. Even an internal or .edu address can be compromised. “Undisclosed recipients” or an unusual recipient list can be warning signs, but do not prove a message is fraudulent.
- Verify before clicking. Avoid links and attachments in suspicious messages, especially those claiming to contain confidential complaints or incident details.
- Confirm through a trusted channel. Contact the relevant office using contact details from the official directory and not those provided in the suspicious email.
- Report suspicious emails. Use the Report Phishing option. If a suspicious link has already been clicked or sensitive information disclosed, contact IT promptly. For assistance, contact NYU Abu Dhabi IT:
Call: +971 2 628 8888
Email: nyuad.it@nyu.edu

Can You Fool an AI Authenticator?
Join BioHACK3D, an exciting biochip hackathon taking place at NYU Abu Dhabi as part of CSAW’26!
Participants will receive a dedicated dataset and baseline code to help build and refine fabricated images designed to trick a deep-learning security system. By working with microscopy images of 3D-printed, melt-electrowritten QR codes (MEW-QRCs), you will sharpen your deep learning skills for image analysis while trying to make the authenticator classify non-genuine samples as "Genuine".
Key Highlights:

- Hands-on Experience: Get direct access to starter code and datasets—a great way to learn and refine deep learning concepts in image security.

- No Coding Experience Required: AI tools are fully permitted.

- Event Date: November 13, 2026

- Location: In-person track at NYU Abu Dhabi (MENA/UAE).

NYUAD’s Center for Brain and Health invites you to participate in a MRI study here on campus. The institute’s mission is to gain a better understanding of conditions prevalent in the region.
What will you do?
The study will take approximately 2.5 hours. We will collect demographic data, behavioral and visual data, brain scans in the MRI scanner, a saliva sample for whole-genome sequencing, and an OCT scan. You will be compensated up to 150 AED in vouchers.

You can participate if you are above 18 years of age, do not have a history of neurological conditions, are not pregnant at the time of the study, and do not have non-removable metal. You can only participate once.
