title: Academic Resource Center · NYUAD Students
text:
John Sexton and Lisa Goldberg Academic Resource Center (ARC)

The John Sexton and Lisa Goldberg Academic Resource Center (ARC) is dedicated to supporting student success throughout the NYU Abu Dhabi academic journey. Through personalized guidance, academic support services, and opportunities for mentorship, the ARC helps students navigate their educational experience and make the most of the resources available to them.

Whether students are exploring academic interests, planning their degree path, seeking support in challenging courses, or preparing for future opportunities, the ARC serves as a central hub for academic planning.

Academic Advising

Academic advisors partner with students to help them make informed decisions about their educational goals. Advisors provide guidance on degree requirements, major exploration and declaration, academic policies, course selection, and long-term academic planning.

Peer Tutoring

Students can access peer tutoring services for select courses across a range of disciplines, including Mathematics, Foundations of Science, Computer Science, Social Science, and Engineering. Peer tutors offer collaborative support that helps students strengthen their understanding, build confidence, and develop effective learning strategies.

Faculty Mentoring

ARC works with Pre-Major Faculty Mentors to provide students with an additional layer of academic and professional guidance. Mentors help students explore their academic interests, understand opportunities within their field of study, and prepare for graduate school and future careers.

At the ARC, students find the support, resources, and connections needed to thrive academically and pursue their goals.

title: Academic Advising · NYUAD Students
text:
What to Expect from Academic Advising

Academic advising is an essential part of the NYUAD academic experience. At the John Sexton and Lisa Goldberg Academic Resource Center (ARC), academic advisors support students in achieving their academic goals. Our advisors meet with students one on one to create individualized plans to progress through their degree successfully. We believe in holistic advising that supports the whole student, taking into account non-academic factors of success.

Here are a few things that we can help you with:

-
Course Selection: We can help you choose courses based on your interests, academic requirements, and career goals. — Read more on Course Selection

-
Four-year Planning: We assist in creating a four-year plan to fulfill requirements for your chosen degree or program.

-
Degree Progress Monitoring: We support in reviewing degree progress throughout your academic journey.

-
Academic Problem Solving and Support: We help navigate challenges you may encounter during your academic journey.

-
Resource Referral: We connect you with additional campus resources like the Writing Center, Student Persistence and Well-Being, and the Career Development Center.

- Academic Policies and Procedures: We help you understand NYUAD academic policies. — View NYUAD Academic Policies

Accessing Academic Advising

You can meet with an advisor by booking an individual thirty-minute appointment, or stop in during drop-in hours.

Should you drop in or book an appointment?

- Drop-In Advising

Drop-in advising is best suited if you have a quick question that can be answered within 10-15 minutes. Visit us in-person during walk-in hours or via Zoom . Here are some instances when drop-in advising can be advantageous:

- Quick Questions or Concerns: For brief inquiries or issues that require immediate assistance; for example, clarification on course selection, academic policies, or general academic information.

- Urgent Issues: Pressing matters, such as a time-sensitive registration problem or a sudden change in their academic situation.

- Time Constraints: For quick access to an advisor without needing to book an appointment in advance.

- Initial Guidance: New to NYUAD, or new to seeking services at the ARC? Receive general information, and learn about campus resources before scheduling a more in-depth appointment.

- Booked Appointments

Booked appointments involve scheduling a 30-minute appointment with an academic advisor in advance through NYUConnect .

This format can be advantageous in the following situations:

- In-Depth Discussions: that require detailed and in-depth academic advising, such as major exploration or complex four-year academic planning.

- Comprehensive Academic Planning: For assistance with long-term academic planning, such as a 4-year plan or navigating intricate degree requirements

Watch a tutorial on booking advising appointments at the ARC.

title: Academic Petition Process · NYUAD Students
text:
Occasionally students may encounter circumstances for which they seek exceptions to academic policy. In such cases, students may request consideration for their request by submitting an academic petition.

What is an Academic Petition?

An academic petition is a formal request made by a student seeking:

- an exception to an academic policy, or,

- an additional semester, beyond the regular eight semesters, to complete degree requirements

Petitions are typically submitted by students who have encountered significant challenges that impact their academic progress, such as health issues, personal emergencies, or other factors.

How do I Submit a Petition?

- Consult with an Academic Advisor: Connect with an academic advisor in the Academic Resource Center (ARC). An advisor can help assess your situation, provide you with the petition application link and guide you through the submission process. This is a required first step to start the process.

- Prepare Your Case: After consulting with an academic advisor, you will need to prepare a detailed petition outlining your extenuating circumstances. Be sure to include any supporting documentation you feel will support your case.

- Submit Your Petition: Submit your petition online via the online form your academic advisor provides you.

Review Process

- Review: Your completed petition, along with any supporting documentation, will be reviewed by the Undergraduate Petition Committee which includes leadership from the Office of Undergraduate Education, the Registrar’s Office, and the ARC.

- Timeline: Please allow up to three weeks for the committee to review and decide on your petition.
Decision Notification: Once a decision is reached, you will receive a letter from the Office of Undergraduate Education.

- Appeals: Appeals are only considered if you have new information or details that were not available at the time of your initial request. Consult with an advisor in the ARC if you think you have grounds for an appeal.

If you have any questions or need additional guidance connect with an advisor in the ARC or email us at nyuad.arc@nyu.edu .

Related official links:
https://students.nyuad.nyu.edu/academics/academic-resources/academic-advising/

title: Course Selection Process · NYUAD Students
text:
Last updated: May 19, 2026

The Course Selection Process for New Students

Course selection is a multi-step process that begins with considering your interests and goals and reviewing a number of resources to prepare for registration.

Considerations

Consider the following before beginning the process of course selection for your first semester at NYUAD.

- Your interest. Your first year is a great time to explore new courses / subjects that interest you even if it isn't going to be your major.

- Your intended major. If you have a major that you are interested in, explore the required courses in that major using the Bulletin and Sample Schedules .

- Your schedule. Consider the schedule you’d like to have. For example, are you a morning person or a night owl? This can help you decide if you should take a course at 8:30am or choose courses that are later in the day.

- University Requirements. Become familiar with University requirements like First Year Writing Seminar and the Core Curriculum .

- Balanced Schedule. Work towards enrolling in exploratory courses, major courses, and university requirements to ensure a balanced schedule.

Course Selection

Before you begin to choose courses, you should get acquainted with the following resources:

- Registration dates, found on the Academic Planning Timeline

- New Student Course Registration Checklist

- The NYUAD Bulletin has information you need to choose courses, such as listing of majors and minors, policies, graduation requirements, and more. You should refer to the bulletin for the year you start at NYUAD.

- Sample Course Grids for the Major(s) you are interested in.

- Course Registration Quick Guide (PDF) on courses you should take in your first year and how to register for them.

- The Course List and Syllabi page to better understand course offerings.

- These pages on the student portal:

- Graduation Requirements

- FAQs

- Exploring Major Options

- Preparing for Post-grad Studies

- New Student Brightspace modules

Course Selection Tips

- First-year students typically take four courses (16 credits) during their first semester.

- Completing a First-year Writing Seminar (FYWS) in your first year is required.

- Given that math is required for many majors, consider taking the math course you were placed into in your first year.

- Read the Academic Major part of the Graduation Requirements section.

- Try to take a few Core courses during your first two years of study. You can also take Core Competency courses when you study away.

- When selecting Core courses, explore topics that are different from the courses for your anticipated major. For example, if you are planning to enroll in Foundations of Science 1 and 2, don't simultaneously enroll in a science-focused course. The purpose of the Core Curriculum is to broaden your education.

- Balance the different kinds of demands on your time by taking courses that have different kinds of assignments and require different modes of thinking.
For example, don't choose four courses that are all likely to have a lot of reading and writing.

- If you select a seven-week course that meets for one half of the semester, consider adding another seven-week course that meets in the other half of the semester.

- If you’re interested in studying away, review the study away pathways for the major or majors you are interested in.

- Take a course just because it seems interesting or because you want to! First year is a good time to explore your interests.

Get Ready for Registration

To prepare for registration review the Registration Process on the student portal.

title: Frequently Asked Questions · NYUAD Students
text:
Last updated April 29, 2025

- Can I get academic credit or advanced standing for the AP (or IB, A-level or dual-enrollment) courses that I took in high school?

NYU Abu Dhabi does not award credit for work completed prior to enrollment at NYU Abu Dhabi. However, you can take a proficiency assessment for advanced standing in Arabic, Chinese, French, and Economics. In most cases, if a student does place out of a course, they will be expected to complete an additional advanced course in its place.

- Can I get credit for university-level courses that I take at my local university this fall?

No. First-year students are limited only to NYUAD courses.

- Can I take more than 16 credits?
You can’t take more than 18 credits your first semester and are strongly recommended to take only 16. This usually equates to four 4-credit courses. Almost all NYUAD courses are four credits. However, there are a handful of exceptions. Beyond this initial fall semester, students are generally also limited to 18 credits per term.

- Can I be sure that the courses that don't fit into my schedule will all be offered again later?

The vast majority of courses will be offered again the following year, but some may not. As a general rule, courses that are required for a major or minor will be offered at least once a year — although there may be exceptions for some upper-level courses. There will always be multiple options for each of the core areas and many of the courses will be repeated on an annual basis. However, some may not be offered again. Similarly, elective courses for majors and minors will generally be offered again, but we will also strive to offer new and different courses every year. You can be certain that if you follow the suggested plan of study for your major, you will be able to complete all of your requirements.

- Is Foundations of Science 1 & 2 one course or two?

For the purpose of planning your schedule, each Foundations of Science course counts as one 14-week course except the labs. Should you decide after completing Foundations of Science 1 that you no longer wish to major in a science or engineering field, you will have the option to withdraw from Foundations of Science 2 by the 14-week withdrawal deadline. Formally, each of these courses is actually divided into three separate pieces of 3-1 credit components.

-

- If I want/need to take Calculus this first semester but my math placement does not allow it, what do I do?

If you are not ready, it would be a mistake for you to enroll in the course. Even if you wish to be a science or engineering student, you must delay taking Calculus until you are adequately prepared. With careful planning, it will still be possible to complete a science major, even if you delay Foundations of Science until your second year.

- What if I was placed into a Math class but think I was placed incorrectly?

The decisions regarding the placement of students into appropriate math classes are final. They are taken in accordance with the highest academic standards required to achieve the best learning outcomes out of the calculus curriculum. The math placement of each student is therefore determined with the greatest care.

- What do I do if two courses I want/need to take are scheduled at the same time?

You will need to choose between the conflicting courses. The best option is to select the course that is most essential for your planned major or is most interesting to you.

- I heard that there is an Islamic Studies requirement. What is it and what does it mean for me?

We do have an Islamic Studies requirement that must be completed before you can graduate. There are a variety of ways to complete this requirement. It can be completed with two semesters of Arabic language classes or with any one of an expansive list of courses that contain a substantial component of Arabic or Islamic content. Courses satisfying the requirement have an X at the end of their course number (e.g., ACS-UH 1010X Anthropology and the Arab World).

- How do I integrate study away with all of the other academic requirements?

Studying away is a great way to augment your NYUAD academic experiences. The optimal timing and locations for study away vary by major. The Global Education Office has worked with the various academic programs to think through the many options. Their best advice is available in the Study Away Pathways page .

- A course that I REALLY want or need is listed as “Closed.” What does that mean and what should I do?

Closed courses have reached their maximum capacity and no more students are allowed to enroll. If a class is full, you won’t be able to register for it. In most cases you may be able to add yourself to a wait list. This means that if a space opens up, you may be able to move into the class. Be sure to use the edit/swap function in Albert so that you can move in off of the waitlist if a space opens up. Update your edit/swaps if you no longer want to enroll in the class — otherwise you could end up enrolled and not aware of the swap.

It is important that you identify some other alternative class so that you do have a full course load, 16 credits. There may be opportunities to enroll in the class in a later semester.

- I noticed that the NYUAD website and the Albert student information system lists courses as being offered on MTWRF. What does that mean?

These are the one-letter abbreviations for the days of the week.

- M is Monday

- T is Tuesday (but you probably already figured that out!)

- W is Wednesday

- R is Thursday

- F is Friday

- S is Saturday - classes are rarely offered on Saturdays except during J-Terms.

- U is Sunday - classes are rarely offered on Sundays except during J-Terms.

- I read somewhere that there are cross-listed courses. What does that mean and how do I find cross-listed courses?

A is a course that can be counted toward different things. For example ANTH-UH 2113 Memoir and Ethnography can be counted as an Art, Design, and Technology core course, or as a Cultural Exploration and Analysis core course, or as an elective for Literature and Creative Writing, or as an elective for Social Research and Public Policy in addition to its “home” minor of Anthropology.

Generally cross-listed courses can count for multiple majors or minors at the same time. Courses that are cross listed with the core, though, can only count toward the core or toward one or more majors or minors, but not toward the core AND toward one or more majors or minors. Thus LITCW-UH 2315X Postcolonial Turn can count for both Literature and Film and New Media. However, if you wanted it to count toward either or both of them, it couldn’t also count as a Cultural Exploration and Analysis core course.

Finding cross-listed courses on our Student Portal by visiting the Course List & Syllabus page and filter for the fall semester and the category that you are interested in.

- Do physical education courses count in the four courses that I can select for my first semester?
No, they are in addition to your four-course academic load. Physical education (PE) courses are 0-credit courses. Enrolling in PE classes won’t have any impact on when or how many regular academic courses you can enroll in.

- How do I request accommodations if needed?

Reasonable accommodations are adjustments to policy, practice, and programs that “level the playing field” for students with disabilities (physical, learning, neurodiversity, mental health, etc.) and provide equal access to NYU‘s programs and activities. Each student who registers with the Moses Center for Students Accessibility works with an Accessibility Specialist to develop a reasonable accommodation plan. For more information about how to apply please visit the Moses Center for Student Accessibility portal.

- When do I declare a major?

Students declare their major starting during spring break of their first year.

- Why can’t I validate courses?

In some cases, you would need department consent or there are prerequisites that you would need to take in order to take this course. Contact the Registrar’s Office at nyuad.registrar@nyu.edu .

title: First-Year Glossary · NYUAD Students
text:
Last updated June 23, 2025

The following are a list of terms that first year students at NYUAD should understand. You can also use the NYU glossary for a more comprehensive list of terms.

- Academic Advisor

A staff member who provides guidance and advice to students regarding academic plans and decisions, including course registration, school policies, choosing and declaring a major and/or minor. You can connect with an academic advisor in the Academic Resource Center .

- Academic Calendar

A calendar that includes all the key dates and events that occur in an academic year including holidays, legislative days, and deadlines. Check the Academic Calendar .

- Academic Division

A subdivision of NYU Abu Dhabi that is responsible for instruction and research in a specific group of disciplines. NYUAD has four academic divisions: Arts and Humanities, Engineering, Science, and Social Science.

- Academic Integrity

A foundational set of values that supports the free exchange of ideas and promotes scholarly excellence through independent, active, and creative thought. It ensures that all members of the NYU Abu Dhabi community are able to achieve, and be recognized for achieving, their highest potential. Upholding academic integrity requires a commitment to the core principles of responsibility, honesty, and respect.

Some more common violations of academic integrity include, but are not limited to:

- Plagiarism — copying and pasting from or paraphrasing minor or substantial portions of another’s work or secondary sources and presenting it as your own;

- Cheating — the unauthorized use of information, materials, devices, or other sources during an exam, quiz, or test;

- Collusion — unauthorized collaboration with others to purposely cheat or influence the outcome of an assignment; and

- Fraud — creating false data or the alteration of data to deliberately mislead on an assignment, or the citing of fabricated sources.

- Academic Resource Center

The John Sexton and Lisa Goldberg Academic Resource Center (ARC), provides students with resources and support to help them achieve their academic goals. At the ARC, students can access academic advising, peer tutoring and ARC Faculty Mentors. You can find more information on how to connect with an advisor or mentor on the ARC student portal page. Or email the ARC at nyuad.arc@nyu.edu .

- Academic Standing

The system is used to evaluate a student’s academic progress and determine their eligibility to continue in good standing at the University. A student is considered to be in good academic standing when they complete at least 16 credit hours each fall and spring semester and maintain both a term and cumulative GPA of 2.0 or higher. If a student’s term or cumulative GPA falls below 2.0, they are no longer considered to be in good academic standing.

- Add/Drop Period

Refers to adding or dropping a course on Albert. Review these helpful videos on how to add/drop a course. Refer to the Academic Calendar to check deadlines.

- Albert

NYU’s student information system and the home of a student’s academic record. Students, faculty, and staff can access Albert from NYU Home . Students can use Albert to find and sign up for classes, check requirements for and progress toward their degree, request transcripts, verify their enrollment, update their preferred name, name pronunciation, and pronouns in NYU’s systems, and accept or decline financial aid packages, view any financial aid missing forms or paperwork, see grades, and view any holds on their account.

- Anti-requisite

Two courses are considered anti-requisites when a student is not allowed to take both for credit. Students can take one or the other, but if they have taken one of the courses, they may not enroll in the other.

- Bulletin

An annual publication that outlines NYU Abu Dhabi’s academic programs, course offerings, major requirements, prerequisites, and detailed course descriptions. Always refer to the bulletin from the year you enter the university when planning your academic pathway. For example, if you began your studies in fall 2024, you should consult the 2024–2025 Bulletin. All bulletins are available on the student portal .

- Career Development Center

The Career Development Center (CDC) plays an integral role in the undergraduate experience at NYU Abu Dhabi, providing career and postgraduate guidance, advising, programs, and resources to students during their time at NYUAD, and beyond. The CDC is located on the ground level of the Campus Center (C2) in the Student Life Suite.

- Center for Academic Technology (CAT)

The Center for Academic Technology is where NYU Abu Dhabi students, faculty, and staff can receive help with their academic technology needs. The team supports students, faculty, and staff in using technology, software, and equipment for their teaching and research. This team also supports classroom technology services and audiovisual services on campus. They are located in the NYUAD Library. More information on the Library's website .

- Center for Writing

The NYUAD Center for Writing supports students at any stage in the writing, articulation, and expression of ideas. Writing Instructors are experienced readers and writers who work with students in one-on-one writing consultations, help to develop strategies for revision of assignments or papers, teach specific writing skills, and facilitate a deeper understanding of the student's own writing process. They welcome students from any field or discipline and work with all types of writing assignments, papers, and projects. In addition to writing consultations, they also offer specific consultations for oral expression and public presentations, Capstone projects, and support for students with ESL needs. You can find the Center for Writing in the Library. Check their timetable and available instructors .

- Core Curriculum

A set of required courses and requirements essential to your NYU Abu Dhabi experience and are taught by faculty from all divisions. The NYUAD Core Curriculum consists of:

- 1 Core Colloquium (14 weeks) which addresses a significant global challenge from multidisciplinary perspectives. These are only located in Abu Dhabi.

- 2 Core Field Colloquia (J-Term) courses which enables a deep dive into a particular aspect of these challenges within a specific site. Can be located in Abu Dhabi or outside the UAE (but will always be organized through NYUAD)

- 4 Core Competency Courses, one each in:

- Arts, Design, and Technology

- Cultural Exploration and Analysis

- Data and Discovery

- Structures of Thought and Society

- Co-Requisite

Some courses require that you be enrolled in another “co-requisite” course during the same semester. For example, Foundations of Science 1 has several different components each with its own grade. These courses must be taken together in the same term. See also Pre-requisite.

- Course Enrollment

(Also referred to as Course Registration) The process of registering, or signing up for a course. The NYUAD Academic Calendar lists registration dates and deadlines for each academic year. Every student has a specific enrollment period based on their seniority and credit count before the semester begins, which you can find on your Albert homepage under the main banner. Students can search and sign up for classes online also using Albert. It is advisable to meet with your academic advisor prior to enrolling.

- Course Registration

(Also referred to as Course Enrollment) The process of registering, or signing up for a course. The NYU Academic Calendar lists registration dates and deadlines for each academic year. Every student has a specific enrollment period based on their seniority and credit count before the semester begins, which you can find on your Albert homepage under the main banner. Students can search and sign up for classes online also using Albert. It is advisable to meet with your academic advisor prior to registering.

- Course Tags

All students are required to take at least one course designated as satisfying a Quantitative Reasoning (Q) requirement, one that satisfies an Experimental Inquiry (E) requirement, and one that satisfies an Islamic Studies (X) requirement.

You can refer to a course’s code and look for the symbols (E, Q, and X) to find out if a course satisfies any of these requirements. Course tags are not limited to double counting restrictions. However, courses with course tags cannot be taken as pass/fail since they fall under the Core course requirements.

- Credits

(Also referred to as credit hours, units, or points) Units to measure a student’s enrollment in a course and track their progress toward a degree. At NYU Abu Dhabi, you are required to complete 128 credits over the course of your undergraduate degree. An average undergraduate plan entails students taking ~16 credits per semester along with two 3-credit J-Term courses to satisfy the 128-credit requirement for graduation.

- Cross-listed Course

A cross-listed course is a course that can be counted toward different things, sometimes simultaneously. For example, ANTH-UH 2113 Memoir and Ethnography is an Anthropology minor elective. However, it can also be counted as an Art, Design, and Technology core course, as a Cultural Exploration and Analysis core course, as an elective for Literature and Creative Writing, or as an elective for Social Research and Public Policy.

- Divisional Dean

An academic leader of a specific division. Each NYU Abu Dhabi Division has one dean supported by several associate and assistant deans. Deans maintain the academic excellence of their schools by working with faculty and staff to develop academic strategies and other programming goals.

- Dropping (a class)

Dropping a course means formally leaving a course you have enrolled in during the add/drop period. You can drop the course through Albert. A course does not appear on your transcript if it is dropped within the add/drop period. If you discontinue a course after the Add/Drop deadline, it will count as a withdrawal.

- Edit/Swap

An Edit Swap tells the system that, if a seat becomes available in your waitlisted class, you will be automatically swapped from whatever enrolled class that you specify into the waitlisted class if it fits with the rest of your schedule and you meet all pre-requirements. Keep in mind that if you’re on a waitlist and already have a full schedule (16 credits) or a time conflict with another course, you will NOT automatically come off the waitlist when a space becomes available.

- Elective

A course that is not specifically required to graduate is called an elective.

- Major/Minor Electives

All academic majors and most minors, have a set of required courses and a set of major electives from which students can choose. For example students majoring in Psychology, must select at least one advanced Psychology lab elective, but have several options to choose from. Students also have a lot of flexibility in selecting specific courses to meet their Core and First-year Writing requirements.

- General Electives

Students in all majors have at least a few spaces in their four-year academic plan to take courses which are not used to satisfy any specific requirement. These courses are called general electives.

- Faculty Member

An individual who is actively involved in teaching and/or research, often called a professor. There are various kinds of faculty members, including adjunct, assistant, associate, and tenured.

- Faculty Mentor

A faculty or staff member who provides guidance and advice to students to help them adjust to NYU Abu Dhabi, navigate university life, and fully engage with the NYUAD community.

- First-Year Writing Seminars (FYWS)

A writing course required for all first-year students at NYU Abu Dhabi. It introduces students to the reading, writing, oral expression, and critical-thinking skills essential to a liberal arts education.

- Grade Point Average (GPA)

A number that measures academic achievement on a scale from 4.000 (an A) to 0.000 (an F). Students have both a term and a cumulative GPA that appear on their transcripts: Term GPA measures academic progress for a given term, and cumulative GPA includes all courses taken for credit.

NYU Abu Dhabi students also have an official GPA and final GPA. The final GPA excludes First-Year grades by marking them as "Successfully Completed" if the student has achieved the passing grade. The official GPA includes freshman year grades for classes "successfully completed" as part of the cumulative GPA calculation.

- Incomplete Grade

A temporary grade that means a student has not yet completed a course and has made an agreement with the faculty member to complete the course at a later date. Incomplete grades are granted at the discretion of the faculty member and are usually granted because there is a circumstance beyond the student’s control that has impacted their ability to complete coursework. Students who may have unexpected or difficult situations that impact their ability to complete work in a particular course should talk with an advisor and faculty about requesting an incomplete.

- January/June Term (J-Term)

J-Term courses are designed as two-week, intensive and highly immersive learning experiences during January. They intensify the student's focus, reach beyond the classroom to incorporate experiential learning, and are site-specific, connecting students to the place where they study. NYU Abu Dhabi students are required to complete two J-Term courses during their four-year undergraduate studies — at least one J-Term course must be taught fully in Abu Dhabi, and at most one can be taught abroad.

- Legislative Day

A day used to balance the academic calendar so courses meet instructional time requirements while keeping proper sequence. In simpler words, a legislative day is when classes meet on a different day's schedule to maintain the progress of the class. For instance, sometimes a Thursday could be considered a legislative day where students attend classes based on their Monday schedule.

- Liberal Arts College

An institution of higher education that emphasizes undergraduate study in the liberal arts and sciences. They provide a curriculum that provides students with extensive general knowledge and helps develop their intellectual capabilities.

- Major

An academic major is an academic discipline to which an undergraduate student formally commits. A student who successfully completes all courses required for the major qualifies for an undergraduate degree. All undergraduate students must declare a major by the end of their second year in order to graduate. Many students choose majors that directly or indirectly relate to their future career goals.

- Midterm Exam

Any of one or more exams in a course offered prior to the final exam. Not all courses have midterms exams, but some may have two or even more.

- Midterm Period

A period during the semester, usually in the middle of the semester, where students undertake examinations and complete bigger assignments that are more comprehensive than quizzes and smaller assignments during the semester but less comprehensive than final exams and assignments.

- Minor

A separate course of study that an undergraduate student may declare to either complement their major or build time for another area of interest into their academic schedule. They are not mandatory for graduation (unlike a major) and require fewer courses than a major (typically 4-6).

- Moses Center for Accessibility and Inclusive Culture

New York University is committed to providing equal educational opportunity and participation for all students across all its campuses. The Moses Center for Accessibility and Inclusive Culture partners with the NYU Community worldwide to ensure an accessible university experience for all students with disabilities by removing or minimizing barriers to education access. We engage in an individualized, interactive process with each student to explore the impact of a disability or disabilities on their education experience. Through this process, appropriate and reasonable accommodations are determined and implemented on a case-by-case basis. Reach out to the Moses Center for Accessibility and Inclusive Culture Liaison in Abu Dhabi at nyuad.spa@nyu.edu if you have any questions or if you would like to explore your accommodation needs.

- Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA)/Duo Mobile

An extra layer of protection to ensure data security for its students, faculty, and staff. When logging in to NYU’s online systems, users will typically need to enter their NetID and password, along with a second form of verification from a cell phone or landline. Duo Mobile is an app that lets users log in by accepting a notification on their phones.

- N-Number

All NYU students, faculty, and staff have N Numbers. N numbers are printed on the back of your NYU ID cards. It is an 8-digit string of numbers and starts with “N.”

- NetID

All NYU students, faculty, and staff have an NYU NetID, or network identification. It is a combination of an individual’s initials and a few random numbers. NetIDs, along with N Numbers, are printed on the back of NYUCards. This form of identification is necessary to log on to many of the internal systems.

- NYU Brightspace

NYU Brightspace is NYU’s learning management system. You can use Brightspace to access course materials, submit assignments, look at your grades, participate in discussion boards, and communicate with your professors.

- NYU Connect

An online platform where students, faculty, advisors, and staff can share and track information in one place to coordinate support for students. Students can also use NYU Connect to access their individualized Success Network, schedule appointments, and request assistance..

- Office Hours

A block of time set aside by instructors, teaching assistants, and other NYU staff members for students to ask questions and receive extra guidance and/or support. Office hours could be held in the individual’s office or via Zoom.

- Online Courses

Students are not able to take online courses offered at other sites during their studies. Enrollment for courses need to be offered at the site where the student is studying for the semester.

- Pass/Fail

A grading option that is either chosen by a student sometime before the Change of Grading Basis deadline or, in rare cases, is automatically applied to those few courses that are available only on a pass/fail basis. Upon completion of the course, instead of receiving a letter grade for the class, students will have a P for pass or F for fail on their transcript. A grade of at least a D must be earned to achieve a passing grade of P.

At NYU Abu Dhabi, a course taken pass/fall will count towards your overall credits, but it will not satisfy the major requirement, minor requirements, or core requirements, nor can courses taken pass/fail be used to satisfy prerequisites. Courses that can be used toward a major, minor, or Core requirement cannot be taken pass/fail.

- PHYED

Students need to successfully complete two Physical Education (PHYED-UH) courses as part of their degree requirements.

- Placement Test

An exam, generally taken near the start of a term, where students can demonstrate sufficient mastery of a given subject that grants them exemption from a particular course. Placement tests may be required or optional.

NYUAD placement tests include the Math Assessment for Math courses, and Language Placement Tests for language courses.

- Plagiarism

Copying and pasting from or paraphrasing secondary sources without proper citation.

- Prerequisite

A course that students are required to take before advancing to a higher-level class in a given subject or discipline. For example, many Engineering courses have Foundations of Science 1 and 2 as prerequisites, as in you must complete FoS 1 and 2 before enrolling in them. Students may be able to place out of certain prerequisites (in languages, or math for example) by taking a placement exam.

- Proficiency Assessment

(Also referred to as a Placement Test) An exam, generally taken near the start of a term, where students can demonstrate sufficient mastery of a given subject that grants them exemption from a particular course. Placement tests may be required or optional. NYUAD placement tests include but are not limited to, the Math Assessment and Language Placement Tests for language courses.

- Registrar

(The Office of the University Registrar) The office is responsible for tasks related to registration, graduation, transcripts, enrollment verification, and academic record keeping. Students can meet in person with representatives from the Registrar. You can reach them at nyuad.registrar@nyu.edu .

- Shopping Cart

Prior to registration, students can log in to Albert and use the Shopping Cart feature to mark any classes they’re interested in taking for the current or upcoming term.

- How to Course Search via Albert Shopping Cart

- How to validate classes

- STEM

A term for classifying fields of academic study and careers oriented around Science, Technology, Engineering, and Math.

- Study Abroad

(Also referred to as Study Away) when students apply to spend a semester studying at a program outside of the home campus in Abu Dhabi. Students can choose to study at one of NYU’s global academic sites or at an approved exchange program.

- Study Away

(Also referred to as Study Abroad) when students apply to spend a semester studying at a program outside of the home campus in Abu Dhabi. Students can choose to study at one of NYU’s global academic sites or at an approved exchange program.

- Swap

During the add/drop period, students may join the waitlist for a course they want to take by setting up a “ swap .” This feature in Albert allows students to register for another course as a placeholder (to ensure that they remain enrolled full-time) and automatically switches the waitlisted course with the placeholder once a seat opens up.

- Syllabus

A document that instructors use to provide students in their class with a general overview of the class for that semester. Syllabi generally include contact information for the instructor and their office hours, a course description, the instructor’s expectations, and policies, required materials like books or other supplies, an overview of major and minor assignments, and a general schedule for the term. You can usually find each course’s syllabus on its Brightspace site.

- Transcript

A complete record of all courses a student has completed, including the final grades earned, at an educational institution. A transcript will also list the student’s Grade Point Average (GPA) and any awards or degrees granted by that institution. NYUAD official transcripts do not contain grades from the first year of courses (fall, J-Term, spring, and summer/June Term of the first year).

- Waitlist

After a course has reached its capacity, or the maximum number of seats for students, students may join the waitlist (not all courses have waitlist seats) to be automatically enrolled in the course should another student drop the class and space become available. Joining a waitlist does not guarantee a seat in the class, students on a class waitlist should always enroll in other courses as a backup and set up swaps with their waitlisted courses. See edit/swap

- Withdraw

Formally unenrolling from a course. Withdrawals happen after the add/drop deadline has passed (you can find the deadline on the Academic Calendar). Courses that students have withdrawn from do not receive credit and appear on their transcripts with a “W” grade. A “W” grade does not impact a student’s Grade Point Average (GPA), but it may impact their degree progress.

title: Proficiency Assessments · NYUAD Students
text:
Last updated: May 15, 2026

To ensure that you are enrolling in the classes most appropriate for you, NYU Abu Dhabi has several placement assessments. Some are offered in the summer and some occur during Marhaba.

Summer Proficiency Assessments

- Writing

Writing Proficiency is a key requirement for success at NYU Abu Dhabi (and in life!). As an NYUAD student, you must complete a semester-long Writing Seminar in your first year. This summer, you will be taking the Writing Diagnostic and Survey to help you determine how urgently you need to enroll in the mandatory First-Year Writing Seminar. We ask that you take this non-binding, self-directed self-assessment by July 15, 2026 .

Once you have taken the diagnostic, we hope you'll consult with your advisor or a member of the team from the Center for Writing to kick off a conversation about your writing.

- Mathematics

Mathematics is often regarded as the language of science, but its significance extends far beyond. It provides the analytical tools necessary for understanding complex systems and making informed decisions in various fields such as business, economics, political science, social science, and psychology. Moreover, it serves as the foundation for computer science, artificial intelligence, cryptography, data analysis, etc. From optimizing business strategies to advancing AI-driven technologies, mathematics is at the heart of innovation across disciplines.

All students entering NYUAD in fall 2026 who plan to take courses in the Calculus Curriculum at any point during their undergraduate studies must complete a math assessment.

Visit the Math Placement page for complete details and instructions.

- Foreign Language Placement

Most of you who are interested in pursuing Arabic, Chinese, Spanish, Japanese, or French language courses will be true beginners and will want to start at the beginner or elementary level. However, some of you may have had previous coursework in one of these languages or may be heritage speakers. If you believe that you could be ready to begin your university study at a higher level than Elementary 1, you will need to take a Foreign Language Proficiency Assessment.

For Arabic , students are asked to read the Arabic Placement FAQ and write directly to Mohammed Muqbel at mm10321@nyu.edu for further inquiries.

For Spanish , students should read about the Spanish program at NYUAD and write directly to Eduardo Lage-Otero at elo204@nyu.edu to take the NYUAD placement test.

For all other languages , you will need to complete an online evaluation . Students will see their test results in Albert within seven working days of completing the exam.

Additional information about the Chinese assessment is available from the East Asian Studies program at NYU New York. Please note that the proficiency assessment result will still be valid throughout your NYU career.

Related official links:
https://students.nyuad.nyu.edu/academics/academic-resources/academic-planning/proficiency-assessments/math-placement/
https://students.nyuad.nyu.edu/academics/academic-resources/academic-planning/proficiency-assessments/arabic-proficiency-assessment/

title: Arabic Proficiency Assessment FAQs · NYUAD Students
text:
Last updated: May 19, 2026.

- Who needs to take an Arabic Proficiency Assessment?

Students who have learned Arabic, formally or informally, prior to taking classes at NYU, and believe they could be ready to begin at a higher level than Elementary 1, should take the Arabic Proficiency Assessment.

- Who does not need to take it?

Total beginners, with no prior knowledge of Arabic, can enroll in Elementary Arabic 1 on their own. No placement test or permission is needed. Also, students who took Arabic classes at NYUAD, in Abu Dhabi, Shanghai, or New York, do not need to take the proficiency assessment.

- What does the Arabic Proficiency Assessment consist of?

It takes three hours to complete and consists of an online exam on Brightspace that tests vocabulary, grammar, reading comprehension, and writing skills.

- When is it scheduled?

Contact Mohammed Muqbel, Assistant Instructor of Arabic ( mm10321@nyu.edu ) to schedule the Arabic placement test over Zoom.

- How do I sign up for the Arabic Proficiency Assessment?

Send an email to Mohammed Muqbel, Assistant Instructor of Arabic, at mm10321@nyu.edu about any previous Arabic study experience (where and how you studied Arabic), topics, materials, or textbooks covered, current skills in speaking, listening, reading, and writing Arabic, when and how often you use Arabic, how recently you studied Arabic, type of Arabic studied (Modern Standard Arabic, specific dialect(s), etc.), and any additional relevant details about your Arabic background or experience. You may be asked to send a sample of your writing, in Arabic, to determine which test is suitable for your level.

- What can I expect after finishing the Proficiency Assessment?

Within 48 hours, you will receive an email informing you of the test results. Shortly after that you will receive an email indicating the appropriate course you can enroll in.

- Can I use the results of a placement test to join a class, a year later?

No, you will need to take another placement test prior to joining that class.

title: Math Placement · NYUAD Students
text:
Updated: June 8, 2026

Math Pathways | Process Overview | Scoring | Course Placement

Math Assessments for the Class of 2030

All students entering NYUAD in fall 2026 are required to take a Mathematics Proficiency Assessment (MPA) before taking a Math course. The results of the MPA determine which Math course a student may begin with.

Initial Assessment, Predicted Score, and Preliminary Course Placement

The first assessment takes place during Marhaba. Results will be available before courses begin. However, in order to register for courses on July 15, students who intend to take the MPA during Marhaba should take an online Math assessment and submit a predicted score by July 4. This predicted score determines their preliminary placement and allows them to provisionally enroll in a Math course. This course placement is provisional.

Final course placement takes place after the MPA at Marhaba. The provisional placement may be adjusted based on the in-person MPA during Marhaba. Below is a detailed description of the process and a list of procedures that will help gain the appropriate placement in the summer so that it will not be changed at Marhaba.

IMPORTANT NOTE : A change in placement will result in alteration of schedule and selected courses, so it is important to follow the procedure below to be able to confirm the predicted placement and avoid disrupting your course schedule right before the semester starts.

Math Pathways

It is wise to plan ahead as much as you can and consider your enrollment options for each of the scenarios. — Learn about scores and math placement

Statistics Pathway (majors that only require Statistics)
Statistics Pathway — for majors that only require Statistics (i.e., Political Science, Social Research and Public Policy, and Psychology)

-

-
MATH-UH 1004: Math for Statistics,

-
SOCSC-UH 1010: Statistics for Social and Behavioral Sciences, or

-
PSYCH-UH 1004: Statistics for Psychology

Calculus Pathway (majors that require Calculus)
Calculus Pathway — for majors that require Calculus (i.e., Engineering, Sciences, Business, Organizations, and Society, and Economics majors)

Calculus Pathway Scenarios

There are several scenarios for starting the calculus curriculum:

- Take the MPA at Marhaba. If your score qualifies for Pre-calculus or higher, use the placement result at Marhaba to start Math courses in fall 2026 or later. You cannot take an MPA after starting a Math course.

- Take the MPA at Marhaba. Even if your score qualifies for Pre-calculus or higher, if you do not take Math classes in fall 2026, you can take the MPA in December again, and use the highest of the two scores to start Math courses in spring 2027.

Your course placement depends on your final placement score and your pathway, as outlined in the chart below. Note that the score ranges will be provided after July 4 when all the predicted scores have been submitted.

Score Range | Calculus Pathway | Statistics Pathway

Range 0 | Placement Prep Coaching | Placement Prep Coaching

Range 1 | Precalculus (MATH-UH 1006) | Mathematics for Statistics (MATH-UH 1004)

Range 4 | Multivariable Calculus with Applications to Science and Engineering / to Economics (MATH-UH 1020 / MATH-UH 1021)

Process Overview

Your math course placement consists of an On-campus Math Placement Assessment (MPA) during Marhaba. In order to revise your preparation and, at the same time, be able to make an early preliminary registration into your courses, a Summer Preparation phase is offered, where you can train and predict your own performance.

Your final placement grade is the one received at Marhaba, partially modified by some rewards or penalties based on how accurately you predicted that performance over the summer. The process is so designed in order to provide an accurate assessment of your current Math level, while rewarding honesty and accurate self-assessment.

Phase 1: Summer Preparation and Predicted Score (T)

Starting June 15, 2026 , you will receive an email with your login credentials for the Webassign Math Placement Practice Platform.

- Workflow : You will access sample exams that you can use to practice by working the problems out on paper and inputting the answers in Webassign to get an evaluation.

- Practice Exams : When ready, you arrange a setup in order to take an exam under strict exam-like conditions similar to those at Marhaba: work the problems out on paper, follow the time limit as prescribed, no calculators, notes, or outside help, and then input your answers into Webassign to receive a score.

- Determining Your Score (T) : After completing at least two practice exams, you will determine your final Predicted Score (T) , which must be an integer from 0 to 100, and return it as instructed in the email.

- Deadline : You must submit your score (T) via the platform by July 4, 2026, at 4pm .

- Fall Enrollment : This predicted score will be used to determine your provisional course allocation and allow you to enroll in a fall math course (e.g., Precalculus, Calculus).

Phase 2: On-Campus Assessment (G)

During Marhaba orientation, you will take the official Math Placement Assessment (MPA) on campus.

- Format : The test is highly similar in length, format, and difficulty to the summer practice exams. It is a Webassign exam printed on paper.

- Evaluation : You will write your answers on the exam sheet and return both the sheet and your handwritten paperwork. Your paperwork will be graded to support and confirm your answers.

- Grade : You will receive an official Marhaba grade (G) based on this test.

Taking the MPA (G)

- You will go to an assigned room for a paper-based assessment using print-outs of Webassign exams.

- The test content and level will be aligned with the practice exams you saw over the summer.

- You will have a fixed amount of time (e.g., 60–120 minutes) to complete the test under standard exam conditions: no notes, material, calculators, or help of any sort.

- Exams will be collected, scanned, and graded by the Math faculty .

- You will obtain a graded score G (0–100 ).

Phase 3: The Final Placement Formula

Your final course placement depends on a calculation that compares your Marhaba grade (G) to your summer predicted grade (T).

- Accurate Prediction (Bonus) : If your prediction was accurate, your Marhaba grade will be slightly increased. This rewards fairness, integrity, and self-awareness during summer testing.

- Inaccurate Prediction (Reduction) : If your prediction was highly inaccurate, your grade will be decreased.

- Underestimating vs. Overestimating : Overestimating your score causes severe course misalignment, so overestimating results in a harsher penalty . If you underestimate your score but improve by the time you take the Marhaba test, the penalty is halved, maximizing your chances of keeping a performance bonus.

- Optimal Behavior : The system is designed so that aiming at the most accurate prediction is the optimal and most rewarding behavior. Any deviation from this leads to a possible loss of points and change of course placement.

Scoring

How Your Final Score (S) is Computed

Once we have your predicted score T and your graded score G, we compute the final score:

S = G + K – (G – T)/2 | 0 ≤T ≤ G ≤ 100,

S = G + K – (T – G), | 0 ≤ G ≤ T ≤100,

Where K ≈ 5. |

Key Points

- If your prediction T exactly matches G , then
S = G + K
You keep the full bonus K.

- If your prediction is close to G , you lose only a small part of K.
Example (with K = 5):
T = 72, G = 75 →
S = 75 + 5 – (75 – 72)/2 = 80 - 1.5 = 78.5

- If your prediction is very optimistic or very pessimistic , the penalty is larger.

Examples (K=5)

- Accurate prediction

- You predict T = 80, actually score G = 80
S = 80 + 5 – (80 – 80) = 85

- You get a 5-point bonus.

- Slightly off but still realistic

- You predict T = 78, actually score G = 72
S = 72 + 5 – (78 – 72) = 77 - 6 = 71

- You lose 1 point relative to G (71 vs 72) because you overestimated by 6.

- Severe overestimation

- You predict T = 95, actually score G = 70
S = 70 + 5 – (95 – 70) = 75 - 25 = 50

- This large mismatch strongly penalizes your final placement score.

- Severe underestimation

- You predict T = 60, actually score G = 85
S = 85 + 5 – (85-60)/2 = 90 – 12.5 = 78.5

- You performed very well, but your pessimistic prediction reduces the bonus.

- Slight underestimation

- You predict T = 65, actually score G = 72
S = 72 + 5 – (72 – 65) /2= 77-3.5=73.5

- As you improved upon the prediction, there is still a reward even with a slightly off prediction.

Because S is highest when T is close to G , your best strategy is to use your practice results and your honest self-assessment to predict as accurately as you can . This involves taking the practice tests in conditions as similar as possible to the actual, in-person test, with no aid and no interruptions.

Why Honest Prediction Is Your Best Strategy
You might wonder:

“Can I game the system by reporting a higher (or lower) predicted score T than I really expect?”

Short answer: No —this can only hurt you .

- For any fixed test performance (G), the formula above for your final score (S) is maximized when (|T - G| = 0), i.e., when T = G.

- If you overstate your prediction (choose T much higher than you expect to score), you risk a large negative adjustment if your actual score is lower.

- If you understate your prediction (choose T much lower than you expect to score), you give up part of the bonus K you could have earned.

In other words, the system is designed so that:

- Being accurate is rewarded.

- Being unrealistic — in either direction — is penalized.

This is not only fair, it also encourages you to:

- take the practice exams seriously,

- reflect honestly on what you know and don't know,

- enter the semester in the course where you have the best chance to succeed.

(For those interested: a theoretical analysis and a small pilot study at NYUAD show that this kind of scoring system encourages students to report their best estimate honestly and improves calibration between expected and actual performance.)

- Please review the NYUAD Academic Integrity Policy and Procedure .

Course Placement

How Your Math Placement Will Be Determined

- Before Marhaba : Based on your predicted score T, you will be assigned a provisional math course.

- After the Marhaba placement test :

- We compute your final score S.

- If S confirms your provisional course placement, you stay enrolled in that course.

- If S suggests that a different level would be better, your enrollment will be adjusted up or down . Be mindful that in this case, courses might have conflicting times or be full, and you might not be able to stay in other courses that you registered for and that have math courses as corequisites.

- In case of a very large mismatch or special circumstances, the math program may review your case individually and may speak with you during Marhaba.

title: Writing Diagnostic and Survey · NYUAD Students
text:
Writing at NYUAD: The Writing Diagnostic and Survey

Welcome to Writing at NYUAD! We are glad you are here, and you are right where you should be. We can't wait to start working with you. But first: who are "we"? The NYUAD Writing Program and the Center for Writing champion process-based approach to the teaching of writing, and we strive to help you not only produce better writing but become better writers.

To aid you in the process of developing your writing skills and your sense of yourself as a writer, we ask that you take a self-directed Writing Diagnostic and Survey by July 15, 2026.

Once you have taken the diagnostic and survey, we hope you’ll consult with your advisor or a member of the team from the Center for Writing to kick off a conversation about your writing.

What Do the Writing Diagnostic and Survey Do?

We’ve designed an opportunity for you to read, write, and reflect on your thinking and writing process. This diagnostic will help you determine the best path for you to push your thinking and writing skills to the next level of analytical excellence and clarity of expression. Please note: though this is a mandatory requirement, this is not a formal assessment of your writing or a placement test .

First-Year Writing Seminar

You can use the Writing Diagnostic and Survey to help make choices about the mandatory First-Year Writing Seminars (FYWS). As you may know, all students must take a Writing Seminar in their first year. The FYWS are theme-driven writing classes designed to introduce you to the rigors of academic writing in English. The class will help you develop and refine your skills as a thinker and writer by asking you to read often, write daily, and engage with source materials in a rigorous and ethical manner as you build persuasive and compelling arguments.

But how will you decide when it is best for you to take the class? What kind of support will you need to thrive as a college-level writer? To help you answer these questions, we have designed the self-directed Writing Diagnostic and Survey.

The experience of reading, writing, and reflecting on your process that we’ve set up for you via the survey will help you talk to your advisor and determine whether you would like to take the FYWS in the first semester or the second.

What’s the best path for you? We’re here to help you decide. And this diagnostic and survey are your first steps.

As a reminder: This is not a placement test ,

nor will it be used by the university to assess your writing skills. Instead, it is a tool designed to help you develop a sense of your strengths as a writer. It will also help you gain insight into the rigors and demands of university-level academic writing in English.

The writing you produce and the survey responses you provide will be archived by the Writing Program. These materials will help us develop classes and curricula tied to student needs.

Deadline

Students should take the Writing Diagnostic and Survey by July 15, 2026 , prior to course registration.

Related official links:
https://students.nyuad.nyu.edu/academics/resources/writing-center/

title: Registration Process · NYUAD Students
text:
Last updated: May 19, 2026

Preparing for Registration

Before registering for courses, be sure to review the Course Selection page and the Course Registration Checklist on the student portal. Next, prepare to register for courses by doing the following:

- Use course offerings to identify ten to twelve 1,000-level courses that seem interesting to you, including courses in the major you want to explore. The course list and syllabi tool will enable you to find courses using filters you are interested in. You can look for specific courses, such as a Core course or a First Year Writing Seminar (FYWS). You can also use the keyword search to identify courses related to particular topics.

- Add First Year Writing Seminar and a Core course to your list because all first-year students must take FYWS and a Core in their first year.

- Given that math is required for many majors, consider taking the math course you placed into in your first year.

- Prioritize your courses by identifying 16 credits (usually four courses) you prefer and backup courses in case you don’t get into your first choices. First-year students must register for 16 credits.

- Once you’ve made a list of preferred and backup courses from NYUAD’s course search tool, use Albert to create a sample timetable and ensure the courses you prefer do not conflict. You can find videos on how to use Albert and search for courses .

- Review how to enroll , add , drop , and edit/swap videos before registering for courses.

- Next, add courses to your shopping cart and validate selections to make sure you meet the prerequisites required and classes do not have any time conflicts. You can then enroll from your shopping cart once registration opens.

- Have a backup plan, in case one or more of the classes that you want are full by the time you get to enroll.

- Check the “ Waitlist if class is full " checkbox when adding classes to your shopping cart (this is available on the "Select classes to add" screen). This ensures that if a class is full by the time you are able to enroll, you will be automatically added to the waitlist if seats are still available.

Full Classes

There is a chance that some of the classes that you are hoping to enroll in will be full before you register. It is even possible that the wait list will be full and you won’t be able to get onto the wait list.

This is a reality of college life everywhere. But don’t worry! In most cases you will have a chance to enroll in those courses another semester.

Remember, any course that you take, that has a credit value, will count toward the requirement of 128 credits to graduate.

Setting up Swaps for Waitlisted Classes

All first-year students must register for 16 credits. If you have been put on the waitlist for one (or more) of your classes, you should enroll in another course or courses in case seats do not become available in your desired courses.

You will then be able to set up “swaps” for these classes using Albert’s Edit Swap functionality. An Edit Swap tells the system that, if a seat becomes available in your waitlisted class, you will be automatically swapped from whatever enrolled class that you specify into the waitlisted class. Remember, this will only be possible if the class you want to go into fits with the rest of your schedule and you have met all requirements. Make sure to double-check that waitlisted classes do not conflict with classes you are already registered in. Check for time conflicts.

Please be aware that without an Edit Swap if you are on a waitlist and already have a full schedule or a time conflict with another course, you will NOT automatically come off the waitlist when a space becomes available. Also remember to check and update your edit swaps before the start of the semester as an Edit Swap can happen at any time.

Registration Assistance

If a class is full, you will have to wait for a spot to become available or take the course another semester. Your mentor, the class instructor, ARC advisors, and even the Registrar are not able to help you get into a full class. However, if you have other difficulties with the registration process itself, please email nyuad.registrar@nyu.edu for assistance.

Foundations of Science (FoS)

Students intending to enroll in Foundations of Science I and II should enroll in the five components at the same time since they are co-requisites with each other (a total of 8 credits).

- SCIEN-UH 1121EQ Foundation of Science 1-2: Physics (1.5 credits)

- SCIEN-UH 1122EQ Foundation of Science 1-2: Chemistry (3 credits)

- SCIEN-UH 1123EQ Foundation of Science 1-2: Biology (1.5 credits)

- SCIEN-UH 1124P Foundation of Science 1 Lab: Physics (1 credit)

- SCIEN-UH 1124C Foundation of Science 2 Lab: Chemistry (1 credit)

Also please remember that you cannot register for Foundations of Science unless you are placed into and enroll Calculus with Apps (MATH-UH 1012Q or MATH-UH 1013Q) or Multivariable Calculus with Apps (MATH-UH 1020Q or MATH-UH 1021Q).

title: Degree Progress Exception (DPE) · NYUAD Students
text:
What Is a Degree Progress Exception (DPE)?

A Degree Progress Exception (DPE) is an administrative adjustment made in a student’s Degree Progress Report that modifies how a course is counted toward a degree requirement.

An Academic Advisor or a Major Mentor can request a DPE so that the student’s record accurately reflects what requirements have been fulfilled.

Examples of When a DPE Might Be Used

- Course Substitution: An alternate course completed can count toward a requirement. Example: You took “Probability and Statistics” instead of “Statistics for the Social and Behavioral Sciences,” and it’s approved as a substitute.

- Course Redirect: A course is appearing in one requirement and needs to be moved to an alternate requirement. Example: You took “Boundaries” for your Political Science major; however, it is counting towards the Structures of Thought and Society Core.

- Double Counting: When a course taken can double count for two requirements. Example: You are a CS major and a Math minor. You took Calculus, however, it is only appearing in your major and you need to request it to also count towards Math.

How Do You Request a DPE?

Core Requirement

If you would like adjustments made to how courses that currently count towards the Core Curriculum appear in your Core requirements, please complete this form .

Once submitted, the changes will appear in your DPR within 5-7 business days.

All Other DPEs

For all other courses, including Core courses you want counted as a major or minor requirement, complete this form through ARC or reach out to your Major Mentor.

Note: The ARC does not submit DPEs for courses that are not approved as cross-listed on the Course List and Syllabi page or listed on the Study Away Alternates page . If you are seeking a true exception for a course to count that does not appear on either of these pages, you must request that your Major Mentor or Associate Program Head submit the DPE.

What Is the Process for Approval of a DPE?

Once the DPE is requested in the Degree Progress Report (DPR), it is then routed to the program of the relevant degree requirement, to review.

After approval by the program the request will go to the Registrar’s Office for verification and processing.

Therefore it is important to note, DPE requests can take some time to process.

Note:

- Only one DPE can be processed at a time.

- All majors and/or minors for which you are requesting DPEs must be officially declared and reflected on Albert.

- During peak periods, DPEs sent to the ARC can take up to two weeks to review.

- DPEs can only be completed for approved course alternates or double counts

- Any DPEs not already approved for all students, in other words, given as an exception by the program for an individual student, must be initiated by a student's Major Mentor.

text:
This Four-year Academic Planning Template is designed to help you map out your courses, prerequisites, study away experiences, and potential summer classes across all four years of study.

We encourage you to download a copy of the template and begin drafting your plan. Once you have created your version, you can check in with your academic advisor if you have any questions or want to review your progress. Remember to stay flexible — your plan should be updated each semester as your goals evolve and as you make progress in your degree.

In addition, you can find some sample four-year plans that you can use as a starting point.

Please note that your Four-year Plan is meant to serve as a guiding tool only. It does not replace or override official degree requirements. Always consult your Degree Progress Report and your advisor to ensure you are on track.

title: Faculty Mentoring · NYUAD Students
text:
Faculty Mentoring

Undergraduate Faculty mentoring is designed to help students make the most of their academic experience at NYU Abu Dhabi. All students have access to a mentor throughout their time at NYUAD.

Pre-major Mentors

New students are assigned a pre-major Faculty Mentor when they first join NYUAD. Pre-major Mentors are selected faculty who work with the Academic Resource Center to connect students with the NYUAD community, access campus resources, plan for graduate school, and understand a student's field of interest. Pre-major mentors meet with new students online during the summer before they arrive on campus and both in person and online during the academic year. Once a student declares a major, students are then assigned a Faculty Major Mentor. You can find a list of current pre-major Mentors on the student portal.

Major Mentors

Once a student declares a major, they are assigned a Major Mentor, a faculty member in their selected major. Major Mentors can help students navigate degree requirements, prepare for graduate school, and understand their field of study. Once you are assigned a major mentor, you can connect with your mentor via email or during their office hours.
