title: Pre-major Mentors · NYUAD Students
text:
- Najwa Belkziz, Lecturer of Writing

I'm an educator who's passionate about youth and human development. I completed a PhD in History at the University of Melbourne and a Master's in International Affairs from Columbia University in New York City. I also worked on issues of good governance, human rights, and irregular migration in various international organizations across the Arab region. At NYUAD, I enjoy working with students both inside and outside the classroom. I also teach writing and research innovative ways of preserving and presenting historical knowledge. Through interactive exhibits and immersive storytelling, I aim to empower individuals to actively participate in shaping their own histories, present, and futures.

- Marwa Chafii, Associate Professor of Electrical Engineering

Marwa Chafii received her PhD in electrical engineering in 2016, and her Master's degree in the field of advanced wireless communication systems (SAR) in 2013, both from CentraleSupélec, France. Between 2014 and 2016, she was a visiting researcher at Poznan University of Technology (Poland), University of York (UK), Yokohama National University (Japan), and University of Oxford (UK).

- Joe Davies, Visiting Assistant Professor of Music

I am a musicologist and educator specializing in the relationship between music and loss, women in music, and global music history. I hold a DPhil from the University of Oxford and have taught at Oxford, Maynooth University in Ireland, and the University of California, Irvine. At NYU Abu Dhabi, my courses include "Thinking and Writing About Music," a Core Colloquium on "Dreaming," and a First-Year Writing Seminar on "Loss." Across my teaching and mentoring, I encourage students to think holistically about their academic journeys — to embrace their dreams, develop their individual voices, and build connections with one another and the world around them.

- Chinasa Ezugha, Assistant Arts Professor of Live Art/Art as Social Practice

Chinasa Ezugha is a PhD candidate at the University of Exeter. Her interdisciplinary practice spans performance art, film, and drawing. Ezugha holds a BA in Fine Art from Aberystwyth University and an MA in Performance Making from Goldsmiths, University of London.

- Karam Fayad, Lecturer in Mathematics

I am a Lecturer in Mathematics and the Associate Program Head for Undergraduate Studies of Mathematics. I joined NYUAD in 2020 after having completed my PhD in pure mathematics at Sorbonne Université in Paris in 2015, and taught in several higher education institutions in France (Sorbonne Université, CY Tech, Sciences Po) from 2011 to 2020. At NYUAD, I teach within the Math Program (Calculus, Linear Algebra, Foundations of Mathematics...) and the Core Curriculum (Infinity). In the ARC faculty mentor role, and as an educator, I am dedicated to fostering academic excellence, wellness, and belonging. I hope to see you soon!

- Suzanne Manizza Roszak, Associate Professor of Literature and Creative Writing

I am an Associate Professor of Literature and Creative Writing here at NYUAD. I have been teaching university students since 2011; prior to coming to Abu Dhabi, I taught at the University of Groningen in the north of the Netherlands and at US colleges and universities including Scripps College, Occidental College (where I was an academic advisor for pre-majors), and East Carolina University. At NYUAD, I teach courses in creative writing across genres, creative nonfiction writing, and children’s literature. I received my PhD in comparative literature from Yale and my MFA in creative writing from UC Irvine in 2015. I am the author of six books; a couple that you might be interested in include my monograph They Also Write for Kids and my poetry collection Sicilianas , which won the Lauria/Frasca Poetry Prize and was first finalist for the North American Poetry Book Award. I also have two new books forthcoming: a collection of lyric essays and a writing handbook for students of literature who hope to write for publication, which will be published by Rutgers University Press in 2027. When I am not teaching or writing, I serve as the managing editor of Seneca Review , a leading US literary magazine. As an advisor and mentor, I prioritize openness, enthusiasm, and carving out space for joy amid the stresses of student life.

- Pauline Rutsaert, Associate Professor of Practice of Economics

I am an economist with expertise in the fields of Industrial Organization, especially Competition and Regulatory Economics, Industrial and Strategic Trade Policy, Innovation, and R&D. Since joining NYUAD in 2021 I have been teaching Markets and Managerial Economics. Over the years, I worked in different countries (Belgium, Netherlands, United Kingdom, and the UAE) and in various sectors (academic, government, regulatory agencies, economic consultancy firms). I enjoy teaching and interacting with students. My hobbies include walking, cooking, reading, yoga, and meeting with family and friends.

- Hanan Salam, Assistant Professor of Computer Science

Hanan Salam is an AI and robotics expert, an academic, and an entrepreneur. She is the co-founder of Women in AI, an international non-profit Do-Tank whose mission is to close the gender gap in the field of Artificial Intelligence through education, research, and events. She is currently an assistant professor in Computer Science and the director of the Social Machines and Robotics (SMART) Lab at NYUAD. The SMART lab focuses on the development of smart machines endowed with social and emotional intelligence, and their applications in education and well-being. She is a public speaker and an advisor on AI. She has participated as a keynote speaker and panelist in major events and organizations such as UNESCO and OECD world forum. She is currently a member of the UNESCO Women for Ethical AI expert group (Women4Ethical AI), a new collaborative platform to support governments and companies’ efforts to ensure that women are represented equally in both the design and deployment of AI. Prior to this, Hanan was an associate professor in AI at Emlyon Business School in France. She has taught in different higher education French universities, worked in the robotics industry, and as a consultant in AI for several companies. Hanan holds a PhD, an MSc, and an engineering degree in Telecommunications, Information, and Communication Sciences and Technologies. She is an advocate of technology for common good and an activist for women empowerment.

- Khaled Shahin, Senior Lecturer of Civil and Urban Engineering

Khaled Shahin is a Clinical Associate Professor of Structural Engineering and Coordinator of Engineering Assessments at NYU Abu Dhabi, specializing in computational structural mechanics, reliability-based design, and fiber-reinforced polymer composites.

Before joining NYUAD, Khaled served as an assistant professor in the Department of Civil Engineering at Abu Dhabi University, UAE, and prior to that as a senior research engineer at Lloyd’s Register - Martec Ltd. in Halifax, Canada. While at Lloyd’s Register, Khaled completed a two-year postdoctoral industrial R&D fellowship focusing on the reliability-based design of marine composite structures. Khaled received his PhD in Civil Engineering from Dalhousie University in Halifax, Canada where he also completed his undergraduate degree in Civil Engineering.

- Rana Tomaira, Lecturer in Social Research and Public Policy

I am a senior lecturer in Social Research and Public Policy. I joined NYUAD in 2015. I teach three undergraduate courses, "Understanding Urbanization", "Social Change and Development in the Arab World," and "Colonization of Palestine." I received my PhD in City and Regional Planning from UC Berkeley. I also have a masters degree in Architecture from Berekeley and a BSc in Architectural Engineering from the University of Jordan.

title: Meet the ARC Team · NYUAD Students
text:
Last updated April 21, 2026

The John Sexton and Lisa Goldberg Academic Resource Center (ARC), provides students with resources and support to help them achieve their academic goals. Meet our team members:

The ARC Team

- Hema Nair — Director, Academic Advising and the Academic Resource Center

I’m so excited to be the founding Director of the new Academic Resource Center! As an NYU graduate myself, I’m honored to help build a resource for students at the institution I love. I was born in India, grew up in the US, lived in Canada for 14 years with my husband and three girls, and now love being in Abu Dhabi and traveling the world. I was a teacher and Vice Principal in NYC public high schools and, most recently, was an advisor with the NYUAD CDC. I was an Indian classical dancer and dance better than I look like I do! I love hiking, the beach, and game nights. My idea of happiness is a table full of friends and family, good food, and good laughs.

- April Sanders — Associate Director, Academic Resource Center

April is the Assistant Director of the Academic Resource Center and is so excited to help students on their academic journey at NYUAD! April has a passion for advocating, empowering, and supporting international students holistically. She has experience working in public and private higher education institutions in four countries.

April earned her Doctor of Education in Educational Leadership and Policy and her Bachelor of Arts in International Studies in Arabic from the University of Utah in the United States. She also has a Master of Science in Academic Advising from Kansas State University. April conducted research on understanding how international students select higher education and their experiences as students.

April was born in the United States, grew up in the Southeast, and lived in Utah for over 10 years. Outside of work, she loves watching and playing sports, cooking, baking, and traveling.

- Patricia Bandar — Academic Advisor

I’m Patricia, the Academic Advisor at the ARC. I’m here to help you navigate your academic journey with confidence and support by creating a supportive space where you can explore your goals and grow your strengths with clarity and self-awareness.

I have a Master’s in Communication from Northwestern University and experience working in higher education across Europe and the US.

I love spending quality time with family and friends, sharing good food, laughter, and meaningful conversations. I also enjoy travelling and discovering new places and experiences.

- Reenas Mohamed — Academic Advisor

Hi, I’m Reenas!

As an Academic Advisor at the ARC, I’m passionate about helping students find their footing and, more importantly, ensuring they feel they truly belong. Having grown up in the diverse city of Toronto, I learned early on the beauty of a multicultural community. That foundation followed me through my undergraduate degree at the University of Toronto and Master's degree at York University, which then led me to international development work across Africa.

Those experiences shaped my deep commitment to creating inclusive, equitable spaces where every student feels seen and supported. I’m here to be your advocate and a resource as you navigate the complexities of university life.

I believe life is about the journey, whether that’s an academic one, a flight to a new country, or a meal at a restaurant. I can’t wait to meet you all, hear about your own adventures, and help you thrive here at NYUAD!

- Firdous Rafiqueddin — Academic Advisor

Firdous is thrilled to join the ARC Team as an Academic Advisor. Born and raised in Dubai, she holds an MBA and has spent several years working in education, helping students find their best path because she understands firsthand how challenging that can be. She enjoys making student's academic lives a bit less stressful and more manageable, and she finds it rewarding to help people navigate their way, even when things get a little confusing.

Outside of work, you will often find Firdous hopping between cafés. No coffee for her, but she is all about the vibes. She enjoys trying to master new board games, even though she is usually the one losing, and blasting everything from sad songs to Spanish, Arabic, French, and anything else that catches her ear. Her playlists are all over the place, so one minute it might be a mellow tune and the next a full on dance party.

- Husain Shafei — Academic Advisor

Husain is a higher education professional committed to supporting students in dynamic, cross-cultural environments. He helps institutions to design programs and policies that help equip students and professionals with the leadership skills and experiences needed to thrive in an increasingly diverse and competitive world. Before joining NYU Abu Dhabi, Husain worked as a Program Manager and Advisor, where he supported both undergraduate and graduate students through study abroad and international programs. Husain is a recipient of the Marxe International Scholarship, He holds a Master’s degree in Higher Education Administration from Baruch College - City University of New York, and a Bachelor’s degree in Web Media from Bahrain Polytechnic. Husain’s research interests include student organizations, campus diversity, and student success. Outside of work, he enjoys running, Esports, and volunteering with international organizations like the Global Shapers Community. He’s always open to chat with students about their university experience and leadership development.

- Amna Alketbi — Administrative Coordinator

Hi! I’m Amna Alketbi, the Administrative Coordinator at the Academic Resource Center at NYU Abu Dhabi.

I have a bachelor's degree in Biomedical Engineering, and in my role, I help with department operations and coordination of the peer tutoring program, and provide front-line advising to students. I enjoy interacting with students and helping them navigate their academic journey, ensuring they have the support and resources they need to succeed.

Outside of work, I spend my time with family, going to the gym, or unwinding at the beach. Staying active and connected keeps me balanced and motivated. Being part of the NYU Abu Dhabi community allows me to contribute to students’ success and support the smooth functioning of the ARC.

title: Peer Tutoring · NYUAD Students
text:
The Academic Resource Center in partnership with NYUAD Academic Divisions offer peer tutoring services to students in a number of areas.

Peer Tutors are undergraduate students and students who performed well in specific courses and have been trained to provide support and guidance.

- Peer tutoring is not a substitute for support from your instructor or professor.

- Students should consult with a Peer Tutor in addition to , not instead of, the instructor or professor.

- Tutors are there to support, guide, and teach topics. They are not there to do the assignment. Please refer to the University Academic Integrity policy .

Peer tutors are NYUAD undergraduates in the following subjects:

- Computer Science

- Intro to Computer Science

- Discrete Math

- Data Structures

- Algorithms

- Computer Systems Organizations

- Software Engineering

- Operating Systems

- Computer Networks

- Select electives

- Engineering

- Computer Programming for Engineers

- Conservation Laws

- Statics

- Numerical Methods

- Circuits

- Digital Logic

- Advanced Digital Logic

- Advanced Circuits

- Fundamentals of Complex Variables

- Solid Mechanics

- Fluid Mechanics

- Dynamics

- Foundations of Science

- Foundations of Science 1-4: Biology, Chemistry, and Physics

- Foundations of Science 5-6: Biology and Physics

- Math

- Math 1000A and 1000B

- Calculus with Applications to Science and Engineering

- Calculus with Applications to Economics

- Multivariable Calculus with Applications to Science and Engineering

- Multivariable Calculus with Applications to Economics

- Linear Algebra

- Foundations of Mathematics

- Social Science

- Statistics for Social and Behavioral Sciences

- Global Economic, Political and Social Development since 1500 (GEPS)

- Markets

- Data Analysis

What to Expect with Peer Tutoring

Important things to know about Peer Tutoring:

Students can access peer tutoring services by appointment or by drop-in, depending on the subject.

Drop-in Tutoring

- Subjects: Drop-in tutoring is available for Computer Science, Engineering, and Math subjects.

- The drop-in schedule is updated every semester and is reflected on NYUConnect .

- Required Check-in: For drop-in tutoring services, all students must follow the check-in instructions:

- Scan the QR code at the drop-in location.

- Select the course for tutoring.

- Describe what they need help with in the detailed description area.

Appointments

- Subjects: Appointments are available for Engineering, Foundations of Science, Math, and Social Science.

- Booking: For scheduled appointments, all students must book an appointment through NYUConnect and describe what they need help with in advance in the detailed description area.

- Appointments are scheduled for 60 minutes.

All Sessions

- Location: All sessions must take place in designated spaces, as outlined by the ARC.

- Preparation: Students should come to each session prepared with relevant materials, and an idea of the topics they need assistance with, so that the tutor can be most helpful.

- Cancellation: Students must give at least advance notice if they want to cancel an appointment. Multiple no-shows or late cancellations can result in restricted access to tutoring sessions.

How to Book An Appointment

To book a peer tutoring appointment through NYU Connect, follow these steps:

- Visit the NYU Connect website.

- Log in to your account.

- Click on the “Academic Resource Center (ARC) @ Tutoring” card.

- Select whether you need tutoring in Computer Science, Engineering, Math, Foundations of Science, or Social Science.

- Select a tutor in the course you need assistance with

- Select a time.

- Indicate whether this is for exam prep, course content, assignment help, or other.

- In the Description box, provide information about the specific topics you need help with.

- Check your email to receive the location of the session.

Related official links:
https://students.nyuad.nyu.edu/academics/registration/academic-policies/academic-integrity/

sections.title: What to Expect with Peer Tutoring · Drop-in Tutoring

sections.title: What to Expect with Peer Tutoring · All Sessions
sections.text:

sections.title: How to Book An Appointment
sections.text:

title: Capstone Projects · NYUAD Students
text:
During the fourth year, every NYUAD student will produce a Capstone project, which may be either an individual or team project. Students do a Capstone project in their major field. The Capstone project is a demanding, year-long endeavor aiming at a significant piece of research or creative work — a historical narrative, musical composition, performance, invention, documented experiment, scholarly thesis, or other form appropriate to the student's goals.

Arts & Humanities

Students explore fundamental questions of human thought, cultural values, and modes of expression, and develop their own creative capacities as scholars, writers, and artists in a variety of media.

Engineering

The goal of the Capstone Design Project is to provide students with a major design experience that leverages the knowledge and skills acquired through the curriculum and incorporates appropriate engineering standards and multiple realistic constraints.

Science

The interdisciplinary nature of modern scientific research requires that biologists, chemists, computer scientists, engineers, mathematicians, and physicists have a fundamental understanding of multiple scientific disciplines and their interrelationships.

Social Science

Social science majors will produce a piece of original research to meet the capstone requirement. Students may collect their own data, conduct simulations, or analyze available data to make a contribution to the research in the field of their choice.

title: Arts & Humanities · NYUAD Students
text:
The Capstone AY25/26 Timeline and Deadline Overview can be found here .

The Capstone project is a demanding year-long endeavor aimed at creating a significant piece of research and/or creative work. This can take the form of a thesis project: for example, an historical narrative; an analysis and discussion; and/or participation within an ongoing philosophical or theoretical debate. Capstone projects can also take the form of (for instance) a musical composition, a performance, a film or documentary, a series or prints or other visual “inventions.”

The Capstone experience culminates in the public presentation of the student project during the Capstone festival and a Capstone defense.

Capstone Advising and Seminars

The Capstone experience consists of a seminar offered by the respective major (taken in the first and second semester of the senior year) and a year-long individualized thesis tutorial with an individual advisor.

It provides seniors with the opportunity to work closely with a faculty mentor in the form of a (weekly) tutorial and to produce a senior thesis project. In the tutorial, students work on a one-to-one basis with a faculty director to hone their research and produce successive drafts of a senior thesis throughout the senior year.

Program heads and/or program committees will vet the proposals, and Capstone advisors will be assigned to the students. Students will be permitted to request particular faculty capstone advisors, who may already be engaged in advising the students, though the final assignment rests with the program head of the student’s major. Students may be asked to revise and resubmit their proposal.

The Capstone advisor, the Capstone seminar leader, as well as the program head will monitor and be in regular exchange about the progress of each Capstone project.

title: Capstone FAQs · NYUAD Students
text:
Capstone Funding FAQs

- What mechanisms will be set up for students to receive funds for Capstone research?

Students will have to submit a detailed budget to their Capstone advisors for approval. Once the capstone advisor has reviewed and approved the budget, students will have to submit their advisors’ approval and the budget online through the A&H Capstone Student Portal page.

More information will be provided by a divisional representative. Any questions or concerns can be sent to: nyuad.ah.capstones@nyu.edu .

- What funds are available for Capstones?

Limited funding will be available on a competitive basis. Capstone budgets will go through a rigorous review and approval process and the funding awarded will be determined on a discretionary basis. We want to encourage you to utilize the resources that are available on campus, from your respective disciplinary programs, the Library, and so on.

Students who meet the summer funding guidelines, and are taking part in research over the summer (capstones or not) may apply for funding via the Summer Undergraduate Research Grant Application form .

- Do collaborative Capstones receive combined budgets?

No. Students working together will be funded for one project.

- Can I raise money to supplement my budget?

No. We want to encourage you to find the maximum of your creativity within constraints and fiscal resourcefulness.

General Capstone FAQs

- Do we accept a Capstone Adviser from outside our standing faculty?

Rarely, and only with permission from the Dean.

- What will the grading be like?

The grade for first semester will be a combination of the grade for the seminar and the advisor’s assessment.

The grade for the second semester will be the grade given by the panel for the final thesis/project and defense with input from the seminar director.

- Can I take more than the recommended number of classes while I am finishing my Capstone?

We would discourage that, as the work on the Capstone project will be very absorbing.

- Can film students film anywhere?

No. Film students can film only in the UAE.

- How does one solicit crews, actors and performers for film projects?

Other NYUAD students can serve as your crew and are the most likely pool of performers. Please consult the program’s guidelines for specific direction.

- Can theater and music students stage shows anywhere?

Theater students are restricted to city of Abu Dhabi. Music students can produce work or stage concerts in Abu Dhabi.

- Where can visual art students produce work?

Visual arts students can produce work in the Abu Dhabi.

https://students.nyuad.nyu.edu/academics/research/summer-research-grants/

title: Capstone Funding Reconciliation · NYUAD Students
text:
Capstone Funding Reconciliation

When your project has concluded, you will need to submit documentation (detailed receipts) of appropriately spending the funds you received. This is called reconciliation and is a separate submission process called the Capstone Funding Reconciliation.

You can view an example Capstone Expense Reconciliation Packet here .

Failure to complete the Capstone Funding Reconciliation will result in a hold on your diploma after graduation and until you have completed the reconciliation and it is approved by the university.

To complete your reconciliation, follow the step-by-step instructions below:

Step 1: Complete the “ Capstone Expense Reconciliation ” sheet with all information, including:

- The full amount of funding that was added to your card (no need to list funds that were spent on your behalf, but not provided directly to you, i.e. your program ordered an item and paid for it with program funds).

- If you need more rows to list out receipts, you can add them by doing the following:

- Highlight a row, right-click, and select “Insert”, or click on the Insert option on the Home Tab.

- Ensure the numbers of each line item (the first column) are in the same order of your receipts

- List the currency on the receipt. If it is not in AED already, you will also need to convert the amount to AED, and put the converted amount in the AED column.

- For USD/AED conversions, the form automatically does the conversion. For USD, multiply the figure by 3.673.

- For additional currency conversions, use Oanda.com enter the amount in the original currency, and convert it to AED. Attach the currency converter page and combine it with the related receipt.

- Once you have completed the reconciliation sheet, the balance will be listed in red at the end of the sheet.

Step 2: Compile all of the below documents in the following order into a single PDF file** to complete your reconciliation packet

- Cover letter: “ Capstone Reconciliation Form ”; to be filled and signed by yourself

- “ Capstone Expense Reconciliation ”(sheet); completed as per the directions in step 1 above.

- Scanned Receipts (numbered and in the same order as the line items/column 1 number in your “Capstone Expense Reconciliation” sheet). Remember to review the receipt instructions in the above section Step 6 “Track receipts and invoices”

- Email nyuad.ah.capstoneadmin@nyu.edu as soon as possible if you are missing any receipts.

Step 3: Return borrowed items and any non-consumable items (i.e. not single use items like fabric, stage makeup, etc.) you purchased with divisional Capstone funding to the respective storage place for the item type (i.e. prop loan for props and furniture/set pieces, equipment center for technology and devices, IM lab for IM specific technology and devices, etc.). Perpetual Software Licenses (University-Owned & Transferable) p urchased under a divisional account, installed on university or personal devices (if justified) should also be returned upon project completion. Kindly refer to the Capstone Capstone Project Software and Hardware Purchasing Guidelines for more details.

Step 4: Share the completed single PDF packet as above with your Capstone advisor and have them go over it to make sure it is complete. Ask them to e-sign their section of the “Capstone Reconciliation Form” in your PDF packet.

Step 5: Once you have the fully completed and signed single PDF reconciliation packet, email the full packet to nyuad.ah.capstoneadmin@nyu.edu for their review and final approval.

Step 6: Respond to any requests for additional information or adjustments to your reconciliation packet.
Once the administration team has reviewed your application they may have some questions, request additional information, or ask you to make adjustments to your application. Your reconciliation packet will be pending until all final adjustments are made and the packet is approved by the administration team. After that, the administration team will send your approved packet to the Office of Student Finance for processing.

Step 7: Keep an eye out in your email inbox for an email from the Office of Student Finance to settle your funding balance. Note that failure to settle any outstanding balance with the university will result in a hold on your diploma until the process has been completed.

You can view an example Capstone Expense Reconciliation Packet here .

title: Preparing Your Advanced Funding Application · NYUAD Students
text:
Preparing Your Advanced Funding Application

You can apply for your Advanced Funding Application here .

General overview

To manage your Capstone funding, start by planning your project budget. Once the budget is drafted, submit your advanced funding application during the open application window. If any additional information or adjustments are requested, respond promptly, and once approved, sign the funding award letter. After approval, student finance will upload the funds to your account, allowing you to order the necessary materials. Be sure to track all receipts and invoices as you go. Finally, submit your Capstone funding reconciliation and return items borrowed and/or purchase using university funds before the deadline towards the end of the semester.

You can view an example Advanced Funding Application .

Tip! Once you submit your Advanced Funding Application, it may take 4-6 weeks for processing. Please ensure that you plan your project timelines accordingly.

Step 1: Plan your project budget

This step is a moment for you to brainstorm the practical needs of your project and to research items and resources that you will need. Once you have determined your resource needs and costs you can compile them into a budget proposal using the Capstone Budget Template .

Tips for planning your budget:

-
Develop a financial plan for producing your project. Start by creating a comprehensive list of anticipated expenses and categorizing them by expense type to ensure you cover all necessary items. Make sure to think about items you need for process/development as well as items for the final showcase of your project.

-
Evaluate: Are there free alternatives available? Can you borrow items instead of purchasing them? What items are the highest priority?

-
Cross-check your list of needs with existing resources before putting together your budget request.

-
Refine your list and research prices to ensure everything fits within your total budget.

-
Compare vendors before making a purchase. Determine whether it’s more cost-effective to order from international or local sources.

-
Attach price quotes for items to your budget application.

-
Make sure you include shipping costs into your estimates.

- For Capstone Film students, you can allocate a maximum amount of 50 AED per person/day for meals for the crew.

-
Include a financial buffer. Set aside 15-25% of your budget for unexpected costs that might arise.

Step 2: Submit your advanced funding application during the open application window

This step is for you to organize all of your Capstone budget planning into an application packet, which will need to be reviewed and signed off by your Capstone advisor and technical consultant before you submit the application. After you have their approvals and signatures and your Capstone application packet is complete with each required document, you will submit the application. From there, the A&H Divisional Administration Team will review your application.

To prepare your Advanced Funding Application, compile all of the below documents in the following order into a single PDF file :

- Letter of Support to be filled out by your advisor and technical consultant (if applicable). This document is meant to be filled and signed by your advisor and technical consultant after they have reviewed and approved your Capstone funding application packet, this will be the first page of your application packet.

- Budget Template filled with all expected expenses, links to price quotes (price given by vendor, Amazon listing link, etc.), and a detailed budget justification for each line item. You are welcome to use the budget template provided or create your own chart using the same layout in the program of your choice (Microsoft Word, Excel, etc.)

You can view an example Advanced Funding Application here .

PDF Merging tip! To merge all of your documents into a single PDF as required, you can use Adobe’s free PDF merge website and follow their easy steps. You can also do this with the Adobe Acrobat desktop application, by signing in to the application on a university computer with your NetID email.

Step 3: Respond to any requests for additional information or adjustments to your application, and once approved, sign the funding award letter

Once you submit your application it will be sent to the A&H Divisional Administration Team who will review your application for the first round of approvals. Once the administration team has reviewed your application, they may have some questions, request additional information, or ask you to make adjustments to your application.

Once your application packet has been approved, the A&H divisional administration will request for you to read carefully and sign an award letter.

Step 4: Upon approval of funding application, Student Finance will upload the money to your account

Once the administration team has received your signed award letter, they will share your approved packet with Student Finance to process payment. Please note that from the moment student finance receives the payment request it may take some time before it is paid to your account as they will need to process the request.

Tip! Once you submit your Advanced Funding Application, it may take 4-6 weeks for processing. This includes review and potential adjustments by the A&H Divisional Administration Team, approval, and the final distribution of funds by the Office of Student Finance. Please ensure that you plan your project timelines accordingly, allowing sufficient time not only for the approval and funding process but also for making purchases and receiving any materials or equipment. Be mindful that delivery times can vary, so request funding and place orders as early as possible to avoid delays.

Step 5: Order materials

Now that you have your funding approved and money available, you can begin purchasing your items as per your approved budget.

*For FNM Students , once you purchase your props, have your filming set ready, please ensure you follow the NYUAD On Campus Filming Procedure for Students .

Step 6: Track receipts and invoices

Save all your receipts. Organize them in one place, and maintain a running total of your expenses to keep track of your remaining budget and potential reimbursements.

At the time of payment, please request both the proof of payment receipt as well as an itemized receipt/invoice that lists the item(s) purchased, date, and name of the vendor. Collect and keep every piece of documentation possible. For any cash expenses, you must provide an itemized receipt for all the items purchased with cash. Any remaining cash withdrawn from an ATM that was not used for purchases will be considered unused funds and must be returned to the university when you complete the funding reconciliation.

Unacceptable receipts

Some types of receipts are unacceptable or insufficient as proof of payment. Submitting any of the following types of receipts will result in the purchase being classified as unused funds, which must be returned to the university from your personal funds when you complete the funding reconciliation.

- ATM receipts are not acceptable as proof of payment and will result in the purchase being classified as unused funds.

- SMS screenshots showing your credit card being charged a certain amount are not acceptable and will result in the purchase being classified as unused funds.

- Credit card transaction receipts without the supporting itemized receipts are not acceptable and will result in the purchase being classified as unused funds.

- Receipts with incomplete vendor information, such as when the vendor details are cut off, are not acceptable and will result in the purchase being classified as unused funds.

Step 7: Submit Capstone funding reconciliation before the deadline

When your project has concluded, you will need to submit documentation (detailed receipts) of appropriately spending the funds you received. This is called reconciliation and is a separate submission process called the Capstone Funding Reconciliation.

Failure to complete the Capstone Funding Reconciliation will result in a hold on your diploma after graduation and until you have completed the reconciliation and it is approved by the university.

Click here to follow the step-by-step Capstone Funding Reconciliation instructions.

title: Juniors · NYUAD Students
text:
Time Frame for Capstone Project

Fall of Junior Year

Contact and/or meetings with arts and humanities majors to map out the Capstone process. Students will have already begun thinking about a Capstone in conjunction with the choice to major in certain disciplines and/or from work done in courses and will have been discussing ideas with their professors.

Fall and Spring of Junior Year

Students must submit their capstone proposal as per the deadline provided by their program. The proposal must be submitted via this form .

In general, proposals will consist of a written document of about five pages indicating the research topic and/or creative project; a plan/time-frame for getting the work done; an indication of the bibliography or source materials to be used in realizing the project; and a budget detailing what monies will be necessary to complete the project.

Students must also consult the specific guidelines for their major(s) when completing the proposal form.

Program heads and/or program committees will vet the proposals, and Capstone advisers will be assigned to the students. Students will be permitted to request particular faculty Capstone advisers, who may already be engaged in advising the students, though the final assignment rests with the program head of the student’s major. During April and early May, you will work with your advisor and program head on revisions, and will submit to them a final draft by the deadline set by your program.

Summer Between Junior and Senior Years

Appropriate work to ground the Capstone should be launched (script-writing, researching, collecting data, exploring, amassing bibliography, reading, etc.). The Capstone advisor(s) will help determine the parameters for this work and stay in touch over the summer.

Arts

This seminar will focus on supporting students as they develop their individual projects and begin writing their reflective papers. Throughout this process, students will gradually be guided towards a more precise focus of their project (outlines, pre-production work, presentation, exhibition, and/or performance).

The detailed design for each seminar will be determined by the respective program.

Students will also work individually with their specific adviser(s), usually seeing them once a week.

Humanities

In the fall semester, particular attention will be paid to the organization and practice of research in the respective major to master the specific questions and requirements of discipline, as well as evidence, method, and scholarly habit and process.

Skills and concepts discussed and developed in the context of the workshop will always be tailored according to the needs of each project and shared with students’ individual Capstone advisers.

Arts

Humanities

Continuation of research for, as well as writing sections or chapters of thesis.

Spring of Senior Year

Arts

The seminars continue for the first half of the semester and focus on critiquing works in progress. Practice students will complete their projects.

Humanities

In the spring semester, the Capstone seminar will pay particular attention to drafting, editing, and developing oral presentation skills both for the Capstone.

text:
Capstone Festivals

Arts and Humanities | April 2026 — View details

Engineering | May 8, 2026 — View details

Science | May 7, 2026 — View details

Social Science | May 8, 2026 — View details

Arts and Humanities

During the fourth year, all NYUAD students produce a capstone project — either as an individual or team — in their major field. The Capstone Project is a demanding, yearlong endeavor aiming at a significant piece of research or creative work — an historical narrative, musical composition, performance, invention, documented experiment, scholarly thesis, or other form appropriate to the student’s goals. Unlike other courses in which faculty establish the structure and set assignments, students work independently with guidance from NYUAD faculty. The fundamental challenge is to extend oneself in making knowledge, reframing conventional approaches to an issue, or creating something new.

Program Summary

The Arts and Humanities Capstone Festival is the culmination of this yearlong process and a celebration of the work created across the arts and humanities.

Dates: April 2026

Engineering

The Engineering Capstone Festival celebrates the culmination of a year-long design experience in which senior engineering students develop innovative solutions to real-world challenges. Drawing on the knowledge and skills gained throughout their undergraduate education, students present projects that integrate technical rigor with human, aesthetic, and business considerations. The Festival highlights creativity, research, and applied problem-solving while marking the completion of our seniors’ Capstone journey.

- Program
Date : Friday, May 8th 2026
Venue : A5 Lobby

Science

The Science Capstone Festival is a University-wide celebration of student research, bringing together the NYUAD community to recognize the achievements of graduating Science majors. It provides an opportunity for students to share their Capstone projects with peers, faculty, and guests in an engaging and interactive setting. The Festival is designed to be a fun, celebratory event, a chance for students to showcase their hard work, connect with the scientific community, and celebrate the completion of their Capstone journey.

- Program
Date : Thursday, May 7th 2026
Venue : Computational Research Building (A2) Lobby

Social Science

During their final year at NYUAD, Social Science majors have collected their own data, conducted simulations, and reanalyzed available data in order to produce an original piece of research, making a meaningful contribution to the field of their choice. Working closely with faculty, our seniors have addressed a vast array of pressing contemporary issues that affect individual and societal well-being.

We invite you to attend the Social Science Capstone Festival, where we showcase a sample of the best research across our majors: Business, Organizations and Society; Economics; Political Science; and Social Research and Public Policy.

title: Engineering Design Project · NYUAD Students
text:
The goal of the Capstone Design Project is to provide students with a major design experience that leverages the knowledge and skills acquired through the curriculum and incorporates appropriate engineering standards and multiple realistic constraints.

The Capstone Design Project is collaborative and trans-disciplinary across several engineering streams. The emphasis is on educating students to solve real-world problems in an environment resembling a technologically advanced 21st century global workplace. Capstone projects address engineering and technology topics that may also involve science, business, social sciences and liberal arts. A team of students are challenged to design innovative engineering-based solutions after examining multiple aspects of the problem. Simulations/physical prototypes as well as other types of validations are highly recommended for the solution designed. The composition of the team is based on the nature of the problem, student interests and the needed skill set. It provides an opportunity for teams to integrate technical, human, aesthetic and business concerns with engineering design.

Design Project Details

- Objectives

Each team tackles an engineering challenge, a problem of importance, or an engineering aspiration, and develops a problem statement, including constraints.

The team is to design innovative engineering-based solutions by leveraging the knowledge and skills acquired through the curriculum.

Appropriate engineering standards must be considered.

Capstone projects may be collaborative and interdisciplinary, combining several engineering streams or including disciplines such as science, business, social sciences, liberal arts, and others.

Realization of the design solution and validation/testing through simulations and/or building physical prototype is expected.

- Timeline

Junior Fall

- Faculty members identify possible projects and topics.

Junior Spring

- "Ideas week" for faculty to present their interests and possible project areas to students, and for students to convey their interests.

- Student discussions with faculty one-to-one

- Teams register for a capstone project.

- Identify gaps in skills.

Senior Fall

- Attend lectures and continue to acquire skills as needed.

- Students attend seminars given by engineering faculty (standing & affiliated) and invited speakers.

- Design solutions for the problem being addressed.

- Generate proposal identifying the solution pathway. The rationale for the choices made should be included in the proposal.

- Identify the items/parts/components required to implement the solution designed.

J-Term

- Procure the items required for the implementation of the design solution as needed.

Senior Spring

- Implement the chosen solution.

- Presentation of the implemented project.

- Course Structure

The Capstone sequence consists of four 7-week Modules:

Senior Capstone Design Project I (ENGR-UH-4010) — Fall

- Module I: Planning the Project: project management, design theory, etc.

- Module II: Designing the Solution

Senior Capstone Design Project II (ENGR-UH-4011) — Spring

- Module III: Implementation: prototype construction, etc.

- Module IV: Testing and verification

The fall modules are very structured, including weekly lectures, homework assignments, and midterm, to help guide you through the design process. The format in the spring is more flexible, but will still contain important milestones to be met.

- Project Requirements

- Team Composition: Typically at least three members. However, for the class of 2014 teams of two members will be considered. Team members need not be engineering majors, but must be chosen such that their skills bring specific value to the project.

- Each Capstone Project requires a faculty mentor. The faculty mentor must:

-
Approve the Capstone Project Prospectus

- Have professional expertise the primary areas of the Capstone Project

- Be physically present in Abu Dhabi for regular mentoring during both semesters

- Capstone Project Prospectus

- Outlines the purpose and scope of the project, introduces significant prior work and provides a list of specifications for the final design.

- Identifies the skills, experience, equipment, and resources required to successfully complete the project.

- Project Approval Process

Capstone Project applications will be submitted to the Dean of Engineering. The engineering faculty (including the Dean of Engineering) will discuss the merits of each Capstone Project and determine its suitability as a Capstone Project. A complete application for Capstone contains the following:

- Cover sheet

- Prospectus (Project Overview)

- Project specification

- Student team member resumes

- Faculty mentor CV

- Statement of support from faculty mentor

- Proposed project budget

- Pre-approved Projects

Project | Mentor(s)

FPGA-based Fast Microprocessor Simulation (PDF) | Prof. Michail Maniatakos

Sustainable Living Space (PDF) | Prof. Masoud Ghandehari

Automatic Test Pattern Generation System for VLSI Stuck-at-Faults (PDF) | Prof. Ozgur Sinanoglu

A Portable Sea Water Desalination System (PDF) | Prof. Rafael Song Prof. Ramesh Jagannathan Prof. Sachin Khapli

Ultrasensitive Point-of-Care Diagnostic Chip for Global Health (PDF) | Prof. Rafael Song Prof. Ramesh Jagannathan Prof. Sachin Khapli

A Microfluidic Chip for Marine Microbiology (PDF) | Prof. Rafael Song Prof. Ramesh Jagannathan Prof. Sachin Khapli

A Serious Game for Teaching Engineering Statics (PDF) | Prof. Douglas Cook Dr. Mohamad Eid

Inventing a Saxophone Mute (PDF) | Prof. Douglas Cook

Arabic Sign Language Interpreter using Microsoft Kinect (PDF) | Prof. Abdulmotaleb El Saddik Dr. Mohamad Eid

A Robust Process Control Module for Supercritical CO2 Aerosol System (PDF) | Prof. Ramesh Jagannathan Prof. Sachin Khapli Dr. Philip Panicker

An Inkjet Aerosol Generator to Create Metal Oxide Nanostructures (PDF) | Prof. Ramesh Jagannathan Prof. Sachin Khapli Prof. Rafael Song

- Timeline and Important Dates

Immediately: Start forming student teams and discussing project topics with faculty mentors.

April 15: Deadline for submitting Capstone Application to Dean of Engineering.

May 31: Final date for teams to register for capstone project

August 18-22: Immersive skill building workshop

- Students with Double Majors

Need to complete only one capstone project.

If engineering is one of the majors the student must be enrolled in engineering capstone to satisfy accreditation.

Students from other divisions can be part of engineering capstone after the Deans (engineering and other division) approve.

- Engineering Curriculum Handbook

Download the Engineering Curriculum Handbook here .

title: Science Capstone · NYUAD Students
text:
The Capstone Project is the culminating experience of every Science major at NYU Abu Dhabi. It represents the transition from student to researcher, and is an opportunity to apply scientific training, creativity, and critical thinking to a focused, original research question.

Working under the guidance of a faculty supervisor, students design and conduct research, analyze data, and communicate their findings in both written and oral form. The project concludes with a final written thesis, an oral presentation, and a public presentation at the annual Science Capstone Festival, where students showcase their discoveries to the wider NYUAD community.

Before beginning the Capstone, all Science majors complete a Research Seminar in their junior year. This course introduces students to current faculty research, helps them identify potential supervisors, and guides them in developing a formal Capstone Project proposal.

Capstone Pathways by Program

Each Science program has its own structure and timeline for completing the Capstone, including when students take the Research Seminar and when the Capstone Project itself begins. While the overall process is similar across the Division, the specific course codes, prerequisites, and semester offerings vary by discipline.

Students should always refer to the NYU Abu Dhabi Academic Bulletin for the most up-to-date information about:

- The semester in which the Research Seminar is offered

- Prerequisites and eligibility requirements

- The timing and sequence of Capstone courses

- Requirements for secondary majors

Capstone Deliverables

Regardless of program, every Capstone experience includes the following components:

- Research Proposal : Developed during the junior-year Research Seminar course.

- Independent Research : Conducted under faculty supervision during the senior year.

- Written Thesis : A formal report documenting the research and its findings.

- Oral Presentation : Delivered during a scheduled Capstone Defense, to a selected committee of faculty members or, in the case of Psychology students, at the Science Capstone Festival itself.

- Archival Submission : Final thesis uploaded to the NYUAD Library Repository.

-

Capstone Proposal

Complete the Senior Capstone Proposal for your project.

-

Capstone Submission

Submit your final Science Capstone project with this form.

title: Science Capstone Festival · NYUAD Students
text:
Science Capstone Festival 2026 : Thursday, May 7th 2026

The Science Capstone Festival is a University-wide celebration of student research, bringing together the NYUAD community to recognize the achievements of graduating Science majors. It provides an opportunity for students to share their Capstone projects with peers, faculty, and guests in an engaging and interactive setting.

An administrative representative will contact all eligible students closer to the event with detailed instructions, including submission deadlines, format specifications, and logistics.

As a general guideline, all Science students are required to prepare and submit the following materials:

- A scientific poster summarizing your Capstone research

- A PDF document including your name, project title, and a 100–200-word synopsis of your work

Submission of these materials is mandatory. While attendance for the full day of the festival is not required, students are expected to attend for a time to present their poster and discuss their research with visitors. Psychology seniors must be present during their assigned presentation session.

The Festival is designed to be a fun, celebratory event, a chance for students to showcase their hard work, connect with the scientific community, and celebrate the completion of their Capstone journey.

title: Science Capstone Funding · NYUAD Students
text:
- Each student is eligible for up to USD 1,500 in Capstone funding.

- Funding is limited, not guaranteed, and subject to approval by the Office of the Dean.

- Requests may cover research materials, non-available software, participant survey costs, and Capstone-related travel.

Key Guidelines

- All funding must be requested in one submission . It is expected that students plan and request funding with foresight, as multiple separate requests for the same project will not be processed.

- If requesting conference travel, a second funding letter can be submitted later once the presentation of Capstone work is confirmed and finalized.

- The funding letter must indicate how funds are to be received (departmental purchase, quote/purchase order, or FAB student card load).

- Funding letters must be dated and signed by both the student and mentor.

- Participant survey costs require prior IRB approval, submitted with the request.

- Any tangible items purchased with Capstone funds are property of NYUAD and must be returned to the Science Division at the end of the project.

- Travel funding will only be considered after the student has completed the Undergraduate Research Conference Grant Funding Application Form and only if the travel is directly related to the Capstone project.

- If total requested funding exceeds USD 1,500, the excess must be covered by the mentor’s 76 Research Fund.

- Applications are accepted on a rolling basis. Capstone funding is unavailable during Summer (from May 1, 2027).

- For J-Term housing, the primary Capstone mentor must be physically on campus to oversee the project.

- Student card loads take approximately 10 business days to reflect in the student’s account after submission to Student Finance.

- Any tangible items purchased using Capstone funds remain the property of the University and must be returned to the administration at the end of the project, and no later than May 1, 2027.

- Unused funds need to be returned by May 1, 2027.

title: Science Project Proposal · NYUAD Students
text:
Students begin their Capstone journey by developing a research proposal in consultation with their faculty advisor. The proposal should define a clear research question, outline objectives and methodology, and identify the relevance and potential contribution of the project.

Each program sets specific deadlines and requirements for proposal submission and approval. Once approved, students begin data collection, experimentation, or modeling as appropriate to their discipline. Throughout the process, students are expected to maintain regular contact with their advisor and submit progress updates as required by their program.

title: Social Science Projects · NYUAD Students
text:
All majors in the social sciences will produce a piece of original research to meet the Capstone requirement. Students will work closely with their faculty mentor to develop and implement a research design for the Capstone project.

Students may collect their own data, conduct simulations, or analyze available data to make a contribution to the research in the field of their choice. The resulting paper should aim at a format common for the best academic journal articles in the student's discipline.

Fieldwork

Students who wish to do fieldwork abroad should develop the project in the spring of junior year and obtain approval from the faculty mentor to collect data during study abroad or in the summer before senior year. The NYUAD Institutional Review Board must approve all projects that involve human subjects before data collection begins. Fieldwork abroad will likely require further approval by the relevant institutions in the place where the data will be collected. For IRB related questions please contact Nancy Wallach at nyuad.undergraduateresearch@nyu.edu .

Capstone Advising

While social science majors are largely developing a project of their own choice, they do so by working closely with a faculty member, the Capstone adviser. Often, the Capstone adviser will not be your major mentor — rather, it will be a faculty member who knows the literature and research methodology that is relevant for your Capstone project and is therefore best equipped to work with you. To get help with finding a Capstone adviser, talk to your major mentor or program head.

Capstone Seminars

Seniors will attend a two-term, mandatory bi-weekly Capstone seminar, which is moderated by a faculty member and serves as a forum for peer review and feedback on progress with the senior thesis. Students are assigned to sections of the Capstone seminars based on the nature of their project.

SSEL Laboratory General Policies

The SSEL resources are available upon request to NYUAD faculty and students. For more information about our laboratory and our services, please visit us at ssel-lab.com .

Please see our guidelines for Capstone students (PDF) and SSEL's official rules and procedur00es (PDF).

Capstone Funding

NYUAD has limited funding to support Capstone projects. We may be able to fund travel, and research related expenses (such as expenses related to acquiring datasets, setting up experiments, or transcribing interviews). Funding for housing or accommodation will only be considered under exceptional circumstances. Please be aware that funding is limited and students must submit a full rationale for all funding requests.

Apply for funding to support the research for your project (juniors and seniors only).

Funding Application Deadlines

For students requiring J-Term housing : TBC

Final deadline for all students :

- All students must submit their Capstone Funding Application by the final deadline of Friday, November 13, 2026, at 11:59pm GST .

To avoid delays in processing, please use the provided templates and submit a detailed funding proposal. Incomplete applications will be returned. All applications will be reviewed and approved based on merit.

Please contact Shaikha Alobaidalla at saa847@nyu.edu for queries.

text:
Eligibility: Open only to juniors and seniors who have declared a major in the Social Sciences.

Capstone Funding applications should be approved by the Funding Committee before carrying out any work that involves spending funds . In principle, reimbursements are not allowed and will be dealt with on a case-by-case basis.

Application Process

- Student drafts Capstone proposal.

- Student submits proposal to their Capstone Advisor and refines the academic/research content of the proposal based on the advisor’s feedback.

- Once the Capstone Advisor approves the proposal, the advisor signs the Capstone Advisor Approval Form (DOCX).

- Student submits the proposal online.

- Social Capstone administrator processes the application and works with the student on refining the funding aspect of the application.

- Funding application submitted to the Funding Committee for approval.

- The Social Science Capstone administrator reaches out to the student with the Funding Committee’s decision.

- At the end of the project, the student submits a reconciliation of their expenses using the expense listing template (XLXS); relevant receipts must be submitted along with the expense listing sheet. Any unused funding must be returned to NYUAD. It is the student’s responsibility to retain receipts for any expenditures; any amount the student received for which receipts are not submitted will need to be returned to NYUAD unless a justification is sent to the Capstone Administrator. Kindly contact the Capstone Administrator for further details..

title: Core Curriculum · NYUAD Students
text:
Overview

NYU Abu Dhabi’s Core Curriculum forms the heart of our mission to provide an international student body with an outstanding, expansive education. The Core draws on the diversity and cultural wealth of the world’s traditions and spans the content and methodologies of 21st-century disciplines across the Arts and Humanities, Engineering, Science, and Social Science. It offers Core Competencies that will help graduates address major global challenges, including the pursuit of equality, justice, peace, health, sustainability, and a rich understanding of humanity. It fosters modes of thinking and habits of mind central to well-rounded intellectual development and to global citizenship and leadership. All Core courses develop students’ abilities to formulate precise questions and arrive at well-reasoned and effectively communicated conclusions about themselves and the world we share.

Structure

The NYUAD Core consists of:

- One 14-week First Year Writing Seminar (coded FYWS ), located in Abu Dhabi, which introduces students to the reading, writing, oral expression, and critical-thinking skills essential to a liberal arts education.

- One 14-week Core Colloquium (coded CCOL-UH ), which addresses a significant global challenge from multidisciplinary perspectives, located in Abu Dhabi.

- Two January-term Core Field Colloquia (coded CCOL-UH with a J tag ), which enable a deep dive into a particular aspect of these challenges at a specific site.

- They are located in Abu Dhabi or outside the UAE, but will always be organized through NYUAD.

- At least one of them should be taken in Abu Dhabi.

- Four 14-week Core Competency Courses, one each in each of the following competencies:

- Arts, Design, and Technology (coded CADT-UH )

- Cultural Exploration and Analysis (coded CCEA-UH )

- Data and Discovery (coded CDAD-UH )

- Structures of Thought and Society (coded CSTS-UH )

- One course that fulfills the Islamic Studies requirement. It can be drawn from courses across the curriculum (including courses outside of the Core). These courses are identified by the X tag (example: CSTS-UH 1234X )

Core Colloquia

Core Colloquia are small, discussion-oriented seminars designed to help students deepen their understanding of significant global challenges, including the pursuit of Equality, Justice, Peace, Health, Sustainability, and a rich understanding of Humanity. Taught by faculty from all divisions, these seminars offer multidisciplinary, global perspectives and substantively engage two or more of the Core Competencies.

Core Colloquia aim to nurture the civic awareness fundamental to global citizenship and leadership by developing students’ abilities to grapple with the complex conceptual and ethical dimensions of global issues, to communicate respectfully across cultural differences, and to devise problem-solving strategies.

Colloquia are fourteen-week courses taught in Abu Dhabi.

Core Field Colloquia

Students take two intensive Core Field Colloquia during J-Term that emphasize the relevance of the course questions and material to life beyond the classroom by foregrounding immersive, experiential, and community-based learning.

While the semester-long Colloquium grapples with complex issues and questions through a range of disciplines and contexts in a seminar-style classroom setting, the Core Field Colloquia enables a deep dive into a particular aspect of these challenges within a specific site. It is through these interdisciplinary Field Colloquia that students gain real-world exposure to and an understanding for the unique concerns of those who face these challenges and the limits and opportunities of those working to address them.

Students take one Abu Dhabi-based Field Colloquium and up to one Field Colloquium away.

title: Core Competency Courses · NYUAD Students
text:
Core Competency Courses offer students an in-depth grounding in one of four foundational competencies. These courses demonstrate the role of academic and artistic disciplines in developing these competencies, and their relevance to the world beyond the university. They also enable critical reflection on students’ primary courses of study. Core Competency requirements can be satisfied from offerings in Abu Dhabi and select courses in NYU's global network.

All students take a minimum of one course from each of the categories below. In choosing courses, students are strongly encouraged to complement their major studies by exploring faculty and subjects outside their primary fields or programs. Although some divisional courses are designated as cross-listing with the Core, coursework that applies toward a student’s major may not be double-counted as a Core requirement.

- Arts, Design, and Technology courses teach students to think critically and work creatively toward innovations in arts practice, design and engineering, creative writing, data visualization, programming, and performance.

- Cultural Exploration and Analysis courses pursue understanding and appreciation of diverse cultural forms and perspectives, and the ability to navigate differences to establish cross-cultural understanding.

- Data and Discovery courses develop the ability to use experimental and quantitative methods to understand the world.

- Structures of Thought and Society courses allow students to examine past, current, and potential future global frameworks for thinking, social organization, and behavior.

title: Writing Lexicon · NYUAD Students
text:
The Lexicon for the Core is organized around three key areas outlined below (Writing with Purpose; Understanding Audience; and Understanding Conventions), drawn from the Core Writing Guidelines. These guidelines state that students in the Core should practice academic writing and as a baseline should learn to:

- Develop well-reasoned and persuasive arguments;

- Use evidence in the service of their arguments;

- Engage with the thinking of others;

- Credit and cite appropriate sources accurately;

- Write clear, grammatically correct prose.

Writing with Purpose

Thesis
A paper's main insight or central claim. "A thesis is your main insight or idea about a text or topic, and the main proposition that your essay demonstrates. It should be true but arguable (not obviously or patently true, but one alternative among several), be limited enough in scope to be argued in a short composition and with available evidence, and get to the heart of the text or topic being analyzed (not be peripheral). It should be stated early in some form and at some point recast sharply (not just be implied), and it should govern the whole essay (not disappear in places)" (Harvey).

Motive
Motive is "the intellectual context that you establish for your topic and thesis at the start of your essay, in order to suggest why someone, besides your instructor, might want to read an essay on this topic or need to hear your particular thesis argued — why your thesis isn’t just obvious to all, why other people might hold other theses (that you think are wrong)" (Harvey). According to Walk, "in both humanistic and scientific disciplines, the motive is typically an incongruity, puzzle, or surprise in the primary sources or data; and/or holes, limitations, or disagreements in the secondary literature. All good academic papers have a well-defined motive." According to Harvey, "Your motive should be aimed at your audience: it won’t necessarily be the reason you first got interested in the topic (which could be private and idiosyncratic) or the personal motivation behind your engagement with the topic. Indeed it’s where you suggest that your argument isn’t idiosyncratic, but rather is generally interesting."

Crucially, as Harvey puts it, "The motive you set up should be genuine: a misapprehension or puzzle that an intelligent reader (not a straw dummy) would really have, a point that such a reader would really overlook. Defining motive should be the main business of your introductory paragraphs, where it is usually introduced by a form of the complicating word 'But.'"

Understanding the Needs of an Academic Audience

Evidence
Scholars consider evidence to be "the data — facts, examples, or details — that you refer to, quote, or summarize to support your thesis. There needs to be enough evidence to be persuasive; it needs to be the right kind of evidence to support the thesis (with no obvious pieces of evidence overlooked); it needs to be sufficiently concrete for the reader to trust it (e.g., in textual analysis, it often helps to find one or two key or representative passages to quote and focus on); and if summarized, it needs to be summarized accurately and fairly" (Harvey).

Analysis
Analysis can be understood as "the work of breaking down, interpreting, and commenting upon the data, of saying what can be inferred from the data such that it supports a thesis (is evidence for something). Analysis is what you do with data when you go beyond observing or summarizing it: you show how its parts contribute to a whole or how causes contribute to an effect; you draw out the significance or implication not apparent to a superficial view. Analysis is what makes the writer feel present, as a reasoning individual; so your essay should do more analyzing than summarizing or quoting" (Harvey).

Key Words
"Key words are the recurring terms or basic oppositions that an argument rests upon (....). These terms usually imply certain assumptions — unstated beliefs about life, history, literature, reasoning, etc. that the essayist doesn’t argue for but simply assumes to be true. An essay’s key terms should be clear in their meaning and appear throughout (not be abandoned half-way); they should be appropriate for the subject at hand (not unfair or too simple — a false or constraining opposition); and they should not be inert clichés or abstractions (e.g., "the evils of society"). The attendant assumptions should bear logical inspection, and if arguable they should be explicitly acknowledged" (Harvey).

Key words usually appear in the title, are defined early on (often with the aid of sources), and could be used in a library or Web search to locate the paper if it were published.

Reflecting
If we trust that writing is a form of thinking, then how can we write clearly about complex ideas? One way to achieve this is via "reflecting"— when a writer slows down and makes sense of data, evidence, or evolving ideas. According to Harvey, practicing the art of reflection can take a variety of forms. For instance, "when you pause in your demonstration to reflect on it, to raise or answer a question about it — as when you (1) consider a counter-argument — a possible objection, alternative, or problem that a skeptical or resistant reader might raise; (2) define your terms or assumptions (what do I mean by this term? or, what am I assuming here?); (3) handle a newly emergent concern (but if this is so, then how can X be?); (4) draw out an implication (so what? what might be the wider significance of the argument I have made? what might it lead to if I’m right? or, what does my argument about a single aspect of this suggest about the whole thing? or about the way people live and think?), and (5) consider a possible explanation for the phenomenon that has been demonstrated (why might this be so? what might cause or have caused it?); (6) offer a qualification or limitation to the case you have made (what you’re not saying). The first of these reflections can come anywhere in an essay; the second usually comes early; the last four often come late (they’re common moves of conclusion)" (Harvey).

Structure
According to Harvey, "the sequence of main sections or sub-topics, and the turning points between them. The sections should follow a logical order, and the links in that order should be apparent to the reader (see "stitching"). But it should also be a progressive order — there should be a direction of development or complication, not be simply a list or a series of restatements of the thesis ("Macbeth is ambitious: he's ambitious here; and he's ambitious here; and he's ambitions here, too; thus, Macbeth is ambitious"). And the order should be supple enough to allow the writer to explore the topic, not just hammer home a thesis. (If the essay is complex or long, its structure may be briefly announced or hinted at after the thesis, in a road-map or plan sentence.)"

Understanding the Conventions Appropriate to Constructing Academic Arguments

Stitching
Great essays in the humanities have a sense of cohesion readers and writers tend to call "flow." Flow can be achieved in a number of ways — for example, via "stitching." You can identify an essay’s stitching via words that tie together the parts of an argument, "most commonly (a) by using transition (linking or turning) words as signposts to indicate how a new section, paragraph, or sentence follows from the one immediately previous; but also (b) by recollection of an earlier idea or part of the essay, referring back to it either by explicit statement or by echoing key words or resonant phrases quoted or stated earlier. The repeating of key or thesis concepts is especially helpful at points of transition from one section to another, to show how the new section fits in" (Harvey).

Sources
Persons or documents, referred to, summarized, or quoted, that help a writer demonstrate the truth of his or her argument are considered sources. Your sources need to be efficiently integrated and fairly acknowledged by citation.

Sources can be categorized as follows: "Primary sources are uninterpreted documents, artifacts, data, or information that, when analyzed, function as evidence. Secondary sources, also known as "the literature" or "the secondary literature," are texts that make direct claims about the topic and may be used to establish a problem or question worth addressing, the standard opinion(s) on the topic, the standard way in which the problem or question is approached, or the current state of knowledge in the field. Other relevant sources are texts that relate indirectly to the topic and may be used to provide context or background information, key words or concepts, or points of comparison — all of which help serve your thesis and evolving idea" (Walk).

How writers use sources can vary, but here are several basic moves: "they may be quoted (if the style of writing is special or significant), paraphrased (if the style of writing is complex or jargon-laden), summarized (if the source is long and complicated), or referenced (if the source is briefly mentioned). In humanistic disciplines, sources appear in each of these forms. In scientific disciplines, sources are usually referenced or summarized, almost never quoted or paraphrased" (Walk).

Citations
Bibliographic information that enables readers to track down a paper's sources. "In academic writing, sources are always cited; the citation style employed (e.g., MLA, APA, CMS, CSE) depends on the discipline. A list of sources is called the Works Cited, Bibliography, or References, depending on purpose and discipline" (Harvey).

Orienting
Use "bits of information, explanation, and summary [to] orient the reader who isn’t expert in the subject, enabling such a reader to follow the argument. The orienting question is, what does my reader need here? The answer can take many forms: necessary information about the text, author, or event (e.g., given in your introduction); a summary of a text or passage about to be analyzed; pieces of information given along the way about passages, people, or events mentioned (including announcing or "set-up" phrases for quotations and sources). The trick is to orient briefly and gracefully" (Harvey).

Stance
What is the "the implied relationship of you, the writer, to your readers and subject?" Stance is "how and where you implicitly position yourself as an analyst. Stance is defined by such features as style and tone (e.g., familiar or formal); the presence or absence of specialized language and knowledge; the amount of time spent orienting a general, non-expert reader; the use of scholarly conventions of form and style. Your stance should be established within the first few paragraphs of your essay, and it should remain consistent" (Harvey).

Style
Style manifests in the choices you make of words and sentence structure. Your style should be exact and clear (should bring out the main idea and action of each sentence, not bury it) and plain without being flat (should be graceful and a little interesting, not stuffy).

Mechanics
Grammar, punctuation, spelling, and citation format. Writing guides that focus on mechanics are readily available online, as are guides to the citation styles used in various disciplines. Plus, please visit the NYUAD Center for Writing, located in the Library (Campus Center (C2), 3rd floor).

Reference

This Lexicon draws heavily upon Gordon Harvey's " Elements of the Academic Essay " (developed for Yale and widely cited). It also draws upon Kerry Walk’s "A Writing Lexicon" (written for Princeton University).
