title: Standardized Test Preparation Grant · NYUAD Students
text:
Important Update as of September 1, 2026:

This page is currently being updated with application dates and deadlines for the upcoming grant cycle. Please check back soon for updated application information.

Program guidelines remain unchanged. The Test Preparation Grant is intended to support eligible test preparation courses for standardized exams not currently covered by NYU New York Kaplan All Access.

Please note that meeting the eligibility requirements and submitting an application does not guarantee funding. All eligible applications are subject to review, and grant awards are made based on program guidelines and available funding.

Given the launch of the NYU New York Kaplan All Access initiative, which offers NYU students free access to Kaplan’s industry-leading test preparation courses, the standardized test preparation grant program beginning with the 2024-25 Academic Year is only eligible for test preparation courses for exams that are not covered by Kaplan.

We are actively monitoring the initiative and the Standardized Test Preparation Grant Committee will meet annually to update our policies. Any future changes to the grant will be promptly communicated to all NYU Abu Dhabi students through official Career Development Center channels, including newsletters, the student portal, Handshake, and more.

The Grant

The Career Development Center (CDC) offers a Standardized Test Preparation Grant (STPG) to eligible NYUAD undergraduate students through a competitive application process. The grant can be used to take one preparation course for one standardized test required for acceptance into graduate and professional programs worldwide. The preparation course must be for an exam that is not already being administered through the NYU New York Kaplan All Access program .

Best Practices for Utilizing the Kaplan All Access / FAQ

As part of our commitment to your academic and professional success, students have access to Kaplan’s All Access test preparation courses for standardized tests such as the DAT, GMAT, GRE, LSAT, MCAT, OAT, and FE. Here are some tips on how to make the most out of this resource:

- Plan Ahead

All Kaplan test prep courses available to NYU students have a 12 month access period which begins the date you enroll. You should take this into account when planning the best time to register. For example, if you're hoping to take the GRE exam the summer before your senior year, it might be best for you to enroll in a Kaplan course 12 months prior to ensure you can access the content and complete the course.

Additionally, there are people at NYUAD who can help you plan for your next steps. You can schedule an appointment with our Graduate School and Career Advisors on Handshake or visit us during our walk-in hours at the CDC for quick questions.

- Schedule Regular Study Times

Consistency is key in preparation. Schedule regular study sessions and stick to them. Kaplan’s online resources are accessible 24/7, making it easier to fit test prep into your busy schedule.

- Take Practice Tests

Utilize Kaplan’s full-length practice tests to assess your progress. These tests provide a realistic experience and help you identify areas where you need further study.

- Engage with Interactive Resources

Take advantage of interactive study tools like video lessons, flashcards, and quizzes. These resources can help reinforce learning and make complex concepts more manageable.

- Seek Help When Needed

If you find certain topics challenging, use Kaplan’s live support or tutoring options. Asking questions and understanding answers thoroughly can boost your confidence and preparation level. You can call Kaplan customer care at 1-800-KAP-TEST or reach out to the team online .

- Utilize On-Demand Video Lessons

For topics you find particularly challenging, Kaplan’s on-demand video lessons allow you to learn and review at your own pace, ensuring you fully understand before moving on.

- Regularly Review Course Updates

Stay updated with any changes or additions to the Kaplan courses, as these might include vital information or improved strategies for test-taking.

FAQ

Q: How do I access the Kaplan All Access courses ?

A: You can access the Kaplan All Access courses by logging into the Kaplan portal with your NYU credentials to get started. If you have any questions about navigating the Kaplan site, you can view or download the user guide for NYU students .

Q: What if I encounter issues accessing the courses ?

A: Please contact the Kaplan team . You can also email us at nyuad.career@nyu.edu . We’re here to ensure you have everything you need for your test preparation.

Q: Are there any limits on how many courses I can take ?

A: No, there are no limits. You have full access to all the courses in the fields supported by Kaplan All Access. It is best for you to prioritize the test preparation course for the exam that you know for sure you need to take because you only get 12 months access to a course at a time.

Grant Guidelines

Current NYU students are now able to take the following Kaplan test preparation courses for free:

- Dental Admissions Test (DAT®)

- Graduate Management Admission Test (GMAT®)

- Graduate Record Examination (GRE®)

- Law School Admissions Test (LSAT®)

- Medical College Admission Test (MCAT®)

- Optometry Admissions Test (OAT®)

- Fundamentals of Engineering Exam (FE)

If there is a standardized exam required for admission to a graduate school and Kaplan All Access does not currently provide a preparation course for that exam, you can email nyuad.career@nyu.edu to inquire about the exam. Please include the following information in your email:

- The link(s) to the graduate program(s) you’re applying to with information in regard to the standardized exam requirements

The grant can cover up to the cost of the preparation course up to 2000 USD. The course can be online or in-person. Priority will be given to students of financial need.

The following is not covered by the Standardized Test Preparation Grant. However, students who receive Falcon Dirhams can elect for funds to be set aside for graduate school and professional expenses by establishing an individual graduate school expense account . This is a great option for students who would like to set aside some funds to cover expenses for exams or fees that fall outside of the grant:

- English proficiency exam preparation or registration

- CFA exams or other professional qualifying exams

- The purchase of test preparation materials

- The cost of registration for a standardized exam

- For students pursuing the London Track or have an interest in taking the Solicitor's Qualifying Examination (SQE): At this time, the SQE exam is not eligible for the Standardized Test Preparation Grant because it does not meet the grant requirements set by the committee given it is not an entrance exam for graduate studies.

The STPG program does not cover test preparation course reimbursements. The grant committee will only fund eligible and awarded students for payments to be made for a test preparation course going forward from the date a student would be awarded. Any program/costs incurred before the grant announcement are not eligible.

Before Applying

Applicants are highly encouraged to:

- research the various test preparation options to consider which one is most beneficial for them,

- take a diagnostic test to gauge their preparation needs,

- connect with their academic mentor to discuss preparation and graduate school plans,

- and meet with a CDC advisor to discuss graduate school plans and review the completed application before submission.

Important Requirements and Information

Eligibility Requirements

To be eligible for a standardized test preparation grant, students must meet the following eligibility requirements:

- Be a full-time sophomore, junior, or senior enrolled at NYUAD (first years are not eligible) at the time of application. Students on Leave of Absence are not eligible to apply.

- Be in good disciplinary standing* as per a conduct check.

- Be in good academic standing with a minimum cumulative GPA of 3.0

- Have not received a standardized test preparation award previously during their tenure at NYUAD.

- Complete a CDC Orientation prior to submitting an application. You can view if you are credited with taking the CDC Orientation in the lower left hand corner of your Profile in Handshake under Labels. If you haven't participated in or completed a CDC Orientation yet, kindly proceed to this page to complete a brief online orientation and once completed. Once finished, please send an email to nyuad.career@nyu.career to notify us of your completion.

Selection Criteria

The grant committee, made up of CDC staff, reads and scores all applications. Applications are evaluated on how well applicants have articulated their understanding of themselves, preparation for the exam, and planning for graduate school.

For more insight into the elements of a strong application please see the following scoring rubric which is used by the committee when reviewing applications.

Application Questions | Answered Effectively | Answered Somewhat Effectively | Not Answered Effectively

How will you benefit from a test prep course and the course format you are considering? | The applicant clearly articulates why this particular test prep program works for their learning style, schedule and /or needs. The applicant is specific and addresses their individual needs. The applicant describes the specific structure or components of the program and why it works for them. | The applicant articulates why this particular test prep program works for their learning style, schedule and /or needs but does not provide specific details. The applicant provides a limited description of the program structure or components and why it works for them. | The applicant does not clearly articulate why this particular test prep program works for their learning style, schedule and /or needs. The applicant is not specific and does not address their individual needs. The applicant does not provide details about the structure or components of the prep program and why it works for them.

Provide details of how you have prepared and will prepare for the exam and your plans for providing your exam score to the CDC before you graduate from NYUAD. | The applicant has prepared for the exam by reviewing, researching and/ or taking practice tests. They describe how and when they will study for the exam. They also articulate specifically when they will provide the test scores to the CDC. | The applicant has not prepared for the exam by reviewing and/or taking practice tests. They don’t describe how and when they will study for the exam. Or they do not articulate specifically when they will provide the test scores to the CDC. | The applicant does not describe effectively how they prepared for the exam and does not describe how and and when they will study for the exam. They do not articulate specifically when they will provide the test scores to the CDC.

Explain your rationale for applying for graduate school and how it fits into your future career trajectory. What specific skills and knowledge do you stand to gain by continued education? | The applicant describes what they plan on studying, the specific skills and knowledge they will acquire through graduate education and how it will help them in their career, or to figure out their career goals. | The applicant describes what they plan on studying, the skills and knowledge they will acquire and how it will help them in their career with limited detail and scope. And/or the applicant does not describe their career goals effectively. | The applicant does not describe the skills and knowledge they will acquire and how graduate school will benefit their career. The applicant does not articulate their career goals.

Provide an example of a school(s) you may apply to and note your rationale for selecting this program. Include a summary of their academic profile and then assess your feasibility of being accepted. | The applicant identifies one or more graduate/professional school(s) they plan on applying to. They describe the requirements of the program and explain how they meet, or plan to meet, the requirements of the program. The choice of school and plan is convincingly feasible and well reasoned for acceptance. | The applicant identifies one or more graduate/professional school(s) they plan on applying to and describes the requirements of the program with limited detail and scope. The applicant does not explain how they meet or plan to meet the requirements of the program. The plan for being accepted may not seem feasible and/or the reasoning is lacking. | The applicant does not identify one or more graduate/professional schools they plan on applying to and does not identify the requirements of the program. The applicant also does not explain how they meet or plan to meet the requirements of the program. Acceptance to their choice of school does not seem feasible.

Overall quality of application (thoroughness/clarity of answers, etc.) | The applicant is thorough, clear and detailed in their answers. | The applicant is somewhat clear and detailed in their answers. | The applicant is unclear in their answers.

Please note, once an application is submitted any changes to the application information (i.e. grant type, course type, etc.) may impact your eligibility to receive the funding.

It is strongly advised that students review their application with a CDC advisor, for feedback, before submitting it.

Terms and Conditions

The Standardized Test Preparation Grant is granted to eligible students through a competitive application process. Receiving this grant confers the responsibility of upholding the program requirements. Failure to adhere to the stated criteria will result in the consequences outlined below.

Recipients of the grant must adhere to the following:

- provide a receipt of purchase for the test preparation program and amount detailed in their application

- take the course and standardized test for which they received the preparation funding before they graduate

- provide the CDC with the official resulting test score for the standardized test they received preparation funding for before they graduate

Note:

- The review process is blind and there is no appeal process. Grant decisions are based on the strength of applications and all decisions made regarding each application are final.

- Students who cancel a score of a standardized exam will be required to return the full amount of funding they received.

- Students who take the LSAT exam and choose to use the Score Preview option but decide not to keep their score will be required to return the full amount of funding they received.

If the funding recipient (1) changes the course or does not complete the course for which they receive funding, (2) is found to have provided inaccurate information in support of their application, and/or (3) does not report their score to the CDC before graduation, the student will:

- meet with the Assistant Dean of Students/Director of the Career Development Center,

- be required to return up to the full amount of funding, and

- receive a Dean's Academic Hold if the required funds are not returned by the specified date. A Dean’s Academic Hold withholds your final transcript and diploma.

Application Dates and Deadlines

**Applications received after the deadline will be reviewed in the next application cycle.

Application Cycle 1: Fall 2025

Application Opens | September 15, 2025

Application Deadline | October 6, 2025 (9 am GST / Abu Dhabi time)

Notification Date | October 20, 2025

Deadline to accept the award | October 22, 2025

Grant upload to FAB card | November 17, 2025

Application Cycle 2: Spring 2026

Application Deadline | February 9, 2026 (9 am GST / Abu Dhabi time)**

Notification Date | February 25, 2026

Deadline to accept the award | February 27, 2026

Grant upload to FAB card | March 27, 2026

Application Cycle 3: Spring 2026

Application Deadline | March 23, 2025 (9 am GST / Abu Dhabi time)**

Notification Date | April 7, 2026

Deadline to accept the award | April 9, 2026

Grant upload to FAB card | May 8, 2026

Career Development Center

Location:
Campus Center (C2-E), Ground Floor

Office Hours:
Monday-Friday, 9am-5pm

Contact us:
nyuad.career@nyu.edu

Schedule an Appointment to see an advisor via Handshake

Related official links:
https://students.nyuad.nyu.edu/services/financial-services/study-support/graduate-school-related-expenses/

- Be a full-time sophomore, junior, or senior enrolled at NYUAD (first years are not eligible) at the time of application. Students on Leave of Absence are not eligible to apply.

- Be in good disciplinary standing* as per a conduct check.

- Be in good academic standing with a minimum cumulative GPA of 3.0

- Have not received a standardized test preparation award previously during their tenure at NYUAD.

- Complete a CDC Orientation prior to submitting an application. You can view if you are credited with taking the CDC Orientation in the lower left hand corner of your Profile in Handshake under Labels. If you haven't participated in or completed a CDC Orientation yet, kindly proceed to this page to complete a brief online orientation and once completed. Once finished, please send an email to nyuad.career@nyu.career to notify us of your completion.

sections.title: Important Requirements and Information · Selection Criteria
sections.text:
The grant committee, made up of CDC staff, reads and scores all applications. Applications are evaluated on how well applicants have articulated their understanding of themselves, preparation for the exam, and planning for graduate school.

For more insight into the elements of a strong application please see the following scoring rubric which is used by the committee when reviewing applications.

Application Questions | Answered Effectively | Answered Somewhat Effectively | Not Answered Effectively

How will you benefit from a test prep course and the course format you are considering? | The applicant clearly articulates why this particular test prep program works for their learning style, schedule and /or needs. The applicant is specific and addresses their individual needs. The applicant describes the specific structure or components of the program and why it works for them. | The applicant articulates why this particular test prep program works for their learning style, schedule and /or needs but does not provide specific details. The applicant provides a limited description of the program structure or components and why it works for them. | The applicant does not clearly articulate why this particular test prep program works for their learning style, schedule and /or needs. The applicant is not specific and does not address their individual needs. The applicant does not provide details about the structure or components of the prep program and why it works for them.

Provide details of how you have prepared and will prepare for the exam and your plans for providing your exam score to the CDC before you graduate from NYUAD. | The applicant has prepared for the exam by reviewing, researching and/ or taking practice tests. They describe how and when they will study for the exam. They also articulate specifically when they will provide the test scores to the CDC. | The applicant has not prepared for the exam by reviewing and/or taking practice tests. They don’t describe how and when they will study for the exam. Or they do not articulate specifically when they will provide the test scores to the CDC. | The applicant does not describe effectively how they prepared for the exam and does not describe how and and when they will study for the exam. They do not articulate specifically when they will provide the test scores to the CDC.

Explain your rationale for applying for graduate school and how it fits into your future career trajectory. What specific skills and knowledge do you stand to gain by continued education? | The applicant describes what they plan on studying, the specific skills and knowledge they will acquire through graduate education and how it will help them in their career, or to figure out their career goals. | The applicant describes what they plan on studying, the skills and knowledge they will acquire and how it will help them in their career with limited detail and scope. And/or the applicant does not describe their career goals effectively. | The applicant does not describe the skills and knowledge they will acquire and how graduate school will benefit their career. The applicant does not articulate their career goals.

Provide an example of a school(s) you may apply to and note your rationale for selecting this program. Include a summary of their academic profile and then assess your feasibility of being accepted. | The applicant identifies one or more graduate/professional school(s) they plan on applying to. They describe the requirements of the program and explain how they meet, or plan to meet, the requirements of the program. The choice of school and plan is convincingly feasible and well reasoned for acceptance. | The applicant identifies one or more graduate/professional school(s) they plan on applying to and describes the requirements of the program with limited detail and scope. The applicant does not explain how they meet or plan to meet the requirements of the program. The plan for being accepted may not seem feasible and/or the reasoning is lacking. | The applicant does not identify one or more graduate/professional schools they plan on applying to and does not identify the requirements of the program. The applicant also does not explain how they meet or plan to meet the requirements of the program. Acceptance to their choice of school does not seem feasible.

Overall quality of application (thoroughness/clarity of answers, etc.) | The applicant is thorough, clear and detailed in their answers. | The applicant is somewhat clear and detailed in their answers. | The applicant is unclear in their answers.

Please note, once an application is submitted any changes to the application information (i.e. grant type, course type, etc.) may impact your eligibility to receive the funding.

It is strongly advised that students review their application with a CDC advisor, for feedback, before submitting it.

sections.title: Terms and Conditions
sections.text:
The Standardized Test Preparation Grant is granted to eligible students through a competitive application process. Receiving this grant confers the responsibility of upholding the program requirements. Failure to adhere to the stated criteria will result in the consequences outlined below.

Recipients of the grant must adhere to the following:

- provide a receipt of purchase for the test preparation program and amount detailed in their application

- take the course and standardized test for which they received the preparation funding before they graduate

- provide the CDC with the official resulting test score for the standardized test they received preparation funding for before they graduate

Note:

- The review process is blind and there is no appeal process. Grant decisions are based on the strength of applications and all decisions made regarding each application are final.

- Students who cancel a score of a standardized exam will be required to return the full amount of funding they received.

- Students who take the LSAT exam and choose to use the Score Preview option but decide not to keep their score will be required to return the full amount of funding they received.

If the funding recipient (1) changes the course or does not complete the course for which they receive funding, (2) is found to have provided inaccurate information in support of their application, and/or (3) does not report their score to the CDC before graduation, the student will:

- meet with the Assistant Dean of Students/Director of the Career Development Center,

- be required to return up to the full amount of funding, and

- receive a Dean's Academic Hold if the required funds are not returned by the specified date. A Dean’s Academic Hold withholds your final transcript and diploma.

title: Global Education · NYUAD Students
text:
Global education is an essential component of the four-year curriculum. It is comprised of a sequence of intellectually rigorous, culturally and linguistically engaging research-focused learning opportunities that complement students' coursework. The constellation of NYUAD global education experiences includes semester-long study away programs, January-term programs (called J-Terms), and course-related study trips in the UAE as well as the broader Middle East, which may be combined with J-Term or spring semester courses.

Global education opportunities are managed by the Office of Global Education. Students will be invited to attend information sessions and request individual appointments to receive advice on planning and achieving their study away goals. Careful academic and logistical preparation is required for students who intend to participate in study away. Students should also consult with their academic mentors early in their studies to be certain study away experiences can fit well with their major requirements and progress toward graduation.

title: Intercultural Learning Goal · NYUAD Students
text:
Intercultural Learning Goal for Study Away

Developing Greater Intercultural Understanding Towards Social Responsibility Globally and Locally

The ability to

- respect, engage, and negotiate difference toward greater common ground and common good.

- act with ethical intelligence as responsible local citizens within communities you engage abroad or at home.

What can help develop those abilities?

- Learning how to create social ties across difference, including recognizing boundaries and deference behaviors common to the community you are engaging.

- Learning the languages and socio-linguistic behaviors needed in that community to create social ties, navigate boundaries and apply deference behaviors.

- Learning how to access, elicit, interpret, and generate knowledge with ethical intelligence within the culture(s) of that community.

- Learning to respect a variety of knowers and ways of knowing in the host community – appreciating and applying epistemological diversity.

- Learning how to reflect critically on your own positionality (personal identity, socio-cultural identity, political identity).

- Learning how to foster and convey empathy in the face of difference.

- Learning to hold the tension of the opposites within formal and informal community contexts to create a safe space for dialogue.

What Teaching and Learning Environments are Conducive to Developing these Skills?

- Preparation for study abroad that is specific to the countries, cultures, and communities you will be entering; that helps you reflect on your own cultural positionality; and that provides you with training in ethically conducting community-based research abroad.

- Sustained engagement with a variety of knowers in the community through homestays with local families, host country roommates, volunteer or academic internships, and community-based research projects.

- Language learning that requires you to use your language with a broad range of knowers in the community.

- Conducting research within that community and being attentive to ethical practices as required by our Institutional Review Board principles and as appropriate in the local community.

- Reflecting critically on your cognitive and affective learning through regular writing and guided discussion.

- Sharing the results of your learning and research with those with whom you worked to generate the knowledge in the host community, at NYUAD, and beyond.

- Reflecting on (writing about, talking about) how the issues you are encountering abroad help you understand related or other issues in your own society and how to address them within that society.

- Mentoring in resolving the inherent conflict you will encounter simply by living and learning in a culture and language very different from your own (seeing things from multiple viewpoints, examining alternatives to solving problems, reserving judgment, etc.)

title: J-Term · NYUAD Students
text:
J-Term Requirements and Guidelines

Two J-Terms : All students, new and returning, are required to successfully complete two J-Term courses to graduate. One J-Term course must be taught fully in Abu Dhabi, and only one may be taught abroad.

Students who entered NYUAD prior to fall 2024, may still opt to complete three J-Terms. Only one of the three J-Term courses may be taught abroad.

Students may be permitted one extra J-Term course (meaning a third one) only through an Academic Petition submitted to the Academic Resource Center (ARC). Permission may be granted only when the extra credits earned from a J-Term course are essential for on-time completion of one’s degree. A third J-Term course can only be a course taught fully in Abu Dhabi. Completing minors or double majors is NOT considered a compelling reason to take an extra J-Term course.

All first-year students are required to enroll in a course in January 2027 . If a student has a compelling reason that prevents them from completing a J-Term course this year, they must contact Dr. Ram Natarajan , Director of J-Term, to outline their circumstances and to request permission to skip J-Term this year.

J-Term and Study Away Semesters : Students who entered Fall 2026 or later must successfully complete at least one J-Term course before they can become eligible for a study away semester.

Credits and Course Length : As of January 2025, J-Term courses contain 10 or 11 class days and count for 3 credits. J-Term courses are not cross-listed with any other degree requirements, and count solely toward the J-Term Core Field Colloquium requirement. All J-Term courses contain a significant experiential learning component.

J-Term courses are offered only in January. Academic year 2025-2026 was the last year in which – as an exception – some J-Term classes were also offered in June.

Abu Dhabi J-Terms : All students must take at least one J-Term course that is fully taught in Abu Dhabi. Moreover, students may elect to take both of their required J-Term courses fully in Abu Dhabi.

Design & Innovation Course for Engineering Students : While this course is offered in January and/or June every year, and must ordinarily be taken in the first year, the course does not count as a J-Term course. Design & Innovation registration information will take place later this fall. Keep an eye out for announcements coming soon on the student portal and newsletter.

Leaves of Absence and J-Term : Students who are on leave for the fall semester immediately preceding January Term, or who take a term withdrawal for that semester are not eligible to take a J-Term course in the following term.

Study Away and J-Term : Students who are studying away in the fall semester immediately preceding the January Term are not eligible to take a J-Term course that is taught fully abroad in that same year. This is prohibited due to the significant increase in refusals from various countries to consider visa applications from students studying abroad.

Students who are studying abroad in the spring semester immediately following the January Term are not allowed to take any J-Term courses if there is a calendar conflict between the end of J-Term and the required arrival date for their spring semester abroad. For AY 26-27, January Term conflicts with the start of the spring semester at the majority of the NYU global sites. The only exceptions are NYU Buenos Aires, NYU New York, and NYU Sydney, so if you are approved to study abroad in the spring at one of these 3 locations, you may be able to take a J-Term course. Students must plan accordingly.

Minimum Age : Students must be at least 18 years old prior to attending an Away J-Term course. Please do not apply for an Away course if you will not meet this requirement prior to the start of J-Term.

J-Term Grading : J-Term courses must be taken for a letter grade. Pass/Fail grading is not permitted. Incomplete (I) grades are not allowed during J-Term – all coursework must be completed within the scheduled J-Term course duration.

Prerequisites : J-Term courses typically have no prerequisites, and a few are not available to students who have already taken a very similar course (i.e., they have “anti-requisites”). These restrictions will be enforced via Albert as in any other semester.

Enrollment Holds : Students must clear all Finance, Library, and Health Center holds before selecting J-Term coursework. Students will not be able to enroll in J-Term coursework with holds.

J-Term Withdrawal Deadline : Students may choose to withdraw (with a W grade) from a J-Term course they have started only on the first day of class and only if they have a documented, legitimate reason. After the first day of class, withdrawal is no longer permitted, and the course will be graded with a letter grade. Students who withdraw from an Away J-Term course should expect to travel home immediately following their withdrawal regardless of their location at the time.

Important Note : Students who withdraw from an Away J-Term course will not be eligible to take another Away J-Term course in a future academic year.

Attendance Policy : Due to the condensed nature of J-Term, each day of absence is the equivalent of missing more than a full week in a regular semester – with less of an opportunity to make up for missed material. An unexcused absence results in the deduction of one full letter grade from the final course grade (e.g., from an A- to a B-). Excusing absence is at the discretion of the instructor.

Students who miss more than two classes will not be able to complete the course: if one or more of these absences are excused, students will be withdrawn; if all of the absences are unexcused, students will fail.

Missing required co-curricular activities outside of formal class time will result in the same grade penalties (and potential withdrawal or failure) as class absences.

J-Term Attendance Expectations :

-
On-time attendance at every class meeting is mandatory. Students may be marked ‘late’ if they arrive more than 5 minutes after class begins. In some classes, three “lates” are considered an unexcused absence.

-
J-Term courses are academically rigorous and because of their intensive nature demand a lot from students. Every day of a J-Term course is the equivalent of at least a week's worth of classes in a regular semester. Students should expect to spend several hours each day preparing assignments for their course.

-
Students must keep their calendars free of other commitments during J-Term for weekdays, weekends, and evenings.

-
All J-Term courses require community-based learning (CBL) as part of the distinctive J-Term curriculum. For the duration of J-Term, you must be free to participate in required activities outside of class, including in the evenings and on the weekend. Do not schedule personal engagements during J-Term that you cannot cancel in order to participate in your course activities. These may not be announced or scheduled until after the class begins because we are dependent on the availability of our community partners.

-
All Community-based learning (CBL) activities taking place outside of class are a required part of the course. Missing a CBL activity will have a consequence similar to missing a regular class session and may negatively affect your final grade.

-
Missing two consecutive classes or three classes overall in J-Term will result in your failing the class.

-
If you become ill at any time during the J-Term course and cannot rejoin the class activities for more than 2 days, you may have to withdraw from the course.

Accessibility : Students with Moses Center approved accommodations need to request a new accommodation specifically for J-Term, since accommodations approved for the fall and/or spring semester do not automatically apply for J-Term. Students who believe they need a special accommodation should contact the Moses Center Liaison for NYUAD at nyuad.spa@nyu.edu as soon as they know which J-Term course they will be taking. Students should request approval for a J-Term accommodation in October and provide the official approval from the Moses Center no later than November 1.

J-Term Courses Abroad : If you are eligible to select Away J-Term courses, please note the following and prepare accordingly:

-
You will most likely need a visa to enter your J-Term course country. You will need to prepare and submit all visa materials accurately and on time. You may be required to appear in person at the embassy or consulate issuing the visa. This could cause you to miss class(es). If you are not approved for the visa, you will need to drop the class and work with the Registrar to take a J-Term course in Abu Dhabi instead, if you absolutely need to take a J-Term this academic year.

-
The J-Term classes abroad are tightly scheduled to take full advantage of being in the country for a short period of time. You should expect to have little free time and must participate fully in all scheduled activities related to your class. In that sense, please do not expect to be a tourist.

-
Some courses require long local bus or train rides, extensive walking, and frequent engagement with the unfamiliar. They also facilitate engagement with local community members that may require you to carefully follow local customs. You must be ready and willing to adapt to these learning environments.

-
You may need to obtain specific vaccinations or take certain medicines to participate in J-Term courses abroad (e.g. yellow fever or malaria medicine for some countries.) You will need to consult with your physician about any possible side effects.

-
All J-Term sites abroad are able to provide medical care in case of emergency, but if you have special medical conditions that require unique care, you should consult with the NYUAD Student Health Center before you make your J-Term course selection.

title: J-Term 101: The Need-to-Know Guide · NYUAD Students
text:
J-Term Unfiltered: Everything You Need to Know Before It Starts

Welcome to J-Term! 🎉

J-Term is exciting, immersive, intense—and fast. You’re essentially completing a full semester course in just under two weeks. That makes the J-Term experience powerful and transformative, but it also means expectations are higher and everything moves more quickly.

🌍 Why J-Term Is Different

J-Term compresses an entire semester into a short, twelve-day window. Taking only one course full-time during J-Term allows you more time for concentrated reflection on a dedicated topic. Each day equals more than a full week of a regular semester course in terms of teaching and learning. Because of this:

-
Attendance policies are stricter

-
Deadlines come quickly

-
Participation in fieldwork is a mandatory part of class and counts towards attendance

-
All university policies are in effect, including policies on academic integrity and AI use.

Taking your studies outside the classroom is a game-changer. You’re about to get an experience that’s unique even by NYUAD standards. You'll be making connections with people and organizations from all walks of life. New languages, kilometers of getting your steps across new cities, and the best of local foods: welcome to the world as your new campus.

Bring the gift of your fullest attention to each new experience. Listen deeply. Look slowly. Soak it all in. Appreciate generously those who are giving of their time and expertise to you by. Share your curiosity and enthusiasm energetically with them. Open your mind and heart to the unfamiliar, the new, the different. Fight the jet lag and the desire to be a leisurely tourist in this new place, to win new ways of seeing and engaging with the world.

📅 Attendance = Everything

J-Term isn’t something you can fit around other personal plans. During these twelve days

-
Keep your weekdays, evenings, and weekends completely open. You need to stay fully available until you receive your final syllabus and course schedule on day one and see exactly what is required both in and out of the classroom. And you need to stay fully available after receiving the syllabus. Travel, personal plans, or overlapping commitments are not valid reasons for missing class or required activities.

-
Expect to spend about 2-3 hours per day doing assignments.

-
In addition to an average of three hours of class time each day, your course will require you to do no fewer than 12 hours of fieldwork outside of class over the span of J-Term. This means if class is in the morning, you will likely have fieldwork in the afternoon, or the opposite if your class is in the afternoon and you have fieldwork in the morning. Some fieldwork may take place in the evenings or on the weekend. You should expect to have little free time outside of class.

-
You must remain fully available (days, evenings, weekends) for all in-class instruction and all fieldwork activities. Missing a fieldwork activity is equivalent to missing a class session and will negatively affect your final grade.

❗ Absences & Consequences

Here’s how it usually works:

-
One unexcused absence (whether class or a required field activity) = one full letter grade deduction
(Example: A- becomes B-.)

-
Whether an absence is excused is at the instructor’s discretion.

-
If you miss more than two class sessions or required course activities, you cannot complete the course:

-
If one or more absences are excused due to illness, for example, you will be withdrawn (W grade).

-
If all absences are unexcused, you will receive a grade of F.

Yes, it’s strict. With each day counting as one week, your presence at each class and each course activity is essential to your own learning, your contribution to your classmates’ learning, and your active engagement with the community partners for the course.

⌛ Tardiness

Arriving more than 5 minutes late counts as being late.

📊 Grading Policies

-
Grades are letter grades only:
A, A-, B+, B, B-, C+, C, C-, D+, D, F

-
No Pass/Fail option for J-Term courses.

-
Late assignments may be penalized.

📝 Final Grades

-
All coursework must be completed by the last day of J-Term.

-
Incomplete grades are generally not allowed, except in extraordinary circumstances.

-
Final grades are submitted within 72 hours after the last class and posted in NYU Albert.

🔄 Withdrawal Policy (Once J-Term Starts)

-
The deadline to withdraw is the first day of classes.

-
After that, withdrawal is not an option.

-
To request withdrawal by the first day of classes, contact Dr. Ram Natarajan , Director of J-Term and Special Programs.

Additional Consequences:

For Abu Dhabi Courses

-
You receive a W grade.

-
You must return any J-Term funding received.

-
You may not remain in campus housing during J-Term.

For Courses Abroad

-
You receive a W grade.

-
You lose eligibility for another J-Term course abroad.

-
You must return in full the J-Term allowance you received, the visa costs (if any), and the airfare costs.

-
You will be flown home immediately.

💙 Support Resources

As with all courses, If you need support, reach out as soon as possible.

Accessibility

Student Persistence and Accessibility

📧 nyuad.spa@nyu.edu

Moses Center for Accessibility and Inclusive Culture
📧 mosescenter@nyu.edu

The Student Persistence and Accessibility provides reasonable learning accommodations and keeps information confidential. Please note that if you need to seek a certain learning accommodation specifically for J-Term, you must approach the Moses Center at least 6 weeks prior to the start of your J-Term course.

Health & Well-Being

-
NYUAD Counseling Center (NYUAD Campus Center, Ground Floor)
📞 +971-2-628-8100
📧 nyuad.healthcenter@nyu.edu

-
NYU Wellness Exchange (24/7)
📞 02-628-5555

For students taking a J-Term course outside the UAE, remote assistance is available through the NYU Wellness Exchange. The NYU sites abroad also have on-site resources for health and well-being support, and you will learn about those during the on-site J-Term orientation.

Writing Support

The NYUAD Writing Center can help at any stage—structure, clarity, brainstorming, and polishing. The Center provides help online as well.
Appointments: https://nyuad.mywconline.com

title: J-Term 2027 Course Selection Form · NYUAD Students
text:
J-Term 2027 Course Selection and Placement Guidelines

- Each course has an assigned point value. Each student has been assigned a specific number of points — i.e., a “points budget” – based on their particular J-Term history to date, including the number and location of previously attempted J-Term courses. Only course selections that are within a student’s point budget are allowed.

- Students must select six courses as they complete the J-Term course selection form. The order of the selected courses shows your preferences, with the first course on your list representing your most preferred choice. Although we will do our best to place students in one of their more preferred courses, please note you may be placed in ANY of the six courses you have listed in your selection form. NOTE: Just because a student is eligible for an Away course does not mean that they can’t be placed in an Abu Dhabi course if they list it. Think carefully about this if you are contemplating listing three lower-point Abu Dhabi options as your last three choices so that you can select three Away courses with higher point values as your top three choices.

- Spaces in individual J-Term courses are limited. Students are placed in J-Term courses based on a variety of factors, such as seniority, number of J-Term courses already taken, and the overall level of demand for each specific course.

- The overarching placement goal is to place as many students as possible in one of their three most preferred choices. The most important working assumption is that each choice you have listed in your selection form is a course you are genuinely interested in taking. Students must recognize that they may be placed in ANY one of their six choices.

- While seniority is considered in making placements, it is of notably less importance than assuring that as many students as possible get one of their top three or four choices.

- Placements in J-Term are not negotiable. Once students have been placed in specific courses, that is their only option. Trades, swaps, or requests for alternatives are not allowed.

- Placements will be posted in Albert by October 2, 2026. Students who request to withdraw from their assigned course will receive a W grade. Even students who have a compelling reason to withdraw from their J-Term course will receive a grade of W for the course. If this course is an Away course, the withdrawn students will not be eligible for a future Away course.

- A final grade of C or higher is required to fulfill the J-Term degree requirement.

The J-Term 2027 Course Selection Form can be found below:

Think carefully about this if you are contemplating listing three lower-point Abu Dhabi options as your last three choices so that you can select three Away courses with higher point values as your top three choices.

- Spaces in individual J-Term courses are limited. Students are placed in J-Term courses based on a variety of factors, such as seniority, number of J-Term courses already taken, and the overall level of demand for each specific course.

- The overarching placement goal is to place as many students as possible in one of their three most preferred choices. The most important working assumption is that each choice you have listed in your selection form is a course you are genuinely interested in taking. Students must recognize that they may be placed in ANY one of their six choices.

- While seniority is considered in making placements, it is of notably less importance than assuring that as many students as possible get one of their top three or four choices.

- Placements in J-Term are not negotiable. Once students have been placed in specific courses, that is their only option. Trades, swaps, or requests for alternatives are not allowed.

- Placements will be posted in Albert by October 2, 2026. Students who request to withdraw from their assigned course will receive a W grade. Even students who have a compelling reason to withdraw from their J-Term course will receive a grade of W for the course. If this course is an Away course, the withdrawn students will not be eligible for a future Away course.

- A final grade of C or higher is required to fulfill the J-Term degree requirement.

The J-Term 2027 Course Selection Form can be found below:

J-Term 2027 Course Selection Form

title: J-Term 2027 FAQs · NYUAD Students
text:
Frequently Asked Questions about J-Term

How do I enroll in a J-Term course?

Registration in J-Term courses is based on a placement process. Eligible students must submit a J-Term Course Selection Form, after which the placements are made and recorded in Albert.

Where can I find the J-Term Course Syllabi?

J-Term syllabi will be made available on the first day of J-Term classes. Please do not reach out to faculty to ask for the syllabi of courses in which you are interested. The syllabi are still being developed. You can review the course descriptions in Albert or here as you make your decision on which courses to select.

What is a passing grade for J-Term courses?

For J-Term courses to count toward the Core Field Colloquium a student must earn a grade of C or above. As required degree requirements, J-Term courses are not eligible for pass/fail grading and must be taken for a letter grade. Additionally, students must complete the J-Term coursework within the scheduled duration of J-Term. Incomplete (I) grades are not permitted.

What if I earn less than a C in one or more J-Terms?

You will need to take an additional (Abu Dhabi-based) J-Term course and earn a minimum of a C in two J-Terms.

Is there an add/drop period for J-Term?

Not exactly. Students may choose to withdraw (with a W grade) from a J-Term course they have started only on the first day of class and only if they have a documented, legitimate reason. After the first day of class, withdrawal is no longer permitted, and the course will be graded with a letter grade. Students who withdraw from an Away J-Term course should expect to travel home immediately following their withdrawal regardless of their location at the time. Students who withdraw from an away J-Term class are not eligible for future J-Term away class enrollment.

I didn't get into the J-Term that I wanted, can I be on a waitlist?

There are no waitlists for J-Term. Placements are final as posted in Albert.

I took ENGR-UH 1021J Design and Innovation when it was a J-Term Course. Does that mean I need another J-Term course?

No. As long as you took it when it was designated as a J-Term course (i.e., prior to January 2025), it satisfies one course toward the J-Term requirement. The course is now listed as ENGR-UH 1021 (without the J) as it does not count as a J-Term course anymore

I took ENGR-UH 1021J Design and Innovation when it was a J-Term Course. Can I choose not to count it as a J-Term course and, consequently, be eligible for an extra J-Term?

No. If you took the course when it was designated as a J-Term (i.e. prior to January 2025), it remains a J-Term.

Will all J-Term courses fulfill the Core Field Colloquium?

Yes, and in fact, the J-Term courses ONLY fulfill the Core Field Colloquium requirement. J-Term courses no longer count toward any other degree requirements (major, minor, Core competencies.)

Since it takes two J-Term courses to satisfy the Core Field Colloquium requirement, does that mean that the two courses have to be related in some way?

Not at all. Students can take any two J-Term offerings.

I noticed that semester courses at some of the study away sites contain significant experiential learning opportunities. Can I substitute one of them for the J-Term Core Field Colloquium requirement, or at least for half of it?

No. The NYUAD Core Field Colloquium requirement can only be met through successfully completing two NYUAD J-Term Core Field Colloquium courses.

I've heard that course descriptions sometimes change after course registration. Is that something I should worry about?

Not really. While there are occasionally changes made after registration, they are typically minor and made after the Curriculum Committee works with the faculty member to improve the course. NYUAD's J-Term Program works months, sometimes years, in advance to offer a wide variety of high-quality courses. The posted schedule as shown is the most up-to-date information and the final class schedule is posted by the end of December for students. The university will inform students at the earliest possible opportunity if/when significant changes occur to a J-Term course offering. Barring a truly significant change in the course, NYUAD expects students to select and remain in courses based on the overriding nature of the course and not on any specific detail. Students wishing to abandon a course due to a change in the course description will ordinarily be expected to withdraw from the course with a grade of W rather than being able to drop the course without a penalty.

I don't see the class timings in Albert for the courses I am interested in? How do I find these out?

Class timings are determined closer to the start of J-Term. Please keep in mind that all J-Term classes meet intensively each day throughout the J-Term session. Refer to the information included in the Student Commitment and Expectations section for more information about attendance expectations.

Are there any special health or safety considerations with Away courses?

Rest assured that if deemed necessary, we will provide location-specific guidance for health and safety for any courses that include travel outside of campus, and outside of the UAE.

Related official links:
https://students.nyuad.nyu.edu/academics/course-list-and-syllabi/undergraduate-program/

Are you applying to study away for a semester? Please review the following steps to make sure that you have all the information required to apply.

title: Application Selection Process · NYUAD Students
text:
Applications are reviewed by a committee. Final approval to study away is based on:

- Students applying to study away in their junior year must have declared their capstone major before submitting a study away application

- Minimum cumulative GPA of 3.0 at the time of application– unless otherwise specified by the program in the pathway

- Good academic and disciplinary standing

- Positive overall review of academic, disciplinary, and financial aid records

- Normal progress toward the completion of graduation requirements

- Academic preparation for the chosen study away program

- Suitability of the study away program to the student’s academic goals

- Strength of the application materials, including well-written essays

- Meeting program-specific prerequisites (e.g. foreign language level, area-specific coursework)

- Mentor’s approval of the courses of study away and how they apply to fulfilling core, major, and minor requirements

- Completion of four core courses and two physical education activities prior to studying abroad is highly recommended.

title: Course Alternates · NYUAD Students
text:
A primary principle of NYU’s global network is student mobility. Courses in counterpart majors generally count toward NYUAD majors (e.g., a course in history at any NYU site would usually count toward our history major in Abu Dhabi). Some NYUAD majors do not have perfect counterparts at the other NYU global network sites. Additionally, there are courses in the NYU global network that are essentially identical to some of our courses and care should be taken to make sure that you don't inadvertently repeat a course. Please see Study Away Courses and NYUAD Academic Requirements (https://students.nyuad.nyu.edu/academics/global-education/study-away/course-equivalencies/study-away-equivalencies/) for information regarding course alternates per site as well as the Alternate Course Proposal Form (https://students.nyuad.nyu.edu/academics/global-education/study-away/course-equivalencies/equivalency-proposal/).

Course alternates are reviewed and updated at all times. Please check them frequently as you plan your study away.

As a reminder, courses taught only online are not eligible for credit and students should not take them while on study away. Students should look for in-person coursework.

With respect to Core courses and courses within a multidisciplinary concentration, we seek to balance the ideal of mobility with maintaining the integrity of our unique curriculum. This is accomplished through a generally generous acceptance of courses toward these areas but with a restriction that at least one Core course in each category and at least two courses in a multidisciplinary concentration must be completed in Abu Dhabi. Core course alternates taught at the NYU Global Program locations can be found here (https://students.nyuad.nyu.edu/academics/core-curriculum/global-core-alternates/).

The academic deans and Undergraduate Curriculum Committee have reviewed offerings at the various study away sites and at most of the courses in which students have indicated an intent to study in New York. The links below provide information on the courses that are appropriate for the varying major, Core, and concentration requirements indicated. If a course is listed on the location page it has been reviewed and students will only be able to receive credit as indicated.

Course numbers that contain " -SH " are offered at the NYU Shanghai campus. Other course numbers that contain a " G " or start with a " 9 xxx" are typically offered at one of the global sites. All other course numbers are normally offered at the New York campus. When developing a schedule students should filter on the site location that they will be attending to see the current list of offerings.

Review of courses will ordinarily take several weeks for review and processing and you should have a backup plan in case the course is not approved. You will be notified by email when the review has been completed. The course alternate pages themselves will be updated periodically and may not reflect all recent reviews. As a reminder, courses taught only online are not eligible for credit and students should not take them while on study away. Students should look for in-person coursework. Please DO NOT submit proposals for non-NYU courses with this form.

title: Study Away Alternates · NYUAD Students
text:
Study Away Courses and NYUAD Academic Requirements

If a course does not appear and you would like to enroll in it you will need to complete an Alternate Course Proposal Form (https://students.nyuad.nyu.edu/academics/global-education/study-away/course-equivalencies/equivalency-proposal/). Every effort will be made to review these courses before registration begins as long as the request is submitted at least three weeks before the start of registration. It is unlikely that the review can be fully completed and you may have to make some adjustments to your schedule during add/drop. Due to the press of time, please nominate only courses that are listed in Albert as being offered in the semester that you plan on taking the course. There will be adequate time later to nominate future courses.

Course alternates are reviewed and updated at all times. Please check them frequently as you plan your study away.

As a reminder, courses taught only online are not eligible for credit and students should not take them while on study away. Students should look for in-person coursework.

Please be sure to check degree requirements as some are based on the number of credits, while others are based on the number of courses. Courses taken for 2 credits count as half courses, and courses taken for 3 credits count as full courses, however only actual credits earned will count towards credit-based requirements (e.g. a course taken for 3 credits will not be given 4 credits). sections.title: Study Away Courses and NYUAD Academic Requirements
sections.text:
If a course does not appear and you would like to enroll in it you will need to complete an Alternate Course Proposal Form (https://students.nyuad.nyu.edu/academics/global-education/study-away/course-equivalencies/equivalency-proposal/). Every effort will be made to review these courses before registration begins as long as the request is submitted at least three weeks before the start of registration. It is unlikely that the review can be fully completed and you may have to make some adjustments to your schedule during add/drop. Due to the press of time, please nominate only courses that are listed in Albert as being offered in the semester that you plan on taking the course. There will be adequate time later to nominate future courses.

Course alternates are reviewed and updated at all times. Please check them frequently as you plan your study away.

As a reminder, courses taught only online are not eligible for credit and students should not take them while on study away. Students should look for in-person coursework.

Please be sure to check degree requirements as some are based on the number of credits, while others are based on the number of courses. Courses taken for 2 credits count as half courses, and courses taken for 3 credits count as full courses, however only actual credits earned will count towards credit-based requirements (e.g. a course taken for 3 credits will not be given 4 credits). Please note NYUAD students may not count courses from the School of Professional Studies toward their NYUAD degrees nor will NYUAD financial aid cover the costs of those courses. These courses are typically designated with subject code suffixes “-CE” (and some courses with the suffix of "-UC" and "-GC").

Search for the degree requirement (example: Applied Mathematics Elective) for a listing of courses that have been accepted from NYU Study Away sites. Next check Albert (https://albert.nyu.edu/albert_index.html) course search to see if the course is offered during the semester at the site you plan to attend. Course schedules for the Spring semester are published by the end of October in the preceding year, and the course schedules for the Fall semester are published by the end of March of the same year.

Course numbers that contain " -SH " are offered at the NYU Shanghai campus. Other course numbers that contain a " G " or start with a " 9 xxx" are typically offered at one of the NYU global sites. All other course numbers are normally offered at the New York campus. When developing a schedule students should filter on the site location that they will be attending to see the current list of offerings.

Attention: The process for Study Away Course Alternate Proposals is being reviewed. Due to a large number of submissions it will take time for departments to review requests and make decisions. This can take weeks, and in some cases even months.

- In the meantime, if you need a course to be reviewed urgently because you are graduating this semester or next, please contact the respective program head for the course to be individually reviewed as an exception.

- If you are not graduating this semester or next, please proceed with a contingency plan in case your proposal is not accepted in time for enrollment changes.

- Accra, Ghana

- Berlin, Germany

- Buenos Aires, Argentina

- Florence, Italy

- London, United Kingdom

- Los Angeles, USA

- Madrid, Spain

- New York, USA

- Paris, France

- Prague, Czech Republic

- Shanghai, China

- Sydney, Australia

- Tel Aviv, Israel
