title: Physical and Health Education · NYUAD Students
text:
Mission

The mission of the Physical and Health Education (PHE) program is committed and focused on the development of the whole student: physical, mental, social, and intellectual. The program enables undergraduate students to develop an understanding of the correlations between physical activity, academic studies, and overall well-being and exposes students to new activities and learning that aim to provide confidence and inspiration to maintain a healthy, physically active life whilst a student and beyond.

Requirements

The PHE program offers a wide variety of classes covering a range of health, fitness, and sporting topics relevant to all students regardless of their ability and experiences. Undergraduate students are required to complete two unique 7-week courses before graduation with each successfully completed course appearing on the official student transcripts. One PHE credit can also be earned through successful participation in a University Sports Team, participating in a minimum 80 percent of training sessions and competitive fixtures across a single semester. Students are encouraged to complete at least one PHE credit prior to studying away and those who successfully complete two courses within their first year, acknowledged for their achievement.

How to Enroll

Enrollment occurs through Albert. The list below provides examples of the types of courses offered throughout the school year. For more information on any of these PHE courses, please visit the Undergraduate Program Course list or email pequestions@nyu.edu.

Attendance Policy

Success in PHE is based on student's attendance.

This includes being:

Punctual — Students must arrive on time. Arrival 10 minutes or more after class begins will result in an absence.

Proactive — Plan ahead to avoid delays. If you have a class scheduled before your PHE course, inform your professor to ensure you can leave promptly. Students must notify their instructor via email in advance if they are unable to attend a class and cc pequestions@nyu.edu

Present — The expectations are that students must attend all scheduled PHE classes over the course duration. Students should only miss a class under exceptional circumstances and are permitted a maximum of x2 exceptions per course. For courses that meet only once per week, students are permitted to miss a maximum of one class. Attendance is recorded from the time of enrolment. Missed classes during add/ drop week will count as an absence(s).

Engaged — Participation and effort during class. While our goal is to ensure that you have fun and learn in a safe and supported environment, students are expected to participate fully in class, both in the theory and practical sessions. Students may be asked to lead class discussions, warm-ups, and workouts. Quizzes may also be given during some classes. To ensure that all students are staying safe during practice and are participating fully, no cell phones (unless permission given by instructor) are allowed.

View the full attendance policy .

Examples of PHE Courses Offered

- Introduction to Group Fitness Classes

This introductory course orients students to the various exercise equipment and fitness classes in the Saadiyat Fitness Center and provides a framework for the students to design their own personal fitness programs. Through strength and cardio training, TRX, Kettlebells, spinning, yoga, and pilates, students will learn how to exercise safely and effectively to maximize progress. The guided and progressive workouts teach individuals to achieve personal fitness goals by creating and implementing healthy fitness routines.

- Beginner Swimming

Typically offered: fall, spring. The beginner swimming course is designed for students who are non-swimmers and those who have little to no skills in the water. This course is designed to help the non-swimmer learn basic water safety skills including instruction of proper body position in the water, floating, treading water, holding breath underwater, and introductory to swim strokes, freestyle, and backstroke.

- Intermediate Swimming

Intermediate swimming is a course designed for students who are comfortable treading, floating, and swimming in deep water, can swim front crawl with rotary breathing and can swim basic backstroke and breaststroke. Students learn drills for skill improvement. Emphasis is on body form, stroke efficiency, and conditioning in all the strokes.

- WO Swimming

The beginner swimming course is designed for students who are non-swimmers and those who have little to no skills in the water. This course is designed to help the non-swimmer learn basic water safety skills including instruction of proper body position in the water, floating, treading water, holding breath underwater, and introductory to swim strokes, freestyle and backstroke. This is a women’s only course.

- Hip Hop

Hip Hop dance is designed for students with an interest in Hip Hop dance/culture. This class introduces students to Hip Hop through movement that includes freestyle dancing, locomotive movements, and choreography.

- WO Pilates

Pilates is a conditioning program emphasizing the concepts of core strength and stabilization. Through highly focused and controlled movements, individuals experience increased body awareness, flexibility, coordination, and strength. This is a women's only course.

- Jiu Jitsu

Jiu Jitsu is a strategic grappling sport where one manipulates an opponent’s force against her/ himself rather than confronting it with one’s own force. Individuals will learn how to apply the fundamental techniques of Jiu Jitsu, including positioning, leverage, joint locks, escapes, submissions, and self-defense.

- Mindfulness

-

Koru Mindfulness® is an evidence-based curriculum specifically designed for teaching mindfulness, meditation, and resiliency to college students and other young adults. You will learn several skills, including meditation, breathing exercises, guided imagery, body scan, and more. Each of these skills is designed to help you manage stress and enrich your life.

- Tennis

This class is geared towards novice tennis players and exposes individuals to the basics of tennis. In addition to receiving technical instruction in serve, volley and forehand and backhand strokes, individuals learn the rules of tennis.

- Foundations of Boxing

-

Students will focus on the correct techniques for punching, focus pad holding, basic defense, and footwork. This course ensures a safe and supportive environment without the inclusion of sparring, providing an empowering space for students to build confidence and strength.

- WO Foundations of Boxing

-

Students will focus on the correct techniques for punching, focus pad holding, basic defense, and footwork. This course ensures a safe and supportive environment without the inclusion of sparring, providing an empowering space for students to build confidence and strength.

- Indoor Cycling

This course aims to teach students the essential components of Indoor Cycling.

- Yoga

Yoga will commence with an introduction to yoga practice, infusing breathing techniques, physical movement, detox, meditation, strength, flexibility, and balance conditioning with balance of body and mind. This program will allow students to work within their own individual body's capacity to ultimately let go of any physical or mental barriers.

- Badminton

This course is designed to introduce basic badminton skills, techniques, rules, and strategies for singles and doubles play with a focus on development of various strokes, serves, and offensive and defensive strategies. No previous experience necessary.

- Foundations of Running

-

This course focuses on improving the student's running technique and form. Students will advance through a variety of track sessions where students will be introduced to proper warm-up and running drills with an emphasis on injury prevention. Students will leave the course empowered to continue running for sport or pleasure.

One PHE credit can also be earned through successful participation in a University Sports Team, participating in a minimum 80 percent of training sessions and competitive fixtures across a single semester. Students are encouraged to complete at least one PHE credit prior to studying away and those who successfully complete two courses within their first year, acknowledged for their achievement.

sections.title: How to Enroll
sections.text: Enrollment occurs through Albert. The list below provides examples of the types of courses offered throughout the school year. For more information on any of these PHE courses, please visit the Undergraduate Program Course list or email pequestions@nyu.edu.

sections.title: How to Enroll · Attendance Policy
sections.text:
Success in PHE is based on student's attendance.

This includes being:

Punctual — Students must arrive on time. Arrival 10 minutes or more after class begins will result in an absence.

Proactive — Plan ahead to avoid delays. If you have a class scheduled before your PHE course, inform your professor to ensure you can leave promptly. Students must notify their instructor via email in advance if they are unable to attend a class and cc pequestions@nyu.edu

Present — The expectations are that students must attend all scheduled PHE classes over the course duration. Students should only miss a class under exceptional circumstances and are permitted a maximum of x2 exceptions per course. For courses that meet only once per week, students are permitted to miss a maximum of one class. Attendance is recorded from the time of enrolment. Missed classes during add/ drop week will count as an absence(s).

Engaged — Participation and effort during class. While our goal is to ensure that you have fun and learn in a safe and supported environment, students are expected to participate fully in class, both in the theory and practical sessions. Students may be asked to lead class discussions, warm-ups, and workouts. Quizzes may also be given during some classes. To ensure that all students are staying safe during practice and are participating fully, no cell phones (unless permission given by instructor) are allowed.

View the full attendance policy .

sections.title: Examples of PHE Courses Offered
sections.text:
- Introduction to Group Fitness Classes

This introductory course orients students to the various exercise equipment and fitness classes in the Saadiyat Fitness Center and provides a framework for the students to design their own personal fitness programs. Through strength and cardio training, TRX, Kettlebells, spinning, yoga, and pilates, students will learn how to exercise safely and effectively to maximize progress. The guided and progressive workouts teach individuals to achieve personal fitness goals by creating and implementing healthy fitness routines.

- Beginner Swimming

Typically offered: fall, spring. The beginner swimming course is designed for students who are non-swimmers and those who have little to no skills in the water. This course is designed to help the non-swimmer learn basic water safety skills including instruction of proper body position in the water, floating, treading water, holding breath underwater, and introductory to swim strokes, freestyle, and backstroke.

- Intermediate Swimming

Intermediate swimming is a course designed for students who are comfortable treading, floating, and swimming in deep water, can swim front crawl with rotary breathing and can swim basic backstroke and breaststroke. Students learn drills for skill improvement. Emphasis is on body form, stroke efficiency, and conditioning in all the strokes.

- WO Swimming

The beginner swimming course is designed for students who are non-swimmers and those who have little to no skills in the water. This course is designed to help the non-swimmer learn basic water safety skills including instruction of proper body position in the water, floating, treading water, holding breath underwater, and introductory to swim strokes, freestyle and backstroke. This is a women’s only course.

- Hip Hop

Hip Hop dance is designed for students with an interest in Hip Hop dance/culture. This class introduces students to Hip Hop through movement that includes freestyle dancing, locomotive movements, and choreography.

- WO Pilates

Pilates is a conditioning program emphasizing the concepts of core strength and stabilization. Through highly focused and controlled movements, individuals experience increased body awareness, flexibility, coordination, and strength. This is a women's only course.

- Jiu Jitsu

Jiu Jitsu is a strategic grappling sport where one manipulates an opponent’s force against her/ himself rather than confronting it with one’s own force. Individuals will learn how to apply the fundamental techniques of Jiu Jitsu, including positioning, leverage, joint locks, escapes, submissions, and self-defense.

- Mindfulness

-

Koru Mindfulness® is an evidence-based curriculum specifically designed for teaching mindfulness, meditation, and resiliency to college students and other young adults. You will learn several skills, including meditation, breathing exercises, guided imagery, body scan, and more. Each of these skills is designed to help you manage stress and enrich your life.

- Tennis

This class is geared towards novice tennis players and exposes individuals to the basics of tennis. In addition to receiving technical instruction in serve, volley and forehand and backhand strokes, individuals learn the rules of tennis.

- Foundations of Boxing

-

Students will focus on the correct techniques for punching, focus pad holding, basic defense, and footwork. This course ensures a safe and supportive environment without the inclusion of sparring, providing an empowering space for students to build confidence and strength.

- WO Foundations of Boxing

-

Students will focus on the correct techniques for punching, focus pad holding, basic defense, and footwork. This course ensures a safe and supportive environment without the inclusion of sparring, providing an empowering space for students to build confidence and strength.

- Indoor Cycling

This course aims to teach students the essential components of Indoor Cycling.

- Yoga

Yoga will commence with an introduction to yoga practice, infusing breathing techniques, physical movement, detox, meditation, strength, flexibility, and balance conditioning with balance of body and mind. This program will allow students to work within their own individual body's capacity to ultimately let go of any physical or mental barriers.

- Badminton

This course is designed to introduce basic badminton skills, techniques, rules, and strategies for singles and doubles play with a focus on development of various strokes, serves, and offensive and defensive strategies. No previous experience necessary.

- Foundations of Running

-

This course focuses on improving the student's running technique and form. Students will advance through a variety of track sessions where students will be introduced to proper warm-up and running drills with an emphasis on injury prevention. Students will leave the course empowered to continue running for sport or pleasure.

title: Group Classes · NYUAD Students
text:
Group Classes

To support the community in pursuit of wellbeing, the Department of Athletics offers you the chance to participate in a variety of classes each week. Classes offered include Yoga, Tibetan Singing Bowls, Fitness Boxing, Indoor Cycling and more. All classes are booked and scheduled on the Class Registration page on FABS . All classes are 50 minutes in duration, unless stated otherwise.

Classes are open to all of the NYUAD community including students, faculty, staff, family members age 16 and older, and Tamkeen. The term schedule is displayed in both Fitness Centers, Instagram and on FABS .

Class Booking and Cancellation

Booking is necessary and can be done through the Fitness and Athletics Booking System ( FABS ) .

- Classes can be booked three days in advance and booking ends 30 minutes before the start of class.

- Booked classes can be canceled up to 2 hours prior to its start.

- If you can't make your class, please make sure to cancel the class you have registered for to avoid a "NO-SHOW" warning. Classes have limited capacity so p lease be considerate of other campus residents.

No-Show Policy

- If you fail to show up to a class without cancelling on two occasions, your FABS reservation privileges will be suspended for 7 days.

Please arrive 5-10 minutes before the scheduled start-time, dressed appropriately, and with a towel and water bottle. You will be asked to check-in with the instructor.

title: Career Development · NYUAD Students
text:
Get updated CDC information in the Temporary Operations section.

Celebrating Diverse Ideas of Success

The Career Development Center (CDC) plays an integral role in your undergraduate experience at NYU Abu Dhabi, providing guidance, advising, programs, and resources. From choosing a major, to helping you write your very first CV, finding your first role, and all the next steps in your unique career path, we empower you throughout your time at NYUAD, and beyond.

Learn More About the CDC

- Getting Started

Handshake is the CDC’s go-to career platform where students will register for events, schedule advising sessions, apply for on and off campus positions, and explore resources.

- Review our Ultimate Career Guide for CV and Cover Letter templates, interviewing and networking tips and more.

- Explore the 4-year plan as it guides you through various steps and tips for your next four years.

- Reflect on our list of career competencies that you can build through volunteering, leadership positions and internships to help you be career ready when you graduate.

- Join a career community to explore career possibilities, gain hands-on experience, develop career readiness skills, build connections, and get industry insights across different areas of interest.

- Events and Workshops

The CDC offers a variety of different events, workshops and panels throughout the academic year. These are a great way to meet professionals and alumni in your area of interest, develop and learn skills to help you apply for various opportunities and learn more about pathways to graduate school, global awards and more.

- You can RSVP and our list of workshops and events on Handshake .

- Don’t forget to sign up for Career Communities so you can get updates on relevant events.

- Advising

Whether you are finding your first job, applying to graduate school, or transitioning to a new career, NYUAD CDC advisors are always happy to help.

- 30-min Advising Appointments: Log in to Handshake and select Appointments under the Career Center tab to schedule your advising appointment. Advising is available through in-person or virtual sessions. Here is a list of various topics you could discuss with an advisor.

- Choosing Your Major

- Career Exploration and Planning

- CVs and Cover Letters

- Strength and Interest Assessments

- Walk-in Hours: This is another great option if you have a quick question, or would like the CDC to review your application materials.

title: Career Communities · NYUAD Students
text:
Career Communities are designed to help students and alumni explore career possibilities, gain hands-on experience, develop career readiness skills, build connections, and get industry insights across different areas of interest.

Benefits of Joining a Career Community

- Be Part of a Curated Resource Hub
Members of Career Communities get tailored communication and information about programming, employment opportunities, skill development tools, and career exploration and preparation resources all in one place.

- Insight into Careers and Industries
Gain industry specific information, understand career pathways, attend relevant panels and workshops, gain insight on companies and trends, and access to curated resources.

- Build Connections
Engage with your peers as you explore a career community. Connect with industry professionals or alumni that can share industry insight and advice.

Our Communities

- Arts and Creative

Start your search here to explore a career in arts, media, and entertainment. Connect with practicing artists, arts administrators, or professionals in marketing and entertainment. Explore arts education organizations, galleries, museums, cultural centers, and marketing and entertainment companies in the UAE and beyond. Learn about residencies, graduate programs, competitions, and festivals to help you gain experience in the arts and creative industry.

Join the Arts and Creative Career Community by signing up on Handshake .

- Consulting, Finance, and Business

Start your search here to explore a career in consulting, finance, or business. Connect with consultants, analysts, entrepreneurs, and industry professionals. Explore and network with the top consulting firms, e-commerce, and tech companies. Learn how to tailor your CV, participate in case competitions, practice case interviews, and much more.

Join the Consulting, Finance, Business Career Community by signing up on Handshake .

- Career Exploration

Start your search here to explore different career paths and industries. Engage with career assessments and learn how your interests, values, strengths, and skills connect to potential pathways. Attend panels and workshops to gain insight about different industries and how to engage in activities that help you gain skills and insight, like joining student interest groups, or applying for student internships or volunteer opportunities.

Join the Career Exploration Career Community by signing up on Handshake .

- Diplomacy, Law, and International Relations

Start your search here to explore a career in diplomacy, law, or international relations. Connect with diplomats, lawyers, legal advisors, policy analysts. Explore and network with the UN, Embassies, and Law firms. Learn how to engage in related internships, training or volunteer programs and conferences.

Join the Diplomacy, Law and International Relations Career Community by signing up on Handshake .

- Health and Medicine

Start your search here to explore a career in health and medicine. Connect with health professionals, doctors, nurses, researchers, and industry professionals. Explore and network with hospitals, clinics, and medical school programs. Learn how to gain shadowing experience, join a volunteer program or explore graduate school and medical school programs.

Join the Health and Medicine Career Community by signing up on Handshake .

- Science, Engineering, and Technology

Start your search here to explore a career in science, engineering, and technology. Connect with software developers, coders, engineers, and data analysts. Explore and network with companies leading the charge in technology advances, or help to inform decisions and drive innovation for companies, startups, or research centers. Learn how to gain hands-on experience, participate in competitions and related projects, or engage in research.

Join the Science, Engineering, Technology Career Community by signing up on Handshake .

- Social Impact and Education

Start your search here to explore a career in social impact and education. Connect with educators, non-profit leaders and policy experts. Explore and network with organizations and companies committed to social change and education. Develop an understanding of the field, what skills and experiences are in demand, and the different ways you can make an impact. Learn how to gain community based experiences, volunteer, or explore graduate programs.

Join the Social Impact and Education Career Community by signing up on Handshake .

- PhD and PostDoc

This community is for PhD students, Global PhD, and PostDoc fellows. Explore your options and prepare for a career in academia or industry. Connect with alumni, faculty, and industry professionals. Learn how to tailor your application materials (industry/academia), gain insight into industry trends and hiring, and connect with potential employers locally as well as globally.

Join the PhD, PostDoc Career Community by signing up on Handshake .

title: Explore Your Interests · NYUAD Students
text:
Ways to Explore Career Options

- Craft career experiments to explore your options

Leverage your time as a student to try out or experiment with new industries, skills, and possible work contexts. Experiments can be brief, like a lecture series or workshop hosted by a professional about a topic of interest, or more in-depth, like an internship. Our career advisors can help you decide where to start.

- Get some industry perspective

Do research to get a bird’s eye view of an industry (check out our industry maps and databases below), which companies operate in that space, as well what graduate programs, conferences, and trainings are relevant.

- Expand your idea of options

Check out the eclectic paths of NYUAD alumni in the Life Beyond Saadiyat reports or on LinkedIn. Explore what internships students have pursued by industry through the Internship Map .

- Assess mobility

Review the work status requirements for different countries for internships as well as full-time work through GoinGlobal or individual country immigration departments. Navigating your global mobility is a lifelong skill you can begin to develop in university.

- Benchmark your skills

Develop your sense of what it will take to be competitive in your field of interest by reviewing job descriptions for jobs you’d like to have in the future. Meet with a career advisor to evaluate your current skills as they relate to your goals and discuss a plan of action.

- Evaluate the outlook

Look into possible job titles and expected growth for occupations in the United States or the UAE . If you’re considering a PhD, think ahead with Versatile PhD , a resource of STEM, humanities, and social science PhDs sharing non-academic career choices.

- Meet the people doing the work

Watch videos clips of real people talking honestly about their jobs with Candid Career . Reach out to professionals for information interviews to help build your industry knowledge. As an NYUAD student, you can attend our employer information sessions, which bring various employers to campus throughout the academic year.

- Consider the unconventional

If you sense that traditional employment or graduate school isn’t for you, talk to an advisor about the paths less traveled. Explore books like How to Work Your Way Around the World , Teaching English Overseas , Volunteer Vacations , You Majored in WHAT? or What Color is Your Parachute? These are all available in the CDC library.

Uncover Your Skills and Strengths

Knowing your own preferences can help you understand your strengths, and the type of work environment and activities you might enjoy. Assessments can help develop a vocabulary for your skills and interests, which helps guide you in career-related decisions.

- Myers-Briggs Type Indicator (MBTI)

The most widely used personality inventory in the world, the MBTI will provide you with insight about yourself in four areas:

- How you energize and re-energize.

- How you perceive and acquire information.

- How you make decisions.

- How you prefer to engage the world around you.

The career report of the MBTI provides occupational lists, showing the occupations most selected and least selected by your personality type.

To take a free version of the MBTI using 16 personalities , then we recommend scheduling an appointment with an advisor to discuss your results. contact nyuad.career@nyu.edu .

- Strong Interest Inventory

The Strong Interest Inventory assessment is another widely respected and frequently used career planning tool. It can help with choosing a major because it helps identify interests and corresponding areas of study, and also ties interests to various occupations and careers. Schedule an appointment with an advisor via Handshake to discuss your interest in a career assessment.

- Skills and Values Checklist

This simple worksheet is a great start place for exploring the skills you currently have and the skills you want to build. It also invites you to prioritize your values, so you can integrate this into your decision making process. You can review your checklist with a career advisor to generate action steps.

See What You can do With Your Major

Use this resource to see what are common career areas, employers, and strategies for different majors. Note that this is a US-based resource, but the information remains applicable globally. You can always stop by our office to help translate it to a different region.

Helping Plan for Your Future

From self-discovery of your skills and interests, all the way to acclimation to the world of work, we will help you each step of the way. Make use of our four-year timelines to help track your progress.

Individual appointments (in person and Skype) are available for you to talk through career-related concerns, get feedback, and develop strategies to move forward. Some of the topics we cover include:

- Career Advising

Our counselors and advisors are equipped to help you navigate your career: the in-betweenness and uncertainty you may face in your career decisions, self-discovery of your skills and interests, development of your professional skills, preparation for graduate school, exploration of scholarships and prestigious awards, and acclimation to the world of work. Some of the topics we can cover include:

- Choosing Your Major

- Career Exploration and Planning

- CVs and Cover Letters

- Strength and Interest Assessments

- Job/Internship Search Strategy

- Networking

- Interviewing

- Internships and Experiential Learning

- Negotiating an Offer

- Graduate and Professional School

- Global Mobility

- Industry Knowledge and Recruitment

- Funding/Grant/Award Applications

- Student Assistantships

- Events and Workshops

CDC events, big and small, are a great way to actively explore career topics, meet professionals in your area of interest, and develop skills. Our events and workshops include:

- Career Fair (fall and spring): Explore jobs, internships, and volunteer opportunities with organizations from across the UAE.

- Networking Night: Engage in conversations with professionals from all different fields in the UAE.

- Employer Sessions: Get a more in-depth look at an organization as they share industry knowledge and company insights.

- Workshops and Meetups: Group discussions about the skills and strategies you need to build in order to achieve your goals.

- Programs and Services

The CDC provides a wide array of programs and services that empower students to take ownership of their ongoing career development process, such as:

- CV Books: Join the collection of student CVs which are distributed to hundreds employers each year, so you can be actively recruited.

- On-campus Recruitment: Interview on-campus for opportunities with local organizations.

- Campus Work Experience: Develop employability skills through on-campus jobs and internships.

- Grant Programs: Apply for a limited number of competitive grants which can support your summer internship, graduate school admissions test preparation, or final-round interview costs.

sections.title: Uncover Your Skills and Strengths
sections.text:
Knowing your own preferences can help you understand your strengths, and the type of work environment and activities you might enjoy. Assessments can help develop a vocabulary for your skills and interests, which helps guide you in career-related decisions.

- Myers-Briggs Type Indicator (MBTI)

The most widely used personality inventory in the world, the MBTI will provide you with insight about yourself in four areas:

- How you energize and re-energize.

- How you perceive and acquire information.

- How you make decisions.

- How you prefer to engage the world around you.

The career report of the MBTI provides occupational lists, showing the occupations most selected and least selected by your personality type.

To take a free version of the MBTI using 16 personalities , then we recommend scheduling an appointment with an advisor to discuss your results. contact nyuad.career@nyu.edu .

- Strong Interest Inventory

The Strong Interest Inventory assessment is another widely respected and frequently used career planning tool. It can help with choosing a major because it helps identify interests and corresponding areas of study, and also ties interests to various occupations and careers. Schedule an appointment with an advisor via Handshake to discuss your interest in a career assessment.

- Skills and Values Checklist

This simple worksheet is a great start place for exploring the skills you currently have and the skills you want to build. It also invites you to prioritize your values, so you can integrate this into your decision making process. You can review your checklist with a career advisor to generate action steps.

sections.title: See What You can do With Your Major
sections.text: Use this resource to see what are common career areas, employers, and strategies for different majors. Note that this is a US-based resource, but the information remains applicable globally. You can always stop by our office to help translate it to a different region.

sections.title: Helping Plan for Your Future
sections.text:
From self-discovery of your skills and interests, all the way to acclimation to the world of work, we will help you each step of the way. Make use of our four-year timelines to help track your progress.

Individual appointments (in person and Skype) are available for you to talk through career-related concerns, get feedback, and develop strategies to move forward. Some of the topics we cover include:

- Career Advising

Our counselors and advisors are equipped to help you navigate your career: the in-betweenness and uncertainty you may face in your career decisions, self-discovery of your skills and interests, development of your professional skills, preparation for graduate school, exploration of scholarships and prestigious awards, and acclimation to the world of work. Some of the topics we can cover include:

- Choosing Your Major

- Career Exploration and Planning

- CVs and Cover Letters

- Strength and Interest Assessments

- Job/Internship Search Strategy

- Networking

- Interviewing

- Internships and Experiential Learning

- Negotiating an Offer

- Graduate and Professional School

- Global Mobility

- Industry Knowledge and Recruitment

- Funding/Grant/Award Applications

- Student Assistantships

- Events and Workshops

CDC events, big and small, are a great way to actively explore career topics, meet professionals in your area of interest, and develop skills. Our events and workshops include:

- Career Fair (fall and spring): Explore jobs, internships, and volunteer opportunities with organizations from across the UAE.

- Networking Night: Engage in conversations with professionals from all different fields in the UAE.

- Employer Sessions: Get a more in-depth look at an organization as they share industry knowledge and company insights.

- Workshops and Meetups: Group discussions about the skills and strategies you need to build in order to achieve your goals.

- Programs and Services

The CDC provides a wide array of programs and services that empower students to take ownership of their ongoing career development process, such as:

- CV Books: Join the collection of student CVs which are distributed to hundreds employers each year, so you can be actively recruited.

- On-campus Recruitment: Interview on-campus for opportunities with local organizations.

- Campus Work Experience: Develop employability skills through on-campus jobs and internships.

- Grant Programs: Apply for a limited number of competitive grants which can support your summer internship, graduate school admissions test preparation, or final-round interview costs.

title: Cover Letter · NYUAD Students
text:
Your Cover Letter is a single-page document often sent along with your CV when applying for opportunities. What makes it different from a CV? While your CV highlights your overall professional and academic experiences, the Cover Letter is your chance to delve deeper and explain how these experiences make you a great candidate for the specific opportunity you're applying for.

Use a cover letter to explain why you want to work for the organization, and highlight your related skills and experience. This letter should be tailored to the opportunity you’re applying for and clearly state how your qualifications will make a contribution to the organization.

Learn how to craft a successful Cover Letter with Ale from our Back to Basics Series:

Review our Ultimate Career Guide (Ch3: Crafting a Cover Letter) (PDF) with a Cover Letter template, samples, and more. Visit the CDC during our office hours and have your CV reviewed by a Global Career Peer or visit our walk-in’s for a quick appointment with an advisor.

What's in a Cover Letter?

- First Paragraph

The first paragraph needs to do three things:

- Explain why you are writing (to apply for this job; name it!)

- Tell them how you heard about the position.

- Offer a one-sentence argument — essentially a thesis statement — as to why they should hire you. If you didn't get a full letter, but just one sentence, what would you say?

- Body Paragraphs

With 2-3 body paragraphs, make the case for hiring you by telling stories. People love to hear anecdotes and stories: they provide evidence for the assertions you are making, they are interesting, they make you stand out from everyone else, and they are memorable. You have to tell these stories very briefly, but you can do so by following a very clear formula:

- Here's what I did.

- Here's what I learned from that experience.

- Here's how I can use that skill or experience to do this job for you.

- Conclusion

Conclude your letter with a thank you, reiterate how excited you are about this position, and note that you look forward to discussing your qualifications in an interview. Sign off with an appropriate valediction, such as “Sincerely,” followed by a space for your signature (hand-signed and scanned at high-quality, or insert your signature electronically).

How to Stand Out

- Make Sure it Travels Well

Cover letters should be attached as PDF files to an email, unless otherwise requested by the employer. PDF files preserve formatting as opposed to MS Word documents, and you don't want your hard work arriving in disarray because of technological incompatibility.

- Keep it Consistent

The CV and cover letter travel together, so give them the same font, size, and margins. It will make them look like a pair, rather than one document being an afterthought.

- Business Letter Format

Business letters have a unique format. Use it. The main elements include date, addressee name and location, and your contact information (in the header).

- Reuse Your Header

It's like your stationery. Copy/paste the header from your CV onto your cover letter for consistency and to brand your other documents. If required, you can also do this for your list of references.

- Tell a Story

If CVs are like fact sheets, then cover letters are like stories. Make them readable and interesting. Why should you in particular be chosen for this specific role? Elaborate on what you want them to notice. Don't expect them to "read between the lines," because most likely they won't. Be explicit about what you can offer as it relates to the opportunity.

- Do Your Homework

The best cover letters are written after doing a significant amount of research on the company. It helps you know what they care about, what language they use to describe their goals, and how you fit into all of it.

- Write to People

When possible, address your cover letter to a specific individual rather than a general "To Whom It May Concern" or "Dear Hiring Manager." If the job description does not list it, check on LinkedIn for the senior person in the office of reference.

- Stick to One Page

Just like with the CV, a longer letter does not mean they will spend more time reading it; it means they will read it less thoroughly.

title: Curriculum Vitae (CV) · NYUAD Students
text:
Your CV (Curriculum Vitae) is a listing of applicable and important experiences and accomplishments that demonstrate that you have the skills and qualifications to be successful in the opportunity you are applying for.

Learn how to craft a successful CV with Kevin from our Back to Basics Series:

Review our Ultimate Career Guide (Ch2: Building a CV) (PDF) with a CV template, samples, and more. Visit the CDC during our office hours and have your CV reviewed by a Global Career Peer or visit our walk-in’s for a quick appointment with an advisor.

What's in a CV?

- Name and Contact Information

Put your name at the top so it stands out. The contact information must include your current email address, phone number, and mailing address.

- Make sure your email is professional and appropriate; avoid monikers like “getfierce1012@aol.com”

- If you are a currently-enrolled student and go to university outside of your home country, but are applying for a position in your home country, include both your current and permanent addresses.

- Education

As a college student, your Education should be the first section. Include the name of your university, its location, the month and year you anticipate graduating, the degree you are studying for, and your major or intended major.

- Include non-class-related research, such as a senior thesis, as bullet points under your university. Focus on the skills you obtained, rather than the research topic.

- Add study-away experiences, including where you went and when. If the study-away program had a focus that is relevant for the position you are applying for, include that information, too.

- If you are not submitting a transcript as a part of your job application (most companies and organizations don’t ask for one) and you have taken courses that are relevant to this position, you can list those as “relevant coursework.”

- Don’t list your high school education; very few people get a job based on their high school experience, even if you were valedictorian of your class.

- Related Experience

This is usually the most important part! Show the employer that you have the skillset to be successful in this job. List jobs, volunteer positions, internships, and other activities—formal and informal—that have given you the skills to do this job.

- This should not be a laundry list of everything you have ever done; if it is not relevant, you should not list it. Employers should be able to see what skills you gained, and how those skills apply to the job they are hiring for.

- Be sure to list the name of the employer or organization, your title, the dates you were involved with it, and the location.

- Describe exactly what you did for that organization utilizing bullet points; see the “Writing a Strong Bullet Point” section below.

- Other Related Activities

This is an optional section in which you can include other activities you have engaged in that demonstrate your interest in and commitment to this job or field. For example, if you are applying for a paralegal job, and you were a member of a pre-law society, you can list that here.

- Don’t list activities if they are not relevant. If you are applying for a paralegal job, they don’t need to know that you were on the volleyball club.

- For each activity, give the same information that you gave in the related experience section. You may not need to use bullet points to explain the activity. If you were just a member of the pre-law society and are applying for a paralegal position, you do not need a bullet point saying “Expressed interest in legal career by being member of pre-law society.” That’s obvious.

- Awards and Honors

Time to brag! This is where you show them how other people have recognized you for being exceptional or outstanding in some way. It’s particularly helpful and important to list those awards and honors that are relevant to the position you are applying for.

- Be sure to give the reader context as to what the award was that you won. If you just list that you won the Super Awesome Award for Excellence, nobody will know why you won it, how selective it was, or what you received for winning this award. Instead, write “Super Awesome Award for Excellence: Only recipient of merit-based $10,000 college scholarship for outstanding basket weaving, out of over 150 submissions.”

- Only list awards and honors that are, at least in part, merit-based; financial aid that is solely based on need should not be listed on a CV.

- Be cautious about listing any awards or honors that you received before college.

- Awards and Honors, Skills and Languages

This is another optional section. Use it for two main reasons: (a) to convey that you have specific skills and abilities that are needed for this job, and (b) to tell them something (appropriately!) interesting about you that might show them a different side of you.

- If you have skills that will be enormously helpful for this job that are not listed elsewhere on your CV, you should list them here.

- Language skills are often a good thing to list in this section, especially if the job you are applying for is in a cross-cultural setting. When you do so, give the reader a parenthetical sense of how strong your skills are, such as “English (fluent), Mandarin (advanced), and Hausa (basic).” Don’t claim language skills that you don’t have; you never know when an employer might ask a question in that language!

- You generally do not need to list basic computer skills such as MS Office, familiarity with iOS, or “proficient in social media” #ItIs2016 #EveryoneHasThoseSkills.

How to Stand Out

- Formatting

- The entries in each section should be in reverse chronological order, so that the most recent activities are higher up on the page.

- Stick to one page. Employers, on average, spend a very short amount of time reviewing each CV.

- Use the full page. Don’t leave excess blank space; it looks empty and lonely. Nobody likes a lonely CV.

- Be consistent in your formatting. Readers will quickly figure out, for example, that your employer is always in bold, and the dates of your employment are always right-justified.

- Use visual tricks to set each section apart. Whether it is a horizontal line, use of ALL CAPS, or some combination of bolding and italics, make it clear to the reader where one section ends and another one starts. Don’t go crazy though! It does not take much to visually set text apart.

- Writing a Strong Bullet Point

Use bullet points to describe what you did and the skills that you gained for each of your experiences. Think about painting a picture of your work; would someone else be able to look at it, and understand what you did and how it relates to the position that they are hiring?

- Start every bullet point with a well-chosen, specific action verb, try here or here for lists of good action verbs, written in the past tense (for a job you currently have, you can write these in the present tense). Spend time selecting the perfect verb to describe what you did, avoiding generalized words like “worked” or “organized,” that do not specify your exact tasks. Try very hard not to repeat verbs anywhere in your CV.

- Numbers, numbers, numbers! We love numbers in CVs. Numbers add context, size, and scope. Use numbers wherever you can to add significant details to your accomplishments.

- Eliminate all articles, such as a, an, and the, and avoid first-person references to yourself. A sentence like, “I introduced a new product line that was the top-seller for the year,” write “Introduced new product line that became top-seller of year”. And then add some numbers to that bullet point to define what you mean!

- Because you are writing in this truncated style, you do not need to end each bullet point with a period.

- More important or relevant jobs can have more bullet points as a way of visually encouraging the reader to spend more time looking at those experiences.

CV Samples

- CV Guide and Template

Use the CV guide and templates found in Chapter 2: How to Build a CV in our Ultimate Career Guide to help you format and write your CV. As you continue to develop your CV throughout your time at NYUAD, play with different formats. You don't want your CV to look the same as everyone elses!

- CV Samples by Major

Sometimes it is helpful to see what students who have similar courses of study do with their CV, as well as what experiences they pursue. Check out these sample CVs from NYUAD students by major (be sure you are trying to access them from your NYU email account). Remember that one of the great things about studying at NYUAD is that the degree allows you to pursue a variety of fields, regardless of what you study.

- CV Samples That are Designed

Spice up your CV with these creative CV samples by NYUAD students (be sure you are trying to access them from your NYU email account) . This does not work for everyone, so do not force it.

If you need help designing your CV, Canva is a free online tool that provides a lot of templates.

FAQs

- How long should my CV be?

Your CV should never go beyond one page. Imagine that you were looking through a pile of CVs. The vast majority of industries prefer one page documents. Not only does it allow for readability but it also demonstrates that you can communicate concisely.

- What if I don't have enough information to fill one page?

Don't discount your past experiences. You can put many different experiences on your CV; they don't have to be formal internships or jobs. You can include all of the following:

- Volunteer positions

- Leadership experiences

- Awards or scholarships

- Relevant coursework

- Study abroad experiences

- Research projects and publications

- Extracurricular or sports leadership positions

If you need assistance in finding experiences to add, our career counselors can help you brainstorm and find ways to format your CV to highlight your skills.

- How can I best describe my past responsibilities to get an employer's attention?

Use the STAR method to assist with writing your bullets under each experience. STAR stands for Situation, Task, Action, and Result. Using this method changes your CV from a description-based CV to an accomplishments-based CV; rather than describing just your responsibilities, you describe your accomplishments in each experience which sets you apart from other applicants. For each experience you list, it can be helpful to ask these questions when writing out your bullets:

- Situation: What was the situation? Was there a specific problem you were trying to solve? Who/what was involved? Be specific.

- Task: What was the key objective? What issues were you trying to address?

- Action: What action did you take? What specific skills did you use to achieve your goal

- Result: What was the result of your action(s)? Be specific and quantify if possible.

Examples:

-
Before: "Led a student fundraising group"

After using the STAR method: "Led a student fundraising group of 30 students which raised over $5,000 for cancer research through various on-campus and off-campus events and outreach efforts."

-
Before: "Made a rating tool"

After using the STAR method: "Created a vendor rating system to identify reliable suppliers, resulting in an 80% reduction in product defects."

Another helpful way to insure the best description of your responsibilities: use strong action verbs!

- What other categories can I use on my CV?

Your particular situation, experiences, and goals will dictate which of the following optional categories are more appropriate to include:

- Objective, Profile, or Summary

- Honors or Awards

- Relevant Coursework

- Relevant/Additional Experience

- Leadership Activities

- Research Activities

- Affiliations or Memberships

- Interests

- Where can I get feedback on my CV?

Schedule an appointment with a career counselor to review your CV format and content. Counselors can also help orient your document for particular employers and industries and troubleshoot reasons you may not be getting interviews.

sections.title: FAQs
sections.text:
- How long should my CV be?

Your CV should never go beyond one page. Imagine that you were looking through a pile of CVs. The vast majority of industries prefer one page documents. Not only does it allow for readability but it also demonstrates that you can communicate concisely.

- What if I don't have enough information to fill one page?

Don't discount your past experiences. You can put many different experiences on your CV; they don't have to be formal internships or jobs. You can include all of the following:

- Volunteer positions

- Leadership experiences

- Awards or scholarships

- Relevant coursework

- Study abroad experiences

- Research projects and publications

- Extracurricular or sports leadership positions

If you need assistance in finding experiences to add, our career counselors can help you brainstorm and find ways to format your CV to highlight your skills.

- How can I best describe my past responsibilities to get an employer's attention?

Use the STAR method to assist with writing your bullets under each experience. STAR stands for Situation, Task, Action, and Result. Using this method changes your CV from a description-based CV to an accomplishments-based CV; rather than describing just your responsibilities, you describe your accomplishments in each experience which sets you apart from other applicants. For each experience you list, it can be helpful to ask these questions when writing out your bullets:

- Situation: What was the situation? Was there a specific problem you were trying to solve? Who/what was involved? Be specific.

- Task: What was the key objective? What issues were you trying to address?

- Action: What action did you take? What specific skills did you use to achieve your goal

- Result: What was the result of your action(s)? Be specific and quantify if possible.

Examples:

-
Before: "Led a student fundraising group"

After using the STAR method: "Led a student fundraising group of 30 students which raised over $5,000 for cancer research through various on-campus and off-campus events and outreach efforts."

-
Before: "Made a rating tool"

After using the STAR method: "Created a vendor rating system to identify reliable suppliers, resulting in an 80% reduction in product defects."

Another helpful way to insure the best description of your responsibilities: use strong action verbs!

- What other categories can I use on my CV?

Your particular situation, experiences, and goals will dictate which of the following optional categories are more appropriate to include:

- Objective, Profile, or Summary

- Honors or Awards

- Relevant Coursework

- Relevant/Additional Experience

- Leadership Activities

- Research Activities

- Affiliations or Memberships

- Interests

- Where can I get feedback on my CV?

Schedule an appointment with a career counselor to review your CV format and content. Counselors can also help orient your document for particular employers and industries and troubleshoot reasons you may not be getting interviews.

title: Interviewing · NYUAD Students
text:
An interview for an internship or job is a conversation between the employer and potential candidates. This is a common way that companies will decide who they'd like to hire.

Get prepared for your interview with Ale from our Back to Basics Series:

Review our Ultimate Career Guide (Ch6: Interviewing) (PDF) with tips for interviewing, sample interview questions and more. Practice interviewing by utilizing Big Interview . If you have a casing interview utilize CaseCoach to help you prepare.

Visit the CDC during our office hours to learn more about our interview resources from a Global career Peer or set up a mock interview appointment via Handshake.

Before the Interview

- Research the Organization

It’s essential that you research an organization before you walk into your interview. You’re giving an employer the first taste of how you approach your work, so you want to show them how thorough and hard-working you are.

- Use resources like Vault , TheMuse , and GlassDoor to figure out as much as you can about this company, its culture, and how it positions itself within its field. Who are its closest competitors, and what are its advantages and disadvantages? What do current and past employees say about what it is like to work there?

- Read the organization’s website thoroughly. Know their mission, general company statistics, and what projects they are currently working on.

- Search for recent news stories about this company to contextualize their work in relation to the community.

- Social media gives organizations the opportunity to present the best version of themselves to the public. What messages are they trying to push? What successes have they had recently that you can talk about? How are they interacting with consumers in interesting or unique ways?

- If you are provided the names of your interviewers in advance, use LinkedIn, the company website, and Google to learn more about them. Knowing someone’s background, work responsibilities, and professional interests may help you figure out potential avenues of questioning they are likely to raise. But don’t go overboard: if you happen to find out that an interviewer is president of their local Britney Spears fan club, that’s information you don’t necessarily need to raise in your conversation with them.

- Preparing for the Interview

There is no way for you to predict and prepare for every question they might ask you, but that doesn’t mean that you shouldn’t undertake thorough preparations.

- Begin with the end in mind: What do you want them to think of you when you walk out of that interview room? If they write a summary of the interview, what adjectives do you want them to use to describe you? What stories do you want them to remember about your past? What key qualifications and skills do you want to be sure they know?

- Write down a couple of dozen questions that you think they might ask you. These can range from the generic (Why do you want this job? What are your main strengths and weaknesses? What do you enjoy about your current job? What are your long-term goals?) to specific questions based on the job description, the company, or your resume. Then, write a couple of bullets for each question, with main points or phrases you would want to use if you get that question. Lastly, practice...practice...practice! Sit by yourself, or with a friend, and practice your answers, reminding yourself of the main points you want to make, and noting any key points or turns of phrase you come up with as you practice. The key is to hit an elusive middle ground, where you sound confident but unrehearsed in your answers.

- The best way to prepare for the inevitable questions you were not expecting is to come prepared with many different anecdotes and stories from your professional experience. Interviewers love to hear examples: Anyone can claim that they are hard-working, but your story of how you voluntarily took on an extra task at work, stayed late to finish it, and won an award for the company at the conference demonstrates your hard work. When you arrive at the interview armed with stories, then it is just a matter of telling them at the appropriate time when those unexpected questions come up.

- Dress for Success

The interviewer, whether or not they know it, has an expectation as to the level of formality of your dress before you arrive. This expectation is based on the kind of job you are interviewing for, the company’s culture, and a host of other factors. Imagine, for example, if a presidential candidate showed up in a hoodie at a nationally televised debate (perhaps the ultimate job interview!), or if an interviewee showed up at an interview at Apple in a business suit (thus violating Steve Jobs’ maxim : “We’re Apple. We don’t wear suits. We don’t even own suits.”). By doing your research, you can know the company’s culture and figure out what their expectations are, and then meet them appropriately.

During the Interview

- First Impressions

Let’s own from the start that this advice is based on an assumption that your interview is with a Western-style company. The qualities that go into a positive first impression are culturally-based, and vary around the world. CDC advisors can help you navigate interviews in other cultural situations.

You rarely lose in Western cultures by being enthusiastic, optimistic, and confident. From the moment you first meet your interviewers—whether in a formal setting or if they meet you in the parking lot—your job is to show them that you want this job, you are excited about this job, and that you can do this job well. Be sure to:

- Smile. You would not believe how much a smile helps. If you are having fun, your interviewers will have fun.

- Have an appropriately firm handshake. Not sure what to do interviewing in an unfamiliar cultural setting? Come see us at the CDC for help.

- Make good eye contact. Look your interviewers in the eye when you walk in the room. Look at the person asking the question while they are talking. When answering, start by looking at them, but break eye contact by looking around the room. If you are talking with multiple people, start and finish your answer by looking at the person who asked the question, but spend the middle part of your answer looking at other people in the room, too.

- Lastly, be polite and professional to everyone you meet at the company, from the CEO to an outside vendor who is cleaning a bathroom. Small interactions with everyone you meet say a lot about your character.

- Show them You're a STAR

There is a simple yet highly effective way to structure your answers: the STAR method. Concise, purposeful, and intentional storytelling is at the heart of the STAR method. Whether or not your interviewer asks you for an example (“What are your strengths?” vs. “Tell us a story that demonstrates your strengths.”), use the STAR method to create evocative, memorable answers:

- Situation: Briefly set-up the background to the story. Where were you, when, and who were the key players?

- Task: What needed to be done, and what was your role in it?

- Action: What, specifically, did you do?

- Result: What was the outcome of your actions?

Then, apply this outcome to your prospective employer: “And that is the kind of result I am excited about bringing to this company in this role.”

- Asking Questions

It is common for interviewers to invite you to ask them questions, too. Keep in mind that “Do you have any questions for us?” does not signal the end of the interview! It is itself another interview question, and the questions that you ask say something very important about you: they can demonstrate how much you have researched the company, how thoughtful and curious you are, and provide an opportunity for you to show them how you would approach this job. This is not actually a time for you to ask questions about the company which you want to have answered before you accept or decline their offer; those can come later on. Keep the focus at this point on convincing them that you are the right person for the job.

- Ask questions that demonstrate your level of research: “I see in last week’s New York Times that one of your main competitors has launched a new line in Asia. Do you see this company expanding overseas in the coming years?”

- Ask questions that demonstrate your critical thinking: "When I examine your company’s mission statement and values, I recognize aspects of a holacratic corporate structure. Can you tell me more about what this looks like and how it impacts your employees' day-to-day?"

- Ask questions that demonstrate how you will approach this job: “I see that this school has a large number of extracurricular activities for students, most of which are led by teachers. As a teacher here, how involved can I become in helping to lead some of those clubs and groups?”

- Closing the Interview

Interviews can be stressful, and you might have an urge to bolt from the room at the first sign that your time is up. Resist that temptation! You have three main things you need to do before you leave:

- Reiterate your interest in the job. Remember that you are trying to show them how enthusiastic, optimistic, and confident you are about this position. One of the last things you want them to hear from you is that you want this job, you are excited about it, and that you are confident that you can do this job exceptionally well.

- Shake their hand and look them in the eye, and say thank you. They have taken time out of their day to consider you for this position, and you should thank them for doing so.

- If you do not already have their name and contact information, ask for their business card. You’ll be sending a thank-you note (more on that below), so you want to be sure that you have the correct spelling of their name and know where to send that note.

Good interviewers will usually give you a sense of their timeline for a decision, and how you will hear from them next. If they do not do so, it is OK to note that you are excited about this possibility, and are curious as to whether they have a sense as to when you might hear from them next, or what the next stages in the hiring process will be.

After the Interview

- Making Notes

As soon as you get to a private spot away from the interview location, you should stop, take a deep breath, high-five yourself, and then take out a piece of paper and start jotting down notes:

- What did they ask you, and how did you answer those questions? If you were asked a question once, it is likely you will be asked it again in the future, either in another round of interviewing at this company, or with another. Were you happy with your answer? What would you change about it?

- Who did you talk to, and what did you talk about? Make specific notes about each person, which you can mention in the thank-you notes you are about to write.

- What did you learn about this company, and what questions do you need answered before you accept or decline the job if offered?

- Following Up

You must send a personalized thank-you note to each person who interviewed you within 24 hours. While a handwritten note on an actual thank-you card is traditional, use your judgement as to whether the employees at this company would prefer an email. In each thank-you note, be sure to:

- Say thank you.

- Connect 1:1 with that person about a comment they made, an answer to a question of yours that they gave, or an answer of yours that they seemed to respond particularly well to. You can also r emind them of anything you forgot to tell them. Stand out from other interviewees by making that human connection to them.

- Reiterate your interest in the position once more.

Sample Questions

In addition to the questions listed below, Big Interview and Interview Stream, accessible through Handshake house thousands of other practice questions.

- 20 questions to expect

- Tell me about yourself.

- Why did you apply for this position? Why do you want this job?

- What makes your global experiences valuable? How did they make you more hireable?

- What are your greatest strengths and weaknesses?

- What do you have to offer my organization?

- Where do you see yourself in five years?

- What specific goals, other than those related to your occupation, have you established for yourself for the next five years?

- How would you describe yourself?

- How would your friends describe you? How would your professors describe you?

- What motivates you to put forth your greatest effort?

- How has your college experience prepared you for a career?

- Why should I hire you for this opportunity?

- What qualifications do you have that you think will make you successful in this profession?

- How do you know that you have been successful?

- Discuss two or three accomplishments that have given you the most satisfaction.

- Describe your most rewarding college experience.

- Do you think that your grades are a good indication of your academic achievement?

- What have you learned from participation in extracurricular activities?

- What do you know about our organization? What is our mission? Describe our core values.

- Do you have a geographical preference? Why?

- What are your minimum salary expectations for this opportunity?

- 20 Questions to Ask

- How is the organization structured in terms of divisions, departments, etc.?

- Could you please describe your corporate culture. How would you compare it with the culture of your competitors?

- Will relocation be required in the future?

- Is this opportunity the result of increased expansion or new growth?

- What skills helped previous employees in this role succeed?

- What advice do you share with new hires?

- What kind of training program does the organization have? How long is the training program? Is there a mentoring system? Can an individual go through it in a shorter length of time? At his/her own pace?

- What is the organization's policy on advancement? What is the realistic time frame for advancement?

- Could you describe typical career paths employees have taken in your organization?

- What about those employees who began in the same position for which I am interviewing? How recent are these examples and have opportunities changed enough so that someone in this position today may not follow the same path?

- Could you please describe your own career path/advancement in the organization? How much travel is required? How often? To what cities?

- What are the organization's plans for future growth?

- How has the organization changed in the past five years? What direction will the organization be taking in the next five years?

- When could I expect to complete my first performance evaluation? How often are evaluations conducted and is a salary adjustment connected to the evaluation?

- Could you please describe your management philosophy/style?

- What are your policies regarding continuing education for employees? Is there a tuition reimbursement policy?

- What makes your organization different from its competitors?

- How much contact would I have with management?

- Who are the other people I would be working with? Will I have a chance to meet them in the interview process?

- Can you tell me about the last two employees that held this position? What are they doing now? (This either will reaffirm the recruiter's assertion about the organization's preference for promoting from within or it will offer a glimpse into a possible problem area.)

- What is your time frame for the decision-making process about this position? When do you expect to make a decision regarding the next step in the interview process?

General Tips

- The job description is your friend

When available, job descriptions provide an excellent reference point by showing you precisely what the company is looking for. Select the examples from your experience that best align with the job description.

- Think in terms of what you can add

Interviewers need to know what you can offer their organization. The interview is your critical window to tell them. Don't wait for the interviewer to draw your intentions out; be ready to say what you can bring to the table that is unique.

- Be prepared to steer

Some interviews ask a series of questions all in a row, others prefer more of a conversational dialogue, and still others will talk for 20 minutes without ever asking you a thing. For less structured interviews, have your stories and points on hand to bring into the conversation. Whether they ask or not, you still have a limited amount of time to communicate yourself as a potential asset to the organization.

- Practice, practice, practice!

Choose your most vivid examples of the skills required for the position, and practice your stories. Get feedback on your examples from a career counselor in a mock interview. Employ the STAR method to ensure your responses are well rounded but not too long.

When available, job descriptions provide an excellent reference point by showing you precisely what the company is looking for. Select the examples from your experience that best align with the job description.

- Think in terms of what you can add

Interviewers need to know what you can offer their organization. The interview is your critical window to tell them. Don't wait for the interviewer to draw your intentions out; be ready to say what you can bring to the table that is unique.

- Be prepared to steer

Some interviews ask a series of questions all in a row, others prefer more of a conversational dialogue, and still others will talk for 20 minutes without ever asking you a thing. For less structured interviews, have your stories and points on hand to bring into the conversation. Whether they ask or not, you still have a limited amount of time to communicate yourself as a potential asset to the organization.

- Practice, practice, practice!

Choose your most vivid examples of the skills required for the position, and practice your stories. Get feedback on your examples from a career counselor in a mock interview. Employ the STAR method to ensure your responses are well rounded but not too long.

title: Case Interviews · NYUAD Students
text:
There are myriad of case interview questions and the average successful candidate prepares for 70 hours. These interviews are particularly common in consulting and finance. Students can download the Vault Case Interview Guide and Sample Case Questions through Handshake , Review Case in Point in the CDC Library, listen to sample cases through the Interview Stream or Big Interview modules (available through Handshake ), and schedule a mock interview with a career counselor.

- Do

- Review frameworks and types of questions before the interview

- Bring paper and pen with you to the interview

- Repeat questions back to recruiter to ensure you consider all the information provided

- Double-check your calculations (count the zeroes)

- Maintain a dialogue with the recruiter and listen for their feedback

- Don't

- Use filler words (um, you know, like, etc.).

- Jump right in. Take a few moments to think about your first approach

- Lose your composure (especially if you miss a calculation)

- Contradict yourself in your final analysis

- Be overconfident. A tentative but confident approach is better received.

Sample Questions

- Increasing Profits Case

The client is a regional retail bank. Recently, it has begun facing threats from internet-based financial services firms and other non-traditional firms. Deposits are declining and the bank has approached us with a strategy to grow the bottom line. Walk me through some of the issues that you consider and work streams you would set up in coming up with recommendations.

- Growth Strategies Case

The client is a large pharmaceutical firm with a market cap of USD 85 billion. They have about 4% market share and are currently enjoying a 34 P/E ratio. The industry average P/E is about 29. Over the next five years they are looking at a healthy growth in their EBIT margins. However, for three years thereafter, the EBIT margin growth is likely to stagnate when three of their blockbusters come off patent. Subsequently, blockbusters currently in the pipeline will hit the market and their EBIT margins are expected to continue healthy growth levels. The CFO of the firm asks you to help her figure out if the three-year plateau five years out is an issue she should be worried about and if so what external options she can pursue to fix it?

- Entering a New Market Case

The client is a division of an industrial chemicals firm. They are in the business of manufacturing fibers and have had sales of USD 1 billion. Their concern is that the sales have been declining steadily over the past five years. Their objective is to identify three to five new lines of business with total revenues of USD 300-500 million utilizing existing capacity in the fiber manufacturing facilities. They have come up with a new fiber that has very good absorbency, around 10 times its weight, which is a breakthrough in the industry. The client is looking to enter the urban pet care market in the US with this new high-absorbency fiber. They want to manufacture pet care pads, sort of diapers for pets in urban areas. The client would like us to evaluate the potential of this idea, which is where you come in.

- Mergers & Acquisitions Case

The client is a US based wine manufacturing firm looking to expand globally. They have retained us to advise them on the valuation of a South African based wine company that they are looking to acquire. Why don't you walk me through some of the things you would consider in advising the client?

- New Product Case

A client's company operates one passenger and two cargo ships in the Baltic Sea, between Finland and Germany. The ships are old and need to be replaced. The choices before him are to continue with the same configuration, one passenger and two cargo ships, or to go in for two hybrid ships, which can handle both cargo and passengers.
