title: Online/Phone Interviews · NYUAD Students
text:
Need space for a virtual interview?

Use this guide on how to use the CDC space to set up your virtual interview.

Do

- Get your technology in order

Test the internet connectivity, as well as the microphone and camera to ensure you'll be able to proceed without a hitch. Technology glitches on the day of the interview send the wrong impression, casting doubts on your interest in the job, your technological savvy, and your ability to problem solve.

- Prepare your environment

If possible, position your computer and webcam so there's a blank wall in back of you. If that's not possible, manipulate the background so it appears you are in a professional setting. Think bookshelves in the background, rather than your unmade bed. Turn off the television, radio, or other noise before beginning, and make sure roommates are aware of your interview so they don't make unannounced -- and unappreciated -- guest appearances.

- Dress for success

Dress for a virtual interview the same way you would for an in-person interview. Avoid wearing bright or distracting colors, or jewelry that is remarkable. You want the interviewer to focus on you, not on your outfit.

- Position yourself to win

Because you won't have the benefit of a face-to-face connection, your body language becomes even more obvious -- and important to manage -- in a virtual interview. Sit up straight, maintain the illusion of eye contact by looking at the webcam and not at the image on your computer screen, and don't slouch, yawn, or fidget. Some virtual interview software programs allow the employer to rewind, meaning bad moments can be viewed over and over again.

- Go for a practice run

Enlist the help of a trusted friend or career counselor--someone who will be honest with you--and ask them to run through a mock interview with you using the virtual interview technology. In addition to testing the technology, your trusted advisor can tell you whether you are adequately seen and heard, how the lighting is, how you appear on the camera, and whether you come off as professional, prepared, enthusiastic, and interested.

- Show AND Tell

During in-person meetings, an interviewer may get a sense of how a person will fit into an organization based simply on their presence and the "vibe" they throw off. Not so in virtual interviews. It's extra important to do some research on both the company and the job, and tell the interviewer in detail why your qualifications, experience, and skill set makes you deserving of a second interview. Because the miles between you won't allow the interviewer to "feel" your enthusiasm, make sure you convey interest using voice intonation and facial expression.

Don't

- Eat or drink during the interview

You should not have food in sight, and you should not drink during the interview. You do not need it, it will not make you look more relaxed, it will not make you feel relaxed, and it will not make it feel as if you are talking to them in a café. It makes it appear as if you do not care about the job and that you are disinterested.

- Don't forget to smile

Smile, but make it more that you are smiling because you are having the interview. Remember the feeling you had when you discovered you got an interview? Be as genuine as possible. First impressions still apply online, and you do not want to make a bad one straight off the bat.

- Don't forget to use your hands

In a real interview, you would allow your hands to move around as you talk, and this is what you should do during your interview. Don’t sit there with your hands on the table as if you are being interviewed by the police, or having your hands down by your side as if you are having your photo taken at the police station.

- Don't be a jerk or be boring

If you perceive the video interview as less formal than a face-to-face interview, you may forget to check your ego. The key is coming across as confident but not overconfident.

- Don't get distracted

Be cautious of falling into the same distraction-prone tendencies you might in class or at the office, like checking e-mail, reading notes, or browsing social media.

title: Networking · NYUAD Students
text:
Networking and informational interviewing involve having a “career conversation” with someone for the purpose of exploring careers or job searching. These conversations are about building authentic relationships with people who can give you information and advice, not job interviews.

Get started networking with Kevin from our Back to Basics Series:

Review our Ultimate Career Guide (Ch5: Networking) (PDF) for tips on developing an elevator pitch and how to build your LinkedIn profile. Join the Violet Network to get connected with other NYU and NYUAD alumni. To learn about our networking events, visit the CDC during our office hours to meet with a Global Career Peer or attend a walk-in for a quick appointment with an advisor

Maximize the Experience

- Make a Strong Introduction

30-second Introduction

Develop a 30-second introduction or “elevator pitch” to make your outreach efforts in-person as effective as possible.

Consider the following questions:

- Who are you? Introduce yourself and begin to tell your story. Indicate your name, school, and major (or area of a focus).

- What do you have in common? Are they an alumni? Do you have a shared contact? Are you members of the same social organization or network? What is the context of your meeting?

- What sets you apart? Incorporate a high-level overview of your unique skills, experiences, or accomplishments. This piece of your introduction will likely change the most often.

- What are you seeking? Are you looking for insight about the field through an informational interview? Are you seeking more in-depth internship and job search advice in your field of interest? Make your intentions clear to the people you’re connecting with, but do not ask for a job.

During the Conversation

- Respect their time by honoring the time agreed upon and moving the conversation to a close 5 minutes prior to the end of your meeting.

- Remember that even though you may want an internship or job, it is not appropriate to ask for one.

- Inquire about other professionals or organizations you can contact and if you can say you were referred by them.

- Dress appropriately and be courteous to everyone you encounter.

- Observe what types of skills and knowledge someone needs to perform this role.

- Thank your contact and others at the site who were helpful.

- Ask Good Questions

Maximize your experience by preparing specific questions in advance.

- What led you into this career?

- What does a typical day look like?

- Which professional organizations would you recommend I join?

- Which publications should I be reading to learn more about this field?

- What types of education and experience are most needed in this field?

- What types of skills and knowledge are important to perform this job well?

- What is the most challenging and/or frustrating aspect of your position?

- Where do you see the profession going?

- How did you go about finding this job?

- What would you advise me if I chose to pursue this career?

- Who else would you recommend I talk to? Are you willing to introducing me to them?

- Are you open to giving me feedback on my CV?

- Cultivating Relationships

The people you meet now can be influential in your life now or later. Consider the best way to stay in touch.

- Request a business card/contact information following new conversations and connect with them through LinkedIn.

- Send a thank-you email expressing your gratitude for their time within 24 hours.

- Maintain contact by sending existing contacts brief updates on how you’re progressing through your career.

- Share relevant articles or news when appropriate.

- Keep notes on your conversations so you can follow-up appropriately and accurately.

- Follow through on all leads and deliver what you promised, building your positive reputation and that of the person who referred you.

- Do

- Be prepared and know the basics. If you're going to attend an event, know the dress code, what time it starts, and what speakers will be there. Avoid awkward situations by dressing appropriately and showing up on time.

- Be open to being nervous and put yourself out there anyway. It's okay to fumble at your first networking event. Use the practice to get better at introducing yourself and making small talk.

- Go in with small goals, such as talking to 5 new people, getting their contact information, and following up with them after the event.

- Use every opportunity to build connections. You don't need to be at a formal networking event to meet new people. Be open to meeting others at casual social gatherings, lectures, concerts, and any other venue or event where there are people. You never know who you might meet!

- Be prepared with some conversation starters:

- Hi! I wanted to introduce myself...

- What did you think of the talk?

- What brings you to this event?

- I couldn't help but overhear…

- Have you traveled far to be here?

- Where did you go to university?

- What do you think about (the venue, the latest news, the weather)?

- When reaching out via email, make sure you have a professional email signature and use your @nyu.edu email address. Always employ professional language and be cautious of assuming the gender of the recipient with your pronouns.

- Leverage in-person conversations to learn about people's experiences in a given industry. Be curious and ask open-ended questions. Your questions communicate how much you already know about the industry and can establish rapport very quickly.

- Don't

- Never ask for a job or internship right after meeting someone (e.g., saying "Can I have a job?"). You can ask about the company and say that you'd be interested in opportunities there, but this should be part of a larger conversation. Networking should be about building relationships — not reaching an end goal.

- Don't take up too much of one person's time. Be mindful of body language and understand that they may want to talk to other people at the event. If you see that someone's eyes are wandering or that they are fidgeting, it is probably best to wrap up your conversation.

- Don't forget to follow-up. Too many times, people will ask for an employer's contact information but neglect to send an email to follow-up.

- Never be arrogant or overzealous with marketing yourself. While you should be able to speak about your talents, you also want to come across as self-aware and interested in the other person you are talking with.

- Don't forget: quality is better than quantity. It is better to have an authentic connection with a small number of individuals than to run around an event collecting business cards. Genuine connections are more apt to lead to future opportunities.

Developing Your Network

While the CDC facilitates career panels, networking nights, career fairs, graduate school fairs, and other events as networking opportunities, students are encouraged to take initiative and reach out to professionals on their own with our guidance.

- Finding Contacts

Who | Why |

Family, friends, university staff and professors | You’ll be amazed how many contacts you can make through existing relationships. Although you might not have a relationship with someone in a particular field, you may know someone who does. |

Social networks | Are you on LinkedIn? Facebook? Twitter? WeChat? Tap into alumni networks, professional organizations, as well as existing connections by reaching out to them for the information you’re seeking. |

Employer Sessions and Opportunities Fairs | These events can be very useful even if you aren’t looking for an internship or job: you can meet the types of people you want to know. |

Campus or community events | The NYUAD Institute, academic departments, and professional organizations in Abu Dhabi are regularly hosting events that you can join to meet people.

- Opportunities for Networking

- Volunteer for a cause you are passionate about. You are likely to meet like-minded individuals from various industries and backgrounds.

- Reach out to alumni. Alumni are most likely to understand where you are coming from and will be motivated in assisting you and paying it forward. Use the LinkedIn and other social media or talk to your peers to get alumni contact information.

- Keep your connections strong. You already have a strong network; consider your family, friends, community members, clubs, professors, and former colleagues and supervisors. Don’t forget to check in with these people periodically as they can be a huge help in your future success.

- Actively engage with faculty and staff on campus. Ask about a professor’s research or see if you can volunteer for an upcoming big event.

Career advisors are also available to consult with students about networking etiquette and to brainstorm additional opportunities to interface with professionals. Request an appointment with a counselor via Handshake for additional help.

LinkedIn

Employers are researching job and internship applicants online and 91% of employers are using social networking sites to screen candidates. LinkedIn is the best platform for promoting yourself professionally online; it gives you the ability to connect with other professionals and to learn more about industries of interest. Your LinkedIn connections can develop into real-world relationships which can shape your future opportunities.

In addition, Google loves LinkedIn. If you have a LinkedIn profile, it is likely to be at the top of a Google search result when anyone searches for you online. Why is this important? People, including employers and graduate school admissions officers, naturally go to Google to search for someone new. If your LinkedIn profile is at the top of the search results list, you are able to control the information they see and their overall first impression of you.

Do's, Don'ts, and Tips for LinkedIn

- Do

- Complete your profile to the fullest extent possible. The more information you provide, the higher the chances your profile will be found.

- Use a professional headshot.

- Join groups and professional associations related to your field. Join or start discussions within groups.

- Be strategic with whom you connect with — this is a professional network.

- Develop professional relationships. Connect with others who share your career interests and set up informational interviews.

- Help others by being a resource and sharing your knowledge and connections.

- Endorse or recommend your colleagues when appropriate.

- Ask for recommendations from past employers or colleagues.

- Don't

- Request to connect with just anyone. In your invitation, be specific about why you want to connect or where you met (try not to wait too long after big events to request to connect!).

- Overwhelm the news feed. Be intentional with your posts on LinkedIn.

- Make personal posts. Keep it professional.

- Ask everyone you connect with for a job. It is unprofessional and will get you nowhere. Build relationships first.

- Use the template message when connecting. Write a personalized note instead.

- Tips

Use the LinkedIn alumni tool to find alumni who have studied your major or who work in your field. You can send personalized connection requests to build your network and set up informational interviews (see How to Ask for a 1:1 Conversation below).

Complete all sections of your LinkedIn profile. Having a complete profile increases your chances of being seen by employers.

How to Ask for a 1:1 Conversation

You will need to introduce yourself, establish why you’re writing, and make your request in a personal, concise, and clear way. People usually are very willing to help and lend advice, but they need to understand who you are and what you want.

The number one rule? Don't ask for a job or internship outright.

How to Send a Cold Email

- 1. Search for Contacts

Find contacts at companies of interest or people who have jobs that match your interests. Use LinkedIn, search professional social media accounts, company websites and the like.

- 2. Find their emails

This can be easier said than done and your first point of contact may need to be via LinkedIn or another social media network (only if the person is using it as a professional platform). Regardless, Google is a great place to start searching.

- 3. Draft and send your message

Keep it short and simple if possible:

Introduce yourself. State why you are contacting them and what you hope to gain from meeting with them (virtually or in person). Offer to buy them coffee if you can (if it's an in-person meeting).

Example 1:

Dear ____,

I am a senior currently studying Economics at New York University Abu Dhabi. I have interned with ____ and ____, and conducted research on ____. I came across your LinkedIn profile and I'm interested in your career path and how you were able to connect economics and social research. Would it be possible to schedule a Skype meeting so I can learn more about your path? (Or — I would love to buy you a coffee soon and learn more about your path into ____. Please let me know if you might be available for a short meeting.). I hope to hear from you soon. Thank you for your time.

Best,

Your Full Name

Examples 2:

Dear Vivek,

As a student at New York University Abu Dhabi studying economics and finance, I have been following the Deutsche Bank response to the current volatility with interest rates, economic slowness, and currency issues. I recently came across the interview you did with the Financial Times, and saw that you are an NYU alumnus. I would love to hear more about how you transitioned from New York to banking in London, and how you’ve adapted to the European and Middle Eastern markets in light of the current economic climate.

I am studying away in London over the next 12 weeks. Would you be free for 20-minutes in the next few weeks for a chat? I understand that your schedule is really full, and I am happy to bring lunch by your office or meet you after work.

Sincerely,

Mohammed

--

New York University Abu Dhabi
B.A. Economics, Specialization in Finance, Class of 2020
PO Box 129188
Abu Dhabi, UAE

- 4. Follow up

Always wait a week before following up with another email, but follow up! Don't take it personally if you don't hear back. People are busy and it's possible they just don't have the time to respond.

- 5. Thank them

If you hear back from someone, thank them for their time in getting back to you and commit to making time for your meeting, whether virtual or in-person. If you meet with them, don't forget to send a follow-up thank you email.

Reaching Out to an Existing Contact

- Employer Session or Event Follow Up

Dear Joanna,

My name is Mahra and I am a second year student at NYU Abu Dhabi, studying Film and New Media. After hearing your talk about commercials at TwoFour54, I was fascinated about the potential of video content. The illustrations you shared inspired me to think more broadly and be more curious about new outlets. I would love to learn from you about the direction of this industry in the UAE and get your input about how I can best develop my skills.

Would you be open to a 15-minute conversation sometime in the next two weeks? I am happy to meet you at your office — and I can bring some coffee. Alternatively, we could just talk on the phone or email, whichever works best for you.

Best,

Mahra

--

New York University Abu Dhabi
B.A. Film and New Media, Class of 2019
PO Box 129188
Abu Dhabi, UAE

Questions to Ask

- Sample Questions

- What made you interested in this field?

- What is a typical day like for you in this position?

- What past jobs and experiences have led you to this current position?

- How would you describe your working atmosphere and the people you work with?

- Do you have any advice for someone who wants to work in this field?

- What skills are most important to being successful in this career?

- Who has been most influential in your career?

- What are the types of jobs that exist where you work and in the industry in general?

- Are there any professional or trade associations I should connect with?

- How do you see your industry changing in the next 10 years?

- What’s unique about your company compared to your competitors or to your past work experiences?

Always remember to follow up with a thank you email after an informational interview. This is incredibly important as the person you interviewed took time out of their schedule with the intention of helping you — show your gratitude! You can use the information you gained from your interviews to assist with making career decisions and you can use your new contact for future opportunities if you continue to keep in touch — it's a win-win!

Student Email Signatures

Email signatures provide evidence of your affiliations and orient the reader. In short, they make you more easy to answer, and can build quick credibility.

- Do

- Add your anticipated degree

- List any key student leadership roles that you choose to list are explicitly referenced as student groups or clubs

- Don't

- Avoid overstating your qualifications (e.g., inflated titles that imply more influence than is actual)

- Avoid using language that implies you are a full-time employee of the university, which can confuse and disorient external stakeholders

See the example signature below:

Faiza Falcon (Name)
NYU Abu Dhabi, B.S. Computer Science, 2020 (Anticipated Degree, Graduation Year)
Girls Education Network, Student Facilitator
NYUAD Department of Computer Science, Student Research Assistant
UAE M: +971 50 106 9672
NYU Abu Dhabi, Saadiyat Campus
PO Box 129188
Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates

If you have questions about how to present yourself in your email signature, please stop by the CDC or reach out to nyuad.career@nyu.edu .

Related official links:
https://students.nyuad.nyu.edu/campus-life/career-development/post-graduate-preparation/interviewing/

To learn about our networking events, visit the CDC during our office hours to meet with a Global Career Peer or attend a walk-in for a quick appointment with an advisor

sections.title: Maximize the Experience · 30-second Introduction
sections.text:
Develop a 30-second introduction or “elevator pitch” to make your outreach efforts in-person as effective as possible.

Consider the following questions:

- Who are you? Introduce yourself and begin to tell your story. Indicate your name, school, and major (or area of a focus).

- What do you have in common? Are they an alumni? Do you have a shared contact? Are you members of the same social organization or network? What is the context of your meeting?

- What sets you apart? Incorporate a high-level overview of your unique skills, experiences, or accomplishments. This piece of your introduction will likely change the most often.

- What are you seeking? Are you looking for insight about the field through an informational interview? Are you seeking more in-depth internship and job search advice in your field of interest? Make your intentions clear to the people you’re connecting with, but do not ask for a job.

sections.title: Maximize the Experience · During the Conversation
sections.text:
- Respect their time by honoring the time agreed upon and moving the conversation to a close 5 minutes prior to the end of your meeting.

- Remember that even though you may want an internship or job, it is not appropriate to ask for one.

- Inquire about other professionals or organizations you can contact and if you can say you were referred by them.

- Dress appropriately and be courteous to everyone you encounter.

- Observe what types of skills and knowledge someone needs to perform this role.

- Thank your contact and others at the site who were helpful.

- Ask Good Questions

Maximize your experience by preparing specific questions in advance.

- What led you into this career?

- What does a typical day look like?

- Which professional organizations would you recommend I join?

- Which publications should I be reading to learn more about this field?

- What types of education and experience are most needed in this field?

- What types of skills and knowledge are important to perform this job well?

- What is the most challenging and/or frustrating aspect of your position?

- Where do you see the profession going?

- How did you go about finding this job?

- What would you advise me if I chose to pursue this career?

- Who else would you recommend I talk to? Are you willing to introducing me to them?

- Are you open to giving me feedback on my CV?

- Cultivating Relationships

The people you meet now can be influential in your life now or later. Consider the best way to stay in touch.

- Request a business card/contact information following new conversations and connect with them through LinkedIn.

- Send a thank-you email expressing your gratitude for their time within 24 hours.

- Maintain contact by sending existing contacts brief updates on how you’re progressing through your career.

- Share relevant articles or news when appropriate.

- Keep notes on your conversations so you can follow-up appropriately and accurately.

- Follow through on all leads and deliver what you promised, building your positive reputation and that of the person who referred you.

- Do

- Be prepared and know the basics. If you're going to attend an event, know the dress code, what time it starts, and what speakers will be there. Avoid awkward situations by dressing appropriately and showing up on time.

- Be open to being nervous and put yourself out there anyway. It's okay to fumble at your first networking event. Use the practice to get better at introducing yourself and making small talk.

- Go in with small goals, such as talking to 5 new people, getting their contact information, and following up with them after the event.

- Use every opportunity to build connections. You don't need to be at a formal networking event to meet new people. Be open to meeting others at casual social gatherings, lectures, concerts, and any other venue or event where there are people. You never know who you might meet!

- Be prepared with some conversation starters:

- Hi! I wanted to introduce myself...

- What did you think of the talk?

- What brings you to this event?

- I couldn't help but overhear…

- Have you traveled far to be here?

- Where did you go to university?

- What do you think about (the venue, the latest news, the weather)?

- When reaching out via email, make sure you have a professional email signature and use your @nyu.edu email address. Always employ professional language and be cautious of assuming the gender of the recipient with your pronouns.

- Leverage in-person conversations to learn about people's experiences in a given industry. Be curious and ask open-ended questions. Your questions communicate how much you already know about the industry and can establish rapport very quickly.

- Don't

- Never ask for a job or internship right after meeting someone (e.g., saying "Can I have a job?"). You can ask about the company and say that you'd be interested in opportunities there, but this should be part of a larger conversation. Networking should be about building relationships — not reaching an end goal.

- Don't take up too much of one person's time. Be mindful of body language and understand that they may want to talk to other people at the event. If you see that someone's eyes are wandering or that they are fidgeting, it is probably best to wrap up your conversation.

- Don't forget to follow-up. Too many times, people will ask for an employer's contact information but neglect to send an email to follow-up.

- Never be arrogant or overzealous with marketing yourself. While you should be able to speak about your talents, you also want to come across as self-aware and interested in the other person you are talking with.

- Don't forget: quality is better than quantity. It is better to have an authentic connection with a small number of individuals than to run around an event collecting business cards. Genuine connections are more apt to lead to future opportunities.

sections.title: Developing Your Network
sections.text:
While the CDC facilitates career panels, networking nights, career fairs, graduate school fairs, and other events as networking opportunities, students are encouraged to take initiative and reach out to professionals on their own with our guidance.

- Finding Contacts

Who | Why |

Family, friends, university staff and professors | You’ll be amazed how many contacts you can make through existing relationships. Although you might not have a relationship with someone in a particular field, you may know someone who does. |

Social networks | Are you on LinkedIn? Facebook? Twitter? WeChat? Tap into alumni networks, professional organizations, as well as existing connections by reaching out to them for the information you’re seeking. |

Employer Sessions and Opportunities Fairs | These events can be very useful even if you aren’t looking for an internship or job: you can meet the types of people you want to know. |

Campus or community events | The NYUAD Institute, academic departments, and professional organizations in Abu Dhabi are regularly hosting events that you can join to meet people.

- Opportunities for Networking

- Volunteer for a cause you are passionate about. You are likely to meet like-minded individuals from various industries and backgrounds.

- Reach out to alumni. Alumni are most likely to understand where you are coming from and will be motivated in assisting you and paying it forward. Use the LinkedIn and other social media or talk to your peers to get alumni contact information.

- Keep your connections strong. You already have a strong network; consider your family, friends, community members, clubs, professors, and former colleagues and supervisors. Don’t forget to check in with these people periodically as they can be a huge help in your future success.

- Actively engage with faculty and staff on campus. Ask about a professor’s research or see if you can volunteer for an upcoming big event.

Career advisors are also available to consult with students about networking etiquette and to brainstorm additional opportunities to interface with professionals. Request an appointment with a counselor via Handshake for additional help.

sections.title: LinkedIn
sections.text:
Employers are researching job and internship applicants online and 91% of employers are using social networking sites to screen candidates. LinkedIn is the best platform for promoting yourself professionally online; it gives you the ability to connect with other professionals and to learn more about industries of interest. Your LinkedIn connections can develop into real-world relationships which can shape your future opportunities.

In addition, Google loves LinkedIn. If you have a LinkedIn profile, it is likely to be at the top of a Google search result when anyone searches for you online. Why is this important? People, including employers and graduate school admissions officers, naturally go to Google to search for someone new. If your LinkedIn profile is at the top of the search results list, you are able to control the information they see and their overall first impression of you.

sections.title: LinkedIn · Do's, Don'ts, and Tips for LinkedIn
sections.text:
- Do

- Complete your profile to the fullest extent possible. The more information you provide, the higher the chances your profile will be found.

- Use a professional headshot.

- Join groups and professional associations related to your field. Join or start discussions within groups.

- Be strategic with whom you connect with — this is a professional network.

- Develop professional relationships. Connect with others who share your career interests and set up informational interviews.

- Help others by being a resource and sharing your knowledge and connections.

- Endorse or recommend your colleagues when appropriate.

- Ask for recommendations from past employers or colleagues.

- Don't

- Request to connect with just anyone. In your invitation, be specific about why you want to connect or where you met (try not to wait too long after big events to request to connect!).

- Overwhelm the news feed. Be intentional with your posts on LinkedIn.

- Make personal posts. Keep it professional.

- Ask everyone you connect with for a job. It is unprofessional and will get you nowhere. Build relationships first.

- Use the template message when connecting. Write a personalized note instead.

- Tips

Use the LinkedIn alumni tool to find alumni who have studied your major or who work in your field. You can send personalized connection requests to build your network and set up informational interviews (see How to Ask for a 1:1 Conversation below).

Complete all sections of your LinkedIn profile. Having a complete profile increases your chances of being seen by employers.

sections.title: How to Ask for a 1:1 Conversation
sections.text:
You will need to introduce yourself, establish why you’re writing, and make your request in a personal, concise, and clear way. People usually are very willing to help and lend advice, but they need to understand who you are and what you want.

The number one rule? Don't ask for a job or internship outright.

sections.title: How to Ask for a 1:1 Conversation · How to Send a Cold Email
sections.text:
- 1. Search for Contacts

Find contacts at companies of interest or people who have jobs that match your interests. Use LinkedIn, search professional social media accounts, company websites and the like.

- 2. Find their emails

This can be easier said than done and your first point of contact may need to be via LinkedIn or another social media network (only if the person is using it as a professional platform). Regardless, Google is a great place to start searching.

- 3. Draft and send your message

Keep it short and simple if possible:

Introduce yourself. State why you are contacting them and what you hope to gain from meeting with them (virtually or in person). Offer to buy them coffee if you can (if it's an in-person meeting).

Example 1:

Dear ____,

I am a senior currently studying Economics at New York University Abu Dhabi. I have interned with ____ and ____, and conducted research on ____. I came across your LinkedIn profile and I'm interested in your career path and how you were able to connect economics and social research. Would it be possible to schedule a Skype meeting so I can learn more about your path? (Or — I would love to buy you a coffee soon and learn more about your path into ____. Please let me know if you might be available for a short meeting.). I hope to hear from you soon. Thank you for your time.

Best,

Your Full Name

Examples 2:

Dear Vivek,

As a student at New York University Abu Dhabi studying economics and finance, I have been following the Deutsche Bank response to the current volatility with interest rates, economic slowness, and currency issues. I recently came across the interview you did with the Financial Times, and saw that you are an NYU alumnus. I would love to hear more about how you transitioned from New York to banking in London, and how you’ve adapted to the European and Middle Eastern markets in light of the current economic climate.

I am studying away in London over the next 12 weeks. Would you be free for 20-minutes in the next few weeks for a chat? I understand that your schedule is really full, and I am happy to bring lunch by your office or meet you after work.

Sincerely,

Mohammed

--

New York University Abu Dhabi
B.A. Economics, Specialization in Finance, Class of 2020
PO Box 129188
Abu Dhabi, UAE

- 4. Follow up

Always wait a week before following up with another email, but follow up! Don't take it personally if you don't hear back. People are busy and it's possible they just don't have the time to respond.

- 5. Thank them

If you hear back from someone, thank them for their time in getting back to you and commit to making time for your meeting, whether virtual or in-person. If you meet with them, don't forget to send a follow-up thank you email.

sections.title: How to Ask for a 1:1 Conversation · Reaching Out to an Existing Contact
sections.text:
- Employer Session or Event Follow Up

Dear Joanna,

My name is Mahra and I am a second year student at NYU Abu Dhabi, studying Film and New Media. After hearing your talk about commercials at TwoFour54, I was fascinated about the potential of video content. The illustrations you shared inspired me to think more broadly and be more curious about new outlets. I would love to learn from you about the direction of this industry in the UAE and get your input about how I can best develop my skills.

Would you be open to a 15-minute conversation sometime in the next two weeks? I am happy to meet you at your office — and I can bring some coffee. Alternatively, we could just talk on the phone or email, whichever works best for you.

Best,

Mahra

--

B.A. Film and New Media, Class of 2019
PO Box 129188
Abu Dhabi, UAE

sections.title: How to Ask for a 1:1 Conversation · Questions to Ask
sections.text:
- Sample Questions

- What made you interested in this field?

- What is a typical day like for you in this position?

- What past jobs and experiences have led you to this current position?

- How would you describe your working atmosphere and the people you work with?

- Do you have any advice for someone who wants to work in this field?

- What skills are most important to being successful in this career?

- Who has been most influential in your career?

- What are the types of jobs that exist where you work and in the industry in general?

- Are there any professional or trade associations I should connect with?

- How do you see your industry changing in the next 10 years?

- What’s unique about your company compared to your competitors or to your past work experiences?

Always remember to follow up with a thank you email after an informational interview. This is incredibly important as the person you interviewed took time out of their schedule with the intention of helping you — show your gratitude! You can use the information you gained from your interviews to assist with making career decisions and you can use your new contact for future opportunities if you continue to keep in touch — it's a win-win!

sections.title: How to Ask for a 1:1 Conversation · Student Email Signatures
sections.text:
Email signatures provide evidence of your affiliations and orient the reader. In short, they make you more easy to answer, and can build quick credibility.

- Do

- Add your anticipated degree

- List any key student leadership roles that you choose to list are explicitly referenced as student groups or clubs

- Don't

- Avoid overstating your qualifications (e.g., inflated titles that imply more influence than is actual)

- Avoid using language that implies you are a full-time employee of the university, which can confuse and disorient external stakeholders

See the example signature below:

Faiza Falcon (Name)
NYU Abu Dhabi, B.S. Computer Science, 2020 (Anticipated Degree, Graduation Year)
Girls Education Network, Student Facilitator
NYUAD Department of Computer Science, Student Research Assistant
UAE M: +971 50 106 9672
NYU Abu Dhabi, Saadiyat Campus
PO Box 129188
Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates

If you have questions about how to present yourself in your email signature, please stop by the CDC or reach out to nyuad.career@nyu.edu .

title: What GPA to submit · NYUAD Students
text:
Determining your GPA

NYU Abu Dhabi's policy on whether or not first-year grades are included in the calculation of GPA changes based on whether a student is enrolled or has already graduated. This page is designed to help students and alumni understand which grades are included in the GPA calculation, what documentation exists of their GPA, and which documents should be submitted when applying for opportunities.

In short: in applying for opportunities, NYU Abu Dhabi students and alumni should always list their GPA as recognized by the university at the time of application.

Enrolled students

- First-year grades are included in GPA calculation.

- First-year grades and GPA are not shown on official transcripts.

- First-year grades and GPA are shown on unofficial transcripts. This GPA should be used in all applications.

- In general, students should use their unofficial transcript in applying for opportunities, because it shows their GPA and their first-year grades. Students who are applying for opportunities that require the submission of an official transcript should also submit an unofficial transcript along with the official transcript, since the unofficial transcript includes information (first-year grades and GPA) that are excluded from the official transcript.

- Students should not submit their GPA exclusive of their first-year grades (colloquially and incorrectly referred to as an "official GPA") as a part of any application, since NYUAD will not issue documentation of this number.

Alumni who have already graduated

- First-year grades are not included in GPA calculation nor shown on official transcripts.

- GPA, calculated without first-year grades, is shown on official transcripts

- First-year grades are shown on unofficial transcripts, along with a potentially inaccurate GPA which includes first-year grades. Alumni should not use or submit this GPA or an unofficial transcript in any applications.

title: Global Awards · NYUAD Students
text:
What are Global Awards?

Global awards are highly-competitive, merit-based opportunities that are conducted at a national or international level. Some of the best-known global awards include the Rhodes Scholarship , Fulbright Scholarship , and Schwarzman Scholarship . Most of these awards, like those three, fund further study after your NYUAD education.

Our goal at NYUAD is to help you identify your passions, interests, and future paths; work closely with you to identify global awards competitions that will help you pursue those goals; and assist you throughout the application process.

- What Kind of Support Does NYUAD Offer for Students?

We offer an active, hands-on, individualized approach to advising our students and alumni who are applying for global awards. We maintain a roster of about 40 awards for which we actively recruit, reaching out to currently-enrolled students who we think might be a good fit for the criteria each foundation has set out.

Then, we work 1:1 with those students to determine whether a given award is right for them, and then help them at every stage of the application process.

- Why Should I Apply for A Global Award?

The most obvious reason to apply for a global award is because you are interested in the opportunity offered by the funding organization, and you want to participate in their program. As there are many more highly-qualified applicants for these programs than there are positions available, and selection processes are necessarily subjective in nature. The vast majority of applicants, no matter how well-qualified they are or how strong their applications are, are not going to win.

- The Importance of the Application Process

Here at NYUAD, we put the emphasis not on the outcome of the global awards competition, but on the process of applying. We believe that there are significant and important benefits from going through the process of applying for a global award, whether or not you are selected to receive such an honor.

- What You Learn Through Applying

- Greater self-knowledge

- A plan for life after NYUAD

- Excellent writing samples

- Increased interview skills

- Outstanding letters of recommendation

Just because we put the emphasis on process over product, though, does not mean that we do not think about or care about winning. We do! We work very hard on an individual basis with scores of students every year to help them prepare the best possible application, and to present themselves as well as possible in interviews. The difference is that while winning a global award is a measure of success, it is not our only measure of success.

Related official links:
https://students.nyuad.nyu.edu/campus-life/career-development/global-awards/scholarships-and-awards/

title: Application Timeline · NYUAD Students
text:
You are about to embark on a long but rewarding journey. Use the following steps as a guide to stay on track. Always keep in mind the specific deadlines for the scholarship(s) to which you are applying. Work closely with the Global Awards Office because each applicant will have his or her own timeline.

Need a printable copy? Download the PDF here .

Action | Timing

Read the website of the award(s) in which you are interested: Be sure to go over eligibility requirements and selection criteria carefully. | Fall-Spring

Meet with a Global Awards Advisor: We can help you find the scholarship that best fits your interests and goals. Do not worry if you unsure what scholarship(s) to consider. This process can take a while and we are here to guide you. | Fall-Spring

Fill out the Global Awards Application Questionnaire: Be as specific and detailed as possible. It will help you later when you fill out the actual scholarship application. | April 15

Ask for Letters of Recommendation: Start this process early. Obtaining good letters of recommendation is a key aspect of the application process. It is also one of the most challenging because you have the least control over them. Be sure to read the resource titled ‘ Letters of Recommendation ’ and follow the directions closely. | April-May

Work on your application with a Global Awards Advisor: Scholarship applications take time. Be prepared to revise many times and to think critically about yourself and your future goals. This process is a very personal one. | Spring-Fall

Polish and finalize application materials: Spend more time proof-reading your application materials. Have others read over for grammar, punctuation and spelling. Making a simple, careless mistake in the application does not reflect well on your candidacy. | Fall

Prepare for an interview if necessary: The interview is usually one of the final stages of the scholarship process. Prepare for it well because it means you are being seriously considered for the award. | Fall-Winter

Submit all required documents in proper form to the scholarship foundation: Scholarships are particular in the way they receive application material. Follow their instructions meticulously or your application will be disqualified, no matter how good of a candidate you are. If you have any questions, as the Global Awards Office. | Fall-Winter-Spring

Related official links:
https://students.nyuad.nyu.edu/students/campus-life/career-development/global-awards/letters-of-recommendation/

title: Application Tips · NYUAD Students
text:
Need a printable copy? Download the PDF here .

Application Tips

- Start early! Take your time. Do not apply for a scholarship in a single night. Your chances of winning will be minimal and it defeats the purpose of self-exploration that is key to the application process.

- Follow the directions on the application! Scholarship committees are particular and will disqualify applications for being late, not containing each required document, etc.

- Proof-read everything. A spelling mistake or writing the name of the wrong scholarship looks careless. Careless applicants do not win scholarships.

- Read our guides on ‘Asking for Letters of Recommendation’ and ‘The Personal Statement’.

- Give yourself time. It is not easy to apply for a scholarship. Make sure you allocate time to the application so that you are not rushed.

- If you get stuck, put the application aside for a few days or send it to someone to look over. Fresh eyes always help.

- Don’t be afraid of overhauling your application. Just because a paragraph or sentence is brilliant does not mean that it fits within your application.

- Remember the entire application is a narrative about you. It should be cohesive and true to who you are. Nothing should stick out or be out of place. Connect everything to your theme.

- Revise, revise, revise. Nothing will be perfect the first time around. It may even be bad. With revision you can take that bad first draft and turn it into a scholarship winning one.

- Be open and be vulnerable. Push the limits of your self-awareness and your potential.

- Ask for help. If you are stuck, unsure of what to do, or just want assurance, reach out to us at the Office of Global Awards. You can also reach out to a mentor, a professor, or a friend.

- Remember the entire application is a narrative about you. It should be cohesive and true to who you are. Nothing should stick out or be out of place. Connect everything to your theme.

- Revise, revise, revise. Nothing will be perfect the first time around. It may even be bad. With revision you can take that bad first draft and turn it into a scholarship winning one.

- Be open and be vulnerable. Push the limits of your self-awareness and your potential.

- Ask for help. If you are stuck, unsure of what to do, or just want assurance, reach out to us at the Office of Global Awards. You can also reach out to a mentor, a professor, or a friend.

title: Letters of Recommendation · NYUAD Students
text:
Letters of Recommendation (LoR) are one way selection committees gain an outside perspective on an applicant.

LoRs are not a stand-alone piece of your application. They are an integral part of a complete narrative that is meant to capture who you are, why you are applying, and why you are the best candidate for an award. While you cannot write your own, nor see your LoRs, you can influence the strength of them. Follow these instructions to obtain the best possible letters.

Need a printable copy? Download the PDF here .

Writing for the Fulbright ETA? Get specific advice here .

Writing for the Fulbright Full Grant? Get specific advice here .

Requesting a Letter of Recommendation

- Be sure to identify all possible recommenders/references in the Global Awards Application Questionnaire.

- Meet with a Global Awards Advisor about why you are choosing those recommenders and what information you need to provide to make sure that they are writing the best possible recommendation.

- Send a personalized, formal invitation to each recommender for them to write you a letter.

- You can work with the Global Awards Advisor on how this should look.

- Meet with your recommenders if necessary to explain any requirements or aspects that you want them to highlight in your letter.

- Follow-up with recommenders at appropriate intervals to make sure they are staying on top of the recommendation process and that they have all of the resources they need.

- Make sure all letters of recommendation are sent to the proper source for each scholarship application.

- Send personalized thank you notes when someone agrees to write you a LoR

Obtaining Strong Letters of Recommendation

- Build strong relationships from the start. It is easiest to ask for letters from someone who knows you well.

- Work with a Global Awards Advisor on compiling the list of best possible recommenders for you.

- Ask well in advance. Give writers up to 6 months and at the very least 4 weeks to complete the letter.

- Offer to meet with the writer in person or via Skype to explain the purpose of the LoR.

- Make sure the writer has the option to say ‘no’. It is tough to hear that, but it is better than sending a bad LoR in with an application.

- Provide the writer with the following:

- Copy of your CV

- Copy of your personal statement or cover letter for the application. Explain why you are applying for the award.

- Description and requirements of the scholarship, fellowship or award

- Provide the writer with LoR writing resources. The Global Awards Office is always happy to help support recommenders with whatever resources they need.

- Feel free to ask the writer to focus on a particular item to highlight, perhaps an aspect of you to which they have had a lot of exposure.

- Waive your right to see the letter

- Provide clear instructions. Give details such as to whom the writer should address, where it should be sent and in what format.

- Ask for letters from a diverse range of sources. Get writers who can speak to different aspects of who you are: your intellectual strengths, your leadership capacity, your creativity, your work/volunteer experience, your personality etc.

It is always better to have fewer strong LoRs than many weaker ones. If you are struggling to obtain LoRs, go for the minimum required for an application.

Finally, always follow the directions given in a scholarship application. If you do not, your application will be disqualified!

Writing Letters of Recomendation

Letters of recommendation generally cover at least one of three topics: intellectual characteristics and capacity, personal characteristics, and ability to succeed and leadership abilities or potential. These are very broad topics and the extant to which each is covered will depend on how you know the student, the depth of interaction with the student and what the letter is being used for. This guide is designed to help write strong letters of recommendation for our students.

Writing for the Fulbright ETA? Get specific advice here .

Writing for the Fulbright Full Grant? Get specific advice here .

Before Writing a LoR

- Meet with the student: discuss the student’s short-term and long-term goals. Gain precise and specific examples of work or class accomplishments as well as personal characteristics. Draw the student out and put them at ease so s/he is comfortable talking about past accomplishments and future goals.

- Attain a copy of the student’s CV, personal statement or cover letter or other writing sample, transcript, description of what the LoR is for, date the LoR is due and how it must be submitted.

- Say ‘No’ if needed: it is better to not write a letter than to submit a mediocre or bad LoR. Help the student understand why you cannot write the letter and find someone who could. Try to emphasize the student’s potential strengths in these conversations.

- Never ask a student to write their own LoR: instead ask them to brag about their accomplishments in person or through email and then filter that information into your letter.

- Consider the reading conditions: scholarship selection committees read quickly. Be short and to the point. Gather enough information about a candidate to employ vivid examples to support your statements wherever possible.

Writing a Strong LoR

- Identify yourself and the basis of your knowledge of a student.

- Explain your credibility and the credibility of the program briefly.

- Provide context of what the student has accomplished (what textbook was used, rigor of the course(s), how the student compares to the rest of the class).

- Provide context of where the applicant fits within the grander scheme of the university and your experiences writing LoRs for other students.

- Clarify terms that are specific to NYUAD (SIG, SLA, Capstone etc.).

- Consider ranking the student within specific contexts (a class, other students you write LoRs for, student’s ability to articulate thoughts).

- Discuss the specifics required for or asked for by the application.

- Use concrete examples. Superlatives tell nothing about a student.

- Provide details on student’s ability to grasp content, do research, master technology or ideas, solve problems, think creatively, think critically, etc.

- A LoR can be used to explain weakness or ambiguity in the application.

- Refrain from commenting on a candidate’s race, color, citizenship, medical condition, political affiliations, religious beliefs etc.

- Characteristics to enumerate:

- Knowledge of field of study

- Ability to communicate

- Industry and self-discipline

- Interpersonal skills

- Leadership ability

- Personal achievements

- Candidate’s self-awareness: insight into own assets and liabilities

- Potential

- Maturity

- Special attributes

title: Rhodes 2-Page CV · NYUAD Students
text:
One of the most important pieces of your Rhodes Scholarship application is your 2-page CV. You should think of your Rhodes CV as a document that works in tandem with your personal statement. Your CV, along with your transcript, describes what you have done; your personal statement is a narrative that explains your motivation, or why you have done those things.

For tips on writing your 2-page CV for the Rhodes, check out this document .

title: Rhodes Academic Statement Advice · NYUAD Students
text:
Your academic statement of study is an important part of the Rhodes application process; here are some general guidelines for writing it.

- Your opening paragraph should be a concise, clear declaration of what you want to study. Name the specific degree(s), and note how long the course of study is for each. Include a general thesis statement that lets the reader know the argument you are making for why you want to pursue this course of study.

- Use most of the document to dive into each of the degrees that you want to pursue. Describe exactly what you are excited about for this degree, in detail. You need to connect as an individual to this course of study, showing what exactly in your background and interests matches with what the course offers. Are there specific professors you want to work with? Classes you want to take? Resources you hope to access? Each paragraph and each argument should be unique to you; if I read the document without knowing who wrote it, I should be able to figure out that it belongs to you.

- Avoid arguments that are generic or vague in nature. “Oxford is a great university” is a general truism that makes no specific argument for you or your candidacy. “Getting a degree in public policy will help me shape policy in my home country’s government in the future” is an argument that anyone applying for that program could make. “This degree in theoretical physics will teach me a lot about theoretical physics” is just defining what the degree does. Look at every argument you make and think about if anyone else could write it; if so, change it to make it specific to you.

- You do need to cover alternative programs, though not in as much depth as your first-choice programs. Remember that winning a Rhodes does not guarantee you admission to your first-choice programs; if you are not admitted, what other options might you pursue at Oxford.

- Somewhere in your application, it is helpful if you describe why you are generally interested in this topic, field of study, and/or degree. You may already be covering this area in your personal statement, so it may not be necessary to repeat that information here in the academic statement.

- Either in the academic or personal statement, you need to connect your studies at Oxford to your future plans. It’s helpful to state these plans both in terms of big goals (What do you hope to accomplish in your career? What do you want to be remembered for? What are your Big Goals? How will you judge success?) as well as the career pathway you might take to get there (What jobs will help you accomplish those goals? What organizations might you work for?). Show how Oxford helps you get from where you are now to where you want to be in the future; how is it a bridge between the person you are today and the person you hope to be?

- The prompts encourage you to demonstrate that you are qualified for this course of study. The key here is not just to repeat what the committee already knows about you from elsewhere in your application; taking time to recite your major, your GPA, your Capstone topic, your key internships, etc., doesn’t help, since it is just turning your transcript and CV into prose. Instead, say something interesting about what you have done. Which courses prepared you the most and why? What skills did you learn from an internship project that will be particularly useful at Oxford? What researchers have particularly influenced your thinking?

- Your statement should both impress experts in your academic field and be understandable to non-experts. It is helpful to seek advice and review both from faculty members within your field and from smart people who are not experts. In particular, you should not use jargon or refer to ideas or thinkers which may not be common knowledge.

- You should seek advice from your faculty members and your Rhodes advisor in writing this. Unlike the personal statement, there are no restrictions on the help you can get in writing this document; take advantage of that. You should also share this document with the people writing your letters of recommendation so they are clear on what you hope to study at Oxford.

- Because this is a graduate application, you should focus your essay on the program or department or degree you are applying for, and do not need to justify Oxford as an institution to the committee. If you have some compelling reason why Oxford as a place of study is important to you outside of the specific program, you can include that, but this is less common. Avoid non-academic reasons, such as “I have always wanted to study at Oxford; it’s so pretty!” or “I have family nearby;” these are unlikely to be compelling and could undercut the academic seriousness of your application.

- Remember that, ultimately, you are not bound by what you propose here, especially in considering your second year. The general tenure of a Rhodes is two years, and you should propose at least a two-year plan for study at Oxford. However, Rhodes Scholars’ plans change frequently, and you may decide later to alter your plans for the second year. That said, your application should indicate a good-faith plan of what you hope to study at Oxford.

title: Who Should Apply · NYUAD Students
text:
Every NYU Abu Dhabi student has the potential to win a prestigious award. Awards provide limitless opportunities. They exist for every field, every nationality and at every level of study. The Global Awards Office will work with you to find the award that fits your interests, skills and goals. We will also assist you to gain the faculty and confidence required to be a successful applicant.

Remember that applying for awards is not just about winning. Rather it is about what you learn through the process. The application gives the opportunity for self-evaluation—for you to reflect on yourself, your skills, your goals and how you are going to accomplish them. Winning can afford you a once in a lifetime opportunity. If you do not win, you have still gone through an extensive process of self-discovery with the aid and support of an advisor who will help you reach your full potential. You will be able move on with confidence and a clear direction for your future accomplishments.

While applying takes a significant amount of time, effort and dedication, the rewards are great. Take a moment to consider if this is an enterprise to which you wish to dedicate yourself. While you will always receive support, it will also require a substantial amount of self-motivation. Applicants should be willing to work hard, be vulnerable and think critically about themselves.

We encourage you to contact the Global Awards Office ( nyuad.career@nyu.edu ) to explore the possibilities and begin the shaping of a life changing experience.

Need a printable copy? Download the PDF here .

title: Scholarships and Awards · NYUAD Students
text:
Use these pages to get started searching for scholarships and awards available around the world. Reach out to doug.cutchins@nyu.edu , our global awards advisor, for more information and to schedule an appointment.

- Code of Ethics for Applicants

All NYUAD students and alumni are expected to follow the code of ethics for applicants , as laid out by the National Association of Fellowships Advisors:

Prior to applications candidates will:

- Engage in self-reflection, assess long-term goals, and search for appropriate programs and funding;

- Pursue fellowships that support those goals, not fellowships that they must bend their goals to fit;

- Be aware of the high level of competition and respect the value of the process.

During the applications process, candidates should:

- Ensure that all application materials, including but not limited to personal statements, resumes, proposals, essays, shall be the sole and original work of the applicant. Cite any sources quoted or paraphrased;

- Respond to campus and foundation communications in an honest and timely fashion;

- Apply only to those fellowships in which they have a genuine interest;

- Provide adequate and accurate information to recommenders in a timely fashion;

- Neither compose their own letters for faculty to sign (even at the request of faculty) nor ask faculty members to show them their own letters of recommendation;

- Make clear what information revealed to an advisor or recommender should remain confidential;

- Include resume and application response items that reflect an accurate and substantive contribution;

- Provide honest responses to questions in all practice and real interviews without aggrandizing accomplishments or providing deliberately misleading information to committee members;

- Treat other applicants with respect and courtesy.

- Additional Scholarship Databases

In addition to the scholarships listed on this page, there are many other databases out there to help you find opportunities. Try a few of the ones below!

- Petersons.com

- ProFellow.com

- Scholars4Dev.com

- Fastweb.com

- for9a.com (for MENA students)

Roster of 40
sections.text:
Below is the roster of about 40, awards for which we actively recruit, reaching out to currently-enrolled students who we think might be a good fit for the criteria each foundation has set out. If you are interested in these awards or others, please make an appointment with our global awards advisor by emailing doug.cutchins@nyu.edu .

title: Preparation for Graduate Studies · NYUAD Students
text:
Visit the NYUAD Graduate School Map to learn where our alumni have gone to graduate schools

Preparing for and Taking Standardized Tests in the UAE

Check out the NYU New York Kaplan All Access initiative, which offers NYU students free access to Kaplan’s industry-leading test preparation courses for the following exams:

- Dental Admissions Test (DAT®)

- Graduate Management Admission Test (GMAT®)

- Graduate Record Examination (GRE®)

- Law School Admissions Test (LSAT®)

- Medical College Admission Test (MCAT®)

- Optometry Admissions Test (OAT®)

- Fundamentals of Engineering Exam (FE)

The CDC also has preparation books you can borrow. It is important to conduct your own research on standardized test requirements, modes of administration and dates, in order to plan accordingly.

Accreditation and English Proficiency

Graduate schools should not require English proficiency exam scores because NYUAD is accredited in the US and you receive a degree from NYU. If a graduate school asks for TOEFL, IELTS or other English language proficiency test, please reply with the relevant accreditation information from the statement below.

However, some schools are still requiring TOEFL scores. For such instances, please review the ETS TOEFL website for test centers and dates. For IELTS exams, see the British Council in Abu Dhabi who administer the exam. Both the TOEFL and IELTS are offered multiple times a month in Abu Dhabi, Dubai, and Al Ain. Check with schools well in advance of applying to see their English language proficiency requirements.

If you have any issues, please make an appointment to see a career advisor.

Accreditation Statement

If your graduate program requires information about NYU Abu Dhabi institutional accreditations, please refer to the official, publicly available, university statement .

title: Essential Information · NYUAD Students
text:
Timelines

As you are considering graduate school and thinking about how a graduate degree will complement your career goals, it is important to create a timeline for yourself to stay on track. You should be mindful of the time needed to meet the requirements, including application deadlines, given that they differ from region to region.

Schedule a Handshake appointment with a Graduate School and Career Advisor early to create a plan for yourself. It is recommended that you begin your graduate school search and preparation processes at least a year and a half in advance of any application deadlines.

Requirements

Requirements vary from school to school and program to program. A major in your desired field of graduate study is not always required. You must, however, be able to demonstrate your interest in the desired field of graduate study through internship, research and/or volunteering experiences.

You may also be requested to complete the following:

- Standardized Tests, such as GRE, MCAT and LSAT. The Career Development Center offers books for students to take courses that will prepare them for the required tests.

- Check out the NYU New York Kaplan All Access initiative, which offers NYU students free access to Kaplan’s industry-leading test preparation courses.

- Accommodations for Standardized Exams .

- English Language Proficiency Tests, such as TOEFL, IELTS.

Return to the Graduate Study page to learn more about the test providers and the associated costs.
Request a letter from the Office of Registrar to help you waive this requirement.

- 3-5 Letters of Recommendation. The letters are written by academic referees such as professors and instructors, but can also come from work and/or research mentors and supervisors. They’re typically requested 2-3 months in advance of the submission date and should focus on academic achievements, intellectual promise, leadership ability and personal character.

If needed, share your CV, Personal Statement and/or Statement of Purpose with your referees to provide context about your interests. You may also specify experiences, interactions or items that you’ll like to be highlighted in the letters.

Do not forget to waive your right to see the letter.

- Personal Statement and Statement of Purpose: You’re expected to write about your interest in the desired field, graduate program and the university. Please make sure to review this slide deck for how to write a personal statement and statement of purpose .

- Official Transcript: NYU Abu Dhabi's official transcript does not show letter grades for the first year. For grades of C and above, you are granted a Successful Completion (SC). For a C- or below, the course is not recorded on the official transcript. Your GPA is not recorded on your official transcript.

The unofficial transcript shows first year grades and records a GPA including them. If you would like this to be seen by the graduate schools to which you apply, you can upload a copy of your unofficial transcript to be attached when ordering the official transcript online through the National Clearinghouse (see link below on how to order an official transcript). You will still need your official transcript as part of your application. Although certain graduate and professional schools may be lenient when evaluating your freshman year grades, it's important to note that they will likely request them.

Request the transcript from The Office of the Registrar .

Financing

Graduate School is an expensive endeavor. Be aware of the costs, know how a graduate level degree will help you in your career, and make a plan as to how you will fund your studies. To start off your financing search, these are some databases that you can browse by various factors such as school, location, and more:

- Peterson’s

- ProFellow

- Scholarships for Development

- Fastweb

- Forsa

- Funding for US Study

- Postgraduate Funding

- International Education and Financial Aid

It is also important to explore financial aid opportunities through scholarships, grants or awards available at the institutions you’re considering for your studies. In addition, you should explore any funding opportunities through your country’s governmental institutions or NGOs.

While the CDC does not provide direct financial assistance for graduate school expenses, students have the opportunity to allocate a portion of their Falcon Dirhams towards covering various costs, such as application and standardized test fees. — Learn more about and open a Graduate School Expense Account with Student Finance

Interviewing

Some graduate schools may require an interview prior to admission. Use your NYU email address to access Big Interview , an interview training platform. You can receive immediate, personalized feedback on your interviewing skills, including coaching on how to improve. The tool provides guidance on eye contact, use of "ums" and filler, vocabulary, tone, rate of speech, and more. You can also schedule a Handshake appointment with a Graduate School and Career Advisor for a mock interview.

https://students.nyuad.nyu.edu/academics/registration/transcripts/
https://students.nyuad.nyu.edu/services/financial-services/study-support/

title: The Financing · NYUAD Students
text:
Law School is an expensive endeavor. Be aware of the costs and make a plan as to how you will meet them.

- Standardized Tests

The LSAT costs USD 118. Other fees may apply depending on when you register for the exam and other variables. It recommended that you register at least one month in advance.

- Application Fees

Fees for applications are roughly USD 50-100 per school.

The CDC is unable to provide financial assistance for standardized testing fees.

- Enrollment Fees

Law schools often have an enrollment fee. This fee is to secure your place in the incoming class when accepting the offer of admittance to a given law school.

The CDC is unable to provide financial assistance for application fees for NYUAD students.

- Visa Fees

If you are going to graduate school in a country other than your home country, you will likely need a student visa. Most schools have an international office that can guide you through the process of acquiring one.

- Tuition

Tution is no small cost. It can range from tens to hundreds of thousands of dollars. Be aware of this when considering law school. Scholarships, grants, and loans are offered directly from law schools, however, external scholarships exist. Additionally, your home government might offer financial assistance. It is really important for a student to take initiative and research all the potential financial aid options available.

- Room-and-Board

The cost of living varies from city to city. When considering law school, make sure to do your research in order to get an estimate of how much it will cost for room and board and add that to the tuition you have to pay. Some schools offer housing for their students which may be subsidized at a lower cost.

title: The Process · NYUAD Students
text:
There are many components involved when it comes to deciding if law school is the best fit for you and how you should use your time at NYUAD to prepare for law school or a career in law. You should meet with a Graduate School and Career Advisor to develop a 4-year plan that works for you.

- Sample Timeline: What should I be doing during my time at NYUAD?

There are common study paths and types of law practices that students pursue. Most of our students and alumni want to practice law in the US, the UAE, and England, and Wales.

Application Timeline: If you intend to attend law school in the United States directly after graduation, the application process begins in the Fall semester of your senior year. To become a lawyer in the US, you will need to obtain a JD (Juris Doctor).

The Application

You should learn more about the application processes of your desired schools. In the U.S., some schools require the LSAT (Law School Admission Test), and others may require the GRE (Graduate Standard Test). In the United Kingdom, the National Admissions Test for Law (LNAT) is used by a number of universities.

There are five main components that make up the law school application process. While there may be supplemental application materials that each individual institution may require, these are usually the main components:

A Law School Admission Test (LSAT) Score

This is a standardized test that almost all schools have as part of their admission requirements. It is meant to provide the admissions committee with some insight into your performance in your first year of law school.

- Getting Ready for Your LSAT

- LSAT Test Dates (Middle East)

Undergraduate Transcript(s)/GPA

You must submit transcripts for your undergraduate school or any other schools you may have attended. If you are applying in your senior year of your undergraduate studies, it is okay that your transcript only includes your courses during your freshman, sophomore, and junior years. If you use the Credential Assembly Service (CAS) via LSAC, LSAC will calculate a GPA for each year as well as a cumulative GPA for every undergraduate institution that you have a transcript for.

- LSAC Transcript Summarization Process

- Requesting your undergraduate transcripts

Personal Statement

This is a very important part of your application as it gives the admission committee a chance to get to know you as the applicant from your perspective aside from your performance academically. Key components that you should cover include who you are, what brings you to that institution, and why is law the best choice for your professional goals. You can also include information about why you have chosen to apply for that particular law school. Please make sure to review this slide deck for how to write a personal statement and statement of purpose .

Letters of Recommendation

Letters of Recommendation are a good way for law school admissions officers to have some insight into your performance in the classroom from academic sources like your professors or Teaching Assistants. For more insights on who to select for recommendation letter writers and how to obtain the letters, please visit the Essential Information page .

Résumé or CV

The résumé you need to submit as part of your law school application can look a bit different than the one you may use to apply for internships or jobs. Every institution can have specific requirements for what they would like to see in the résumé which can include education, honors and awards you may have earned, work experience, leadership and service, volunteer work, as well as skills and interests. You should avoid putting any of your high school experiences on there as admissions committees are more interested in the things you acquired during your undergraduate studies. You can always have your résumé reviewed by the Pre-Law Graduate School and Career Advisor.

- The No B.S. Guide to the Law School Resume

- The No B.S. Guide to the Law School Application Timeline

Handshake Resources

The Law Handbook is a digital handbook designed to guide you through the process of exploring the idea of pursuing a career in law or applying to law school. It outlines common study paths and types of law practices in the US, the UAE, and England, and Wales.

Review the NYUAD CDC Law Resources on Handshake.
